edge_cases.title: The append that "works" but is still invalid
edge_cases.explanation:
- `const char* p = s.c_str(); s += " world"; puts(p);` may print the full text on libstdc++ when capacity was sufficient.
- The standard says `+=` may invalidate `p` regardless of capacity. Another library, a debug mode, or a future version may behave differently.
- When capacity is exceeded, libstdc++ allocates a new block and frees the old one: ASan reports `heap-use-after-free` on the next use of `p`.
- Rule: never reason from capacity for strings; reacquire the pointer.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity

edge_cases.title: Returning a temporary as a view
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string_view name() { return std::string(60, 'N'); }` compiles without warnings in GCC 13 (`-Wall -Wextra`).
- The temporary is destroyed at the end of the `return` statement, before control reaches the caller. The view returned already dangles.
- With a short string the buffer was on the callee's stack and the program may even print the right text; with a long one ASan reports `heap-use-after-free` in the caller.
- Fix: return `std::string` (by value, NRVO or move makes it cheap).
- Deep dive: Topic 2, std::string_view and std::span

edge_cases.title: Dangling reference from a temporary optional
edge_cases.explanation:
- `const std::string& name = *find_name(id);` where `find_name` returns `std::optional<std::string>` by value:
  - The returned optional is a temporary; `*` returns a reference into it, not the temporary itself, so **no** lifetime extension applies.
  - The temporary (and its string) is destroyed at the end of the full expression; `name` dangles.
- Same bug with `.value()`, `->` and `for (char c : *find_name(id))` (range-for over a member of a temporary: fixed only in C++23 by P2718, which GCC 11/13 do not implement).
- Fix: keep the optional: `auto name = find_name(id); if (name) use(*name);` or copy: `std::string n = *find_name(id);`.
- The reset/reassign variant of this bug (reference into an optional that is later reset) is covered in Memory & Ownership, topic 01.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, std::optional and std::expected

edge_cases.title: A string literal picks a surprising alternative
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::variant<bool, std::string> v = "hello";`
  - C++17 as published: `const char*` to `bool` is a standard conversion and beats the user-defined conversion to `std::string`, so it held `true`.
  - After P0608 (adopted for C++20; GCC 10+ and libc++ also apply it in C++17 mode; MSVC first enabled it only for `/std:c++20` and extended it to C++17 later): pointer-to-bool is excluded, so it holds the string (`index() == 1` on GCC 11 in both `-std=c++17` and `-std=c++20`).
- `std::variant<std::string, const char*> v = "x";` holds the `const char*` (exact match after decay), not the string.
- `std::variant<std::string, std::string_view> v = "x";` does not compile: two user-defined conversions, ambiguous.
- Rule: when the alternative matters, say it: `v = std::string("hello");` or `v.emplace<std::string>("hello");`.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, std::variant, std::visit and std::any

edge_cases.title: Pushing an element of the same vector
edge_cases.explanation:
- `v.push_back(v[0]);` at full capacity looks dangerous: the reference argument points into the block being replaced.
- The standard requires it to work, and libstdc++ constructs the new element (copying from the old block) before releasing the old block.
- The same holds for `insert(pos, v[i])`: implementations copy the value first. It is a hand-written container that usually gets this wrong.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::vector Internals

edge_cases.title: Range-for plus push_back
edge_cases.explanation:
- `for (int x : v) v.push_back(x);` looks like "duplicate the vector".
- The hidden `last` iterator is the old `end()`. On reallocation, `first` points into freed memory: ASan reports heap-use-after-free.
- With enough capacity reserved, it often appears to work, but the cached `end()` is invalid, so it is still UB.
- Fix: `v.insert(v.end(), v.begin(), v.end())` is also wrong (source range aliases the destination and is invalidated). Copy first, or index: `auto n = v.size(); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) v.push_back(v[i]);` (topic 05 explains why `push_back(v[i])` itself is safe).
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Iterators and Invalidation Rules

edge_cases.title: deque is random access but not contiguous
The wrong pair type in range-for copies every element
edge_cases.explanation:
- `for (const std::pair<std::string, int>& p : m)` does not match `std::pair<const std::string, int>`; the compiler builds a temporary converted pair (copying the string) per iteration and binds the reference to it.
- Costs an allocation per long key, and `&p.first` is not the address of the key in the map.
- GCC warns: "loop variable 'p' ... binds to a temporary constructed from type 'std::pair<const ...>'" (`-Wrange-loop-construct`, part of `-Wall`).
- Write `const auto& [k, v]` or `const auto& p`.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, std::map and std::set

edge_cases.title: Floating-point keys: NaN and negative zero
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::unordered_set<double> s; s.insert(NAN); s.insert(NAN);` gives size 2, and `s.count(NAN)` is 0: equality says NaN equals nothing, not even itself.
- `0.0` and `-0.0` compare equal, so they are one key; `std::hash<double>` must (and does) hash both to the same value.
- Prices as `double` keys also suffer from rounding (`0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`). Use integer ticks or fixed-point keys.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Unordered Containers and Hashing

edge_cases.title: Missing typename, template or this->
edge_cases.explanation:
- `T::value_type x;` is parsed as a value expression: error "need 'typename' before 'T::value_type' because 'T' is a dependent scope".
- `t.get<0>()` where `t` depends on `T`: may parse `<` as less-than; write `t.template get<0>()`.
- In `template <class T> struct D : Base<T> { void g() { helper(); } };`, `helper` is not found in the dependent base: "there are no arguments to 'helper' that depend on a template parameter, so a declaration of 'helper' must be available". Fix: `this->helper()`.
- Some compilers in permissive modes historically accepted these; GCC and Clang reject them.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, Templates: Deduction, Specialization and Variadics

edge_cases.title: static_assert(false) in a discarded branch
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) { ... } else { static_assert(false, "unsupported type"); }`
- GCC 11: "static assertion failed: unsupported type" even when only `int` is used (pre-P2593 rule: a non-dependent false assertion makes the template ill-formed).
- GCC 13+ (any `-std`, P2593R1 as a defect report): compiles; fires only if the else branch is instantiated.
- Portable form: `static_assert(always_false<T>, "...")` (`template <class> constexpr bool always_false = false;`).
- Deep dive: Topic 11, SFINAE, Type Traits and Concepts

edge_cases.title: UB, throw and limits are compile errors, not silent fallbacks
edge_cases.explanation:
- In a constant evaluation: `INT_MAX + 1` → "overflow in constant expression"; `arr[3]` on `int arr[3]` → "array subscript value '3' is outside the bounds"; `*nullptr` → "dereferencing a null pointer"; reading an uninitialized local → "the value of 'x' is not usable in a constant expression".
- A `throw` on the evaluated path → "expression '<throw-expression>' is not a constant expression" (until C++26). Useful as a compile-time assertion inside a constexpr function.
- 1,000,000 iterations of one loop → "'constexpr' loop iteration count exceeds limit of 262144"; deep recursion → "evaluation depth exceeds maximum of 512"; huge total work → "operation count exceeds limit of 33554432" (GCC defaults, adjustable with `-fconstexpr-loop-limit`, `-fconstexpr-depth`, `-fconstexpr-ops-limit`).
- None of these silently turn into run-time computation for a `constexpr` variable: the program does not compile.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, constexpr, consteval and Compile-Time Programming

code_examples.title: An event type with visit and the overloaded idiom
code_examples.explanation:
- A closed set of messages; adding a new message type makes every visitor that lacks a handler fail to compile.

- Output:

- The events are stored contiguously in the vector: no heap allocation per event, unlike `vector<unique_ptr<EventBase>>`.

code_examples.title: The order of a reallocation
code_examples.explanation:
- A noisy type shows that the new element is constructed before the old ones are relocated.

- Output (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64):

- `copy7` happens before `move7 dtor7`: the copy reads the old block while it is still alive.
- Remove `noexcept` from the move constructor and every `move` in the relocation becomes `copy` (details in Memory & Ownership, topic 02).
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::vector Internals
additional_code:
ctor1 ctor2 
at capacity, emplace_back(3): ctor3 move1 dtor1 move2 dtor2 
self push_back at capacity:   ctor7 copy7 move7 dtor7 
end of main: dtor7 dtor7 dtor1 dtor2 dtor3

code_examples.title: Three ways to remove elements correctly
code_examples.explanation:
- `std::erase_if` (C++20) for a vector, the erase-remove idiom for older code, and the iterator loop for a node container with per-element work.

- Output:

- `std::erase_if` returns the number of removed elements (C++20). For `map` and other node containers `std::erase_if` also exists and does the iterator loop internally.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Iterators and Invalidation Rules
additional_code:
erase_if removed 3: 5 7 3 
after remove_if size is still 6
after erase size 3
archiving order 2
open orders: 2

code_examples.explanation:
- `Point` gets `operator==` and a `std::hash` specialization, so the map needs no extra template arguments.
- `PairHash` shows the functor form for `std::pair`, which has no standard hash.

- Output:

- Without the specialization, `std::unordered_map<Point, std::string> names;` fails with "use of deleted function" (the disabled `std::hash<Point>` makes the map's default constructor deleted).
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Unordered Containers and Hashing

code_examples.title: A compile-time lookup table
code_examples.explanation:
- A CRC-32 table computed by a `constexpr` function, verified with `static_assert`, used at run time with zero start-up cost.

- Output (no argument):

- `crc_table` is in read-only data: no initialization code runs at start-up, and the `static_assert`s fail the build if the table logic breaks.
- `crc32` is used both at compile time (the check value) and at run time (user input): one implementation, tested by the compiler.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, constexpr, consteval and Compile-Time Programming

interview_qa.question: What is the small string optimization, and is it guaranteed by the standard?
interview_qa.answer: SSO stores short strings inside the `std::string` object itself instead of allocating a heap block. The standard permits it but does not require it, and the inline capacity is implementation-defined.
interview_qa.explanation:
- libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64: `sizeof(std::string) == 32`, up to 15 characters inline.
- libc++: typically 24 bytes, up to 22 characters inline. MSVC: typically 32 bytes, 15 characters (64-bit release builds).
- Benefits: no allocation, no free, characters on the same cache line as the size.
- Costs: the object is larger than three pointers' worth of "just a handle" in some layouts, and moving a short string copies its characters.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Strings up to 15 characters never allocate in C++." That is libstdc++ and MSVC, not C++.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a stale pointer into an SSO buffer points into the live string object, so ASan cannot detect its misuse.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity
interview_qa.key_takeaway: SSO is universal in practice and unspecified in the standard; quote numbers with the library name.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
SSO stores short strings inside the `std::string` object itself instead of allocating a heap block. The standard permits it but does not require it, and the inline capacity is implementation-defined.

**Explanation:**
- libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64: `sizeof(std::string) == 32`, up to 15 characters inline.
- libc++: typically 24 bytes, up to 22 characters inline. MSVC: typically 32 bytes, 15 characters (64-bit release builds).
- Benefits: no allocation, no free, characters on the same cache line as the size.
- Costs: the object is larger than three pointers' worth of "just a handle" in some layouts, and moving a short string copies its characters.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Strings up to 15 characters never allocate in C++." That is libstdc++ and MSVC, not C++.

- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity

**Key takeaway:** SSO is universal in practice and unspecified in the standard; quote numbers with the library name.

interview_qa.question: Which `std::string` operations invalidate pointers, references and iterators into it?
interview_qa.answer: Any non-const member function except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `rbegin`, `end`, `rend`, plus passing the string by non-const reference to `swap`, `operator>>` or `getline`. Reallocation is not the criterion.
interview_qa.explanation:
- So `+=`, `append`, `push_back`, `insert`, `erase`, `clear`, `resize`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`, `assign` and `swap` all formally invalidate.
- The exempt list is exactly the element-access and iterator-access functions: they can be called through a non-const string without disturbing existing borrows.
- In practice libstdc++ keeps the same buffer when capacity suffices, so code that relies on it "works". It is still UB to use the pointer by the standard's rules.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Same as vector: if it doesn't reallocate, pointers stay valid." The vector rule does not apply to `basic_string`.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the practical fix is to store indices across mutations and call `c_str()` again right before each use.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity
interview_qa.key_takeaway: For strings, every mutating member except element access invalidates; reacquire after each one.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
Any non-const member function except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `rbegin`, `end`, `rend`, plus passing the string by non-const reference to `swap`, `operator>>` or `getline`. Reallocation is not the criterion.

**Explanation:**
- So `+=`, `append`, `push_back`, `insert`, `erase`, `clear`, `resize`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`, `assign` and `swap` all formally invalidate.
- The exempt list is exactly the element-access and iterator-access functions: they can be called through a non-const string without disturbing existing borrows.

- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity

**Key takeaway:** For strings, every mutating member except element access invalidates; reacquire after each one.

interview_qa.question: When should a function take `std::string_view`, `const std::string&`, or `std::string` by value?
interview_qa.answer: `string_view` by value for read-only, synchronous use. `const std::string&` when the function needs a null-terminated string or forwards to an API that takes `const std::string&`. `std::string` by value when the function stores the text (a sink): the caller can move into it.
interview_qa.explanation:
- With a `const std::string&` parameter, a literal longer than the SSO capacity costs one allocation per call; a view costs none (verified by counting `operator new`).
- A view parameter that is later converted with `std::string(sv)` to call a C API or to store it pays the copy anyway; in that case take `std::string`.
- Storing a view parameter in a member is a lifetime bug waiting for the first caller that passes a temporary.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Always use `string_view` for strings now." It is a parameter type for borrowing, not a replacement for `std::string`.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for `std::map<std::string, V>` lookups, a view only helps with a transparent comparator (`std::less<>`); otherwise `find` needs a `std::string`.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, std::string_view and std::span
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Borrow with a view, terminate with `const std::string&`, store with `std::string` by value.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
`string_view` by value for read-only, synchronous use. `const std::string&` when the function needs a null-terminated string or forwards to an API that takes `const std::string&`. `std::string` by value when the function stores the text (a sink): the caller can move into it.

**Explanation:**
- With a `const std::string&` parameter, a literal longer than the SSO capacity costs one allocation per call; a view costs none (verified by counting `operator new`).
- A view parameter that is later converted with `std::string(sv)` to call a C API or to store it pays the copy anyway; in that case take `std::string`.

- Deep dive: Topic 2, std::string_view and std::span

**Key takeaway:** Borrow with a view, terminate with `const std::string&`, store with `std::string` by value.

interview_qa.question: Why is `std::map<std::string_view, int>` dangerous, and what should you use instead?
interview_qa.answer: The map stores views, not characters. Keys built from temporaries or from strings that later change point into dead memory, and every later comparison reads it. Use `std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>>`: the map owns its keys and can still be searched with a `string_view`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- A `string_view` key is fine only when the characters outlive the map (literals, an arena or buffer owned next to the map that never reallocates).
- `std::less<>` is transparent: `find`, `count`, `contains`, `lower_bound` accept anything comparable with `std::string` (C++14 for ordered containers).
- For `std::unordered_map`, heterogeneous lookup needs both a transparent hash and a transparent equality (C++20), see topic 09.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Views as keys save memory, so they are a free optimization."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `std::hash<std::string_view>` equals `std::hash<std::string>` for the same characters, which is what makes transparent hashing consistent.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, std::string_view and std::span
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Containers should own their keys; look them up with views.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**

**Explanation:**
- A `string_view` key is fine only when the characters outlive the map (literals, an arena or buffer owned next to the map that never reallocates).

- Deep dive: Topic 2, std::string_view and std::span

**Key takeaway:** Containers should own their keys; look them up with views.

interview_qa.question: Why is `std::optional<bool>` considered a trap?
interview_qa.answer: Because `if (ob)` tests whether a value is present, not whether the value is `true`. An `optional<bool>` holding `false` is truthy, so "explicitly disabled" behaves like "enabled".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: For `optional<bool>`, the condition asks "is it set?", never "is it true?".

interview_qa.question: What is `std::expected<T, E>` and how does it differ from `std::optional<T>`?
interview_qa.answer: A C++23 vocabulary type holding either a value `T` or an error `E`, in-place like optional. Optional only says "nothing"; expected says "nothing, and here is why", with a typed error the caller can inspect via `error()`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Success: `return value;`. Error: `return std::unexpected(err);`.
- `value()` on an error throws `std::bad_expected_access<E>`, which carries the error; `error()` on a success is UB.
- A default-constructed `expected<T, E>` holds a value-initialized `T` (success); a default optional is empty.
- `expected<void, E>` exists for actions without a result; there is no `optional<void>`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It is optional plus an error string." `E` is any type; an enum is usually better than a string.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: before C++23, `tl::expected` provides the same interface.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, std::optional and std::expected
interview_qa.key_takeaway: optional answers "is there a value?"; expected also answers "why not?".
interview_qa.full_content:

interview_qa.question: When would you choose `std::variant` over an inheritance hierarchy, and vice versa?
interview_qa.answer: Variant for a closed set of types known in one place (protocol messages, states, AST nodes in one module), especially when you keep adding operations. Inheritance for an open set that other modules extend (plugins, strategies), especially when you keep adding types.
interview_qa.explanation:
- New operation: variant needs one new visitor; inheritance needs a new virtual in every class.
- New type: variant needs every visitor updated (the compiler lists them); inheritance needs one new class.
- Variant values are copyable, in place, no heap; polymorphic objects usually need `unique_ptr` and cannot be copied without a `clone()`.
- Variant is not extensible across library boundaries: users of a library cannot add an alternative.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "variant is always better because it is faster."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: this is the "expression problem"; the choice depends on which axis changes more.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, std::variant, std::visit and std::any
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Fixed types, growing operations: variant. Growing types, fixed operations: virtual.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
Variant for a closed set of types known in one place (protocol messages, states, AST nodes in one module), especially when you keep adding operations. Inheritance for an open set that other modules extend (plugins, strategies), especially when you keep adding types.

**Explanation:**
- New operation: variant needs one new visitor; inheritance needs a new virtual in every class.
- New type: variant needs every visitor updated (the compiler lists them); inheritance needs one new class.

- Deep dive: Topic 4, std::variant, std::visit and std::any

interview_qa.question: What does `valueless_by_exception` mean? How do you avoid it?
interview_qa.answer: A variant becomes valueless when switching to a different alternative throws after the old object has been destroyed: it then holds no object, `index()` returns `variant_npos`, and `get`/`visit` throw `bad_variant_access`. Avoid it by making alternatives nothrow-move-constructible, so the implementation can build the new value in a temporary first.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Typical trigger: `v = x` or `v.emplace<T>(...)` where `T`'s constructor (or copy) throws.
- For converting assignment the standard requires: if direct construction cannot throw, or `T` has no nothrow move, construct in place; otherwise build a temporary `T` and move it in, which protects the old value if the temporary's construction throws.
- `emplace` always destroys first, so a throwing `emplace` can make the variant valueless.
- Recover by assigning a new value.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A variant always holds one of its types."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `std::monostate` is the intended empty state; valueless is an error state, and code like `names[v.index()]` must not run on it.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, std::variant, std::visit and std::any
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Valueless = old destroyed, new failed; nothrow moves make it rare.

interview_qa.question: What exactly happens when `push_back` is called on a full vector?
interview_qa.answer: The vector allocates a larger block, constructs the new element there, relocates the existing elements (move if the move constructor is `noexcept`, otherwise copy if copyable), destroys the old elements, frees the old block and updates its pointers. All pointers, references and iterators into it become invalid.
interview_qa.explanation:
- libstdc++ order, observed with a noisy type: `ctor3 move1 dtor1 move2 dtor2`. The new element comes first.
- That order is what makes `v.push_back(v[0])` safe: the source is copied before the old block is released.
- Trivially copyable elements are relocated with one `memmove`.
- If constructing the new element throws, nothing has changed. If relocation by copy throws, the new block is discarded and the vector is unchanged (strong guarantee); see Memory & Ownership, topic 02 for the `noexcept` rule.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "If the allocator is clever, `push_back` at full capacity may not reallocate." `capacity()` is the storage held; inserting beyond it always needs new storage.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the latency spike is O(n) on one unlucky call, which is why hot paths `reserve` up front. Which iterators survive the non-reallocating case (hint: not `end()`) is covered in topic 06.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::vector Internals
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Full vector + insert = new block, new element first, relocate, free old, every borrow dead.

interview_qa.question: What is special about `std::vector<bool>`?
interview_qa.answer: It is a bit-packed specialization: elements are bits, `operator[]` returns a proxy object instead of `bool&`, there is no `data()`, and you cannot take `bool*` to an element. It does not satisfy the container requirements that generic code assumes.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `auto x = vb[0];` is a proxy that keeps referring to the bit.
- Two threads writing different elements of a `vector<bool>` is a data race (adjacent bits share a word); for every other `vector<T>`, distinct elements are safe.
- Template code like `T& r = v[i];` fails to compile for `T = bool`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It is just a vector that stores bools efficiently, otherwise identical."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: use `std::vector<char>` / `std::vector<std::uint8_t>` for addressable flags, `std::bitset` for fixed sizes.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, std::vector Internals
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `vector<bool>` is a bitset with a vector-like interface, not a vector of `bool`.

interview_qa.question: What is the correct way to erase elements from a container while iterating over it?
interview_qa.answer: Use the iterator returned by `erase`: `if (pred(*it)) it = c.erase(it); else ++it;`. For a vector, prefer `std::erase_if(v, pred)` (C++20) or the erase-remove idiom, which are O(n) instead of O(n²).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Continue from `erase`'s return value; for vectors, remove in one pass with `erase_if`.

interview_qa.question: A component keeps pointers to objects in a `std::vector` that keeps growing, and crashes appear after growth. How do you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: Stop handing out pointers into storage that relocates. Use indices or stable ids, or store objects where they never move: `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>>`, a `std::deque` grown only at the ends, or a node container. `reserve` only mitigates the problem if the maximum size is truly known.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Indices survive reallocation but break if middle elements are erased; stable ids plus a lookup map survive both.
- `vector<unique_ptr<T>>` keeps each object at a fixed address; reallocation moves only the pointers. Cost: one allocation and an extra indirection per element.
- `deque` keeps element addresses stable for end insertions, while still allowing indexed access.
- If other threads read while one thread grows the vector, it is also a data race; that needs synchronization (Concurrency chapter), not just a different container.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Call `reserve` with a large number." It works until the size estimate is wrong, then the same bug returns in production.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: name the trade-off: stable addresses cost locality; indices keep locality but need care on erase.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Iterators and Invalidation Rules
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Choose a handle that matches what the container guarantees: indices or ids for vectors, pointers only for stable storage.

interview_qa.question: How is `std::deque` implemented, and how can `d[i]` be O(1) if the storage is not contiguous?
interview_qa.answer: A deque is a map (an array of pointers) to fixed-size blocks that hold the elements. Because every block has the same capacity, `d[i]` computes the block as `(start + i) / per_block` and the slot as `(start + i) % per_block`: two loads and some arithmetic, independent of `n`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Block size is implementation-defined; libstdc++ uses 512-byte blocks (128 `int`s), or one element per block when `sizeof(T) >= 512`.
- O(1) random access needs a constant-time address computation, not contiguity.
- Each access costs one more indirection than a vector (map slot, then block), and iteration has a branch at every block boundary.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Blocks grow like vector capacity (30, 50, 50, ...), so index math walks the blocks." Real implementations use one fixed block size; variable blocks would make indexing O(number of blocks).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the deque iterator is a "fat" iterator (libstdc++: four pointers) that knows its block's bounds, which is also why end insertion invalidates it (topic 06).
- Deep dive: Topic 7, deque, list, forward_list, array and Adaptors
interview_qa.key_takeaway: deque = map of fixed-size blocks; index math replaces contiguity.

interview_qa.question: Both traversals are O(n). Why is iterating a `std::list` much slower than a `std::vector`?
interview_qa.answer: A vector traversal reads consecutive memory, so every cache line brings several elements and the hardware prefetcher runs ahead. A list traversal must load each node's `next` pointer before it knows the next address, so every step can be a cache miss that cannot be overlapped.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Nodes allocated at different times end up scattered across the heap; even freshly built lists lose locality after some inserts and erases.
- Each node also carries two pointers of overhead, so less useful data fits in cache.
- The dependent-load chain also blocks out-of-order execution: the CPU cannot start load k+1 before load k finishes.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Same Big-O, so same speed." Big-O hides the constant, and memory access dominates that constant.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: deeper cache discussion (lines, prefetching, TLB) belongs to the Systems chapter; the interview point is "locality beats asymptotics for realistic N".
- Deep dive: Topic 7, deque, list, forward_list, array and Adaptors
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Pointer chasing makes list traversal latency-bound; vector traversal is bandwidth-bound.

interview_qa.question: How do `insert`, `emplace`, `try_emplace` and `insert_or_assign` differ?
interview_qa.answer: `insert` and `emplace` add the element only if the key is absent and never overwrite. `try_emplace` (C++17) does the same but guarantees its arguments are untouched if the key exists. `insert_or_assign` (C++17) inserts or overwrites. All return `{iterator, bool}` where `bool` means "inserted".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Insert-if-absent: `try_emplace`. Insert-or-overwrite: `insert_or_assign`.

interview_qa.question: How do you choose between `std::map` and `std::unordered_map`?
interview_qa.answer: Use `map` when you need sorted iteration, range or nearest-key queries (`lower_bound`), a guaranteed O(log n) worst case, or iterators that survive every insert. Use `unordered_map` for pure point lookups by key when average O(1) matters and order does not.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `unordered_map` is O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case (bad hash, adversarial keys), and a rehash invalidates all iterators.
- `map` needs only `operator<`; `unordered_map` needs a good hash plus equality.
- Both allocate one node per element; neither is cache friendly. For small or read-mostly data, a sorted vector or `flat_map` often beats both.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "unordered_map is always faster." For small n, string keys with expensive hashing, or workloads with range queries, it often is not.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: latency-sensitive code may prefer `map`'s predictable worst case or, better, an open-addressing flat hash map (topic 09).
- Deep dive: Topic 8, std::map and std::set
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Order or worst-case guarantees: map. Average-case point lookups: unordered_map. Small or static: sorted vector.

interview_qa.question: How is std::unordered_map implemented internally?
interview_qa.answer: As a hash table with separate chaining: an array of buckets, where each bucket leads to a chain of individually heap-allocated nodes holding the key/value pair. The bucket index is computed from `hash(key)` reduced modulo the bucket count.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Lookup: hash the key, go to its bucket, compare keys in that chain with `key_equal` until one matches.
- One node allocation per element; the bucket array is a separate allocation that is replaced on rehash.
- The node design is forced by the standard: references to elements must stay valid across a rehash, so elements cannot live inside a probing array.
- libstdc++ detail: all nodes are on one singly linked list, each bucket points to the node before its first element, and the hash code is cached in the node for non-trivial hashes such as `std::string`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's a balanced tree like `std::map`, just unsorted." Trees give O(log n) and ordered iteration; this is a hash table.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: why this layout is slow in practice (allocation per insert, pointer chasing per lookup) and that open-addressing "flat" maps exist because of it.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Unordered Containers and Hashing
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Buckets plus heap nodes: stable element addresses, at the price of allocations and cache misses.

interview_qa.question: Is lookup in unordered_map O(1)? What is the worst case and why?
interview_qa.answer: Average O(1), worst case O(n). The worst case happens when many keys land in the same bucket (bad hash, adversarial keys, or keys that collide by construction), so lookup degenerates into a linear scan of one chain.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Insertion is average O(1) **and** amortized: an occasional insert triggers an O(n) rehash.
- "Average" assumes a hash that spreads the actual keys; it is not a property of the container alone.
- Hash flooding: if an attacker controls keys and knows the hash, they can push every key into one bucket and make each operation O(n).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "O(1) always, that's why it's faster than map." Big-O hides the hash computation, cache misses and rehash spikes.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: distinguishing "average" (distribution of keys) from "amortized" (rare expensive operations), and mentioning tail latency on a hot path.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Unordered Containers and Hashing
interview_qa.key_takeaway: O(1) on average with a good hash; O(n) worst case; inserts are amortized because of rehash.

interview_qa.question: What does "instantiating a template" mean, and why do template definitions usually live in headers?
interview_qa.answer: Instantiation is the compiler generating a concrete function or class from the template for specific arguments, at the point where it is used. To do that it needs the full definition in the same translation unit, so definitions go in headers; otherwise other translation units fail at link time with "undefined reference".
interview_qa.explanation:
- Each distinct argument set is a separate entity: `Stack<int>` and `Stack<double>` share no code unless the optimizer folds identical functions.
- Explicit instantiation lets you keep the definition in a `.cpp`: `template class Stack<int>;` there, plus `extern template class Stack<int>;` in the header to stop other TUs from instantiating it (C++11). This works when the set of types is closed.
- Duplicate implicit instantiations across TUs are merged by the linker (they are inline-like entities), so the ODR is not violated.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Templates are compiled once into generic machine code." C++ templates are expanded per argument set; it is not type erasure like Java generics.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: compile-time cost and binary bloat grow with instantiations; `extern template`, explicit instantiation and moving type-independent code into a non-template base reduce both.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, Templates: Deduction, Specialization and Variadics
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A template is a recipe compiled per use; the recipe must be visible where it is used.

interview_qa.question: Should you specialize a function template or overload it? Why?
interview_qa.answer: Overload. Explicit specializations do not take part in overload resolution: the compiler first picks the best primary template (or non-template function), and only then checks whether that primary has a specialization for the deduced arguments. A specialization of a primary that loses is silently ignored.
interview_qa.explanation:
- With `template<class T> void f(T)`, a specialization `f<int*>`, and an overload `template<class T> void f(T*)`, the call `f(&x)` picks the overload `f(T*)` (more specialized) and the specialization never runs.
- Moving the specialization after `f(T*)` changes which primary it belongs to (now `f(T*)` with `T = int`) and it is called: the behaviour depends on declaration order.
- Overloads are visible, rank by normal rules, and cannot be "attached" to the wrong primary.
- Exception: specializing `std::` customization points such as `std::hash<MyType>` (a class template) is correct and expected (see topic 09).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A specialization is just a more specific overload, so it wins." It is not a candidate at all.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for type-dependent behaviour inside one function, `if constexpr` is often cleaner than either.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, Templates: Deduction, Specialization and Variadics
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Customize function templates with overloads; full specializations are invisible to overload resolution.

interview_qa.question: What is SFINAE, and what exactly counts as a "substitution failure"?
interview_qa.answer: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: when the compiler substitutes deduced template arguments into a function template's signature and gets an invalid type or expression, that template is quietly dropped from the overload set instead of causing an error. Only failures in the immediate context of the signature count; errors in the body are hard errors.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Immediate context: parameter types, return type (including trailing `decltype`), template parameter defaults, the C++20 `explicit(bool)` condition. Not the `noexcept` specifier: it is substituted only when needed, so an invalid `noexcept(T::value)` is a hard error.
- Hard errors (not SFINAE):
  - The function body (instantiated only after the function is selected).
  - `auto` return type deduction, because finding the type needs the body.
  - Errors inside another template that gets instantiated while forming the signature.
- After substitution, the surviving viable candidates are ranked by normal overload resolution.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "If any overload fails to compile, the compiler tries the next one." Only signature substitution failures are forgiven.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the `auto len(T t) { return t.size(); }` example where `len(5)` is a hard error even with a `len(...)` fallback.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, SFINAE, Type Traits and Concepts
interview_qa.key_takeaway: SFINAE removes candidates whose signature cannot be formed; it never rescues errors inside bodies.

interview_qa.question: What are concepts, and what do they improve over SFINAE?
interview_qa.answer: A concept (C++20) is a named compile-time predicate on template arguments, used to constrain templates: `template <std::integral T> T gcd(T, T)`. Compared with SFINAE they are readable, they produce errors at the call site that name the unsatisfied requirement, and constrained overloads are ordered by subsumption, so a more constrained overload beats a less constrained one.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Constraints are checked after deduction, before the function is considered viable.
- No runtime cost: like SFINAE, they only decide which template is used.
- They also work on non-template members of class templates (`void push(T) requires std::copyable<T>;`), which SFINAE cannot do without making the member a template.
- Concepts check syntax (expressions compile, types exist); semantic requirements (e.g. "`<` is a strict weak order") are documented, not checked.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Concepts are like interfaces with virtual functions." There is no runtime dispatch or vtable; types satisfy them structurally, without inheriting.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the subsumption rule and its source-identity limitation.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, SFINAE, Type Traits and Concepts
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Concepts = named, ordered, readable constraints; same zero runtime cost as SFINAE.

interview_qa.question: `constexpr int sq(int x) { return x * x; }` then `int b = sq(10);`. Is `sq(10)` computed at compile time?
interview_qa.answer: Not by the language rules. `int b` is a non-const local, so its initializer is an ordinary run-time call. The optimizer may fold it to `100` at `-O2`, but that is an optimization, not a guarantee, and `std::is_constant_evaluated()` would still report `false` there.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Compile time is guaranteed only in contexts that require a constant: `constexpr int a = sq(10);`, `static_assert`, array bounds, template arguments, `case` labels. For `const` integral initializers and statics the constant evaluation is attempted first and used when it succeeds.
- At `-O0` GCC emits a real call to `sq` for `int b = sq(10);`.
- To force it: `constexpr int b = sq(10);`, or make `sq` `consteval`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Yes, the arguments are constants, so the compiler evaluates it at compile time."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in the `const int c = sq(10);` case the answer flips to yes, because a const integral variable with a constant initializer is usable in constant expressions; for `const double` it does not.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, constexpr, consteval and Compile-Time Programming
interview_qa.key_takeaway: The calling context, not the arguments, decides whether a constexpr call is compile-time.

interview_qa.question: What does `std::is_constant_evaluated()` do, and what is the classic mistake with it?
interview_qa.answer: It returns `true` when the current evaluation is a manifestly constant-evaluated context, so one function can choose a constexpr-friendly algorithm at compile time and a faster run-time implementation (intrinsics, `memcpy`, SIMD) otherwise. The classic mistake is `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())`, which is always `true`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Use plain `if (std::is_constant_evaluated())`, never `if constexpr`; in C++23 prefer `if consteval`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
UB. On libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 it prints:
[d]
ASan reports nothing.
```

**Explanation:**
- `reserve` is a non-const member that is not exempt, so `p` is invalidated; printing it is UB.
- Why `d`: "Hello" was inline (SSO). `p` points into the string object's 16-byte local buffer. After `reserve(100)` the characters move to the heap and libstdc++ reuses those 16 bytes (a union) for the capacity field. 100 is `0x64`, ASCII `'d'`, followed by zero bytes.
- ASan is silent because `p` points into a live object: nothing was freed. With a 40-character string the old heap block is freed and ASan reports `heap-use-after-free`.
- **Key Concept:** Stale pointers into an SSO buffer are invisible to sanitizers; follow the rule, not the tool.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string s = "Hello";
    s.reserve(100);
    const char* p = s.c_str();          // acquire after the last mutation
    std::cout << '[' << p << "]\n";     // [Hello]
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: qty refers to an int whose lifetime ended.
GCC 11, -O0: printed an arbitrary number (on libstdc++ those bytes now hold part of the string's data pointer),
different on each run. ASan reports nothing: no memory was freed.
```

**Explanation:**
- Assigning a `std::string` destroys the `int` alternative and constructs a string in the same storage. `qty` still points at those bytes, which now belong to the string object (its first member is the heap pointer).
- Reading prints garbage; writing through `qty` would corrupt the string's pointer and crash later in its destructor.
- ASan is silent because the bytes are valid stack memory: only the object changed.
- Assigning another `int` (`field = 7;`) would have kept `qty` valid: same alternative, assignment instead of destroy + construct.
- **Key Concept:** A reference into a variant is valid only while that alternative stays active; re-fetch after every possible alternative change.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, std::variant, std::visit and std::any

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <variant>

int main() {
    std::variant<int, std::string> field = 42;
    int qty = std::get<int>(field);                  // copy the value out

    field = std::string("pending-confirmation-from-venue");
    std::cout << qty << '\n';                        // 42
    if (auto* p = std::get_if<int>(&field)) std::cout << *p << '\n';   // not printed
}
```

```
10 1 10 2 10 1
```

practice_tasks.answer: Undefined behaviour: it is invalidated by the insert. In practice (libstdc++) it prints 200.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Without reallocation, `insert` invalidates every iterator at or after the insertion point. `it` (index 2) is after `begin()`, so it is invalid.
- The buffer did not move, so the iterator still addresses slot 2, which now holds the old `v[1]` (200): the bug produces wrong data instead of a crash.
- ASan reports nothing (the memory is owned by the vector). `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` aborts with "attempt to dereference a singular iterator".
- **Key Concept:** Validity is defined by the operation, not by whether the address is still mapped. Use the iterator returned by `insert` and recompute positions after it.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, Iterators and Invalidation Rules

practice_tasks.answer: Undefined behaviour: after v.erase(it), the loop increments an invalidated iterator. In practice (libstdc++) it prints "4 5": the 4 survives.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `erase` invalidates `it` and everything after it. The loop's `++it` then uses an invalid iterator.
- What actually happens in a release build: erasing 2 shifts 4 into slot 0, `++it` moves to slot 1 (now 5), so 4 is never examined.

- Debug mode aborts at the `++it`: "attempt to increment a singular iterator".
- **Key Concept:** Continue from the iterator `erase` returns, and advance only when you did not erase.

practice_tasks.answer:
Does not compile. The essence of the GCC 11 error (inside std::sort):
error: no match for 'operator-' (operand types are 'std::_List_iterator<int>' and 'std::_List_iterator<int>')
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::sort` needs random access iterators (it computes `last - first` and jumps to midpoints). `list` iterators are bidirectional.
- `l.sort()` is the member merge sort: stable, O(n log n), relinks nodes, keeps all iterators valid.
- With `std::ranges::sort(l)` (C++20) the error message names the unsatisfied constraint (`random_access_range`) instead of failing deep inside the algorithm.
- **Key Concept:** The iterator category decides which algorithms are available; list compensates with member algorithms.

practice_tasks.title: Question 16
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
5 4 2 1 | 1 2 4 5 
```

**Explanation:**
- The comparator means "lower priority than". With the default `std::less`, the largest value has the highest priority: max-heap.
- With `std::greater`, a larger value counts as lower priority, so the smallest comes out first: min-heap.
- `pop()` returns `void`; reading requires `top()` first.
- **Key Concept:** `std::greater` in a priority_queue gives a min-heap, the opposite of what the name suggests.
- Deep dive: Topic 7, deque, list, forward_list, array and Adaptors

practice_tasks.title: Question 20
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Lines A and B are well-defined and print "one".
Line C is undefined behaviour (the rehash invalidated `it`), even though
libstdc++ happens to print "one" as well and ASan reports nothing.
```

**Explanation:**
- `reserve(1000)` changes the bucket count (13 to 1031 on libstdc++), which is a rehash.
- A rehash relinks nodes into a new bucket array; the nodes themselves do not move, so references and pointers stay valid.
- All iterators, including `end()`, are invalidated by the standard. The "it still works" result is an implementation accident (the node is still alive), so no tool flags it.
- **Key Concept:** Rehash invalidates iterators, not references. Re-run `find` after anything that can rehash.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, Unordered Containers and Hashing

practice_tasks.title: Question 22
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: no matching function for call to 'add(int, double)'
note: deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')
Fix: add<double>(10, 20.5), which prints 30.5
```

**Explanation:**
- `T` is deduced from each argument separately: `int` from `10`, `double` from `20.5`. The results must agree, and deduction never applies conversions.
- With an explicit template argument there is nothing to deduce, so `10` is converted to `10.0` as for any normal function call.
- Alternatives: `add(10.0, 20.5)`, or two template parameters with `auto` return type.
- **Key Concept:** All deductions of the same `T` must match exactly; conversions only happen after `T` is fixed.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, Templates: Deduction, Specialization and Variadics

practice_tasks.title: Question 23
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
4 2 4
```

**Explanation:**
- `a{src}`: CTAD prefers the copy deduction candidate for a single argument of the same template, so `a` is a `vector<int>` copy.
- `b{src.begin(), src.end()}`: braces make the `initializer_list` constructor win, so `b` is a `vector<vector<int>::iterator>` holding two iterators.
- `c(src.begin(), src.end())`: parentheses select the iterator-pair constructor and its deduction guide: `vector<int>` with 4 elements.
- **Key Concept:** CTAD plus braces can deduce a container of iterators; use parentheses or spell out the element type.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, Templates: Deduction, Specialization and Variadics

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
handle(int)
handle(long)
handle(T)
```

**Explanation:**
- `handle(1)`: `handle(int)` and `handle<int>` are both exact matches; on a tie the non-template wins.
- `handle(1L)`: same tie with `handle(long)` and `handle<long>`: the non-template wins.
- `handle(s)`: `handle<short>` is an exact match, while `handle(int)` needs a promotion and `handle(long)` a conversion. The better match wins before "prefer non-template" is considered.
- **Key Concept:** The non-template preference is only a tie-breaker; a template's exact match beats a non-template that needs a promotion.

practice_tasks.title: Question 25
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: call of overloaded 'print(double)' is ambiguous
(print(7) alone would compile and print "generic 7")
```

**Explanation:**
- `print(7)`: the `enable_if` overload is removed by SFINAE (`int` is not floating point), only the generic one is viable.
- `print(2.5)`: both overloads are viable, both take a `double`. Partial ordering compares parameter types only, and the `enable_if` condition is not part of that comparison, so neither is more specialized.
- Fix: add `std::enable_if_t<!std::is_floating_point_v<T>, int> = 0` to the generic overload, or use `template <std::floating_point T>` (a constrained template beats an unconstrained one).
- **Key Concept:** SFINAE only removes candidates; it never makes one candidate better than another.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, SFINAE, Type Traits and Concepts

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <concepts>
#include <iostream>

template <std::floating_point T>
void print(T v) { std::cout << "floating " << v << '\n'; }

template <class T>
void print(T v) { std::cout << "generic " << v << '\n'; }

int main() {
    print(7);     // generic 7
    print(2.5);   // floating 2.5
}
```

**Answer:**

```
Compile error: request for member 'size' in 'counter', which is of non-class type 'int'
```

**Explanation:**
- `v.name()` depends on `T`, so in the discarded branch it is never instantiated: no error for it.
- `counter.size()` does not depend on `T`: `counter` is always an `int`. Non-dependent code is checked when the template is defined (phase 1), whether or not the branch is discarded.
- The discarded-branch rule means "not instantiated", not "not compiled".
- **Key Concept:** `if constexpr` only hides code that depends on the template parameters.

practice_tasks.title: Question 27
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
-1 100 100 -1 -1
```

**Explanation:**
- `a`: a `constexpr` variable requires a constant: compile time.
- `b`: a plain local `int`: ordinary run-time call, even though the argument is a literal. At `-O2` the optimizer may fold `10 * 10`, but folding does not change what `is_constant_evaluated()` returns.
- `c`: `n` is a constant, but `c` is a non-const local: run time again. A constant argument does not make the call constant-evaluated.
- `d`: a static local is constant-initialized if possible, and that attempt is a constant evaluation.
- `e`: a `const int` with a constant initializer is usable in constant expressions, so its initializer is constant-evaluated. (`const double` would print 100.)
- **Key Concept:** The context of the call decides compile vs run time, never the arguments alone.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, constexpr, consteval and Compile-Time Programming

practice_tasks.title: Question 28
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
-std=c++14 -O0: link error: undefined reference to `Limits::MaxQty'
-std=c++17:     builds and prints 100
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::max` takes `const int&`. Binding a reference to `Limits::MaxQty` odr-uses it, which needs a definition with storage.
- In C++14 the in-class line is only a declaration; the definition `constexpr int Limits::MaxQty;` must appear in one .cpp file.
- In C++17 `static constexpr` data members are implicitly `inline`, so the in-class declaration is a definition.
- With `-O2` the C++14 build linked in this test: the optimizer inlined the value and removed the reference. The program is still wrong in C++14, the error just hides.
- **Key Concept:** static constexpr members are inline since C++17; before that, odr-use needs an out-of-class definition.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, constexpr, consteval and Compile-Time Programming

quick_reference.content:
#### std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is SSO guaranteed? | No; libstdc++ 15 chars, libc++ 22 chars |
| `sizeof(std::string)`? | Implementation-defined: 32 on GCC/MSVC, 24 on libc++ (64-bit) |
| Copy-on-write? | Forbidden since C++11 |
| Is `data()` null-terminated? | Yes, since C++11; same pointer as `c_str()` |
| Does `+=` within capacity keep `c_str()` valid? | Not guaranteed; reacquire |
| Which calls never invalidate? | `[]`, `at`, `front`, `back`, `data`, `begin`/`end` family |
| Does moving a short string steal a pointer? | No; characters are copied |
| `std::string(nullptr)`? | UB; compile error in C++23 |
| `s.find(x)` in an `if`? | Bug; compare with `npos` or use C++23 `contains` |
| `substr` cost? | New string; throws if `pos > size()` |
| Shrink a string? | `shrink_to_fit` (non-binding); `reserve` never shrinks since C++20 |
| Fastest int to string? | `std::to_chars` into a buffer |

#### std::string_view and std::span
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is a string_view? | Non-owning `(pointer, length)` into characters owned elsewhere |
| Return a view of a local string? | Dangling; return `std::string` |
| When does `return std::string("x")` as a view die? | End of the `return` statement in the callee |
| Is `sv.data()` null-terminated? | Not guaranteed |
| View after the owner appends without reallocating? | Formally invalid; size never updates |
| `string_view` or `const string&` parameter? | View for read-only; `const string&` if you need `c_str()`; by-value `string` if you store it |
| Can `string_view` modify text? | No; `span<char>` can |
| `span` vs `string_view`? | `span<T>` is the generic contiguous view; `string_view` adds string operations |
| Static vs dynamic extent? | `span<T, N>` stores only a pointer; `span<T>` stores pointer + size |
| `ranges::dangling`? | Returned for rvalue non-borrowed ranges; cannot be dereferenced |

#### std::optional and std::expected
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does optional allocate? | No; `T` is stored inside the optional |
| `*o` vs `o.value()` on empty? | UB vs throws `bad_optional_access` |
| Is `value_or(f())` lazy? | No; `f()` always runs |
| What does `reset()` destroy? | The contained `T`, not the optional |
| `optional<bool>` holding false in `if`? | True: tests engagement |
| `optional<T&>`? | Not allowed before C++26; use `T*` |
| Empty vs -5? | Empty is less than any value |
| optional vs expected? | optional: missing; expected: missing with a typed reason |
| How to return an error from expected? | `return std::unexpected(e);` |
| `expected<int,int>`, `return 42;`? | Success with value 42 |
| `and_then` vs `transform`? | Step returns optional/expected vs a plain value |
| When exceptions instead? | Rare, non-local failures; constructors; errors handled far away |

#### std::variant, std::visit and std::any
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Where is a variant's value stored? | In-place, inside the variant; no heap |
| How does variant know the active type? | A stored index |
| `get` vs `get_if`? | Reference + throw vs pointer + nullptr |
| Why `std::visit` over `switch(index())`? | Compile-time check that every type is handled |
| Is visit compile-time dispatch? | No; run-time branch on the index, no vptr |
| variant vs virtual? | Closed set, in-place, easy new operations vs open set, heap, easy new types |
| What is `monostate`? | An intentional empty alternative |
| What is valueless_by_exception? | Old value destroyed, new construction threw: no value |
| `variant<bool, string> v = "hi"`? | string (since P0608) |
| any vs variant? | Run-time open type erasure vs compile-time closed set |
| `any a = "hi"; any_cast<string>(a)`? | Throws: stored type is `const char*` |
| Does any allocate? | Implementation-specific; libstdc++ inline only for pointer-sized nothrow-movable types |

#### std::vector Internals
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| size vs capacity? | Constructed elements vs allocated slots |
| Growth factor? | Geometric, implementation-defined (2x GCC/Clang, 1.5x MSVC) |
| Why geometric? | Amortized O(1) `push_back` |
| `reserve(100); v[50] = 1;`? | UB; size is 0 (ASan silent, `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` aborts) |
| `push_back` at full capacity? | Always reallocates; all borrows die |
| Reallocation order in libstdc++? | Construct new element, relocate old, destroy old, free |
| Is `v.push_back(v[0])` safe? | Yes, required to work |
| Copy or move on growth? | Move if `noexcept` (or not copyable), else copy |
| `emplace_back` vs `push_back`? | Saves one move only when passing constructor arguments |
| `vector<int>{10}` size? | 1 |
| Does `clear()` free memory? | No; capacity stays |
| `std::remove` changes size? | No; erase the tail or use `std::erase` (C++20) |
| `vector<bool>`? | Bit-packed, proxy references, no `data()`, not a real container |
| Need stable addresses? | Indices, `deque`, or `vector<unique_ptr<T>>` |

#### Iterators and Invalidation Rules
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What can you do with an invalid iterator? | Assign to it or destroy it; nothing else (even `==` is UB) |
| vector push_back, no reallocation: what dies? | Only `end()` |
| vector insert, no reallocation: what dies? | Everything at or after the insertion point |
| deque push_back: refs? iterators? | Refs and pointers valid; all iterators invalid |
| deque pop_front: what dies? | Only the erased element |
| list / map erase: what dies? | Only the erased element |
| unordered rehash: what dies? | Iterators; refs and pointers survive |
| Why `it != end()` and not `it < end()`? | `<` exists only for random access; `!=` works for every category |
| `std::advance` on a list? | O(n); `it + n` does not compile |
| `const iterator` vs `const_iterator`? | Fixed position vs read-only element |
| `rit.base()`? | Points one past `*rit` in forward order |
| Does swap invalidate? | No (except string, array values, and `end()`); iterators follow the elements |
| Range-for and push_back? | UB: hidden `begin`/`end` are cached |

#### deque, list, forward_list, array and Adaptors
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is deque contiguous? | No: blocks plus a map; each block is contiguous |
| Why is `d[i]` O(1)? | Fixed block size: index math is division and modulo |
| deque push_back: refs? iterators? | Refs valid; iterators invalid |
| Empty deque cost? | libstdc++: 80 bytes plus two allocations |
| `list::insert(it, x)`? | Inserts before `it`; `it` still points to the same element |
| `list::size()`? | O(1) since C++11 |
| Sort a list? | `l.sort()`; `std::sort` needs random access |
| splice cost? | O(1), except a range from another list: O(range) |
| forward_list size? | No `size()`; use `std::distance` (O(n)) |
| `std::array<int, 3> a;` values? | Indeterminate; use `a{}` |
| Min-heap? | `std::priority_queue<T, std::vector<T>, std::greater<T>>` |
| Why does `pop()` return void? | Returning by value could throw after removal and lose the element |

#### std::map and std::set
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How is std::map implemented? | Red-black tree in practice; standard mandates O(log n) and stable iterators |
| `m[k]` on a missing key? | Inserts `V{}` and returns a reference to it |
| How does set detect duplicates? | Equivalence: `!comp(a,b) && !comp(b,a)`, never `==` |
| `<=` as comparator? | UB: duplicates inserted, lookups fail, `std::sort` can overflow |
| `lower_bound` vs `upper_bound`? | First not before `k` vs first after `k` (per comparator) |
| Greatest key `<= k`? | `upper_bound(k)`, then step back if not `begin()` |
| `emplace` vs `try_emplace`? | try_emplace never consumes args when the key exists |
| Lookup `std::string` keys by `string_view`? | Use `std::less<>` (transparent comparator) |
| Change a key? | `extract` node handle, edit `key()`, re-insert |
| map erase invalidates? | Only the erased element |
| Why can a small vector beat a map? | Contiguous memory, no pointer chasing, no per-node allocation |
| map vs unordered_map? | Need order, ranges, or stable worst case: map; pure point lookups: unordered |

#### Unordered Containers and Hashing
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How is `unordered_map` built? | Buckets of chained nodes; one allocation per element |
| Lookup complexity? | Average O(1), worst O(n) |
| When does it rehash? | Before the insert that would exceed `max_load_factor` |
| `reserve` vs `rehash`? | Elements vs buckets |
| What does rehash invalidate? | Iterators only; references and pointers survive |
| What does erase invalidate? | Only the erased element |
| Custom key needs? | Hash + equality, consistent with each other |
| Why is `h1 ^ (h2 << 1)` bad? | Nearly symmetric, small range, many collisions |
| Avoid a temporary string in `find`? | Transparent hash + `equal_to<>` (C++20) |
| Change a key? | `extract`, modify `key()`, `insert` |
| Faster alternative? | Flat open-addressing map, sorted vector, or direct array |
| `map` instead? | Need ordering, ranges, or a hard O(log n) bound |

#### Templates: Deduction, Specialization and Variadics
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| `add(10, 20.5)` with `T add(T, T)`? | Deduction conflict, no match; `add<double>` works |
| `f(T)` with `const int`? | `T = int` |
| `f(T&)` with `const int`? | `T = const int` |
| Specialize or overload a function template? | Overload |
| Partial specialization of a function? | Not allowed |
| Which wins, `f(T)` or `f(T*)` for `int*`? | `f(T*)`, more specialized |
| Why `typename`? | Dependent name is assumed to be a value |
| Why `this->` in a template derived class? | Dependent base members are not found otherwise |
| Why are templates in headers? | Definition needed at instantiation |
| `(a - ...)` on 10,3,2? | 9; `(... - a)` gives 5 |
| CRTP vs virtual? | Compile-time type, no vptr; no heterogeneous containers |
| Deducing this? | C++23 `this auto& self`: CRTP without the template base |

#### SFINAE, Type Traits and Concepts
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is SFINAE? | Invalid substitution in the signature removes the overload instead of erroring |
| Does a body error count? | No, hard error |
| enable_if overload vs generic `T` for `int`? | Ambiguous |
| Concept-constrained vs unconstrained? | Constrained wins |
| Why `enable_if_t<C, int> = 0`? | Conditions become part of the signature: no redefinition |
| `if constexpr` in a non-template? | Both branches are checked |
| `static_assert(false)` in a discarded branch? | OK since P2593 (GCC 13+); use a dependent false before |
| `requires { sizeof(T) > 4; }`? | Always true if it compiles; use `requires (sizeof(T) > 4)` |
| What decides subsumption? | Atomic constraints identical by source: use named concepts |
| `declval`? | Fake object in unevaluated context |
| Tag dispatch? | Overload on a tag type; inheritance ranks the tags |

#### constexpr, consteval and Compile-Time Programming
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is a constexpr function evaluated at compile time? | Only when called in a context that requires a constant |
| constexpr vs consteval? | May vs must run at compile time |
| constexpr vs constinit? | constinit only requires constant initialization; variable stays mutable |
| Why can't I use a parameter as an array size? | Parameters are never constant expressions |
| `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())`? | Always true |
| How to call consteval from constexpr? | C++23 `if consteval` |
| What happens to UB at compile time? | Compile error: constant evaluation must diagnose it |
| constexpr std::vector global? | Not allowed: allocation must be freed inside the evaluation |
| static constexpr member needs a definition? | C++14 if odr-used; not since C++17 (implicitly inline) |
| Cost of heavy constexpr? | Longer builds, bigger binaries, evaluator limits |
| Use in low-latency code? | Precompute tables and constants; assert layouts at build time |
