topics.topic: std::string: SSO, Buffers and Pointer Validity

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A `std::string` is an **owning, contiguous, null-terminated** buffer of `char`, plus a size and a capacity.
- Two locations to keep apart:
  - **The object** (a few pointers and counters): lives wherever you declared it (stack, heap, static storage, inside another object).
  - **The characters**: either inside the object itself (**small string optimization**, SSO) or in a heap block the object owns.
- The object owns its characters exclusively: copying a string copies the characters (no sharing since C++11), destroying it frees them.
- Every pointer, reference, iterator or `string_view` you take into a string is a **borrow**. The string decides when that borrow dies, and the rules are stricter than for `std::vector` (section 5).
- Three numbers describe the state:
  - `size()` (same as `length()`): characters in use, not counting the terminator.
  - `capacity()`: characters that fit without a new allocation (also not counting the terminator).
  - `max_size()`: theoretical limit; exceeding it throws `std::length_error`.

subsections.title: 2. Layout and the small string optimization (implementation-specific)
subsections.content:
- The standard does **not** require SSO and does not specify `sizeof(std::string)`. Every major library implements SSO anyway, with different numbers:

| Library | `sizeof(std::string)` (64-bit) | Inline capacity (chars) | Layout idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| libstdc++ (GCC, new ABI) | 32 | 15 | pointer, size, union { capacity, 16-byte local buffer } |
| libc++ (Clang/Apple) | 24 | 22 | short/long modes packed into 3 words, one flag bit |
| MSVC STL | 32 | 15 | union { 16-byte buffer, pointer }, size, capacity |

- The libstdc++ row is verified with GCC 11 on x86-64. The libc++ and MSVC rows are the typical values for 64-bit release builds; check your own library before quoting them.

- libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 details:
  - The data pointer always points at the characters: for a short string it points into the object's own local buffer.
  - The local buffer shares storage (a union) with the capacity field. When a string moves to the heap, those 16 bytes start holding the capacity number instead of characters.
  - A default-constructed string has `capacity() == 15`, no allocation at all.
  - `std::string(16, 'a')` allocates exactly 16; growth by `push_back` doubles: 15, 30, 60, 120 ...
- Detecting SSO in a test program (not in production code): check whether `s.data()` lies inside `[&s, &s + 1)`.
- Why SSO matters:
  - Most strings in real programs are short (names, keys, small messages): no allocation, no free, better cache locality.
  - Moving a short string must copy its characters (there is no heap block to steal), so a "move" of an SSO string costs about the same as a copy of 15 bytes.
  - Pointers into an SSO string point into the string object, so they die with the object and can never "follow" the characters to another string after a move.

subsections.title: 3. No copy-on-write since C++11
subsections.content:
- Pre-C++11 libstdc++ (the old ABI) used reference-counted **copy-on-write** (COW): copies shared one buffer until someone wrote.
- C++11 made COW non-conforming:
  - Non-const `operator[]`, `at`, `begin()`, `end()` are not allowed to invalidate references, but a COW string must "unshare" (allocate) on the first non-const access, which moves the characters.
  - Concurrent reads of distinct string objects must not race; a shared refcount turns every copy into an atomic RMW and every non-const access into a check.
- GCC 5 introduced the new ABI (`_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1`, default) with SSO and no COW. The `std::__cxx11::basic_string` symbol you see in error messages is that ABI tag.
- Consequence: `std::string b = a;` always allocates when `a` is longer than the inline capacity. Pass by `const std::string&` or `std::string_view` (see topic 02) when you only read.

subsections.title: 4. Contiguity, null termination and element access
subsections.content:
- Since C++11:
  - Characters are contiguous: `&s[0] + i == &s[i]` for `i <= size()`.
  - `c_str()` and `data()` return the **same** pointer, and both point at a null-terminated sequence (`data()[size()] == '\0'`). Before C++11 `data()` was not required to be null-terminated.
  - `s[s.size()]` is valid and returns a reference to `'\0'`, for both const and non-const strings. Writing any value other than `'\0'` there is UB.
- C++17: non-const `data()` returns `char*`, so a C function can write into `s.data()` (up to `size()` characters).
- C++11 `front()` / `back()`; on an empty string both are UB (no check).
- `at(i)` checks and throws `std::out_of_range` for `i >= size()`; `operator[]` does not check (UB for `i > size()`).
- Embedded nulls are legal: a `std::string` knows its size, so `"ab\0cd"s` has size 5. But `c_str()` handed to a C function stops at the first `'\0'`.

subsections.title: 5. Pointer, reference and iterator validity: the exact rule
subsections.content:
- The standard rule for `basic_string` ([string.require]): references, pointers and iterators into a string **may be invalidated** by:
  - Passing the string as a non-const reference to a library function (`swap`, `operator>>`, `getline`).
  - Calling **any non-const member function**, except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `rbegin`, `end`, `rend`.
- That means `+=`, `append`, `push_back`, `insert`, `erase`, `replace`, `clear`, `resize`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`, `assign`, `operator=` and `swap` **all** formally invalidate, **even when no reallocation happens**.
- This is stricter than `std::vector`, where "no reallocation" keeps pointers before the insertion point valid. Do not transfer the vector rule to strings.
- What actually happens in libstdc++ (useful for explaining symptoms, never for writing code):

| Operation on `s` after `p = s.c_str()` | Standard | libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `s[0] = 'J'` | `p` valid | `p` sees `"Jello..."` |
| `s += "x"` within capacity | `p` invalidated | same buffer, `p` reads the longer string |
| `s += "x"` beyond capacity | `p` invalidated | heap reallocation, old block freed: use-after-free |
| `s.reserve(100)` on SSO string | `p` invalidated | `p` points into the object, now holding the capacity value |
| `s.clear()` | `p` invalidated | same buffer, `p[0] == '\0'` |
| `s.shrink_to_fit()` | `p` invalidated | may move heap data back into the local buffer |
| `a.swap(b)` | iterators invalidated | SSO characters stay in their object: an iterator into `a` now reads `b`'s old content |
| `std::string t = std::move(s)` | `p` invalidated | SSO: `p` still points into `s` (now empty); heap: `p == t.data()` in practice |

- The safe pattern: **reacquire** `c_str()` / `data()` / iterators after every non-const operation, or store an index instead of a pointer.
- Holding an invalidated pointer is fine; **using** it (dereference, printing, passing to a C API) is UB.
- AddressSanitizer only catches the heap cases. For an SSO string the stale pointer still points into a live object, so ASan stays silent while the program prints garbage.

subsections.title: 6. Size, capacity, reserve, clear, shrink_to_fit
subsections.content:
- `reserve(n)`:
  - Ensures `capacity() >= n`; never changes `size()` or the content.
  - Since C++20 `reserve(n)` with `n < capacity()` is a no-op (never shrinks). Before C++20 it was a non-binding shrink request. The no-argument `reserve()` is deprecated in C++20 (removed in C++26).
- `resize(n)` / `resize(n, ch)`: changes `size()`; new characters are `'\0'` (or `ch`).
- `clear()`: `size()` becomes 0, capacity unchanged (libstdc++ keeps the heap block).
- `shrink_to_fit()`: non-binding request to reduce capacity to size. In libstdc++ a short string goes back into the local buffer (capacity 15).
- Growth is **geometric** so `push_back` is amortized O(1). The factor is implementation-defined (libstdc++ doubles; MSVC typically grows by 1.5x).
- Exceptions: allocation failure throws `std::bad_alloc`; exceeding `max_size()` throws `std::length_error`. `push_back` and `append` give the strong guarantee.
- Move constructor is `noexcept` (important so that `std::vector<std::string>` moves instead of copying on growth: see Memory & Ownership, topic 02).

subsections.title: 7. Construction and assignment traps
subsections.content:
| Code | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `std::string s(nullptr);` or `const char* p = nullptr; std::string s(p);` | UB (C++23: `nullptr` literal is a compile error) | The `const char*` constructor calls `strlen`; libstdc++ throws `logic_error` "null not valid" |
| `std::string s = 0;` | UB before C++23, compile error in C++23 | `0` is a null pointer constant |
| `std::string s(5, 'a');` | `"aaaaa"` | count + char constructor |
| `std::string s{5, 'a'};` | 2 characters: `'\x05'`, `'a'` | braces prefer `initializer_list<char>` |
| `std::string s = 'a';` | Compile error | no constructor from `char` |
| `s = 65;` | `"A"` | `operator=(char)`: the `int` converts silently |
| `std::string s("ab\0cd");` | size 2 | the `const char*` constructor stops at `'\0'` |
| `using namespace std::string_literals; auto s = "ab\0cd"s;` | size 5 | the literal operator receives the length |
| `std::string s(sv);` from `string_view` | copy | explicit; there is no implicit conversion from `string_view` |

subsections.title: 8. Searching and substrings
subsections.content:
- `find`, `rfind`, `find_first_of`, `find_last_not_of` ... return a position or `std::string::npos`, which is `size_type(-1)` (the largest `size_t`).
- Classic bugs:
  - `if (s.find("x"))` is true when the text is **not** found (npos is non-zero) and false when it is found at position 0.
  - `int pos = s.find(...)` narrows npos to `-1`; comparing it later with an unsigned value converts it back, and it "works" by accident. Use `auto` or `std::size_t`.
- `substr(pos, n)`:
  - Returns a **new string** (allocation if longer than the SSO capacity).
  - Throws `std::out_of_range` if `pos > size()`; `pos == size()` returns an empty string.
  - `n` is clamped to the remaining length.
  - For parsing, prefer `std::string_view::substr` which is O(1) and allocation-free (see topic 02).
- C++20: `starts_with`, `ends_with`. C++23: `contains`. All three accept a `string_view`, a `char` or a `const char*`.
- Comparison: `==` compares size and content; C++20 `<=>` gives lexicographic `std::strong_ordering` (by `char_traits<char>::compare`, which the standard defines to compare as `unsigned char`, so `'\xE9' > 'a'` even where `char` is signed).

subsections.title: 9. Building strings efficiently
subsections.content:
- `a + b + c` creates intermediate strings; since C++11 the rvalue overloads of `operator+` append into the left temporary, so a chain costs fewer allocations than it looks, but still more than one `reserve` plus `append`.
- In loops: `reserve` the final size once, then `+=` / `append`; reuse a string with `clear()` to keep its capacity.
- Number conversion:
  - `std::to_string(x)`: simple, allocates.
  - `std::to_chars` / `std::from_chars` (C++17): no allocation, no locale, no exceptions; the fastest option.
  - `std::stoi` and friends: throw `invalid_argument` / `out_of_range`.
- `std::format` (C++20, library support in GCC 13): type-safe formatting into a new string; `std::format_to` writes into an existing buffer.
- `resize_and_overwrite(n, op)` (C++23): lets a C API or a hand-written loop write directly into the buffer without first zero-filling `n` characters; `op` returns the final size.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "If there is spare capacity, `+=` keeps my `c_str()` pointer valid." ✅ Any non-const member except the access functions formally invalidates it; that it works in libstdc++ is not a guarantee.
- ❌ "SSO is part of the standard; a short string never allocates." ✅ SSO is an implementation choice; capacities differ (15 vs 22).
- ❌ "Copies share the buffer until one is modified." ✅ COW is forbidden since C++11; every copy owns its characters.
- ❌ "`data()` is not null-terminated, only `c_str()` is." ✅ Since C++11 they return the same null-terminated pointer.
- ❌ "Moving a string is always just stealing a pointer." ✅ A short string's characters are copied; the source is valid but unspecified (empty in practice).
- ❌ "A std::string on the stack keeps its characters on the stack." ✅ Only short strings; longer ones live on the heap regardless of where the object is.
- ❌ "ASan would have told me if the pointer was dangling." ✅ Stale pointers into an SSO buffer point into a live object; ASan sees nothing wrong.
- ❌ "`reserve(10)` on a big string shrinks it." ✅ Since C++20 it never shrinks; use `shrink_to_fit` (non-binding).
- ❌ "`std::string(nullptr)` makes an empty string." ✅ UB; C++23 deletes that overload.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- A `std::string` is an **owning, contiguous, null-terminated** buffer of `char`, plus a size and a capacity.
- Two locations to keep apart:
  - **The object** (a few pointers and counters): lives wherever you declared it (stack, heap, static storage, inside another object).
  - **The characters**: either inside the object itself (**small string optimization**, SSO) or in a heap block the object owns.
- The object owns its characters exclusively: copying a string copies the characters (no sharing since C++11), destroying it frees them.
- Every pointer, reference, iterator or `string_view` you take into a string is a **borrow**. The string decides when that borrow dies, and the rules are stricter than for `std::vector` (section 5).
- Three numbers describe the state:
  - `size()` (same as `length()`): characters in use, not counting the terminator.
  - `capacity()`: characters that fit without a new allocation (also not counting the terminator).
  - `max_size()`: theoretical limit; exceeding it throws `std::length_error`.

#### 2. Layout and the small string optimization (implementation-specific)
- The standard does **not** require SSO and does not specify `sizeof(std::string)`. Every major library implements SSO anyway, with different numbers:

| Library | `sizeof(std::string)` (64-bit) | Inline capacity (chars) | Layout idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| libstdc++ (GCC, new ABI) | 32 | 15 | pointer, size, union { capacity, 16-byte local buffer } |
| libc++ (Clang/Apple) | 24 | 22 | short/long modes packed into 3 words, one flag bit |
| MSVC STL | 32 | 15 | union { 16-byte buffer, pointer }, size, capacity |

- The libstdc++ row is verified with GCC 11 on x86-64. The libc++ and MSVC rows are the typical values for 64-bit release builds; check your own library before quoting them.

- libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 details:
  - The data pointer always points at the characters: for a short string it points into the object's own local buffer.
  - The local buffer shares storage (a union) with the capacity field. When a string moves to the heap, those 16 bytes start holding the capacity number instead of characters.
  - A default-constructed string has `capacity() == 15`, no allocation at all.
  - `std::string(16, 'a')` allocates exactly 16; growth by `push_back` doubles: 15, 30, 60, 120 ...
- Detecting SSO in a test program (not in production code): check whether `s.data()` lies inside `[&s, &s + 1)`.
- Why SSO matters:
  - Most strings in real programs are short (names, keys, small messages): no allocation, no free, better cache locality.
  - Moving a short string must copy its characters (there is no heap block to steal), so a "move" of an SSO string costs about the same as a copy of 15 bytes.
  - Pointers into an SSO string point into the string object, so they die with the object and can never "follow" the characters to another string after a move.

#### 3. No copy-on-write since C++11
- Pre-C++11 libstdc++ (the old ABI) used reference-counted **copy-on-write** (COW): copies shared one buffer until someone wrote.
- C++11 made COW non-conforming:
  - Non-const `operator[]`, `at`, `begin()`, `end()` are not allowed to invalidate references, but a COW string must "unshare" (allocate) on the first non-const access, which moves the characters.
  - Concurrent reads of distinct string objects must not race; a shared refcount turns every copy into an atomic RMW and every non-const access into a check.
- GCC 5 introduced the new ABI (`_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1`, default) with SSO and no COW. The `std::__cxx11::basic_string` symbol you see in error messages is that ABI tag.
- Consequence: `std::string b = a;` always allocates when `a` is longer than the inline capacity. Pass by `const std::string&` or `std::string_view` (see topic 02) when you only read.

#### 4. Contiguity, null termination and element access
- Since C++11:
  - Characters are contiguous: `&s[0] + i == &s[i]` for `i <= size()`.
  - `c_str()` and `data()` return the **same** pointer, and both point at a null-terminated sequence (`data()[size()] == '\0'`). Before C++11 `data()` was not required to be null-terminated.
  - `s[s.size()]` is valid and returns a reference to `'\0'`, for both const and non-const strings. Writing any value other than `'\0'` there is UB.
- C++17: non-const `data()` returns `char*`, so a C function can write into `s.data()` (up to `size()` characters).
- C++11 `front()` / `back()`; on an empty string both are UB (no check).
- `at(i)` checks and throws `std::out_of_range` for `i >= size()`; `operator[]` does not check (UB for `i > size()`).
- Embedded nulls are legal: a `std::string` knows its size, so `"ab\0cd"s` has size 5. But `c_str()` handed to a C function stops at the first `'\0'`.

#### 5. Pointer, reference and iterator validity: the exact rule
- The standard rule for `basic_string` ([string.require]): references, pointers and iterators into a string **may be invalidated** by:
  - Passing the string as a non-const reference to a library function (`swap`, `operator>>`, `getline`).
  - Calling **any non-const member function**, except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `rbegin`, `end`, `rend`.
- That means `+=`, `append`, `push_back`, `insert`, `erase`, `replace`, `clear`, `resize`, `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit`, `assign`, `operator=` and `swap` **all** formally invalidate, **even when no reallocation happens**.
- This is stricter than `std::vector`, where "no reallocation" keeps pointers before the insertion point valid. Do not transfer the vector rule to strings.
- What actually happens in libstdc++ (useful for explaining symptoms, never for writing code):

| Operation on `s` after `p = s.c_str()` | Standard | libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `s[0] = 'J'` | `p` valid | `p` sees `"Jello..."` |
| `s += "x"` within capacity | `p` invalidated | same buffer, `p` reads the longer string |
| `s += "x"` beyond capacity | `p` invalidated | heap reallocation, old block freed: use-after-free |
| `s.reserve(100)` on SSO string | `p` invalidated | `p` points into the object, now holding the capacity value |
| `s.clear()` | `p` invalidated | same buffer, `p[0] == '\0'` |
| `s.shrink_to_fit()` | `p` invalidated | may move heap data back into the local buffer |
| `a.swap(b)` | iterators invalidated | SSO characters stay in their object: an iterator into `a` now reads `b`'s old content |
| `std::string t = std::move(s)` | `p` invalidated | SSO: `p` still points into `s` (now empty); heap: `p == t.data()` in practice |

- The safe pattern: **reacquire** `c_str()` / `data()` / iterators after every non-const operation, or store an index instead of a pointer.
- Holding an invalidated pointer is fine; **using** it (dereference, printing, passing to a C API) is UB.
- AddressSanitizer only catches the heap cases. For an SSO string the stale pointer still points into a live object, so ASan stays silent while the program prints garbage.

#### 6. Size, capacity, reserve, clear, shrink_to_fit
- `reserve(n)`:
  - Ensures `capacity() >= n`; never changes `size()` or the content.
  - Since C++20 `reserve(n)` with `n < capacity()` is a no-op (never shrinks). Before C++20 it was a non-binding shrink request. The no-argument `reserve()` is deprecated in C++20 (removed in C++26).
- `resize(n)` / `resize(n, ch)`: changes `size()`; new characters are `'\0'` (or `ch`).
- `clear()`: `size()` becomes 0, capacity unchanged (libstdc++ keeps the heap block).
- `shrink_to_fit()`: non-binding request to reduce capacity to size. In libstdc++ a short string goes back into the local buffer (capacity 15).
- Growth is **geometric** so `push_back` is amortized O(1). The factor is implementation-defined (libstdc++ doubles; MSVC typically grows by 1.5x).
- Exceptions: allocation failure throws `std::bad_alloc`; exceeding `max_size()` throws `std::length_error`. `push_back` and `append` give the strong guarantee.
- Move constructor is `noexcept` (important so that `std::vector<std::string>` moves instead of copying on growth: see Memory & Ownership, topic 02).

#### 7. Construction and assignment traps
| Code | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `std::string s(nullptr);` or `const char* p = nullptr; std::string s(p);` | UB (C++23: `nullptr` literal is a compile error) | The `const char*` constructor calls `strlen`; libstdc++ throws `logic_error` "null not valid" |
| `std::string s = 0;` | UB before C++23, compile error in C++23 | `0` is a null pointer constant |
| `std::string s(5, 'a');` | `"aaaaa"` | count + char constructor |
| `std::string s{5, 'a'};` | 2 characters: `'\x05'`, `'a'` | braces prefer `initializer_list<char>` |
| `std::string s = 'a';` | Compile error | no constructor from `char` |
| `s = 65;` | `"A"` | `operator=(char)`: the `int` converts silently |
| `std::string s("ab\0cd");` | size 2 | the `const char*` constructor stops at `'\0'` |
| `using namespace std::string_literals; auto s = "ab\0cd"s;` | size 5 | the literal operator receives the length |
| `std::string s(sv);` from `string_view` | copy | explicit; there is no implicit conversion from `string_view` |

#### 8. Searching and substrings
- `find`, `rfind`, `find_first_of`, `find_last_not_of` ... return a position or `std::string::npos`, which is `size_type(-1)` (the largest `size_t`).
- Classic bugs:
  - `if (s.find("x"))` is true when the text is **not** found (npos is non-zero) and false when it is found at position 0.
  - `int pos = s.find(...)` narrows npos to `-1`; comparing it later with an unsigned value converts it back, and it "works" by accident. Use `auto` or `std::size_t`.
- `substr(pos, n)`:
  - Returns a **new string** (allocation if longer than the SSO capacity).
  - Throws `std::out_of_range` if `pos > size()`; `pos == size()` returns an empty string.
  - `n` is clamped to the remaining length.
  - For parsing, prefer `std::string_view::substr` which is O(1) and allocation-free (see topic 02).
- C++20: `starts_with`, `ends_with`. C++23: `contains`. All three accept a `string_view`, a `char` or a `const char*`.
- Comparison: `==` compares size and content; C++20 `<=>` gives lexicographic `std::strong_ordering` (by `char_traits<char>::compare`, which the standard defines to compare as `unsigned char`, so `'\xE9' > 'a'` even where `char` is signed).

#### 9. Building strings efficiently
- `a + b + c` creates intermediate strings; since C++11 the rvalue overloads of `operator+` append into the left temporary, so a chain costs fewer allocations than it looks, but still more than one `reserve` plus `append`.
- In loops: `reserve` the final size once, then `+=` / `append`; reuse a string with `clear()` to keep its capacity.
- Number conversion:
  - `std::to_string(x)`: simple, allocates.
  - `std::to_chars` / `std::from_chars` (C++17): no allocation, no locale, no exceptions; the fastest option.
  - `std::stoi` and friends: throw `invalid_argument` / `out_of_range`.
- `std::format` (C++20, library support in GCC 13): type-safe formatting into a new string; `std::format_to` writes into an existing buffer.
- `resize_and_overwrite(n, op)` (C++23): lets a C API or a hand-written loop write directly into the buffer without first zero-filling `n` characters; `op` returns the final size.

#### 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "If there is spare capacity, `+=` keeps my `c_str()` pointer valid." ✅ Any non-const member except the access functions formally invalidates it; that it works in libstdc++ is not a guarantee.
- ❌ "SSO is part of the standard; a short string never allocates." ✅ SSO is an implementation choice; capacities differ (15 vs 22).
- ❌ "Copies share the buffer until one is modified." ✅ COW is forbidden since C++11; every copy owns its characters.
- ❌ "`data()` is not null-terminated, only `c_str()` is." ✅ Since C++11 they return the same null-terminated pointer.
- ❌ "Moving a string is always just stealing a pointer." ✅ A short string's characters are copied; the source is valid but unspecified (empty in practice).
- ❌ "A std::string on the stack keeps its characters on the stack." ✅ Only short strings; longer ones live on the heap regardless of where the object is.
- ❌ "ASan would have told me if the pointer was dangling." ✅ Stale pointers into an SSO buffer point into a live object; ASan sees nothing wrong.
- ❌ "`reserve(10)` on a big string shrinks it." ✅ Since C++20 it never shrinks; use `shrink_to_fit` (non-binding).
- ❌ "`std::string(nullptr)` makes an empty string." ✅ UB; C++23 deletes that overload.

edge_cases.title: The append that "works" but is still invalid
edge_cases.explanation:
- `const char* p = s.c_str(); s += " world"; puts(p);` may print the full text on libstdc++ when capacity was sufficient.
- The standard says `+=` may invalidate `p` regardless of capacity. Another library, a debug mode, or a future version may behave differently.
- When capacity is exceeded, libstdc++ allocates a new block and frees the old one: ASan reports `heap-use-after-free` on the next use of `p`.
- Rule: never reason from capacity for strings; reacquire the pointer.

edge_cases.title: reserve on a short string prints a stray "d"
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string s = "Hello"; const char* p = s.c_str(); s.reserve(100);`
- In libstdc++ `p` points into the object's local buffer. After `reserve(100)` the characters move to the heap and the same 16 bytes now store the capacity field (a union).
- Capacity 100 is byte `0x64`, which is `'d'`, followed by zero bytes: printing `p` outputs `d`.
- ASan reports nothing: no memory was freed. The bug is real (formal invalidation) but invisible to the tool.
- With a 40-character string the same code reads a freed heap block and ASan does fire.

edge_cases.title: Iterators survive swap but switch strings
edge_cases.explanation:
- For `std::vector`, `swap` keeps iterators valid and they follow the elements into the other vector.
- For `std::string`, `swap` is in the invalidating list. In libstdc++ short strings keep their characters inside each object, so the characters are exchanged by copying: an iterator into `a` keeps pointing into `a`'s buffer, which now holds `b`'s old content.
- A heap string's iterator would follow the buffer to `b` instead. Two different behaviours, both undefined to rely on.

edge_cases.title: `find` truth tests and npos
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if (s.find("key"))` means "found at a non-zero position, or not found at all".
- Correct: `if (s.find("key") != std::string::npos)` or C++23 `s.contains("key")`.
- `int pos = s.find('x');` makes `pos == -1` for not found; `s.substr(pos)` then converts `-1` back to a huge `size_t` and throws `out_of_range`.

edge_cases.title: nullptr and 0 into a string
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string s = nullptr;` and `std::string s = 0;` compile in C++20 (null pointer converts to `const char*`) and are UB: the constructor calls `strlen(nullptr)`.
- libstdc++ checks and throws `std::logic_error` (GCC 11: `"basic_string::_M_construct null not valid"`; GCC 13/14: `"basic_string: construction from null is not valid"`); other libraries may simply crash.
- C++23 adds `basic_string(nullptr_t) = delete`: both lines become compile errors (verified with GCC 13).
- A runtime `const char*` that happens to be null is still UB in C++23; guard at API boundaries.

edge_cases.title: Embedded null characters
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string("ab\0cd")` has size 2: the `const char*` constructor stops at the first null.
- `"ab\0cd"s` (C++14 literal) or `std::string(ptr, 5)` keeps all 5 characters.
- `strlen(s.c_str())` and every C API that takes `const char*` see only the part before the first `'\0'`; binary data belongs in `std::string` only if you never hand it to C string functions.

edge_cases.title: Silent char conversions
edge_cases.explanation:
- `s = 65;` compiles and makes `s == "A"` (`operator=(char)` takes the narrowed `int`).
- `s += 300;` compiles with a warning at best and appends `char(300)`.
- `std::string s{5, 'a'};` is two characters (`'\x05'`, `'a'`), not five `'a'`. Use parentheses for count + char.
- `std::string s = 'a';` does not compile, which surprises people after the line above compiled.

edge_cases.title: A pointer into a moved-from short string
edge_cases.explanation:
- `const char* p = a.data(); std::string b = std::move(a);`
- Long string (libstdc++): the heap block is stolen, so `p == b.data()` in practice; still not guaranteed.
- Short string: the characters are copied into `b`'s local buffer; `p` still points into `a`, which is now empty (`p[0] == '\0'` in libstdc++).
- The moved-from state itself (valid but unspecified) is covered in Memory & Ownership, topic 03.

interview_qa.question: What is the small string optimization, and is it guaranteed by the standard?
interview_qa.answer: SSO stores short strings inside the `std::string` object itself instead of allocating a heap block. The standard permits it but does not require it, and the inline capacity is implementation-defined.
interview_qa.explanation:
- libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64: `sizeof(std::string) == 32`, up to 15 characters inline.
- libc++: typically 24 bytes, up to 22 characters inline. MSVC: typically 32 bytes, 15 characters (64-bit release builds).
- Benefits: no allocation, no free, characters on the same cache line as the size.
- Costs: the object is larger than three pointers' worth of "just a handle" in some layouts, and moving a short string copies its characters.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Strings up to 15 characters never allocate in C++." That is libstdc++ and MSVC, not C++.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a stale pointer into an SSO buffer points into the live string object, so ASan cannot detect its misuse.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: SSO is universal in practice and unspecified in the standard; quote numbers with the library name.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
SSO stores short strings inside the `std::string` object itself instead of allocating a heap block. The standard permits it but does not require it, and the inline capacity is implementation-defined.

**Explanation:**
- libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64: `sizeof(std::string) == 32`, up to 15 characters inline.
- libc++: typically 24 bytes, up to 22 characters inline. MSVC: typically 32 bytes, 15 characters (64-bit release builds).
- Benefits: no allocation, no free, characters on the same cache line as the size.
- Costs: the object is larger than three pointers' worth of "just a handle" in some layouts, and moving a short string copies its characters.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Strings up to 15 characters never allocate in C++." That is libstdc++ and MSVC, not C++.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a stale pointer into an SSO buffer points into the live string object, so ASan cannot detect its misuse.

**Key takeaway:** SSO is universal in practice and unspecified in the standard; quote numbers with the library name.

interview_qa.question: Where does a `std::string` declared as a local variable keep its characters?
interview_qa.answer: The object is on the stack; the characters are on the stack only if they fit in the SSO buffer. Longer strings keep their characters in a heap block the object owns.

interview_qa.question: Does `std::string b = a;` share the buffer with `a` until one of them is modified?

C++20: `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `constexpr` strings (usable inside constant evaluation, but not surviving into runtime), `<=>`, `reserve` no longer shrinks, and `std::format`. C++23: `contains`, `resize_and_overwrite`, `substr() &&`, deleted `nullptr_t` constructor.

**Explanation:**
- `constexpr std::string` (C++20): a string can be built and destroyed inside a `constexpr` function; a `constexpr std::string` variable holding a heap allocation is not allowed (transient allocation only).
- `std::format` library support arrived in GCC 13; GCC 11 and 12 have no `<format>`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`contains` is C++20." It is C++23 (GCC 11 rejects it with `-std=c++20` and accepts it with `-std=c++2b`).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: C++26 adds `std::string + std::string_view` concatenation.

**Key takeaway:** Version-tag the members: `starts_with` C++20, `contains` C++23.

interview_qa.question: Why is the move constructor of `std::string` `noexcept`, and why does that matter?
interview_qa.answer: Moving a string never allocates (steal the heap block or copy at most the inline characters), so it cannot fail and is declared `noexcept`. That lets `std::vector<std::string>` move elements on reallocation instead of copying them.
interview_qa.explanation:
- A vector uses `std::move_if_noexcept` during growth to keep the strong exception guarantee (details: Memory & Ownership, topic 02).
- Move assignment is `noexcept` when the allocator propagates or always compares equal (true for `std::allocator`).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Move is always noexcept for standard types." Not true for every type (for example `std::deque<int>` in libstdc++: `is_nothrow_move_constructible_v` is `false`, its move constructor allocates).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a class that contains a `std::string` and declares its own move constructor without `noexcept` loses this benefit.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `noexcept` string moves make vector growth cheap; keep it when wrapping strings in your own types.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
UB. On libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 it prints:
[d]
ASan reports nothing.
```

**Explanation:**
- `reserve` is a non-const member that is not exempt, so `p` is invalidated; printing it is UB.
- Why `d`: "Hello" was inline (SSO). `p` points into the string object's 16-byte local buffer. After `reserve(100)` the characters move to the heap and libstdc++ reuses those 16 bytes (a union) for the capacity field. 100 is `0x64`, ASCII `'d'`, followed by zero bytes.
- ASan is silent because `p` points into a live object: nothing was freed. With a 40-character string the old heap block is freed and ASan reports `heap-use-after-free`.
- **Key Concept:** Stale pointers into an SSO buffer are invisible to sanitizers; follow the rule, not the tool.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string s = "Hello";
    s.reserve(100);
    const char* p = s.c_str();          // acquire after the last mutation
    std::cout << '[' << p << "]\n";     // [Hello]
}
```

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
3 2 B
```

**Explanation:**
- `a(3, 'x')`: count + char constructor: `"xxx"`.
- `b{3, 'x'}`: braces prefer `initializer_list<char>`: two characters, `'\x03'` and `'x'`.
- `c = 66;`: `operator=(char)` accepts the `int` (implicit conversion), so `c == "B"`.
- `std::string d = 'x';` on the other hand does not compile: there is no constructor from a single `char`.
- **Key Concept:** Braces pick `initializer_list` constructors; `int` silently converts to `char` in string assignment.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
2 5 2
```

**Explanation:**
- The `const char*` constructor determines the length with `strlen`, so it stops at the embedded null: size 2.
- The `s` literal operator (C++14) receives the array length, so all 5 characters are kept.
- `strlen` (and any C API) sees only the part before the first `'\0'`, even though `b.size()` is 5.
- **Key Concept:** `std::string` tracks its size; C APIs track a terminator. Embedded nulls break the second.

-1 [no colon here]
Not UB, but a logic bug that silently returns the whole string.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `find` returns `npos` (`size_t(-1)`); storing it in `int` gives `-1` (GCC warns with `-Wconversion`, not with `-Wall -Wextra`).

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
xyz abc x
```
Using `it` after the swap is UB by the standard; the line shows libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 behaviour.

**Explanation:**
- For `std::string`, `swap` is listed as invalidating (unlike `std::vector::swap`, where iterators stay valid and follow the elements).
- In libstdc++ both strings are inline (SSO), so swapping copies the characters between the two objects' local buffers. `it` still points into `a`'s buffer, which now holds `"xyz"`.
- With heap strings the buffers would be exchanged by pointer, and `it` would follow `"abc"` into `b`: a different result from the same code.
- **Key Concept:** Do not keep string iterators across `swap`; the vector guarantee does not carry over.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
0 1 0 0
```
(libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64; only "moved-from strings are valid" is guaranteed.)

**Explanation:**
- `"tiny"` lives in `shortA`'s local buffer. A move cannot steal it; the characters are copied into `shortB`'s own local buffer, so `p1 != shortB.data()`.
- The 30-character string lives on the heap; the move steals the block, so `p2 == longB.data()` in practice.
- Both sources are left empty by libstdc++; the standard only says "valid but unspecified".
- Using `p1` or `p2` afterwards is formally invalid in both cases.
- **Key Concept:** Moving a short string is a copy of its characters; pointers never follow by contract.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
[] [bc] out_of_range
```

**Explanation:**
- `substr(pos)` with `pos == size()` is allowed and returns an empty string.
- The count is clamped to the remaining characters: `substr(1, 100)` is `"bc"`.
- `pos > size()` throws `std::out_of_range`.
- `operator[]` has no such check; `at()` and `substr` do.
- **Key Concept:** `substr` checks `pos`, clamps `n`, and always returns a new string.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
0 3 15 0 15 0
```
No UB. The capacity value 15 is libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64.

**Explanation:**
- `s[s.size()]` is a valid read of the terminator since C++11 (it returns a reference to `'\0'`; writing anything else there is UB).
- `clear()` sets the size to 0 and keeps the capacity.
- After `clear()`, `data()` points at a valid empty, null-terminated string.
- **Key Concept:** `s[size()]` is `'\0'` by contract; `clear` empties without releasing memory.

quick_reference.content:
#### Does this operation invalidate pointers, references and iterators?
| Operation | Standard |
|---|---|
| `s[i]`, `at`, `front`, `back`, `data`, `c_str`, `begin`, `end`, `rbegin`, `rend` | No |
| `+=`, `append`, `push_back`, `insert`, `replace`, `erase` | Yes (even within capacity) |
| `clear`, `resize`, `assign`, `operator=` | Yes |
| `reserve`, `shrink_to_fit` | Yes |
| `swap`, `operator>>`, `getline` | Yes |
| Move from the string | Yes (SSO: pointers stay in the source object) |

#### Implementation facts (not guaranteed by C++)
- libc++ and MSVC columns: typical values for 64-bit release builds, not verified here.

| Fact | libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 | libc++ (typical) | MSVC (typical) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sizeof(std::string)` | 32 | 24 | 32 |
| Inline capacity | 15 | 22 | 15 |
| Growth on `push_back` | 2x | 2x | 1.5x |
| `shrink_to_fit` of a short heap string | back to inline | back to inline | back to inline |

#### Version timeline
| Version | Change |
|---|---|
| C++11 | Contiguity, `data()` null-terminated, COW forbidden, `front`/`back`, `to_string`, `stoi` |
| C++14 | `"..."s` literal |
| C++17 | non-const `data()`, `string_view` interop, `to_chars`/`from_chars` |
| C++20 | `starts_with`/`ends_with`, `reserve` never shrinks, `<=>`, `std::format`, `constexpr std::string` |
| C++23 | `contains`, `resize_and_overwrite`, `basic_string(nullptr_t) = delete` |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is SSO guaranteed? | No; libstdc++ 15 chars, libc++ 22 chars |
| `sizeof(std::string)`? | Implementation-defined: 32 on GCC/MSVC, 24 on libc++ (64-bit) |
| Copy-on-write? | Forbidden since C++11 |
| Is `data()` null-terminated? | Yes, since C++11; same pointer as `c_str()` |
| Does `+=` within capacity keep `c_str()` valid? | Not guaranteed; reacquire |
| Which calls never invalidate? | `[]`, `at`, `front`, `back`, `data`, `begin`/`end` family |
| Does moving a short string steal a pointer? | No; characters are copied |
| `std::string(nullptr)`? | UB; compile error in C++23 |
| `s.find(x)` in an `if`? | Bug; compare with `npos` or use C++23 `contains` |
| `substr` cost? | New string; throws if `pos > size()` |
| Shrink a string? | `shrink_to_fit` (non-binding); `reserve` never shrinks since C++20 |
| Fastest int to string? | `std::to_chars` into a buffer |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::string_view` (C++17) and `std::span<T>` (C++20) are **non-owning views**: a pointer plus a length into memory that someone else owns.
- `string_view` = `{const char* data; size_t size;}`. `span<T>` = `{T* data; size_t size;}` (the size is dropped for a fixed extent).
- A view never allocates, never frees and never extends the lifetime of anything. It is exactly as valid as the memory it points at.
- Think of a view as a **borrow with no borrow checker**: the compiler accepts a view of a temporary, of a local that is about to die, or of a string that is about to reallocate.
- Rules of thumb:
  - Views are great **parameters** (the caller's object outlives the call).
  - Views are dangerous **return values, members, container keys and captured lambda state** (the owner may die first).
- Copying a view is copying two words: pass it **by value**, not by `const&`.

subsections.title: 2. string_view construction and operations
subsections.content:
| Source | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `"literal"` (`const char*`) | O(n) `strlen` (often constant-folded) | Stops at the first `'\0'` |
| `"literal"sv` (`using namespace std::literals`) | O(1) | Length from the literal; keeps embedded nulls |
| `std::string` | O(1) | Implicit, via `std::string::operator string_view()` |
| `(ptr, len)` | O(1) | Any bytes; no terminator required |
| `nullptr` | UB before C++23, deleted in C++23 | Same trap as `std::string` |
| Range of `char` (C++23) | O(1) | `explicit` constructor |

- Converting back: `std::string(sv)` is **explicit** and allocates (if longer than the SSO capacity). There is no implicit `string_view` to `string` conversion.
- No `operator+` for `std::string + std::string_view` until C++26; use `s.append(sv)` or `std::string(a) += b`.
- O(1) view manipulation (the underlying characters are untouched):
  - `remove_prefix(n)`: `data += n; size -= n;`
  - `remove_suffix(n)`: `size -= n;`
  - `substr(pos, n)`: a new view; throws `out_of_range` if `pos > size()`.
- Read-only access: `operator[]` returns `const char&`; `sv[0] = 'x'` does not compile. The owner can still change the characters under the view.
- Searching: `find`, `rfind`, `find_first_of` ... (return `npos`), C++20 `starts_with`/`ends_with`, C++23 `contains`.
- Comparison compares length and content: `"abc"sv == "abc"` is true; `<=>` is lexicographic.
- `std::hash<std::string_view>` gives the same value as `std::hash<std::string>` for the same characters (standard requirement), which enables heterogeneous lookup.
- `sizeof(std::string_view) == 16` on 64-bit platforms (two words).

subsections.title: 3. Not null-terminated
subsections.content:
- A view of a whole literal or a whole `std::string` happens to be followed by `'\0'`, but a view made by `substr`, `remove_suffix` or `(ptr, len)` usually is not.
- Passing `sv.data()` to `printf("%s")`, `strlen`, `fopen`, `strtol` or any C API reads past the view until it finds a null byte somewhere.
- Safe options:
  - `printf("%.*s", int(sv.size()), sv.data())` for formatted output.
  - `std::string(sv).c_str()` when an API needs a terminator (one allocation for long strings).
  - Keep `const std::string&` parameters for functions that forward to C APIs.
- `std::cout << sv` is fine: the stream inserter uses the size.

subsections.title: 4. Lifetime: views that dangle immediately
subsections.content:
| Code | Safe? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `string_view f() { return "name"; }` | ✅ | String literals have static storage duration |
| `string_view f() { std::string s = "x"; return s; }` | ❌ | `s` is destroyed when `f` returns |
| `string_view f() { return std::string("x"); }` | ❌ | The temporary is destroyed at the end of the `return` statement, inside `f` |
| `string_view sv = std::string("hello");` | ❌ | Temporary dies at the end of the full expression |
| `string_view sv = s.substr(0, 3);` | ❌ | `std::string::substr` returns a new temporary string |
| `string_view sv = std::string_view(s).substr(0, 3);` | ✅ (while `s` lives) | View of `s` itself |
| `string_view sv = s + "x";` | ❌ | `operator+` returns a temporary |
| `string_view sv = flag ? s : "default";` | ❌ | The conditional's type is `std::string`: a temporary copy |
| `string_view f() { static std::string s = "x"; return s; }` | ✅ until `s` changes | Static object lives to program end |
| `void g(string_view); g(std::string("x"));` | ✅ | The temporary lives until the end of the full expression that contains the call |

- No lifetime extension for views: lifetime extension applies only when a temporary is bound **directly to a reference**. A `string_view` is an object, not a reference, so binding it to a temporary extends nothing.
- GCC 13 and 14 with `-Wall -Wextra` do not warn for `return std::string(...)` converted to a view. Clang 14 warns by default for returning a view of a local or a temporary (`-Wreturn-stack-address`) and for `string_view sv = std::string("x");`, `s.substr(...)` and the conditional case (`-Wdangling-gsl`); `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` extends this to your own functions. These catch some cases only: rely on review and ASan, not on warnings.

subsections.title: 5. Lifetime: views into a string that changes
subsections.content:
- A `string_view` into a `std::string` is a pointer into its buffer, so the string invalidation rules apply (topic 01): every non-const member except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `end` (and reverse variants) formally invalidates the view, **with or without reallocation**.
- The view never learns about the change:
  - Its **size stays fixed**: after `s += "FG"` a view of `"XBCDE"` still has size 5.
  - After `s.clear()` the view still has the old size, and libstdc++ has written `'\0'` at position 0: printing it outputs a null byte followed by the stale characters.
  - After reallocation it points into freed memory (ASan: `heap-use-after-free`).
- Writes through `s[i]` are visible through the view (same memory, exempt operation): views are not snapshots.

subsections.title: 6. Choosing a parameter type for text
subsections.content:
| Parameter | Accepts without allocation | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `std::string_view` (by value) | literals, `std::string`, `char` buffers, other views | You only read, synchronously, and do not need a terminator |
| `const std::string&` | only `std::string` (a literal creates a temporary string) | You need `c_str()` or call an API that takes `const std::string&` |
| `std::string` (by value) | moves from rvalues | You **store** the text (sink): `member_ = std::move(param);` |
| `const char*` | literals and C strings | C interop; size unknown, O(n) to find |

- A `string_view` parameter does not protect against the function **storing** the view; storing requires an owning copy.
- Heterogeneous lookup: `std::map<std::string, V, std::less<>>::find(sv)` (C++14) and unordered containers with a transparent hash (C++20) look up a `string_view` without building a temporary `std::string` (details: topics 08 and 09).

subsections.title: 7. Views stored in objects and containers
subsections.content:
- `std::map<std::string_view, int>` built from temporary strings stores dangling keys: lookups later compare against freed memory.
- A struct member `std::string_view name;` is fine only when something with a longer lifetime owns the characters (for example a `std::string` buffer kept next to the index, or literals).
- A lambda capturing a view by value captures the pointer, not the characters; if the lambda runs later (callback, thread, coroutine), the owner may be gone.
- Pattern for "index over a buffer": keep one owning `std::string` (or a `std::vector<char>`) and store views into it **only after** it stops growing.

subsections.title: 8. std::span (C++20)
subsections.content:
- A view over **any contiguous sequence** of `T`: built-in arrays, `std::array`, `std::vector`, `std::string` (as `span<const char>`), `(ptr, n)`, `(first, last)`.
- `std::span<T>` allows writing the elements; `std::span<const T>` is the read-only parameter type.
- Extent:
  - Dynamic (`std::span<int>`): pointer + size, 16 bytes on 64-bit.
  - Static (`std::span<int, 4>`): size is part of the type, only a pointer is stored (8 bytes); constructing from a dynamic range of the wrong size is UB (the constructor is `explicit`).
- Operations: `size()`, `size_bytes()`, `empty()`, `data()`, `front()`, `back()`, `first(n)`, `last(n)`, `subspan(off, n)`, iterators, `std::as_bytes` / `std::as_writable_bytes`.
- `operator[]` does **not** bounds-check; `first`, `last`, `subspan` have preconditions instead of exceptions. C++26 adds `at()`.
- A span over a `std::vector` follows the vector's rules: any reallocation (growth past capacity) leaves the span dangling, and the span's size never changes when elements are added or removed.
- No `span<bool>` over `std::vector<bool>` (not contiguous `bool` objects, see topic 05).
- `std::span` replaces the C pair `(T* p, size_t n)`, and an interface taking `span<const T>` accepts every contiguous container without templates.

subsections.title: 9. Borrowed ranges and std::ranges::dangling
subsections.content:
- A **borrowed range** is a range whose iterators remain valid after the range object itself is destroyed: `string_view`, `span`, lvalue references to containers.
- Ranges algorithms called with an **rvalue non-borrowed range** (for example a temporary `std::vector`) return `std::ranges::dangling` instead of an iterator. Dereferencing it is a compile error, so the bug is caught at compile time.
- `std::ranges::find(std::string_view("abc"), 'b')` returns a usable iterator: the view is borrowed, the characters live in static storage.
- Being borrowed only says the iterators do not depend on the view object; they still depend on the underlying owner.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "A `string_view` keeps the string alive." ✅ It owns nothing and extends nothing.
- ❌ "Returning a temporary string as a view is fine because the temporary lives until the caller's statement ends." ✅ It dies at the end of the `return` statement inside the callee.
- ❌ "If the string does not reallocate, my view is still valid." ✅ Any non-exempt mutation formally invalidates it, and the view's size never updates.
- ❌ "`sv.data()` can be passed to C functions." ✅ Only if you know a terminator follows; views from `substr` usually have none.
- ❌ "`string_view` is always faster than `const std::string&`." ✅ For a function that needs `c_str()`, a view parameter forces a copy later.
- ❌ "`std::string::substr` and `std::string_view::substr` are the same." ✅ The first allocates a new string, the second is O(1).
- ❌ "`span` checks bounds." ✅ `operator[]` is unchecked (C++26 adds `at`).
- ❌ "A `span` over a vector sees new elements." ✅ Its pointer and size are fixed at construction.

- Rules of thumb:
  - Views are great **parameters** (the caller's object outlives the call).

edge_cases.title: Returning a temporary as a view
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string_view name() { return std::string(60, 'N'); }` compiles without warnings in GCC 13 (`-Wall -Wextra`).
- The temporary is destroyed at the end of the `return` statement, before control reaches the caller. The view returned already dangles.
- With a short string the buffer was on the callee's stack and the program may even print the right text; with a long one ASan reports `heap-use-after-free` in the caller.
- Fix: return `std::string` (by value, NRVO or move makes it cheap).

edge_cases.title: `s.substr()` versus `string_view(s).substr()`
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string_view sv = s.substr(0, 5);` views a temporary `std::string` returned by `substr`; it dangles at the semicolon.
- `std::string_view sv = std::string_view(s).substr(0, 5);` views `s` itself and costs nothing.
- Same trap with `s + "x"`, `std::to_string(n)`, `std::string(cstr)`, and any function returning `std::string` by value.

edge_cases.title: The conditional operator makes a temporary
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string_view label = flag ? s : "default";`
- The two operands are `std::string` (lvalue) and `const char[8]`: the common type is `std::string`, so the result is a **prvalue copy** of `s` (or a temporary string built from the literal). The view binds to that temporary and dangles.
- Fix: make both operands views: `flag ? std::string_view(s) : "default"sv`.

edge_cases.title: The view after `clear()`
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string s = "Hello"; std::string_view v = s; s.clear();`
- libstdc++ keeps the buffer and writes `'\0'` at `s[0]`. `v` still has size 5, so `std::cout << v` prints a null byte followed by `ello`.
- "The bytes are still there, so it works" is the wrong lesson: the first byte is already overwritten, and the access is invalid by the rules anyway.

edge_cases.title: Not null-terminated in practice
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string t = "abcdef"; auto v = std::string_view(t).substr(0, 3);`
- `strlen(v.data())` returns 6, not 3: it reads the owner's remaining characters until the terminator of `t`.
- With a view into a raw network buffer there may be no terminator at all: `strlen` runs off the buffer.

edge_cases.title: Embedded nulls depend on how the view was built
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string_view a = "ab\0cd";` has size 2 (constructed through `strlen`).
- `"ab\0cd"sv` and `std::string_view(p, 5)` have size 5.
- Comparisons and hashes include every character, so `a == "ab\0cd"sv` is false.

edge_cases.title: Container of views over temporaries
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::map<std::string_view, int> m; m[make_key(i)] = i;` where `make_key` returns `std::string`.
- Each key views a temporary that is destroyed after the statement; the tree now orders and compares freed memory.
- Use `std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>>` to own the keys and still look them up by `string_view`.

edge_cases.title: A span does not follow its vector
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3}; std::span<int> s = v; v.push_back(4);`
- If `push_back` reallocates, `s` points at freed memory. Even without reallocation, `s.size()` is still 3.
- A span is a snapshot of `(data(), size())`; rebuild it after any change to the vector's size.

interview_qa.question: What is `std::string_view`, and what problem does it solve?
interview_qa.answer: A C++17 non-owning, read-only view of a character sequence: a pointer plus a length. It lets one function accept literals, `std::string`, character buffers and slices of them without copying or allocating.

**Answer:**
A borrowed range is one whose iterators stay valid after the range object is destroyed (`string_view`, `span`, lvalue references). If you pass an rvalue non-borrowed range (a temporary `std::vector`) to a ranges algorithm that returns an iterator, it returns `std::ranges::dangling`, which cannot be dereferenced, so the bug becomes a compile error.

**Explanation:**
- `std::ranges::find(make_vector(), 3)` returns `ranges::dangling`; `*it` fails to compile.
- `std::ranges::find(std::string_view("abc"), 'b')` returns a real iterator.
- A type opts in with `std::ranges::enable_borrowed_range<T> = true`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Borrowed means the range owns its elements." It means the opposite: the iterators do not depend on the range object.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: borrowed protects against the temporary range object dying, not against the underlying owner dying.

**Key takeaway:** `ranges::dangling` is the compiler refusing to hand out an iterator into a temporary container.

interview_qa.question: Why can you not write `std::string r = s + sv;` and how do you concatenate?
interview_qa.answer: Until C++26 there is no `operator+` between `std::string` and `std::string_view`, and `string_view` does not convert implicitly to `std::string`, so it does not compile. Use `s + std::string(sv)`, or better `std::string r = s; r.append(sv);` (or `r += sv`).
interview_qa.explanation:
- `std::string::append`, `operator+=`, `insert`, `compare`, `find` all accept a `string_view` (C++17).
- The conversion `std::string(sv)` is explicit on purpose: it allocates, and implicit allocation was considered a trap.
- C++26 (P2591) adds the `operator+` overloads.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "string_view converts to string implicitly like `const char*`."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for several pieces, `reserve` once then `append` each view.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: View to string is explicit; append views instead of adding them.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.answer:
Dangling view: UB. GCC 13 with -Wall -Wextra gives no warning.
Clang 14 warns by default: returning address of local temporary object [-Wreturn-stack-address].
ASan: heap-use-after-free when the characters are printed in main.
(The size 60 is stored in the view itself, so b.size() still prints 60.)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The temporary `std::string` is created in the `return` statement and destroyed at the end of that statement, inside `banner()`. The view returned to `main` already points into freed memory.
- It is not "alive until the end of the caller's expression": that rule applies to temporaries created in the caller's own expression.
- `b.size()` is safe to read (it is the view's own member), but `b.substr(0, 10)` printed with `<<` reads the freed buffer.
- **Key Concept:** A function that creates text must return an owning `std::string`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
UB (clear() invalidates the view). On libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64:
5 0 ello
```

**Explanation:**
- `clear()` is a mutating member that is not exempt, so `v` is formally invalid.
- libstdc++ keeps the buffer and writes the terminator at `s[0]`; the other bytes are stale leftovers. `v` still has size 5, so it reads a null byte followed by `"ello"`.
- ASan reports nothing: the buffer still belongs to the live string.
- **Key Concept:** A view does not know its owner changed; "the bytes are still there" is not a guarantee, and here the first byte is already gone.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
XBCDE XBCDE 5 XBCDEFG
```
The first print is well defined. The second is formally UB (`+=` invalidates the view even without reallocation); the output shown is libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64.

**Explanation:**
- `s[0] = 'X'` goes through `operator[]`, which does not invalidate: the view sees the new character because it shares the memory.
- `s += "FG"` does not reallocate here (capacity 32), so libstdc++ leaves the buffer in place. The view keeps its original size 5 and never sees `"FG"`.
- By the standard rule for strings, the view is invalid after `+=` regardless.
- **Key Concept:** Views see in-place writes but never size changes; mutating calls invalidate them.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer:
Dangling view: UB. std::string::substr returns a temporary std::string, destroyed at the
end of the statement. ASan: heap-use-after-free (the 32-character substring is on the heap).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `record.substr(...)` is `std::string::substr`: a new owning string, not a view of `record`.
- The view binds to that temporary; the conversion compiles silently.
- Short substrings sit in the temporary's SSO buffer on the stack and may print correctly; long ones fail visibly.
- **Key Concept:** Convert to a view first, then slice: `std::string_view(record).substr(...)`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
2 5 5 0 1
```

**Explanation:**
- Constructing from `const char*` measures the length with `traits::length` (strlen): it stops at the embedded null.
- The `sv` literal and the `(ptr, len)` constructor keep all 5 characters.
- Comparison checks length and every character, including the null, so `a != b` and `b == c`.
- **Key Concept:** How a view was constructed decides its length; embedded nulls survive only with an explicit length.

practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error (GCC 11, C++20; also GCC 13 with -std=c++23):

practice_tasks.answer:
Dangling view: UB, even though use_default is false.
ASan: heap-use-after-free when label is printed.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The conditional operator needs one type for both branches: `const char[8]` and `std::string` give a `std::string` prvalue.
- So the expression produces a **temporary copy** of `configured`, the view binds to the copy, and the copy dies at the semicolon.
- The view never pointed at `configured`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
abc 3 6
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::cout << v` uses the view's size: `abc`.
- `strlen(v.data())` ignores the size and scans for `'\0'`, which only comes after `"def"` in `t`'s buffer: 6.
- Here the scan stays inside `t`, so it is not UB, just wrong. With a view into a raw buffer there may be no terminator and `strlen` runs off the end.
- **Key Concept:** Never hand `string_view::data()` to an API that expects a null-terminated string.

practice_tasks.answer:
Dangling keys: UB. Every key views a temporary string that died after its statement.
ASan: heap-use-after-free inside the map's key comparison (on the second insertion).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `index[make_key(i)]` converts the temporary `std::string` to a `string_view` key and stores only the pointer and length.
- The temporary is destroyed at the end of the statement; the next insertion compares the new key against freed memory.
- Short keys (inside the SSO capacity) would sit in dead stack temporaries and could even appear to work.
- **Key Concept:** A container must own its keys; use `std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>>` and look up with views.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
3 100 4
```
Well defined: `reserve(10)` happened before the span was made, so `push_back` does not reallocate.

**Explanation:**
- For `std::vector`, an insertion without reallocation keeps pointers to elements before the insertion point valid, so the span's pointer is still good.
- The span stored `(data(), 3)` at construction: its size stays 3 and element 4 is invisible through it.
- `v[0] = 100` writes the shared memory, so `s[0]` sees it.
- Without the `reserve`, the `push_back` would reallocate (capacity 3 to 6 on libstdc++) and `s[0]` would read freed memory.
- **Key Concept:** A span is a snapshot of pointer and size; it shares elements but not size changes.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
[/status] [GET /status HTTP/1.1] 4
```

**Explanation:**
- `remove_prefix(4)` moves the view's pointer forward by 4 and shrinks its size; `remove_suffix(9)` shrinks the size only.
- The underlying string is untouched: these functions modify the view object, never the characters.
- The view's data pointer is 4 characters into `s`'s buffer.
- **Key Concept:** Trimming and slicing a view is pointer arithmetic: O(1), no allocation, owner unchanged.

quick_reference.content:
#### Is this view safe?
| Pattern | Verdict |
|---|---|
| View of a string literal | Safe (static storage) |
| View parameter, used only during the call | Safe |
| Return a view of a local or a temporary string | Dangles |
| `string_view sv = s.substr(...)` / `s + x` / `to_string(n)` | Dangles at the semicolon |
| `flag ? s : "lit"` into a view | Dangles (conditional produces a `std::string`) |
| View of `s`, then `s += ...` / `clear()` / `reserve()` | Invalid (even without reallocation) |
| View of `s`, then `s[i] = c` | Valid, sees the change |
| `map<string_view, V>` with keys from temporaries | Dangling keys |
| `span` of a vector, then `push_back` | Dangles if it reallocated; size stale anyway |

#### string_view vs std::string
| | `std::string_view` | `std::string` |
|---|---|---|
| Owns characters | No | Yes |
| Null-terminated | Not guaranteed | Yes |
| `substr` | O(1) view | O(n) copy |
| Modify characters | No | Yes |
| Size (64-bit) | 16 bytes | 32 (libstdc++), 24 (libc++) |
| Pass by | Value | `const&` or value (sink) |

#### Versions
| Version | Feature |
|---|---|
| C++17 | `std::string_view`, `"..."sv` |
| C++20 | `std::span`, `starts_with`/`ends_with`, borrowed ranges, `ranges::dangling` |
| C++23 | `string_view::contains`, range constructor, `nullptr_t` constructor deleted |
| C++26 | `string + string_view` operator, `span::at` |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is a string_view? | Non-owning `(pointer, length)` into characters owned elsewhere |
| Return a view of a local string? | Dangling; return `std::string` |
| When does `return std::string("x")` as a view die? | End of the `return` statement in the callee |
| Is `sv.data()` null-terminated? | Not guaranteed |
| View after the owner appends without reallocating? | Formally invalid; size never updates |
| `string_view` or `const string&` parameter? | View for read-only; `const string&` if you need `c_str()`; by-value `string` if you store it |
| Can `string_view` modify text? | No; `span<char>` can |
| `span` vs `string_view`? | `span<T>` is the generic contiguous view; `string_view` adds string operations |
| Static vs dynamic extent? | `span<T, N>` stores only a pointer; `span<T>` stores pointer + size |
| `ranges::dangling`? | Returned for rvalue non-borrowed ranges; cannot be dereferenced |
