subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::optional<T>` (C++17) is "a `T` or nothing": storage for one `T` **inside** the optional object, plus a flag saying whether a `T` currently lives there (engaged) or not (disengaged).
- `std::expected<T, E>` (C++23) is "a `T` or the reason why not": the same idea, but the empty state carries an error value of type `E`.
- Both are **value types**: copying copies the contained object, comparing compares contents, destroying destroys the contained object. No sharing, no reference counting, no heap.
- Both make absence or failure part of the **type**: the caller cannot use the result without at least seeing that it might not be there.
- What they are not:
  - Not a pointer: `optional<T>` owns its `T`; there is no separate object being pointed at.
  - Not a replacement for every exception: they are for **expected** failures that the immediate caller handles (lookup miss, parse error, validation), not for "cannot continue at all".
- Three questions to answer for any optional-like type: where does the `T` live, what happens to it on reset/reassignment, and what does each accessor do when it is empty.

subsections.title: 2. Storage and layout
subsections.content:
- The `T` lives in-place: an aligned buffer of `sizeof(T)` bytes inside the optional, plus a `bool`. Constructing an optional never allocates (the `T` itself may allocate, like a `std::string` with a long text).
- `sizeof(optional<T>)` is at least `sizeof(T) + 1`, rounded up to `alignof(T)`. The standard does not fix exact sizes.

| Type | sizeof (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64) |
|---|---|
| `optional<char>` | 2 |
| `optional<bool>` | 2 |
| `optional<int>` | 8 (4 + flag, padded to align 4) |
| `optional<double>` | 16 |
| `optional<int*>` | 16 (no "use nullptr as empty" trick) |
| `optional<std::string>` | 40 (string is 32) |
| `expected<int, int>` | 8 |
| `expected<int, std::string>` | 40 |

- Triviality propagates: `optional<int>` is trivially copyable and trivially destructible; `optional<std::string>` is neither. This is why `optional<int>` can be passed in registers and memcpy'd while `optional<std::string>` cannot.
- Consequences:
  - An `optional<BigStruct>` is as big as `BigStruct`, even when empty. Arrays of `optional<Big>` waste space when mostly empty; a `std::unique_ptr<Big>` or a sparse map may be better.
  - The object stays on the stack (or wherever the optional is): an optional local has automatic storage like any other local.
  - Not the same as "pointer + null": there is no indirection, and an `optional<T*>` has two different empty states (disengaged, and engaged holding `nullptr`).

subsections.title: 3. Construction, assignment and lifetime of the contained T
subsections.content:
- Ways to create:
  - `std::optional<T> o;` or `= std::nullopt;` or `= {};`: empty, no `T` constructed.
  - `std::optional<T> o = value;`: engaged, `T` copy/move constructed.
  - `std::optional<T> o{std::in_place, args...};` and `std::make_optional<T>(args...)`: construct `T` directly from constructor arguments (no temporary `T`).
  - `o.emplace(args...)`: destroy the current `T` if any, then construct a new one in place; returns `T&`.
- How each operation affects the contained object:

| Operation | Was empty | Was engaged |
|---|---|---|
| `o = T(...)` | Move/copy **construct** a `T` | `T`'s move/copy **assignment** (same object stays alive) |
| `o.emplace(...)` | Construct | **Destroy**, then construct |
| `o.reset()`, `o = std::nullopt`, `o = {}` | Nothing | **Destroy** `T`; optional now empty |
| `o2 = o` (both optionals) | Depends on both states: construct, assign, destroy or nothing | |
| Destructor of `o` | Nothing | Destroy `T` |

- After `reset()` the optional object is still alive; only the `T` inside it is gone. A reference or pointer obtained earlier (`T& r = *o;`) now refers to a dead object, even though the bytes are still there. This lifetime point is covered in depth in Memory & Ownership, topic 01.
- `emplace` gives only the basic guarantee: if the new `T`'s constructor throws, the old `T` is already destroyed and the optional is left **empty**.
- Moving from an optional moves the contained `T`; the source stays **engaged** (holding a moved-from `T`). See Memory & Ownership, topic 03.

subsections.title: 4. Accessing the value
subsections.content:
| Accessor | When empty | Returns | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `has_value()`, `explicit operator bool` | `false` | `bool` | Branching |
| `*o`, `o->m` | **Undefined behaviour**, no check | `T&` (or `const T&`, `T&&`) | You just checked |
| `o.value()` | Throws `std::bad_optional_access` | `T&` | Empty is a bug you want reported |
| `o.value_or(def)` | Returns `def` converted to `T` | `T` **by value** | A sensible default exists |

- `operator*` performs no check in release builds. libstdc++ checks it only with `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` (or `_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`): "Assertion 'this->_M_is_engaged()' failed", then abort.
- `value_or(def)`:
  - Its argument is evaluated **before** the call, whether or not the optional is engaged (normal function-argument evaluation). `o.value_or(expensive())` always runs `expensive()`.
  - It returns a copy of the contained `T`, never a reference. For a large `T` this is a full copy.
  - `def` is converted to `T`: `optional<unsigned>{}.value_or(-1)` yields 4294967295 with no warning at `-Wall -Wextra`.
- `operator bool` is explicit: `if (o)` and `!o` work; `bool b = o;` does not compile; `int x = o + 1;` does not compile.

subsections.title: 5. Comparisons, hashing and the bool trap
subsections.content:
- Two optionals compare by: both empty equal; empty is **less than** any engaged value; otherwise compare the `T`s.
- Mixed comparisons are allowed: `o == 5`, `o < 5`, `o == std::nullopt`. An empty optional compares less than every value, including negative ones: `std::optional<int>{} < -100` is `true`.
- `std::hash<optional<T>>` exists when `std::hash<T>` exists, so optionals can be keys of unordered containers.
- `optional<bool>` and `optional<T*>` have two different "falsy" ideas:
  - `if (ob)` asks "is there a value?", not "is the value true?". An engaged `optional<bool>` holding `false` is truthy.
  - Write the intent explicitly: `if (ob.has_value() && *ob)` or `if (ob == true)` (the comparison with a value is false when empty).
- `optional<int> o = 0; if (o)` is `true`: the condition tests engagement, not the number.

subsections.title: 6. What optional cannot hold, and where it should not be used
subsections.content:
- Not allowed: references (`optional<int&>` fails with a static assertion in libstdc++), arrays, `std::nullopt_t`, `std::in_place_t`, and `void`.
- Workarounds for an "optional reference": `T*` (null means none), `std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<T>>`, or return an index/iterator. C++26 adds `std::optional<T&>` (P2988) with rebinding assignment; until then use a pointer.
- Parameters:
  - `void f(std::optional<std::string> s)` forces a construction (and possibly a copy and heap allocation) at every call site, even for a callee that only reads.
  - `void f(const std::optional<std::string>& s)` still forces callers that hold a plain `std::string` to build a temporary optional (copying the string).
  - Prefer overloads, a `const T*` (null for "not given"), or a default argument. Optional parameters are fine for small `T`.
- Members: `std::optional<T>` as a data member is a good way to express "not yet set", without a magic value and without the heap.
- As a return type it replaces three older idioms:

| Idiom | Problem | `optional` fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Sentinel (`-1`, `""`, `npos`) | Sentinel may be a valid value; easy to forget the check | Absence is a separate state |
| Out-parameter + `bool` | Clumsy, requires default-constructible `T` | Returns the value directly |
| Pointer to a heap object | Allocation, ownership question | Value in place, no ownership |
| Pointer into a container | Fine for "observe existing object" | Optional would copy it, so keep the pointer here |

subsections.title: 7. Monadic operations (C++23)
subsections.content:
- Chaining without nested `if`s. Available on `std::optional` (C++23, GCC 12+) and `std::expected`.

| Operation | Called when | Function returns | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `o.and_then(f)` | Engaged | `optional<U>` | `f(*o)` or empty |
| `o.transform(f)` | Engaged | Plain `U` | `optional<U>` wrapping `f(*o)`, or empty |
| `o.or_else(f)` | **Empty** | `optional<T>` | `o` itself if engaged, else `f()` |

- Rule of thumb: the step may fail → `and_then`; the step always succeeds → `transform`.
- Passing a function that returns an optional to `transform` yields a nested `optional<optional<U>>`: compiles, rarely what you want.
- `and_then` with a function that returns a plain value does not compile (the result must be a specialization of `optional`).
- `or_else` is the lazy alternative to `value_or`: the fallback is only computed when needed (and it stays an optional).

subsections.title: 8. std::expected<T, E> (C++23)
subsections.content:
- Holds either a `T` (success) or an `E` (error), in-place, plus a flag. No heap, no exception thrown on failure.
- Creating:
  - Success: `return value;` (implicit conversion to `T`).
  - Failure: `return std::unexpected(err);`. The wrapper is required so success and error are never confused.
  - Trap: if `T` and `E` are the same or convertible types, `return code;` is a **success** with value `code`. With `expected<int, int>`, `return 42;` means "value 42".
- Accessing:

| Accessor | On error state | On value state |
|---|---|---|
| `has_value()`, `operator bool` | `false` | `true` |
| `*e`, `e->` | UB | Value |
| `e.value()` | Throws `std::bad_expected_access<E>` (carries a copy of the error) | Value |
| `e.error()` | The error | **UB** |
| `e.value_or(def)` | `def` | Value |
| `e.error_or(def)` (C++23) | The error | `def` |

- `std::expected<void, E>`: success carries nothing; useful for operations like "save", "send", "validate".
- Monadic: `and_then` (next step may fail, must return `expected<U, E>` with the **same** `E`), `transform` (map the value), `or_else` (recover from an error), `transform_error` (convert the error type, e.g. from a low-level code to a domain error).
- A default-constructed `expected<T, E>` holds a value-initialized `T` (success), unlike `optional`.
- Library support: GCC 12+ (libstdc++), Clang 16+ with libc++, MSVC 17.3+. Before C++23 the same idea is available as `tl::expected` or `boost::outcome`.

subsections.title: 9. Choosing an error mechanism
subsections.content:
| Mechanism | Best for | Cost on success | Cost on failure | Can be ignored silently? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exception | Rare, cannot-continue failures; constructors | ~Zero (table-based unwinding) | Expensive (microseconds: allocation, unwinding) | No (propagates) |
| `std::optional<T>` | "Not found" with no further reason | Flag check | Flag check | Possible but visible in the type |
| `std::expected<T, E>` | Expected failures with a reason; parsers, validation, I/O results | Flag check | Flag check, error value copy | Possible; mark functions `[[nodiscard]]` |
| Error code + out parameter | C APIs, very old code | Flag check | Flag check | Easily |
| Sentinel value | Legacy only | None | None | Very easily |

- Exceptions remain the right tool for constructors, operator overloads and deep call stacks where the failure is handled far away.
- Low-latency code paths often ban exceptions on the hot path and use `expected` or error codes: the failure path is predictable and allocation-free.
- `std::optional` loses the reason. If the caller needs to know *why* (bad input vs not found vs timeout), use `expected`.
- `expected`'s `E` should be cheap to copy: an enum or a small struct; `std::string` messages make the error path allocate.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`optional` heap-allocates the value." ✅ The `T` lives inside the optional object; there is no allocation of its own.
- ❌ "`optional<T>` is the same size as `T`." ✅ It needs a flag plus padding: `optional<int>` is 8 bytes and `optional<double>` 16 on GCC x86-64.
- ❌ "`*opt` on an empty optional throws." ✅ It is undefined behaviour; `value()` throws `bad_optional_access`.
- ❌ "`value_or` only computes the default when it is needed." ✅ The argument is always evaluated before the call.
- ❌ "`reset()` destroys the optional." ✅ It destroys the contained `T`; the optional object remains, empty.
- ❌ "Assigning a new value to an engaged optional destroys the old one first." ✅ It uses `T`'s assignment operator; only `emplace` destroys then constructs.
- ❌ "`if (opt_bool)` tests the boolean." ✅ It tests engagement.
- ❌ "`std::optional<T&>` is a cheap optional reference." ✅ It does not compile before C++26; use `T*`.
- ❌ "`expected` is just optional with a string." ✅ It is typed (`E` can be an enum or struct), success/error construction is explicit via `std::unexpected`, and it has `error()`, `transform_error`, `bad_expected_access<E>`.
- ❌ "Returning an `int` error code from an `expected<int, int>` function signals an error." ✅ It creates a success; you need `std::unexpected(code)`.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- `std::optional<T>` (C++17) is "a `T` or nothing": storage for one `T` **inside** the optional object, plus a flag saying whether a `T` currently lives there (engaged) or not (disengaged).
- `std::expected<T, E>` (C++23) is "a `T` or the reason why not": the same idea, but the empty state carries an error value of type `E`.
- Both are **value types**: copying copies the contained object, comparing compares contents, destroying destroys the contained object. No sharing, no reference counting, no heap.
- Both make absence or failure part of the **type**: the caller cannot use the result without at least seeing that it might not be there.
- What they are not:
  - Not a pointer: `optional<T>` owns its `T`; there is no separate object being pointed at.
  - Not a replacement for every exception: they are for **expected** failures that the immediate caller handles (lookup miss, parse error, validation), not for "cannot continue at all".
- Three questions to answer for any optional-like type: where does the `T` live, what happens to it on reset/reassignment, and what does each accessor do when it is empty.

#### 2. Storage and layout
- The `T` lives in-place: an aligned buffer of `sizeof(T)` bytes inside the optional, plus a `bool`. Constructing an optional never allocates (the `T` itself may allocate, like a `std::string` with a long text).
- `sizeof(optional<T>)` is at least `sizeof(T) + 1`, rounded up to `alignof(T)`. The standard does not fix exact sizes.

| Type | sizeof (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64) |
|---|---|
| `optional<char>` | 2 |
| `optional<bool>` | 2 |
| `optional<int>` | 8 (4 + flag, padded to align 4) |
| `optional<double>` | 16 |
| `optional<int*>` | 16 (no "use nullptr as empty" trick) |
| `optional<std::string>` | 40 (string is 32) |
| `expected<int, int>` | 8 |
| `expected<int, std::string>` | 40 |

- Triviality propagates: `optional<int>` is trivially copyable and trivially destructible; `optional<std::string>` is neither. This is why `optional<int>` can be passed in registers and memcpy'd while `optional<std::string>` cannot.
- Consequences:
  - An `optional<BigStruct>` is as big as `BigStruct`, even when empty. Arrays of `optional<Big>` waste space when mostly empty; a `std::unique_ptr<Big>` or a sparse map may be better.
  - The object stays on the stack (or wherever the optional is): an optional local has automatic storage like any other local.
  - Not the same as "pointer + null": there is no indirection, and an `optional<T*>` has two different empty states (disengaged, and engaged holding `nullptr`).

#### 3. Construction, assignment and lifetime of the contained T
- Ways to create:
  - `std::optional<T> o;` or `= std::nullopt;` or `= {};`: empty, no `T` constructed.
  - `std::optional<T> o = value;`: engaged, `T` copy/move constructed.
  - `std::optional<T> o{std::in_place, args...};` and `std::make_optional<T>(args...)`: construct `T` directly from constructor arguments (no temporary `T`).
  - `o.emplace(args...)`: destroy the current `T` if any, then construct a new one in place; returns `T&`.
- How each operation affects the contained object:

| Operation | Was empty | Was engaged |
|---|---|---|
| `o = T(...)` | Move/copy **construct** a `T` | `T`'s move/copy **assignment** (same object stays alive) |
| `o.emplace(...)` | Construct | **Destroy**, then construct |
| `o.reset()`, `o = std::nullopt`, `o = {}` | Nothing | **Destroy** `T`; optional now empty |
| `o2 = o` (both optionals) | Depends on both states: construct, assign, destroy or nothing | |
| Destructor of `o` | Nothing | Destroy `T` |

- After `reset()` the optional object is still alive; only the `T` inside it is gone. A reference or pointer obtained earlier (`T& r = *o;`) now refers to a dead object, even though the bytes are still there. This lifetime point is covered in depth in Memory & Ownership, topic 01.
- `emplace` gives only the basic guarantee: if the new `T`'s constructor throws, the old `T` is already destroyed and the optional is left **empty**.
- Moving from an optional moves the contained `T`; the source stays **engaged** (holding a moved-from `T`). See Memory & Ownership, topic 03.

#### 4. Accessing the value

| Accessor | When empty | Returns | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `has_value()`, `explicit operator bool` | `false` | `bool` | Branching |
| `*o`, `o->m` | **Undefined behaviour**, no check | `T&` (or `const T&`, `T&&`) | You just checked |
| `o.value()` | Throws `std::bad_optional_access` | `T&` | Empty is a bug you want reported |
| `o.value_or(def)` | Returns `def` converted to `T` | `T` **by value** | A sensible default exists |

- `operator*` performs no check in release builds. libstdc++ checks it only with `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` (or `_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`): "Assertion 'this->_M_is_engaged()' failed", then abort.
- `value_or(def)`:
  - Its argument is evaluated **before** the call, whether or not the optional is engaged (normal function-argument evaluation). `o.value_or(expensive())` always runs `expensive()`.
  - It returns a copy of the contained `T`, never a reference. For a large `T` this is a full copy.
  - `def` is converted to `T`: `optional<unsigned>{}.value_or(-1)` yields 4294967295 with no warning at `-Wall -Wextra`.
- `operator bool` is explicit: `if (o)` and `!o` work; `bool b = o;` does not compile; `int x = o + 1;` does not compile.

- Mixed comparisons are allowed: `o == 5`, `o < 5`, `o == std::nullopt`. An empty optional compares less than every value, including negative ones: `std::optional<int>{} < -100` is `true`.
- `std::hash<optional<T>>` exists when `std::hash<T>` exists, so optionals can be keys of unordered containers.
- `optional<bool>` and `optional<T*>` have two different "falsy" ideas:
  - `if (ob)` asks "is there a value?", not "is the value true?". An engaged `optional<bool>` holding `false` is truthy.
  - Write the intent explicitly: `if (ob.has_value() && *ob)` or `if (ob == true)` (the comparison with a value is false when empty).
- `optional<int> o = 0; if (o)` is `true`: the condition tests engagement, not the number.

- Parameters:

  - `void f(const std::optional<std::string>& s)` still forces callers that hold a plain `std::string` to build a temporary optional (copying the string).

- Members: `std::optional<T>` as a data member is a good way to express "not yet set", without a magic value and without the heap.
- As a return type it replaces three older idioms:

| Idiom | Problem | `optional` fixes |
|---|---|---|

edge_cases.title: optional<bool> and optional<pointer> are truthy when they hold false or null
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::optional<bool> ob = false; if (ob)` takes the branch: the condition means "has a value".
- The same applies to `std::optional<int*>` holding `nullptr` and `std::optional<int>` holding `0`.
- Typical bug: a config flag `optional<bool> enable_feature` where "explicitly disabled" is treated as "enabled".
- Fixes: `if (ob.value_or(false))`, `if (ob == true)`, or replace `optional<bool>` with an `enum class` that has three named states.
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <optional>

int main() {
    std::optional<bool> enable = false;      // explicitly disabled
    if (enable) std::cout << "branch taken\n";            // has a value
    if (enable.value_or(false)) std::cout << "enabled\n"; // not printed
    std::cout << (enable == true) << '\n';                // 0
}
```
- Output: `branch taken` then `0`.

edge_cases.title: value_or is eager and returns a copy
edge_cases.explanation:
- `cache.value_or(load_from_disk())` calls `load_from_disk()` every time, even on a cache hit. Arguments are evaluated before the function runs.
- Lazy alternatives: `o ? *o : load_from_disk()`, or C++23 `o.or_else(load)` (returns an optional).
- `value_or` returns `T` by value. `const std::string& s = big.value_or("");` binds a reference to a temporary copy (lifetime-extended, so safe, but it is a full copy of the string). For read-only access to an engaged optional use `*o`.
- The default is converted to `T`: `std::optional<unsigned>{}.value_or(-1)` is 4294967295 with no warning, even with `-Wconversion -Wsign-conversion` (GCC 11): the conversion happens inside a system header.

edge_cases.title: operator* on an empty optional is silent undefined behaviour
edge_cases.explanation:
- `*o` and `o->` do not check. On GCC 11 at `-O0`, `*std::optional<int>{}` printed an arbitrary number that changed on each run: whatever bytes are in the storage.
- With `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` the same program aborts: "Assertion 'this->_M_is_engaged()' failed". Many teams enable this flag in debug and test builds.
- `value()` costs one branch and throws `std::bad_optional_access` ("bad optional access").
- Rule: use `*` only right after a check that the reader can see; use `value()` where emptiness would be a logic error you want reported.

edge_cases.title: Dangling reference from a temporary optional
edge_cases.explanation:
- `const std::string& name = *find_name(id);` where `find_name` returns `std::optional<std::string>` by value:
  - The returned optional is a temporary; `*` returns a reference into it, not the temporary itself, so **no** lifetime extension applies.
  - The temporary (and its string) is destroyed at the end of the full expression; `name` dangles.
- Same bug with `.value()`, `->` and `for (char c : *find_name(id))` (range-for over a member of a temporary: fixed only in C++23 by P2718, which GCC 11/13 do not implement).
- Fix: keep the optional: `auto name = find_name(id); if (name) use(*name);` or copy: `std::string n = *find_name(id);`.
- The reset/reassign variant of this bug (reference into an optional that is later reset) is covered in Memory & Ownership, topic 01.

edge_cases.title: expected<int, int>: a plain return is always a success
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::expected<int, int> parse(...) { if (bad) return -1; ... }` returns a **value** of -1, not an error.
- `std::unexpected(-1)` is required to create the error state. This is deliberate: success is the implicit path, error must be spelled out.
- The same trap appears with `expected<std::string, std::string>` or any `E` convertible to `T`. Prefer a distinct error type (`enum class ParseError`), which also makes `return ParseError::Empty;` fail to compile instead of compiling wrongly.

edge_cases.title: optional<T&> does not compile
edge_cases.explanation:
- libstdc++: "static assertion failed" (`!is_reference_v<_Tp>`), plus the constructors fail.
- People reach for it when a lookup should return "maybe a reference to an existing element".
- Options: return `T*` (null = not found), `std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<T>>` (verbose; `.get()` to access), or an iterator. C++26 standardizes `std::optional<T&>`.
- `std::optional<const T&>` as a parameter type to "avoid copies" is the same error.

edge_cases.title: Assignment to an engaged optional assigns, emplace re-constructs
edge_cases.explanation:
- `o = T(2);` when `o` already holds a `T` calls `T::operator=(T&&)`: the old object stays alive and takes the new value. No destructor runs for the old value at that point (only for the temporary).
- `o.emplace(3);` destroys the current `T`, then constructs a new one in place. If that constructor throws, the optional is left empty.
- Matters for types whose assignment differs from construction (assignment not allowed, `const` members, objects registered by address).
- A type with a `const` member cannot be assigned; `o = T(...)` on an engaged optional then fails to compile, while `emplace` works.

edge_cases.title: Empty compares less than everything
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::optional<int>{} < -1000000` is `true`; `std::optional<int>{} == 0` is `false`.
- Sorting a `std::vector<std::optional<int>>` puts all empties first.
- `std::max(opt_a, opt_b)` picks any engaged one over an empty one, which may hide missing data in a "max price" calculation.
- Mixed comparison `o > 0` is `false` for an empty `o`; `!(o > 0)` is `true`, so the negated check does not mean "o is 0 or less".

code_examples.title: A lookup that may fail: three ways to consume the result
code_examples.explanation:
- Return `std::optional<T>` by value for "found a copy or nothing"; the caller chooses how to handle absence.

- Output:

- `if (auto p = ...)` scopes the optional to the `if`; `*p` is safe because the condition checked it.
- Returning a `double` copy is fine; for a large element, returning `const T*` avoids the copy (see section 6).

code_examples.title: No allocation and the real size
code_examples.explanation:

interview_qa.answer: `value()` on an error throws `std::bad_expected_access<E>`, and the exception holds a copy of the error (`e.error()` on the exception). `error()` on a success is undefined behaviour, like `*e` on an error.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `bad_expected_access<E>` derives from `bad_expected_access<void>`, which derives from `std::exception`; libstdc++'s `what()` is "bad access to std::expected without expected value".
- Since `E` is copied into the exception, `E` must be copy constructible for `value()` to compile.
- Safe spellings: check `has_value()` first, or use `value_or` / `error_or` (C++23).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`error()` returns a default error when there is no error."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: catching `std::bad_expected_access<void>` catches all expected access errors regardless of `E`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `value()` throws on error; `error()` and `*` have no check.

interview_qa.question: When would you use `std::expected<void, E>`?
interview_qa.answer: For actions that either succeed with no result or fail with a reason: send a message, save a file, apply a config. Success is `return {};`, failure is `return std::unexpected(err);`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Replaces `bool` (no reason) and `int` error codes (no type safety, easy to ignore).
- Has `has_value()`, `error()`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `transform_error`; `value()` returns `void` but still throws on error.
- Combine with `[[nodiscard]]` on the function so callers cannot drop the result silently.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Use `std::optional<E>` where empty means success." Works, but reads backwards and loses the monadic API.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the error type should be cheap (enum, small struct); a `std::string` makes every failure allocate.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `expected<void, E>` is a typed, chainable "ok or error".

interview_qa.question: Is `std::optional<T>` trivially copyable? Why does it matter?
interview_qa.answer: When `T` is trivially copyable, `optional<T>` is too: trivial destructor since C++17, trivial copy/move by P0602 (a defect report against C++17). `optional<int>` is trivially copyable; `optional<std::string>` is not.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: optional is as trivial as its `T`; that keeps `optional<int>` free to pass around.

interview_qa.question: What is wrong with `const std::string& name = *find_name(42);`?
interview_qa.answer: `find_name` returns an `optional<std::string>` by value: a temporary. `*` returns a reference into it, which does not extend the temporary's lifetime, so the optional and its string are destroyed at the end of the statement and `name` dangles.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Lifetime extension applies only when a reference binds directly to the temporary (or a subobject via member access), not to the result of a function call like `operator*` or `value()`.
- ASan reports `stack-use-after-scope`: the temporary optional lived in a stack slot of the caller, and reading through `name` touches that dead slot. Without ASan the output is often plausible or partly garbage.
- Same bug: `for (char c : *find_name(42))` before C++23 P2718 (not implemented in GCC 11/13).
- Fix: `auto name = find_name(42);` then use `*name`, or `std::string name = *find_name(42);` (copy, or move out of the temporary).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Binding to `const&` always extends the lifetime."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the same rule applies to `.value()`, `->` and getters on any temporary that return references.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A reference to the inside of a temporary optional dies with the statement.

interview_qa.question: Sketch how you would implement a minimal `optional<T>`.
interview_qa.answer: Store a `bool` and an anonymous union with a single `T` member (or an aligned byte buffer). Construct with placement new (`std::construct_at` in C++20), destroy by calling the destructor explicitly, and make every special member check the flag.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
open 8080
close 8080
caught: bad port
has_value=0
```

**Explanation:**
- `emplace` first destroys the existing `Conn` (prints `close 8080`), then constructs the new one in place.
- The constructor throws, so there is no new object: the optional is left **empty**. The old connection is gone too.
- This is the basic exception guarantee: valid state, but not the original one.
- If the old value must survive a failed replacement, build the new object first (`Conn tmp(-1);`) and then assign or swap.
- **Key Concept:** `emplace` = destroy then construct; a throwing constructor leaves the optional empty.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: name dangles.
GCC 11, -O0: printed "34" followed by garbage bytes and the tail of the name.
With -fsanitize=address: ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `load_name(1)` returns a temporary optional. `.value()` returns a reference into that temporary, which is not lifetime-extended (only binding a reference directly to a temporary extends it).
- At the `;` the temporary optional is destroyed: its string's destructor frees the 34-character heap buffer, and `name` refers to a dead string object.
- ASan reports `stack-use-after-scope`: the temporary optional (and the `std::string` object inside it) lived in a stack slot of `main`, and `name.size()` reads that dead slot. The freed heap buffer is a second problem behind it.
- Without ASan the result varies: right text, garbage (as here) or a crash. Tests that happen to print the right text hide the bug.
- GCC 13+ warns at `-Wall`: "possibly dangling reference to a temporary [-Wdangling-reference]"; GCC 11 says nothing.
- **Key Concept:** Never bind a reference to `*f()` or `f().value()` when `f` returns an optional by value.

practice_tasks.full_content:

**Explanation:**
- `transform(f)` wraps whatever `f` returns: `half` returns `optional<int>`, so `r1` is `optional<optional<int>>`. The outer one is engaged (7 was present), the inner one is empty (7 is odd).

- Using `transform` with a fallible step produces nested optionals that later code checks only halfway.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
_ _ -1 0 3
3
```

**Explanation:**
- `operator<` for optionals orders every empty optional before every engaged one, then compares values.
- `std::max(empty, 3)` returns the engaged one; dereferencing it is safe here. If both were empty, `*` would be UB.
- In a "best bid" calculation, missing quotes sort first: harmless for `max`, wrong if code takes `front()` as "lowest real bid".
- **Key Concept:** Empty optionals sort first; decide explicitly where missing data belongs.

Undefined behaviour: dereferencing an empty optional.
GCC 11, -O0: printed an arbitrary number ("port -282947960", different each run), no error.
With -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS: aborts with
  Assertion 'this->_M_is_engaged()' failed.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error (GCC 11): use of deleted function
  'std::optional<Limits>& std::optional<Limits>::operator=(std::optional<Limits>&&)'
(Limits has a const member, so it is not assignable.)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Assigning a `T` to an optional may have to assign to an existing `T` (when already engaged), so every `optional` assignment operator requires `T` to be assignable. A `const` member deletes `Limits`'s assignment operators.
- The converting `operator=(U&&)` drops out, the compiler falls back to building a temporary `optional<Limits>` and move-assigning it, and that move assignment is deleted too: hence the message mentions `optional<Limits>&&`.
- The check is at compile time, so even the first assignment (to an empty optional) is rejected.
- `emplace` never assigns: it destroys and constructs, so it works with non-assignable types.
- **Key Concept:** `o = value` needs `T` to be constructible **and** assignable; `emplace` needs only constructible.

quick_reference.content:
#### optional accessors
| Expression | Empty | Engaged |
|---|---|---|
| `if (o)`, `o.has_value()` | false | true |
| `*o`, `o->m` | UB | `T&` |
| `o.value()` | throws `bad_optional_access` | `T&` |
| `o.value_or(d)` | `T(d)` (d always evaluated) | copy of value |
| `o.reset()` / `o = std::nullopt` / `o = {}` | no-op | destroys `T` |
| `o.emplace(args)` | constructs | destroys, then constructs |
| `o = t` | constructs | assigns |

#### expected accessors (C++23)
| Expression | Value state | Error state |
|---|---|---|
| `if (e)` | true | false |
| `*e` | value | UB |
| `e.value()` | value | throws `bad_expected_access<E>` |
| `e.error()` | UB | error |
| `e.value_or(d)` / `e.error_or(d)` | value / d | d / error |
| Create | `return v;` | `return std::unexpected(err);` |

#### Monadic operations (C++23)
| Op | Runs on | f returns | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `and_then(f)` | value | `optional<U>` / `expected<U, E>` | step may fail |
| `transform(f)` | value | `U` | step cannot fail |
| `or_else(f)` | empty / error | same optional / `expected<T, G>` | recovery, lazy fallback |
| `transform_error(f)` | error (expected only) | `G` | change error type |

#### Implementation facts (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64, not guaranteed by C++)
| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| `sizeof(optional<int>)` / `<double>` / `<string>` | 8 / 16 / 40 |
| `sizeof(expected<int,int>)` / `<int,string>` | 8 / 40 |
| `*empty` at `-O0` | Reads storage, no error |
| `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` | `*empty` aborts with an assertion |
| `std::optional` monadic ops | GCC 12+ |
| `std::expected` | GCC 12+ |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does optional allocate? | No; `T` is stored inside the optional |
| `*o` vs `o.value()` on empty? | UB vs throws `bad_optional_access` |
| Is `value_or(f())` lazy? | No; `f()` always runs |
| What does `reset()` destroy? | The contained `T`, not the optional |
| `optional<bool>` holding false in `if`? | True: tests engagement |
| `optional<T&>`? | Not allowed before C++26; use `T*` |
| Empty vs -5? | Empty is less than any value |
| optional vs expected? | optional: missing; expected: missing with a typed reason |
| How to return an error from expected? | `return std::unexpected(e);` |
| `expected<int,int>`, `return 42;`? | Success with value 42 |
| `and_then` vs `transform`? | Step returns optional/expected vs a plain value |
| When exceptions instead? | Rare, non-local failures; constructors; errors handled far away |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::variant<A, B, C>` (C++17) holds **exactly one** object whose type is one of a fixed, compile-time list. It is a type-safe tagged union: storage for the largest alternative plus an index saying which one is alive.
- `std::any` (C++17) holds **one object of any copyable type**, decided at run time. It is type erasure: the static type is gone, and you must ask for the exact type back with `any_cast`.
- Both are value types: copying copies the held object, destroying destroys it. Neither shares state.
- The key design question is **closed vs open set**:
  - Closed (all types known where the variant is declared): `std::variant`. The compiler checks that every type is handled.
  - Open (new types added later, by other modules): virtual functions, or `std::any` / `std::function` style type erasure.
- `std::optional<T>` (topic 03) behaves like a `variant<std::monostate, T>` with a friendlier interface.

subsections.title: 2. Storage and layout of variant
subsections.content:
- The active alternative lives **inside** the variant object (no heap allocation by the variant itself). Size is roughly `max(sizeof(Ts...))` plus a small index, rounded up to the strictest alignment.
- The standard specifies the behaviour, not the layout. libstdc++ implements it as a recursive union of the alternatives plus an index of the smallest unsigned type that fits (`unsigned char` for fewer than 255 alternatives). "Tagged union semantics" is the safe way to describe it.

| Type | sizeof (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64) |
|---|---|
| `variant<std::monostate, char>` | 2 |
| `variant<char, int>` | 8 |
| `variant<int, double>` | 16 |
| `variant<int, std::string>` | 40 (string is 32) |
| `std::any` | 16 (one pointer of storage + manager function pointer) |

- Triviality propagates: `variant<int, double>` is trivially copyable; `variant<int, std::string>` is not.
- An alternative's own heap use is unchanged: a `variant<int, std::string>` holding a long string still has the string's heap buffer.
- Not allowed as alternatives: references, arrays, `void`. At least one alternative is required (`variant<>` cannot be instantiated). Duplicate types are allowed but restrict the API (section 4).

subsections.title: 3. Construction and assignment
subsections.content:
- Default construction value-initializes the **first** alternative: `variant<int, std::string> v;` holds `int` 0. If the first alternative is not default-constructible, the variant's default constructor is deleted. Fix: put `std::monostate` first ("empty" state) or reorder.
- Converting constructor `variant<Ts...> v = x;` picks the alternative by overload resolution, as if there were one function `F(T_i)` per alternative, with two filters (P0608, C++20 as a DR; GCC 10+):
  - Narrowing conversions are excluded: `variant<int, double> v = 1L;` does not compile (long to int and long to double are both narrowing).
  - `bool` is only chosen for an argument that is already `bool`: `variant<bool, std::string> v = "hello";` holds the string. Before P0608, the pointer-to-bool conversion won and it held `true`.
  - Ambiguity is a compile error: `variant<std::string, std::string_view> v = "x";` (both are user-defined conversions).
- Explicit selection: `std::variant<A, B> v{std::in_place_type<B>, args...}` or `{std::in_place_index<1>, args...}`; `v.emplace<B>(args...)` / `v.emplace<1>(args...)`.
- What assignment does to the held object:

| Operation | Same alternative already active | Different alternative active |
|---|---|---|
| `v = x` (converting) | `T_j`'s assignment operator | Destroy old, construct new (via a temporary + move when the move is `noexcept` and the direct construction might throw) |
| `v.emplace<T>(args)` | Destroy, then construct | Destroy, then construct |
| `v1 = v2` (variant copy) | Assign alternative | Destroy old, construct copy |

- Any reference, pointer or `get_if` result obtained before an alternative change refers to a dead object afterwards (general lifetime rules: Memory & Ownership, topic 01).

subsections.title: 4. Querying and accessing the active alternative
subsections.content:
| API | Returns | On wrong alternative |
|---|---|---|
| `v.index()` | Zero-based index of the active alternative | `std::variant_npos` if valueless |
| `std::holds_alternative<T>(v)` | `bool` | `false` |
| `std::get<T>(v)` / `std::get<I>(v)` | Reference (`T&`, `const T&`, `T&&` by value category of `v`) | Throws `std::bad_variant_access` |
| `std::get_if<T>(&v)` / `std::get_if<I>(&v)` | Pointer to the alternative | `nullptr` |
| `std::visit(f, v...)` | `f(active alternative)` | Throws `bad_variant_access` only if valueless |

- `get_if` takes a **pointer** to the variant (`&v`), and returns a pointer: the idiom is `if (auto* p = std::get_if<int>(&v)) use(*p);`.
- With duplicate alternatives (`variant<int, int>`), `get<int>`, `get_if<int>` and `holds_alternative<int>` fail to compile ("T must occur exactly once in alternatives"); index-based access still works.
- Asking for a type that is not in the list at all (`get<float>` on `variant<int, double>`) is a compile error, not a runtime one.
- Type-level helpers: `std::variant_size_v<V>`, `std::variant_alternative_t<I, V>`.

subsections.title: 5. std::visit and the overloaded idiom
subsections.content:
- `std::visit(visitor, v)` calls the visitor with the active alternative. The visitor must be callable with **every** alternative: a missing case is a compile error, which is the main safety benefit over `switch (v.index())`.
- Three ways to write the visitor:
  - A generic lambda with `if constexpr (std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<decltype(x)>, int>)` chains (an `else static_assert` branch catches missing types: see topic 11 for the `static_assert(false)` rules).
  - A struct with one `operator()` per type.
  - The **overloaded** idiom: one lambda per type, merged into one overload set:
```cpp
template <class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; };
template <class... Ts> overloaded(Ts...) -> overloaded<Ts...>;   // needed in C++17 (and Clang < 17)
```
- In C++20 the deduction guide is optional (aggregate CTAD, P1816/P2082). Without it, C++17 compilers fail with "class template argument deduction failed".
- Compiler caveat: GCC 11 implements aggregate CTAD, but Clang only from version 17; Clang 14 in `-std=c++20` still fails ("no viable constructor or deduction guide"). Keep the guide in portable code.
- Return type: every call must return the same type, otherwise "std::visit requires the visitor to have the same return type for all alternatives of a variant". C++20 `std::visit<R>(f, v)` converts each result to `R`.
- Multiple variants: `std::visit(f, v1, v2)` calls `f(a, b)` for the active pair; the visitor must handle every combination (N x M overloads, or generic lambdas). Useful for state x event tables and double dispatch.
- Exhaustiveness has a hole: overload resolution still applies implicit conversions. A visitor with only `int` and `std::string` handlers compiles for `variant<int, double, std::string>`, and a `double` goes to the `int` handler (truncated). Generic `auto` handlers have the same effect for "everything else".

subsections.title: 6. How visit dispatches (and what it costs)
subsections.content:
- The index is a run-time value, so dispatch is a run-time branch: implementations build a table of function pointers (one per alternative, or per combination for multi-variant visit) indexed by `index()`, or a `switch` for small variants.
- Compared with virtual dispatch:

| Aspect | `std::variant` + `visit` | Virtual functions |
|---|---|---|
| Set of types | Closed, known at declaration | Open, extendable later |
| Storage | In-place, no heap needed | Usually heap (`unique_ptr<Base>`) for polymorphic containers |
| Dispatch | Branch/jump on the stored index | Load vptr, load function pointer, indirect call |
| Adding a type | Edit the variant; every visitor fails to compile until updated | Add a class; old code untouched |
| Adding an operation | Write a new visitor; no type changes | Add a virtual to the base; every class may need updating |
| Memory for a container | `vector<variant<...>>`: contiguous, cache-friendly | `vector<unique_ptr<Base>>`: pointer chase per element |
| Size per object | Largest alternative, even for small ones | Only what the object needs (+ vptr) |

- Do not claim visit is "resolved at compile time": it is a run-time selection without a vptr. The optimizer can inline the handlers (they are visible lambdas), and when the index is known (constant propagation) the branch can disappear.
- The main performance win is usually memory layout (no heap per object, contiguous containers), not the dispatch instruction itself.

subsections.title: 7. valueless_by_exception
subsections.content:
- A variant can end up holding **nothing** if an exception is thrown while switching alternatives: the old object has already been destroyed and the new one's construction throws.
- Then `v.valueless_by_exception()` is `true`, `v.index() == std::variant_npos`, `std::get` throws `bad_variant_access`, and `std::visit` throws `bad_variant_access` ("std::visit: variant is valueless" in libstdc++).
- When it can happen: converting assignment or `emplace` to a different alternative whose construction may throw. libstdc++ avoids it where possible: for converting assignment, if the new type is nothrow-move-constructible it first builds a temporary, then moves it in.
- Recovery: assign or `emplace` a new value; the variant is then normal again.
- Design rule: make alternatives nothrow-move-constructible and treat valueless as "the operation failed", not as a normal state. `std::monostate` is the deliberate empty state; valueless is the accidental one.

subsections.title: 8. std::any
subsections.content:
- Holds one object of any **copy-constructible** type. `std::any a = std::make_unique<int>(1);` does not compile (move-only types are rejected), because `any` itself is copyable.
- Access requires the **exact** type (after decay, no conversions, no base classes):

| Form | Result | On mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| `std::any_cast<T>(a)` | A copy of the value | Throws `std::bad_any_cast` |
| `std::any_cast<T&>(a)` | Reference to the held object | Throws `std::bad_any_cast` |
| `std::any_cast<T>(&a)` | `T*` | `nullptr` |
| `a.type()` | `typeid` of the held type (`typeid(void)` when empty) | |
| `a.has_value()`, `a.reset()`, `std::make_any<T>(args)`, `a.emplace<T>(args)` | | |

- Decay applies on storage: `std::any a = "hello";` stores a `const char*`, so `any_cast<std::string>(a)` throws. `any a = 42;` holds an `int`, so `any_cast<long>(a)` fails.
- Small-object storage is implementation-specific. libstdc++ (GCC, x86-64): stored inline only if the type fits in one pointer-sized slot, has compatible alignment and is nothrow-move-constructible. So `any(42)`, `any(3.14)` and `any(int*)` do not allocate, but `any(std::string("x"))` (32 bytes) and `any(std::array<char,16>)` allocate once. libc++ and MSVC typically use larger inline buffers (libc++: 3 pointers; MSVC: several pointers, `sizeof(std::any)` is typically 64 on x64); do not rely on either.
- Copying an `any` deep-copies the held object (through a type-erased "manager" function): it is never shared.
- Where it fits: heterogeneous property bags at API boundaries, plugin payloads, passing user data through a library that cannot know the type. In most application code, `variant` (closed set) or a virtual interface (open set with behaviour) is better: `any` gives no compile-time checking and every access is a run-time type comparison.
- `void*` vs `any`: `any` owns and destroys its object and checks the type on access; `void*` does neither.

subsections.title: 9. Choosing among optional, variant, any and inheritance
subsections.content:
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| A value or nothing | `std::optional<T>` |
| A value or an error | `std::expected<T, E>` (topic 03) |
| One of a fixed list of types, handled exhaustively | `std::variant<Ts...>` + `std::visit` |
| Message/event type in a protocol with a known set of messages | `std::variant` |
| Types added by other modules or plugins, common behaviour | Virtual base class (or a type-erased wrapper like `std::function`) |
| Arbitrary user payload passed through untouched | `std::any` |
| Thread sharing | None of these are thread-safe; reassigning while another thread reads is a data race (see Concurrency chapter) |

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`std::variant` allocates the alternative on the heap." ✅ It lives in-place in the variant; size is the largest alternative plus an index.
- ❌ "variant is just a C union." ✅ It tracks the active type, runs the right constructors and destructors, and checks access; a plain union does none of that.
- ❌ "`std::visit` is resolved at compile time." ✅ It branches on the run-time index (no vptr), and the handlers can be inlined.
- ❌ "If my visitor compiles, every type is handled correctly." ✅ Implicit conversions (double to int) and catch-all `auto` handlers can silently absorb alternatives.
- ❌ "`variant<bool, std::string> v = "x";` holds bool." ✅ Since P0608 (GCC 10+ and current libc++ and MSVC) it holds the string; older libraries chose bool.
- ❌ "A variant can never be empty." ✅ It can be valueless after a throwing alternative change; use `monostate` for an intentional empty state.
- ❌ "`get<T>` returns nullptr on the wrong type." ✅ `get` throws `bad_variant_access`; `get_if` returns nullptr.
- ❌ "`std::any` stores small strings inline." ✅ libstdc++ stores only pointer-sized, nothrow-movable types inline; a `std::string` always allocates there.
- ❌ "`any_cast` converts between compatible types." ✅ It requires the exact stored type: `"hi"` is stored as `const char*`.
- ❌ "variant is always faster than virtual functions." ✅ It wins on layout and allocation; dispatch cost is similar; a variant with one huge alternative wastes memory for all elements.

- ❌ "`any_cast` converts between compatible types." ✅ It requires the exact stored type: `"hi"` is stored as `const char*`.
- ❌ "variant is always faster than virtual functions." ✅ It wins on layout and allocation; dispatch cost is similar; a variant with one huge alternative wastes memory for all elements.

edge_cases.title: A string literal picks a surprising alternative
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::variant<bool, std::string> v = "hello";`
  - C++17 as published: `const char*` to `bool` is a standard conversion and beats the user-defined conversion to `std::string`, so it held `true`.
  - After P0608 (adopted for C++20; GCC 10+ and libc++ also apply it in C++17 mode; MSVC first enabled it only for `/std:c++20` and extended it to C++17 later): pointer-to-bool is excluded, so it holds the string (`index() == 1` on GCC 11 in both `-std=c++17` and `-std=c++20`).
- `std::variant<std::string, const char*> v = "x";` holds the `const char*` (exact match after decay), not the string.
- `std::variant<std::string, std::string_view> v = "x";` does not compile: two user-defined conversions, ambiguous.
- Rule: when the alternative matters, say it: `v = std::string("hello");` or `v.emplace<std::string>("hello");`.

edge_cases.title: Narrowing is excluded, so "obvious" conversions fail
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::variant<int, double> v = 1L;` is a compile error: both `long → int` and `long → double` are narrowing, so no alternative is viable ("conversion from 'long int' to non-scalar type ... requested").
- `std::variant<float, double> v = 1;` fails for the same reason (int to float/double is narrowing for a non-constant source inside the library check).
- `std::variant<long, double> v = 1;` holds `long` (int to long is not narrowing).
- `std::variant<int, long> v = 1u;` holds `long` on x86-64 Linux (`unsigned` → `int` narrows, `unsigned` → 64-bit `long` does not). Platform-dependent: with a 32-bit `long` it would not compile.

edge_cases.title: Duplicate alternatives disable type-based access
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::variant<int, int>` is legal (two distinct "slots" with the same type, e.g. "bid qty" vs "ask qty").
- `std::get<int>(v)`, `get_if<int>`, `holds_alternative<int>` and `v = 5` do not compile ("T must occur exactly once in alternatives" / ambiguous).
- Use indices: `std::get<0>(v)`, `v.emplace<1>(5)`, `std::in_place_index<1>`.
- Better design: wrap in distinct types (`struct BidQty { int v; }; struct AskQty { int v; };`) so the meaning is in the type.

edge_cases.title: The first alternative decides default construction
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::variant<Order, int> v;` needs `Order` to be default-constructible; otherwise "use of deleted function 'std::variant<...>::variant()'".
- Even when it compiles, the default state is "a default `Order`", which may be meaningless.
- `std::variant<std::monostate, Order, int>` gives an explicit "nothing yet" state; `std::holds_alternative<std::monostate>(v)` tests for it and visitors must handle it.

edge_cases.title: References into a variant die when the alternative changes
edge_cases.explanation:
- `int& r = std::get<int>(v); v = std::string("x");` destroys the `int` object; `r` now refers to storage occupied by a `std::string`. Reading it is UB, and writing through it corrupts the string.
- Same for pointers from `get_if` and references captured inside a visitor that are kept after the visit.
- Assigning a new value of the **same** alternative keeps the object alive (assignment), so references stay valid then. This asymmetry makes the bug intermittent.
- Shared between threads, a reassignment while another thread holds such a reference is a data race as well as a lifetime bug.

edge_cases.title: valueless_by_exception
edge_cases.explanation:
- If constructing the new alternative throws after the old one was destroyed, the variant holds nothing: `index() == variant_npos`.
- Every access then fails: `get` and `visit` throw `std::bad_variant_access`, `holds_alternative` is false for every type.
- Code that assumes "a variant always has a value" (e.g. a `switch (v.index())` without a default) silently does nothing or indexes out of range.
- Avoid by keeping alternatives nothrow-move-constructible (libstdc++ then builds the new value in a temporary first). Check `valueless_by_exception()` in recovery paths.

edge_cases.title: Visitors with different return types, and conversions that hide missing cases
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::visit([](auto& x) { return x; }, variant<int, std::string>{})` fails: "std::visit requires the visitor to have the same return type for all alternatives of a variant".
- Fix with an explicit return type on the lambda, or C++20 `std::visit<R>(...)`.
- Opposite problem: a visitor built with `overloaded{[](int){...}, [](const std::string&){...}}` compiles for `variant<int, double, std::string>`: the `double` alternative converts to `int`. Exhaustiveness is checked by overload resolution, not by exact type.
- Defence: add a generic guard handler. Exact non-template handlers still win for their own types, and the template catches everything else at compile time:
```cpp
[](const auto& x) { static_assert(sizeof(x) == 0, "unhandled alternative"); }
```
- With that guard the `double` case fails to compile with "static assertion failed: unhandled alternative" (GCC 11).

edge_cases.title: any_cast wants the exact decayed type
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::any a = "hello";` stores `const char*`. `any_cast<std::string>(a)` throws `bad_any_cast`; `any_cast<const char*>(a)` works.
- `std::any b = 42;` stores `int`; `any_cast<long>(b)` throws, `any_cast<unsigned>(b)` throws.
- `std::any c = derived_object;` stores `Derived`; `any_cast<Base&>(c)` throws: no base-class lookup.
- `any_cast<T>(a)` (by value) copies the whole object each time; use `any_cast<T&>` or the pointer form for large objects.

edge_cases.title: any rejects move-only types and may allocate
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::any a = std::make_unique<int>(5);` fails: "conversion from 'std::unique_ptr<int>' to non-scalar type 'std::any' requested". `any` must be copyable, so its content must be copy-constructible. Wrap in `std::shared_ptr` if needed.
- Allocation (libstdc++): inline only for pointer-sized, nothrow-movable types. A type with a throwing move, or anything larger than 8 bytes (including `std::string`), is heap-allocated on every construction and copy.
- On hot paths a variant (closed set) avoids both the allocation and the run-time type comparison.

interview_qa.question: What is `std::variant`, and where does it store the active value?
interview_qa.answer: A type-safe tagged union (C++17): it holds exactly one object whose type is one of a fixed list. The object lives inside the variant itself, in storage big enough for the largest alternative, next to an index recording which alternative is active. The variant never allocates.
interview_qa.explanation:

- Alternatives that allocate internally (a long `std::string`) still do; the variant adds no allocation of its own.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the standard specifies semantics, not layout; libstdc++ uses a recursive union plus the smallest unsigned index type that fits.

interview_qa.question: What does `std::visit` do, and what is the "overloaded" idiom?
interview_qa.answer: `std::visit(f, v)` calls `f` with the active alternative. The visitor must accept every alternative, so missing cases are compile errors. interview_qa.question: Is `std::visit` resolved at compile time? How does it compare to a virtual call?
interview_qa.answer: No. Which alternative is active is a run-time fact, so visit branches on the stored index (through a generated function-pointer table or a switch). - A variant with one large alternative makes every element large; heterogeneous sizes favour pointers.

interview_qa.question: When would you choose `std::variant` over an inheritance hierarchy, and vice versa?

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: this is the "expression problem"; the choice depends on which axis changes more.

interview_qa.question: What is `std::any`, and how is it different from `std::variant` and `void*`?
interview_qa.answer: `std::any` holds one object of any copy-constructible type, decided at run time; you get it back only with `std::any_cast` and the exact type. - ✅ What a strong answer adds: use it at boundaries (user data passed through a library, property bags); inside application logic prefer variant or virtual interfaces.

interview_qa.question: `std::any a = "hello";` Why does `std::any_cast<std::string>(a)` throw?
interview_qa.answer: Because `any` stores the decayed type of its argument: the array `const char[6]` decays to `const char*`. `any_cast` requires that exact type, with no conversions, so asking for `std::string` throws `std::bad_any_cast`.

interview_qa.question: Does `std::any` allocate? Is there a small-object optimization?
interview_qa.answer: It may. The standard encourages (but does not require) storing small, nothrow-movable objects inline. libstdc++ stores a type inline only if it fits in one pointer (8 bytes on x86-64), is suitably aligned and is nothrow-move-constructible; everything else is heap-allocated. So `any(42)` does not allocate, but `any(std::string("x"))` allocates once on GCC.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured with a counting `operator new` (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64): `any(int)` 0, `any(double)` 0, `any(std::string("x"))` 1, `any(std::array<char,16>)` 1.
- libc++ and MSVC use bigger inline buffers (several pointers), so the same code allocates differently per platform.
- The nothrow-move requirement exists so that moving an `any` can be `noexcept`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Small strings are stored inline thanks to SBO." The string object itself is 32 bytes, larger than libstdc++'s buffer.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: if allocation matters, use a variant (closed set) or a custom type-erased wrapper with a buffer size you choose.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: any's small-buffer rules are implementation-specific; on libstdc++ only pointer-sized types avoid the heap.

interview_qa.question: Why can't `std::any` hold a `std::unique_ptr`?
interview_qa.answer: `std::any` is copyable, and copying it must copy the contained object, so the contained type must be copy-constructible. `unique_ptr` is move-only; GCC rejects `std::any a = std::make_unique<int>(1);` ("conversion from 'std::unique_ptr<int>' to non-scalar type 'std::any' requested").

interview_qa.question: `std::variant<int, int>` is legal. Why, and how do you use it?
interview_qa.answer: Alternatives are identified by position, so two `int` alternatives are two different states that happen to share a type. Type-based access (`get<int>`, `holds_alternative<int>`, `v = 5`) does not compile; you must use indices: `get<0>`, `emplace<1>`, `std::in_place_index<1>`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- libstdc++ error for `get<int>`: "static assertion failed: T must occur exactly once in alternatives".
- `v = 5` fails ("no match for 'operator='"): the converting assignment is ambiguous.
- Useful when the meaning differs (e.g. a timeout in ms vs a retry count), but distinct wrapper types (`struct TimeoutMs { int v; };`) make the code self-documenting and keep type-based access.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Duplicate types are a compile error."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: generic code that builds variants from type lists (e.g. `variant<Ts...>` with repeated `Ts`) must use index-based access.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Duplicates are allowed; access them by index, or wrap them in distinct types.

interview_qa.question: How would you implement a minimal variant? What are the hard parts?
interview_qa.answer: Storage: a union (or aligned buffer) of all alternatives plus an index. Construction places the chosen type and sets the index. Destruction, copy and visit dispatch on the index, typically through a table of function pointers generated from the type list. The hard parts are the exception guarantees on assignment, conditional triviality, constexpr support and the converting constructor's overload rules.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Destroy: `table[index](storage)` where each entry calls the right destructor.
- Visit: same table idea, with one entry per alternative (per combination for several variants).
- Assignment between different alternatives must destroy the old object before constructing the new one in the same storage; that is where valueless comes from.
- Triviality propagation needs specialized base classes (or C++20 conditionally trivial special members with `requires`).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Store a `void*` and a `type_info`." That is `any`, with heap allocation.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `get<T>` maps a type to an index at compile time (find `T` in the pack), so a mismatch costs one integer comparison at run time.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: variant = union + index + compile-time generated per-alternative operations.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: qty refers to an int whose lifetime ended.
GCC 11, -O0: printed an arbitrary number (on libstdc++ those bytes now hold part of the string's data pointer),
different on each run. ASan reports nothing: no memory was freed.
```

**Explanation:**
- Assigning a `std::string` destroys the `int` alternative and constructs a string in the same storage. `qty` still points at those bytes, which now belong to the string object (its first member is the heap pointer).
- Reading prints garbage; writing through `qty` would corrupt the string's pointer and crash later in its destructor.
- ASan is silent because the bytes are valid stack memory: only the object changed.
- Assigning another `int` (`field = 7;`) would have kept `qty` valid: same alternative, assignment instead of destroy + construct.
- **Key Concept:** A reference into a variant is valid only while that alternative stays active; re-fetch after every possible alternative change.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <variant>

int main() {
    std::variant<int, std::string> field = 42;
    int qty = std::get<int>(field);                  // copy the value out

    field = std::string("pending-confirmation-from-venue");
    std::cout << qty << '\n';                        // 42
    if (auto* p = std::get_if<int>(&field)) std::cout << *p << '\n';   // not printed
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
1 0 1
```

**Explanation:**
- Variants compare by **index first**: if the active alternatives differ, the one with the smaller index is smaller, whatever the values.
- `a` holds index 0 (`int`), `b` index 1 (`string`): `a < b` is true even though "100 vs 1" might suggest otherwise.
- `c < a`: same index, so the values are compared: `5 < 100`.
- Reordering the alternatives in the type changes the sort order of all stored data.
- **Key Concept:** Variant ordering is (index, then value); alternatives of different types never compare their values.

quick_reference.content:
#### variant API
| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `variant<A, B> v;` | Holds value-initialized `A` (deleted if `A` not default-constructible) |
| `v = x;` | Picks alternative by overload resolution, no narrowing, bool only from bool |
| `v.emplace<T>(args)` / `emplace<I>` | Destroy current, construct in place |
| `v.index()` | Active index, `variant_npos` if valueless |
| `holds_alternative<T>(v)` | `bool` |
| `get<T>(v)` / `get<I>(v)` | Reference, throws `bad_variant_access` |
| `get_if<T>(&v)` | Pointer or `nullptr` (takes `&v`) |
| `visit(f, v1, v2...)` | Calls `f` with active alternatives; same return type required |
| `visit<R>(f, v)` (C++20) | Converts results to `R` |
| `std::monostate` | Explicit empty alternative |

#### Compile errors you should recognize
| Code | Why |
|---|---|
| `variant<int, double> v = 1L;` | Both conversions narrow |
| `variant<string, string_view> v = "x";` | Ambiguous |
| `get<int>(variant<int, int>)` | Type occurs twice |
| `variant<NoDefault, int> v;` | First alternative not default-constructible |
| `variant<int&>` | References not allowed |
| visitor returns `int` and `string` | Return types differ |
| `std::any a = std::make_unique<int>(1);` | `any` needs copyable contents |

#### Implementation facts (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64, not guaranteed by C++)
| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| `sizeof(variant<int, std::string>)` | 40 |
| `sizeof(variant<char, int>)` | 8 |
| Index type | Smallest unsigned type that fits (1 byte for < 255 alternatives) |
| `sizeof(std::any)` | 16 |
| `any` inline storage | Types of at most 8 bytes, suitable alignment, nothrow move |
| `any(std::string)` | 1 allocation |
| P0608 (`variant<bool, string> = "x"` → string) | GCC 10+, also in `-std=c++17` mode |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Where is a variant's value stored? | In-place, inside the variant; no heap |
| How does variant know the active type? | A stored index |
| `get` vs `get_if`? | Reference + throw vs pointer + nullptr |
| Why `std::visit` over `switch(index())`? | Compile-time check that every type is handled |
| Is visit compile-time dispatch? | No; run-time branch on the index, no vptr |
| variant vs virtual? | Closed set, in-place, easy new operations vs open set, heap, easy new types |
| What is `monostate`? | An intentional empty alternative |
| What is valueless_by_exception? | Old value destroyed, new construction threw: no value |
| `variant<bool, string> v = "hi"`? | string (since P0608) |
| any vs variant? | Run-time open type erasure vs compile-time closed set |
| `any a = "hi"; any_cast<string>(a)`? | Throws: stored type is `const char*` |
| Does any allocate? | Implementation-specific; libstdc++ inline only for pointer-sized nothrow-movable types |
