subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A `std::vector<T>` is a handle to one contiguous heap block. In every major library the handle is three pointers:
  - `begin`: first element.
  - `end`: one past the last **constructed** element (`size() = end - begin`).
  - `end_of_storage`: one past the allocated block (`capacity() = end_of_storage - begin`).
- `sizeof(std::vector<T>)` is 24 on 64-bit libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC release builds (implementation detail).
- Only `[begin, end)` holds live objects. The slots in `[end, end_of_storage)` are raw memory: no constructor has run there, so reading or writing them is UB even though the memory is allocated.
- Contiguity is guaranteed: `v.data() + i == &v[i]`, so a vector can be passed to C APIs as `(v.data(), v.size())` or as a `std::span` (topic 02).
- Three costs to keep in mind: allocation (rare, geometric growth), element relocation on growth (move or copy every element), and pointer invalidation (every borrow dies on reallocation).

subsections.title: 2. size, capacity and growth
subsections.content:
- `size() <= capacity()` always. When an insertion would make `size() > capacity()`, the vector **must** allocate a new block: `capacity()` is by definition the storage it holds, so there is no "unusual allocation strategy" that avoids it.
- Growth is **geometric** so that `push_back` is amortized O(1):
  - Total elements moved over n pushes with factor k is about n / (k - 1), a constant per element.
  - Linear growth (`+10` each time) would make n pushes O(n²).
- The factor is implementation-defined:

| Library | Growth on `push_back` | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| libstdc++ (GCC) | 2x (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, ...) | `max(2 * size, size + n)` for multi-element inserts |
| libc++ (Clang) | 2x | similar rule |
| MSVC STL | 1.5x | 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, ... |

- The libstdc++ row is verified with GCC 11; the libc++ and MSVC rows describe their typical documented behaviour and are not verified here.

- Why 1.5x: with factor < golden ratio (about 1.618), the sum of earlier freed blocks can eventually hold the next request, so an allocator could reuse that memory; with 2x it never can. In practice the allocator decides, so the gain is small.
- A default-constructed vector has `capacity() == 0` and usually `data() == nullptr` in libstdc++ (the standard only says `data()` is a valid range pointer; for an empty vector it may or may not be null).
- `max_size()` is the theoretical limit; `reserve(n)` beyond it throws `std::length_error`, allocation failure throws `std::bad_alloc`.

subsections.title: 3. reserve vs resize vs the size constructor
subsections.content:
| Call | `size()` | `capacity()` | Constructs elements? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::vector<int> v(n);` | n | ≥ n | Yes, value-initialized (`0`) |
| `std::vector<int> v(n, x);` | n | ≥ n | Yes, copies of `x` |
| `v.reserve(n);` | unchanged | ≥ n | No |
| `v.resize(n);` | n | ≥ n (never shrinks) | New ones value-initialized; extra ones destroyed |
| `v.clear();` | 0 | unchanged | Destroys all |
| `v.shrink_to_fit();` | unchanged | non-binding request: ≥ size | No |

- `reserve(n)`:
  - Never reduces capacity and never changes size.
  - Makes the next `n - size()` insertions reallocation-free; it does **not** make `v[i]` legal for `i >= size()`.
- `v.reserve(100); v[50] = 10;` compiles and is UB: no element exists at index 50. `size()` stays 0, so a later reallocation drops the value and later `push_back`s overwrite that slot.
- AddressSanitizer does not flag that write (it is inside the allocated block); `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` aborts with `Assertion '__n < this->size()' failed`, and `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` aborts with `Error: attempt to subscript container with out-of-bounds index`.
- Choosing:
  - Know the count and will fill by index: `std::vector<T> v(n);` or `resize(n)`.
  - Know the count and will append: `reserve(n)` then `push_back` / `emplace_back`.
  - `resize` value-initializes, which costs a write per element; for `int` buffers about to be overwritten by `read()` this is wasted work (custom allocator with default-init, or `std::make_unique_for_overwrite<T[]>` in C++20, are the workarounds).

subsections.title: 4. What happens on reallocation
subsections.content:
- For `v.emplace_back(args...)` with `size() == capacity()`, libstdc++ does:
  1. Allocate a new block (larger by the growth factor).
  2. Construct the **new element first**, at index `size()` in the new block.
  3. Relocate the old elements into the new block with `std::move_if_noexcept`: move if the move constructor is `noexcept` (or if the type is not copyable), otherwise copy.
  4. Destroy the old elements, free the old block, update the three pointers. With a `noexcept` move, libstdc++ interleaves steps 3 and 4 (move one, destroy it, next); with copying it copies all, then destroys all (`ctor3 copy1 copy2 dtor1 dtor2`).
- Observable order for a noisy type: `ctor3 move1 dtor1 move2 dtor2`. The often-drawn diagram "move the old elements, then construct the new one" is not what libstdc++ does.
- Constructing the new element first is what makes `v.push_back(v[0])` correct even at full capacity: the argument still refers to the old block, which is alive until step 4.
- Copy vs move on growth, the strong exception guarantee and why `noexcept` on move constructors matters are covered in Memory & Ownership, topic 02. One-line rule: a non-`noexcept` move constructor makes growth copy every element (if the type is copyable).
- Trivially copyable types (`int`, POD structs) are relocated with `memmove`: one bulk copy.
- After reallocation every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector is invalid, including ones obtained from `data()`.

subsections.title: 5. Invalidation in one table (vector only)
subsections.content:
| Operation | Reallocates? | Invalidated |
|---|---|---|
| `push_back` / `emplace_back`, `size < capacity` | No | `end()` only |
| `push_back` / `emplace_back`, `size == capacity` | Yes | Everything |
| `insert` / `emplace` at `pos`, no reallocation | No | `pos` and everything after it, including `end()` |
| `erase(pos)` | No | `pos` and everything after it, including `end()` |
| `pop_back` | No | The last element and `end()` |
| `reserve(n)` with `n > capacity()` | Yes | Everything |
| `resize` | If it grows past capacity | Everything if it reallocates; otherwise like insert/erase at the end (`end()`, plus removed elements when shrinking) |
| `shrink_to_fit` | If capacity changes | Everything when it changes |
| `clear` | No | Everything (no elements left) |
| `swap(a, b)` | No | No element iterators: they stay valid but now refer into the other vector (`end()` may be invalidated) |

- The full cross-container table, erase-in-loop idioms and debug modes are in topic 06.

subsections.title: 6. push_back vs emplace_back
subsections.content:
| Call | Work done (for a type `T` with a converting constructor) |
|---|---|
| `v.push_back(t)` (lvalue) | 1 copy construction |
| `v.push_back(std::move(t))` | 1 move construction |
| `v.push_back(T(args))` | 1 construction of a temporary + 1 move + 1 destruction |
| `v.emplace_back(args)` | 1 construction in place |
| `v.emplace_back(t)` (existing object) | 1 copy: no advantage over `push_back` |
| `v.emplace_back(std::move(t))` | 1 move: no advantage over `push_back` |

- `emplace_back` only saves the temporary when you pass **constructor arguments**, not when you already have an object.
- `emplace_back` uses direct-initialization, so it can call **explicit** constructors:
  - `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v; v.emplace_back(new int(1));` compiles; `push_back(new int(1))` does not.
  - If the reallocation inside `emplace_back` throws, the raw `new int` leaks. Prefer `v.push_back(std::make_unique<int>(1))`.
- Aggregates: `struct P { int a, b; }; v.emplace_back(1, 2);` fails in C++17 (no constructor) and compiles in C++20 (parenthesized aggregate initialization, P0960; GCC 10+).
- `emplace_back` returns a reference to the new element since C++17.
- `insert` / `emplace` in the middle need the type to be move-assignable (elements shift by assignment); `push_back` / `emplace_back` only need move-insertable.

subsections.title: 7. Construction pitfalls
subsections.content:
| Code | Result |
|---|---|
| `std::vector<int> a(10);` | 10 zeros |
| `std::vector<int> b{10};` | 1 element: `10` (initializer list wins) |
| `std::vector<int> c(10, 5);` | 10 fives |
| `std::vector<int> d{10, 5};` | 2 elements: `10, 5` |
| `std::vector<std::string> e(3);` | 3 empty strings |
| `std::vector<std::string> f{3};` | 3 empty strings: `3` cannot make a `std::string`, so the size constructor is chosen |
| `std::vector<std::string> g{{"a", "b"}};` | UB: the inner braces call `std::string(first, last)` with two unrelated pointers |
| `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` | CTAD (C++17): `std::vector<int>` |

- Braces prefer an `initializer_list` constructor whenever one is viable; parentheses never use it.
- `initializer_list` elements are `const`, so `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v{std::make_unique<int>(1)};` does not compile (would need a copy).

subsections.title: 8. Removing elements and returning memory
subsections.content:
- `erase(pos)` / `erase(first, last)`: O(n) because later elements shift left by move-assignment.
- Erase-remove idiom:
  - `std::remove(first, last, x)` moves the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end. It does not change `size()`; the tail holds valid but unspecified values.
  - `v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end());` actually shrinks.
- C++20 `std::erase(v, x)` / `std::erase_if(v, pred)` do both and return the number removed.
- Unordered removal in O(1): swap with the last element, then `pop_back`.
- Returning memory:
  - `clear()` keeps the capacity (good for reuse in a loop).
  - `shrink_to_fit()` is a non-binding request (libstdc++ honours it by reallocating).
  - Pre-C++11 trick: `std::vector<T>().swap(v);` guarantees capacity 0 in practice.

subsections.title: 9. std::vector<bool> is not a container of bool
subsections.content:
- It is a space-optimized specialization that stores bits. `operator[]` returns a proxy object (`std::vector<bool>::reference`), not `bool&`.
- Consequences:
  - `auto r = vb[0];` is a proxy that still refers to the bit; later writes to `vb[0]` show through `r`.
  - `bool* p = &vb[0];` does not compile; there is no `data()`.
  - Generic code that takes `T&` from `v[i]` breaks.
  - Two threads writing **different** elements is a data race (they share a word); the standard explicitly excludes `vector<bool>` from the "different elements are safe" rule.
- Alternatives: `std::vector<char>` or `std::vector<std::uint8_t>` (real elements), `std::bitset<N>` (fixed size), `std::deque<bool>`, or a dynamic bitset library.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`reserve(n)` creates n elements." ✅ It only allocates; `size()` is unchanged and `v[i]` is UB.
- ❌ "Accessing a reserved slot is a compile error or a crash." ✅ It compiles and usually runs silently; even ASan is quiet.
- ❌ "Vectors double their capacity." ✅ Geometric growth with an implementation-defined factor (2x GCC/Clang, 1.5x MSVC).
- ❌ "`push_back` at full capacity might not reallocate." ✅ It must; capacity is the storage held.
- ❌ "With no reallocation, all iterators stay valid." ✅ `end()` (and everything at or after an insertion point) is invalidated (topic 06).
- ❌ "A copy keeps the reserved capacity." ✅ Copies allocate for the elements only; moves keep the block.
- ❌ "Reallocation moves old elements first, then builds the new one." ✅ libstdc++ builds the new element first; that is why `push_back(v[0])` works.
- ❌ "`emplace_back` is always faster." ✅ Only when you pass constructor arguments.
- ❌ "`std::remove` removes elements." ✅ It reorders; `erase` (or C++20 `std::erase`) shrinks.
- ❌ "`clear()` frees the memory." ✅ Capacity stays; use `shrink_to_fit` or swap with an empty vector.
- ❌ "`vector<bool>` is a vector of bools." ✅ It is a bitset with proxy references.

- Constructing the new element first is what makes `v.push_back(v[0])` correct even at full capacity: the argument still refers to the old block, which is alive until step 4.
- Copy vs move on growth, the strong exception guarantee and why `noexcept` on move constructors matters are covered in Memory & Ownership, topic 02. One-line rule: a non-`noexcept` move constructor makes growth copy every element (if the type is copyable).
- Trivially copyable types (`int`, POD structs) are relocated with `memmove`: one bulk copy.
- After reallocation every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector is invalid, including ones obtained from `data()`.

#### 5. Invalidation in one table (vector only)
| Operation | Reallocates? | Invalidated |
|---|---|---|
| `push_back` / `emplace_back`, `size < capacity` | No | `end()` only |
| `push_back` / `emplace_back`, `size == capacity` | Yes | Everything |
| `insert` / `emplace` at `pos`, no reallocation | No | `pos` and everything after it, including `end()` |
| `erase(pos)` | No | `pos` and everything after it, including `end()` |
| `pop_back` | No | The last element and `end()` |
| `reserve(n)` with `n > capacity()` | Yes | Everything |
| `resize` | If it grows past capacity | Everything if it reallocates; otherwise like insert/erase at the end (`end()`, plus removed elements when shrinking) |
| `shrink_to_fit` | If capacity changes | Everything when it changes |
| `clear` | No | Everything (no elements left) |
| `swap(a, b)` | No | No element iterators: they stay valid but now refer into the other vector (`end()` may be invalidated) |

- The full cross-container table, erase-in-loop idioms and debug modes are in topic 06.

#### 6. push_back vs emplace_back
| Call | Work done (for a type `T` with a converting constructor) |
|---|---|
| `v.push_back(t)` (lvalue) | 1 copy construction |
| `v.push_back(std::move(t))` | 1 move construction |
| `v.push_back(T(args))` | 1 construction of a temporary + 1 move + 1 destruction |
| `v.emplace_back(args)` | 1 construction in place |
| `v.emplace_back(t)` (existing object) | 1 copy: no advantage over `push_back` |
| `v.emplace_back(std::move(t))` | 1 move: no advantage over `push_back` |

- `emplace_back` only saves the temporary when you pass **constructor arguments**, not when you already have an object.
- `emplace_back` uses direct-initialization, so it can call **explicit** constructors:
  - `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v; v.emplace_back(new int(1));` compiles; `push_back(new int(1))` does not.
  - If the reallocation inside `emplace_back` throws, the raw `new int` leaks. Prefer `v.push_back(std::make_unique<int>(1))`.
- Aggregates: `struct P { int a, b; }; v.emplace_back(1, 2);` fails in C++17 (no constructor) and compiles in C++20 (parenthesized aggregate initialization, P0960; GCC 10+).
- `emplace_back` returns a reference to the new element since C++17.
- `insert` / `emplace` in the middle need the type to be move-assignable (elements shift by assignment); `push_back` / `emplace_back` only need move-insertable.

#### 7. Construction pitfalls
| Code | Result |
|---|---|
| `std::vector<int> a(10);` | 10 zeros |
| `std::vector<int> b{10};` | 1 element: `10` (initializer list wins) |
| `std::vector<int> c(10, 5);` | 10 fives |
| `std::vector<int> d{10, 5};` | 2 elements: `10, 5` |
| `std::vector<std::string> e(3);` | 3 empty strings |
| `std::vector<std::string> f{3};` | 3 empty strings: `3` cannot make a `std::string`, so the size constructor is chosen |
| `std::vector<std::string> g{{"a", "b"}};` | UB: the inner braces call `std::string(first, last)` with two unrelated pointers |
| `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` | CTAD (C++17): `std::vector<int>` |

- Braces prefer an `initializer_list` constructor whenever one is viable; parentheses never use it.
- `initializer_list` elements are `const`, so `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v{std::make_unique<int>(1)};` does not compile (would need a copy).

#### 8. Removing elements and returning memory
- `erase(pos)` / `erase(first, last)`: O(n) because later elements shift left by move-assignment.
- Erase-remove idiom:
  - `std::remove(first, last, x)` moves the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end. It does not change `size()`; the tail holds valid but unspecified values.
  - `v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end());` actually shrinks.
- C++20 `std::erase(v, x)` / `std::erase_if(v, pred)` do both and return the number removed.
- Unordered removal in O(1): swap with the last element, then `pop_back`.
- Returning memory:
  - `clear()` keeps the capacity (good for reuse in a loop).
  - `shrink_to_fit()` is a non-binding request (libstdc++ honours it by reallocating).
  - Pre-C++11 trick: `std::vector<T>().swap(v);` guarantees capacity 0 in practice.

#### 9. std::vector<bool> is not a container of bool
- It is a space-optimized specialization that stores bits. `operator[]` returns a proxy object (`std::vector<bool>::reference`), not `bool&`.
- Consequences:
  - `auto r = vb[0];` is a proxy that still refers to the bit; later writes to `vb[0]` show through `r`.
  - `bool* p = &vb[0];` does not compile; there is no `data()`.
  - Generic code that takes `T&` from `v[i]` breaks.
  - Two threads writing **different** elements is a data race (they share a word); the standard explicitly excludes `vector<bool>` from the "different elements are safe" rule.
- Alternatives: `std::vector<char>` or `std::vector<std::uint8_t>` (real elements), `std::bitset<N>` (fixed size), `std::deque<bool>`, or a dynamic bitset library.

#### 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "`reserve(n)` creates n elements." ✅ It only allocates; `size()` is unchanged and `v[i]` is UB.
- ❌ "Accessing a reserved slot is a compile error or a crash." ✅ It compiles and usually runs silently; even ASan is quiet.
- ❌ "Vectors double their capacity." ✅ Geometric growth with an implementation-defined factor (2x GCC/Clang, 1.5x MSVC).
- ❌ "`push_back` at full capacity might not reallocate." ✅ It must; capacity is the storage held.
- ❌ "With no reallocation, all iterators stay valid." ✅ `end()` (and everything at or after an insertion point) is invalidated (topic 06).
- ❌ "A copy keeps the reserved capacity." ✅ Copies allocate for the elements only; moves keep the block.
- ❌ "Reallocation moves old elements first, then builds the new one." ✅ libstdc++ builds the new element first; that is why `push_back(v[0])` works.
- ❌ "`emplace_back` is always faster." ✅ Only when you pass constructor arguments.
- ❌ "`std::remove` removes elements." ✅ It reorders; `erase` (or C++20 `std::erase`) shrinks.
- ❌ "`clear()` frees the memory." ✅ Capacity stays; use `shrink_to_fit` or swap with an empty vector.
- ❌ "`vector<bool>` is a vector of bools." ✅ It is a bitset with proxy references.

edge_cases.title: reserve then index
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::vector<int> v; v.reserve(100); v[50] = 10;` compiles and is UB: there is no element 50.
- Typical symptom: the program prints `v[50]` correctly (the raw memory was written), but `v.size()` is 0, range-for prints nothing, and the next reallocation drops the value.
- ASan stays silent: the write is inside the allocated block. Use `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` in test builds.
- Fix: `resize(100)` or construct with `std::vector<int> v(100);`, or keep `reserve` and `push_back`.

edge_cases.title: The function that returns an empty result
edge_cases.explanation:
- A "rotate" or "transform" helper does `result.reserve(n); for (...) result[i] = ...; return result;`.
- Debug prints inside the loop show correct values, the caller receives a vector with `size() == 0`.
- The returned vector's elements never existed; returning it moves only `begin/end/capacity`, and `end == begin`.
- Fix: size the vector (`std::vector<int> result(n);`) or append.

edge_cases.title: reserve does not protect beyond capacity
edge_cases.explanation:
- `v.reserve(100);` then 100 `push_back`s, `int* p = &v[0];`, then one more `push_back`.
- `size() == capacity() == 100`, so the 101st insertion reallocates: `p` dangles.
- reserve only guarantees no reallocation **until** size would exceed the reserved capacity.

edge_cases.title: The copy forgets the reservation
edge_cases.explanation:
- `a.reserve(1000); a.push_back(1); auto b = a;`: `b.capacity()` is 1 on libstdc++, not 1000.
- Copy construction allocates for the elements, not for the source's spare capacity. Moving keeps it (`std::move(a)` hands over the 1000-slot block).
- Copy assignment into an existing vector with enough capacity reuses that vector's storage.
- A buffer `reserve`d in one place and then passed or stored **by value** silently loses its pre-allocation, and the first growth on the hot path reallocates.

edge_cases.title: auto and vector<bool>
edge_cases.explanation:
- `auto first = flags[0];` is `std::vector<bool>::reference`, a proxy, not a `bool`.
- Writing `flags[0] = true;` afterwards changes what `first` reads. If `flags` is destroyed or reallocated, `first` dangles.
- Fix: `bool first = flags[0];` (explicit type), or avoid `vector<bool>`.

edge_cases.title: Brace initialization picks the initializer list
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::vector<int> v{10};` is one element; `std::vector<int> v(10);` is ten.
- `std::vector<std::string> g{{"a", "b"}};` compiles and is UB: the inner `{"a", "b"}` is a `std::string(const char* first, const char* last)` over two unrelated literals. libstdc++ throws `length_error` or crashes.
- Rule: parentheses for sizes and counts, braces for listing element values.

edge_cases.title: emplace_back that cannot default-construct
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Data { Data(const Data&); Data(Data&&); }; v.emplace_back();` does not compile.
- Declaring any constructor (copy and move constructors included) suppresses the implicit default constructor: `error: no matching function for call to 'Data::Data()'`.
- Fix: `Data() = default;`.

edge_cases.title: Pushing an element of the same vector
edge_cases.explanation:
- `v.push_back(v[0]);` at full capacity looks dangerous: the reference argument points into the block being replaced.
- The standard requires it to work, and libstdc++ constructs the new element (copying from the old block) before releasing the old block.
- The same holds for `insert(pos, v[i])`: implementations copy the value first. It is a hand-written container that usually gets this wrong.

edge_cases.title: remove without erase
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2)` on `{1, 2, 3, 2, 5}` returns an iterator to index 3; `v.size()` is still 5.
- The tail (`v[3]`, `v[4]`) holds valid but unspecified values (libstdc++ leaves `2, 5`).
- Fix: erase the tail, or use C++20 `std::erase(v, 2)` which returns 2 (the count removed).

interview_qa.question: How is a `std::vector` laid out in memory?
interview_qa.answer: A small handle (in practice three pointers: begin, end of elements, end of storage, 24 bytes on 64-bit) that owns one contiguous heap block. Elements `[0, size)` are constructed objects; slots `[size, capacity)` are raw, unconstructed memory.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `size() = end - begin`, `capacity() = end_of_storage - begin`.
- Contiguity is guaranteed: `&v[0] + i == &v[i]`, so `v.data()` works with C APIs and `std::span`.
- The handle itself lives wherever the vector object lives; the elements are always in the allocator's memory (the heap for `std::allocator`).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The vector stores its elements inline like an array." Only `std::array` (and C++26 `std::inplace_vector`) do.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: moving a vector is O(1) because only the three pointers move; moving each element is O(n).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Three pointers, one contiguous block, constructed prefix plus raw tail.

interview_qa.question: Does a vector double its capacity when it grows?
interview_qa.answer: It grows geometrically, but the factor is implementation-defined. libstdc++ and libc++ double; MSVC grows by 1.5x. The standard only requires amortized constant time for `push_back`.
interview_qa.explanation:

- MSVC: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, ...

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: an empty vector has capacity 0 in all three libraries; there is no minimum initial allocation.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between `reserve` and `resize`?
interview_qa.answer: `reserve(n)` only allocates: capacity becomes at least `n`, size and content are unchanged, no elements are created. `resize(n)` changes the number of elements: it value-initializes new ones (or destroys extra ones) and allocates if needed.

interview_qa.question: Does copying a vector copy its capacity? Does moving it?
interview_qa.answer: Copying copies the elements, not the capacity: the new vector typically gets `capacity() == size()`. Moving steals the whole block, so the destination gets the source's capacity and the source is left empty (in practice capacity 0).
interview_qa.explanation:

- Copy assignment into a vector that already has enough capacity reuses that storage: `e.reserve(50); e = b;` keeps capacity 50.
- The standard specifies neither number for the copy; only the moved-to vector's ownership of the old block is guaranteed (for `std::allocator`).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A copy is an exact clone, including the reserved space."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a vector that was `reserve`d for a hot path and then passed or returned **by copy** loses the reservation; the copy will reallocate on its next growth.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Capacity travels with moves, not with copies.

interview_qa.question: Does `clear()` release the memory? How do you actually shrink a vector?
interview_qa.answer: No. `clear()` destroys the elements and sets size to 0 but keeps the capacity. To release memory call `shrink_to_fit()` (a non-binding request; libstdc++ honours it) or swap with an empty vector: `std::vector<T>().swap(v);`.
interview_qa.explanation:

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`clear()` frees memory, that is what it is for."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in long-running services, a vector that once held a burst of a million elements keeps that memory until shrunk or destroyed.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `clear` empties, it does not free.

interview_qa.question: Why does `std::remove` not change the size of a vector?

interview_qa.question: What is special about `std::vector<bool>`?
interview_qa.answer: It is a bit-packed specialization: elements are bits, `operator[]` returns a proxy object instead of `bool&`, there is no `data()`, and you cannot take `bool*` to an element. It does not satisfy the container requirements that generic code assumes.

interview_qa.question: In a latency-critical path, why `reserve` even if the final element count is the same?

interview_qa.question: How do you keep stable references to elements in a growing collection?
interview_qa.answer: Store indices instead of pointers, store `std::unique_ptr<T>` elements so the objects never move, use `std::deque` (stable addresses under `push_back` / `push_front`), or `reserve` the maximum up front and never exceed it.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: slot maps / generational indices give stable handles plus contiguous storage and detection of stale handles.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Pointers into a vector are temporary; use indices or a container with stable addresses.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: the range passed to insert must not point into the vector itself.
libstdc++ / GCC 11 and 13 print "10 20 10 20 30 40 50" (wrong values, no crash).
Without the reserve line the same code prints the intended "30 40 10 20 30 40 50".
-fsanitize=address: no report.  -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG: "attempt to insert with an iterator
range [first, last) from this container".
```

**Explanation:**
- The standard's precondition for `insert(pos, first, last)` is that `first` and `last` are not iterators into the same container. C++23 `insert_range` has the same rule ("the range must not overlap the container").
- What happens with spare capacity (libstdc++): to open a gap of 2 at the front, it first shifts `10 20 30 40 50` right by two, then copies from `[begin() + 2, begin() + 4)`. Those slots now hold the shifted `10 20`, so that is what gets copied.
- When the insert has to reallocate, the new block is filled while the old one is still intact, so the source range is read before anything moves: it "works". The bug therefore depends on the capacity at the time, which is why it hides in tests.
- ASan stays silent: every access is inside the vector's own live buffer. Only debug mode knows the iterators belong to `v`.
- Contrast with Q3: `push_back(v[0])` (one element) must work even when it reallocates; the range overloads get no such guarantee.
- **Key Concept:** Never pass a container's own iterators as the source range of `insert`; copy the range out first.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    std::vector<int> tmp(v.begin() + 2, v.begin() + 4);   // copy out first
    v.insert(v.begin(), tmp.begin(), tmp.end());
    for (int x : v) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';                                     // 30 40 10 20 30 40 50
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
1 0
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::vector<bool>::operator[]` returns a proxy (`std::vector<bool>::reference`), so `auto` deduces the proxy type, not `bool`.
- The proxy keeps referring to bit 0, so it reads the later write: `1`.
- `bool copy` converts the proxy to a value at that moment: `0`.
- With `std::vector<int>`, `auto` would have copied the value and printed `0 0`.
- **Key Concept:** `vector<bool>` hands out proxies; spell out `bool` when you want a value.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
5 3 : 1 3 5 2 5
```
The last two values are unspecified by the standard; `2 5` is libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64.

**Explanation:**
- `std::remove` shifts the kept elements (`1, 3, 5`) to the front and returns the new logical end (index 3).
- It cannot change the size: algorithms see iterators, not the container.
- The tail elements are valid but unspecified (moved-from or untouched).
- Fix: `v.erase(it, v.end());` or C++20 `std::erase(v, 2);` (returns 2).
- **Key Concept:** `remove` reorders, `erase` shrinks.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
C++17 (GCC 11): compile error inside the allocator:
  error: new initializer expression list treated as compound expression
  error: no matching function for call to 'Point::Point(int)'
C++20: compiles, prints 7
```

**Explanation:**

- C++20 added parenthesized aggregate initialization (P0960): `Point(3, 4)` now initializes the members in order.
- C++17 alternatives: `pts.push_back({3, 4});` or give `Point` a constructor.
- **Key Concept:** In C++20, `emplace_back` works for aggregates.

practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error:

- The error appears deep inside the allocator's `construct`, which makes it look like a library problem.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
80/100 80/100 200/200 10/200 0/0
```
The guaranteed parts: `reserve` and `resize` never shrink capacity, and the exact 200 and the honoured `shrink_to_fit` are libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64.

**Explanation:**
- `resize(80)` within capacity 100: no reallocation.
- `reserve(30)` below capacity: no-op. It never shrinks and never changes size.
- `resize(200)` beyond capacity: libstdc++ grows to `max(2 * size, size + added) = max(160, 200) = 200`.
- `resize(10)` destroys 190 elements; capacity stays 200.
- `clear()` + `shrink_to_fit()`: libstdc++ releases the block.
- **Key Concept:** Only `shrink_to_fit` (non-binding) or swapping with an empty vector reduces capacity.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
1 1000 0
```
libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64. The copy's capacity is not specified; the move handing over the block is.

**Explanation:**
- The copy constructor allocates for the elements (1), not for the source's spare capacity.
- The move constructor steals the three pointers: `moved` owns the 1000-slot block, `src` is left empty.
- So a vector that was `reserve`d and then passed by value (copied) loses its reservation.
- **Key Concept:** Capacity travels with moves, not with copies.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compiles and prints: 2 4
The commented push_back(new int(2)) would not compile. The emplace_back(new int(1))
line leaks if the vector's allocation throws before the unique_ptr is constructed.
```

**Explanation:**
- `unique_ptr(pointer)` is `explicit`. `push_back` takes a `unique_ptr` parameter, so it would need an implicit conversion from `int*`: compile error ("no matching function for call to 'push_back(int*)'").
- `emplace_back` direct-initializes the element, so it can call the explicit constructor.
- But the allocation of the new block happens before the element is constructed; if it throws `bad_alloc`, nothing owns the raw `new int(1)`.
- **Key Concept:** Do not pass naked `new` to `emplace_back`; use `make_unique`.

quick_reference.content:
#### Operations and costs
| Operation | Complexity | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `v[i]`, `at(i)`, `data()` | O(1) | `at` throws `out_of_range` |
| `push_back` / `emplace_back` | Amortized O(1) | Reallocation at `size == capacity` |
| `insert` / `erase` in the middle | O(n) | Shifts later elements |
| `pop_back` | O(1) | `back()` / `pop_back` on empty: UB |
| `reserve(n)` | O(size) if it grows | Never shrinks |
| `resize(n)` | O(abs(n - size)) | Value-initializes new elements |
| `clear()` | O(size) destructors | Keeps capacity |
| Move construct / move assign / `swap` | O(1) | Steals three pointers |

#### Implementation facts (not guaranteed by C++)
| Fact | libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 |
|---|---|
| `sizeof(std::vector<T>)` | 24 |
| Growth factor | 2x (MSVC: 1.5x) |
| Empty vector capacity, `data()` | 0, `nullptr` |
| Reallocation order | New element first, then relocate, then destroy old |
| `shrink_to_fit` | Honoured (reallocates to exact size) |
| `sizeof(std::vector<bool>)` | 40 |

#### Version notes
| Version | Feature |
|---|---|
| C++11 | `emplace_back`, `shrink_to_fit`, `data()`, move semantics |
| C++17 | `emplace_back` returns a reference; CTAD `std::vector v{1, 2}` |
| C++20 | `std::erase` / `std::erase_if`; parenthesized aggregate init in `emplace_back`; `constexpr std::vector` (transient) |
| C++23 | `append_range`, `insert_range`, `assign_range`, construction `from_range` |
| C++26 | `std::inplace_vector` (fixed-capacity, no heap) |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| size vs capacity? | Constructed elements vs allocated slots |
| Growth factor? | Geometric, implementation-defined (2x GCC/Clang, 1.5x MSVC) |
| Why geometric? | Amortized O(1) `push_back` |
| `reserve(100); v[50] = 1;`? | UB; size is 0 (ASan silent, `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` aborts) |
| `push_back` at full capacity? | Always reallocates; all borrows die |
| Reallocation order in libstdc++? | Construct new element, relocate old, destroy old, free |
| Is `v.push_back(v[0])` safe? | Yes, required to work |
| Copy or move on growth? | Move if `noexcept` (or not copyable), else copy |
| `emplace_back` vs `push_back`? | Saves one move only when passing constructor arguments |
| `vector<int>{10}` size? | 1 |
| Does `clear()` free memory? | No; capacity stays |
| `std::remove` changes size? | No; erase the tail or use `std::erase` (C++20) |
| `vector<bool>`? | Bit-packed, proxy references, no `data()`, not a real container |
| Need stable addresses? | Indices, `deque`, or `vector<unique_ptr<T>>` |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- An iterator is a **position** inside a container, generalized from a pointer: `*it` reads the element, `++it` moves to the next position.
- Every range is **half-open**: `[begin, end)`. `end()` is one past the last element; it is a valid iterator but it is **not dereferenceable**.
- An iterator can be in one of three states:
  - **Dereferenceable**: points at a live element.
  - **Past-the-end**: `end()`; may be compared and decremented (if bidirectional), never dereferenced.
  - **Invalid (singular)**: the container changed in a way that broke it. Using it is undefined behaviour.
- "Invalidated" applies to three different handles, and the rules differ per handle:
  - **Iterators** (including `end()`).
  - **Pointers** to elements (`&v[2]`).
  - **References** to elements (`int& r = v[2]`).
- An iterator becomes invalid for one of three reasons:
  - **Storage moved**: the elements were copied or moved to a new buffer (vector or string reallocation).
  - **Position shifted**: the element at that position is now a different element (vector insert or erase without reallocation).
  - **Bookkeeping changed**: the element did not move, but the iterator's internal data did (deque block map, unordered bucket array).
- The rule that keeps you safe: **a mutating call can invalidate; check the rule for that container and that operation**. "It still prints the right value" proves nothing.

subsections.title: 2. What you may and may not do with an invalid iterator
subsections.content:
- Allowed: assign a new value to it, or destroy it.
- Undefined behaviour: dereference, increment, decrement, **and even compare** it (`it == v.end()` on an invalid `it` is UB).
- Invalid does not mean "points to freed memory":
  - After a vector insert without reallocation, a stale pointer still points into live storage, but at a different element.
  - The standard still calls it invalid, so the program has no defined meaning. Treat "address unchanged" as an observation, not a guarantee.
- Pointers and references follow the same logic: after the invalidating operation they must not be read.

subsections.title: 3. Iterator categories
subsections.content:
| Category | Adds | Containers / sources | Example algorithms |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | single pass read | `istream_iterator` | `std::find`, `std::accumulate` |
| Output | single pass write | `back_inserter`, `ostream_iterator` | `std::copy` destination |
| Forward | multi-pass | `forward_list`, unordered containers | `std::search`, `std::adjacent_find` |
| Bidirectional | `--it` | `list`, `map`, `set` | `std::reverse`, `std::prev` |
| Random access | `it + n`, `it[n]`, `<`, `it2 - it1` in O(1) | `deque` | `std::sort`, `std::nth_element` |
| Contiguous (C++20) | elements adjacent in memory | `vector` (not `vector<bool>`), `array`, `string`, `span`, raw pointers | `std::to_address(it)`, `memcpy` |
- Each category is a superset of the previous one; an algorithm states the weakest category it needs.
- `std::sort` needs random access, so `std::sort(l.begin(), l.end())` on a `std::list` does not compile. Use `l.sort()`.
- C++20 expresses the categories as concepts (`std::random_access_iterator<It>`, `std::contiguous_iterator<It>`), so generic code can constrain on them instead of relying on tag dispatch.
- `deque` is random access but **not** contiguous: O(1) indexing does not imply adjacent storage (see topic 07).
- `it + 2` moves by **elements**, not bytes; `it[1]` is `*(it + 1)`.

subsections.title: 4. advance, next, prev, distance
subsections.content:
| Operation | Random access | Bidirectional / forward |
|---|---|---|
| `std::advance(it, n)` | O(1) | O(n) |
| `std::next(it, n)` / `std::prev(it, n)` | O(1) | O(n) (prev needs bidirectional) |
| `std::distance(first, last)` | O(1) | O(n) |
| `it += n`, `it + n` | O(1) | does not compile |
- `std::advance` modifies its argument and returns `void`; `std::next` returns a copy. Prefer `std::next` in expressions.
- Advancing past `end()` is UB; none of these functions checks bounds.
- `std::ranges::next(it, n, bound)` (C++20) stops at `bound` instead of running off the end.
- Interview point: generic code that uses `std::advance` compiles for a `list`, but silently turns O(1) into O(n). Constrain the template with the category it really needs.

subsections.title: 5. const_iterator versus const iterator
subsections.content:
| Declaration | `*it = x` | `++it` |
|---|---|---|
| `std::vector<int>::iterator it` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `const std::vector<int>::iterator it` | ✅ (the iterator is const, not the element) | ❌ |
| `std::vector<int>::const_iterator it` | ❌ | ✅ |
| `const std::vector<int>::const_iterator it` | ❌ | ❌ |
- Same rule as `int* const p` versus `const int* p`.
- `cbegin()`/`cend()` (C++11) give `const_iterator` even on a non-const container.
- `iterator` converts implicitly to `const_iterator`, not the other way.
- Since C++11, `insert` and `erase` accept `const_iterator` positions, so read-only code can still hold the position it later erases.

subsections.title: 6. The invalidation table (the core of the topic)
subsections.content:
| Container | Insert | Erase | Other |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vector` | Reallocation: **all**. Otherwise: everything **at or after** the insertion point, including `end()` | Everything **at or after** the erased element, including `end()` | `reserve(n)`: all if `n > capacity()`, none otherwise. `clear()`, assignment: all. `pop_back`: erased element and `end()` |
| `string` | Same as vector, plus: any non-const member call except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `end` (and `r` variants) **may** invalidate | Same | `swap` of strings **may** invalidate (SSO buffer lives inside the object); see topic 01 |
| `deque` | At either end: **all iterators**, **no** references or pointers. In the middle: **all** iterators, references, pointers | First or last element: only the erased elements (plus `end()` when erasing the last). In the middle: **all** | `shrink_to_fit`: all |
| `list`, `forward_list` | **None** | Only the erased elements | `splice`, `sort`, `merge`, `reverse`: none (spliced iterators now belong to the destination list) |
| `map`, `set`, `multimap`, `multiset` | **None** | Only the erased elements | `extract`: only the extracted element's iterators |
| `unordered_*` | If it causes a rehash: **all iterators**, **no** references or pointers. Otherwise none | Only the erased elements | `rehash`/`reserve`: all iterators. Details in topic 09 |
| `array` | n/a | n/a | Never invalidated while the array lives |
- Three groups to remember:
  - **Contiguous** (`vector`, `string`): elements move, so the rules depend on capacity and position.
  - **Node-based** (`list`, `forward_list`, ordered and unordered associative): elements never move; only the erased element dies.
  - **Mixed** (`deque`, unordered rehash): elements never move at the ends, but iterators carry bookkeeping that can be rebuilt.
- `swap` on any container except `string` and `array`: no element handle is invalidated; iterators keep pointing to the same elements, which now live in the **other** container. The `end()` iterator may be invalidated.
- Moving a container (`std::vector<int> b = std::move(a);`): in practice the buffer or nodes are stolen, so iterators into `a` now refer to elements of `b`.
  - An explicit guarantee (move construction, and move assignment when the allocator propagates; never for `array`) is proposed in LWG 2321, which is still an **open** issue. Today it rests on the general [container.reqmts] wording and on what every implementation does.
  - `std::string` is not covered: a short (SSO) string is copied on move, so its iterators do not follow.

subsections.title: 7. vector rules in detail
subsections.content:
- Reallocation (new size > capacity): every iterator, pointer and reference is invalid; the old buffer is freed.
- `push_back` / `emplace_back` without reallocation:
  - All iterators, pointers and references **to elements** stay valid.
  - **Only `end()`** is invalidated: it used to be past-the-end, now it would point at the new element.
- `insert(pos, x)` without reallocation:
  - Elements before `pos`: valid.
  - Elements at and after `pos`: invalid. The memory is still there, but every element shifted one slot right, so a stale pointer now reads the element that used to be before it.
- `erase(pos)`: elements after `pos` shift left; everything at or after `pos` (including `end()`) is invalid. `capacity()` does not change.
- `erase` returns an iterator to the element that followed the erased one (or `end()`); `insert` returns an iterator to the inserted element. Always continue from the returned iterator.
- Growth policy, `reserve` and `emplace` are topic 05; this topic only states what they invalidate.

subsections.title: 8. Safe patterns for erasing while iterating
9. Range-for hides two iterators
10. reverse_iterator and base()
subsections.content:
- `std::reverse_iterator` stores a forward iterator `base()` that points **one past** the element it refers to: `*rit` is `*std::prev(rit.base())`.
- This is why `rbegin().base() == end()` and `rend().base() == begin()`, and why reverse ranges need no "before begin" position.
- Erasing through a reverse iterator: `v.erase(std::next(rit).base())`. Passing `rit.base()` directly erases the **next** element in forward order (off by one).
- To keep iterating in reverse after the erase: `rit = std::reverse_iterator(v.erase(std::next(rit).base()));`.

subsections.title: 11. Tools that catch invalid iterators
subsections.content:
| Tool | Catches | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` (libstdc++ debug mode) | Dereferencing, incrementing or comparing singular iterators; iterators from the wrong container; invalid ranges | Stale old `end()` after `push_back` without reallocation (not flagged in GCC 11). Changes the ABI: build every translation unit with it |
| `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` | Cheap precondition checks: `operator[]` out of range, `front()` on empty | Does not track iterator validity at all |
| `-fsanitize=address` | Use after reallocation (heap-use-after-free), out-of-bounds | Insert or erase without reallocation (memory still valid) |
| ASan + `-D_GLIBCXX_SANITIZE_VECTOR` | Reads between `size()` and `capacity()` (container-overflow) | Shifted elements |
- Debug mode is slow (iterators keep a link to their container); run it in tests and CI, not in production builds.

subsections.title: 12. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "If there is no reallocation, all iterators stay valid." ✅ Insert and erase still invalidate everything at or after the position, and `push_back` invalidates `end()`.
- ❌ "The pointer still points into allocated memory, so it is valid." ✅ Validity is defined by the operation, not by the address. After a shifting insert it reads a different element.
- ❌ "Comparing an invalid iterator with `end()` is harmless." ✅ Any use other than assignment or destruction is UB.
- ❌ "`deque::pop_front()` invalidates all iterators because the structure changed." ✅ Erasing at either end invalidates only the erased element (and `end()` for `pop_back`).
- ❌ "deque `push_back` keeps iterators valid, like references." ✅ References and pointers survive; iterators do not.
- ❌ "Erasing from a `std::map` invalidates the iterators after it." ✅ Only the erased node's iterators die.
- ❌ "unordered_map rehash invalidates references." ✅ Only iterators; nodes do not move.
- ❌ "`std::advance(it, n)` is O(1)." ✅ Only for random access iterators.
- ❌ "`const iterator` means read-only access." ✅ That is `const_iterator`; a `const iterator` cannot move but can still write.
- ❌ "ASan will catch any stale iterator." ✅ It only sees freed or out-of-bounds memory; shifted elements look valid to it.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- An iterator is a **position** inside a container, generalized from a pointer: `*it` reads the element, `++it` moves to the next position.
- Every range is **half-open**: `[begin, end)`. `end()` is one past the last element; it is a valid iterator but it is **not dereferenceable**.
- An iterator can be in one of three states:
  - **Dereferenceable**: points at a live element.
  - **Past-the-end**: `end()`; may be compared and decremented (if bidirectional), never dereferenced.
  - **Invalid (singular)**: the container changed in a way that broke it. Using it is undefined behaviour.
- "Invalidated" applies to three different handles, and the rules differ per handle:
  - **Iterators** (including `end()`).
  - **Pointers** to elements (`&v[2]`).
  - **References** to elements (`int& r = v[2]`).
- An iterator becomes invalid for one of three reasons:
  - **Storage moved**: the elements were copied or moved to a new buffer (vector or string reallocation).
  - **Position shifted**: the element at that position is now a different element (vector insert or erase without reallocation).
  - **Bookkeeping changed**: the element did not move, but the iterator's internal data did (deque block map, unordered bucket array).
- The rule that keeps you safe: **a mutating call can invalidate; check the rule for that container and that operation**. "It still prints the right value" proves nothing.

#### 2. What you may and may not do with an invalid iterator
- Allowed: assign a new value to it, or destroy it.
- Undefined behaviour: dereference, increment, decrement, **and even compare** it (`it == v.end()` on an invalid `it` is UB).
- Invalid does not mean "points to freed memory":
  - After a vector insert without reallocation, a stale pointer still points into live storage, but at a different element.
  - The standard still calls it invalid, so the program has no defined meaning. Treat "address unchanged" as an observation, not a guarantee.
- Pointers and references follow the same logic: after the invalidating operation they must not be read.

#### 3. Iterator categories
| Category | Adds | Containers / sources | Example algorithms |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | single pass read | `istream_iterator` | `std::find`, `std::accumulate` |
| Output | single pass write | `back_inserter`, `ostream_iterator` | `std::copy` destination |
| Forward | multi-pass | `forward_list`, unordered containers | `std::search`, `std::adjacent_find` |
| Bidirectional | `--it` | `list`, `map`, `set` | `std::reverse`, `std::prev` |
| Random access | `it + n`, `it[n]`, `<`, `it2 - it1` in O(1) | `deque` | `std::sort`, `std::nth_element` |
| Contiguous (C++20) | elements adjacent in memory | `vector` (not `vector<bool>`), `array`, `string`, `span`, raw pointers | `std::to_address(it)`, `memcpy` |
- Each category is a superset of the previous one; an algorithm states the weakest category it needs.
- `std::sort` needs random access, so `std::sort(l.begin(), l.end())` on a `std::list` does not compile. Use `l.sort()`.
- C++20 expresses the categories as concepts (`std::random_access_iterator<It>`, `std::contiguous_iterator<It>`), so generic code can constrain on them instead of relying on tag dispatch.
- `deque` is random access but **not** contiguous: O(1) indexing does not imply adjacent storage (see topic 07).
- `it + 2` moves by **elements**, not bytes; `it[1]` is `*(it + 1)`.

#### 4. advance, next, prev, distance
| Operation | Random access | Bidirectional / forward |
|---|---|---|
| `std::advance(it, n)` | O(1) | O(n) |
| `std::next(it, n)` / `std::prev(it, n)` | O(1) | O(n) (prev needs bidirectional) |
| `std::distance(first, last)` | O(1) | O(n) |
| `it += n`, `it + n` | O(1) | does not compile |
- `std::advance` modifies its argument and returns `void`; `std::next` returns a copy. Prefer `std::next` in expressions.
- Advancing past `end()` is UB; none of these functions checks bounds.
- `std::ranges::next(it, n, bound)` (C++20) stops at `bound` instead of running off the end.
- Interview point: generic code that uses `std::advance` compiles for a `list`, but silently turns O(1) into O(n). Constrain the template with the category it really needs.

#### 5. const_iterator versus const iterator
| Declaration | `*it = x` | `++it` |
|---|---|---|
| `std::vector<int>::iterator it` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `const std::vector<int>::iterator it` | ✅ (the iterator is const, not the element) | ❌ |
| `std::vector<int>::const_iterator it` | ❌ | ✅ |
| `const std::vector<int>::const_iterator it` | ❌ | ❌ |
- Same rule as `int* const p` versus `const int* p`.
- `cbegin()`/`cend()` (C++11) give `const_iterator` even on a non-const container.
- `iterator` converts implicitly to `const_iterator`, not the other way.
- Since C++11, `insert` and `erase` accept `const_iterator` positions, so read-only code can still hold the position it later erases.

#### 6. The invalidation table (the core of the topic)
| Container | Insert | Erase | Other |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vector` | Reallocation: **all**. Otherwise: everything **at or after** the insertion point, including `end()` | Everything **at or after** the erased element, including `end()` | `reserve(n)`: all if `n > capacity()`, none otherwise. `clear()`, assignment: all. `pop_back`: erased element and `end()` |
| `string` | Same as vector, plus: any non-const member call except `operator[]`, `at`, `data`, `front`, `back`, `begin`, `end` (and `r` variants) **may** invalidate | Same | `swap` of strings **may** invalidate (SSO buffer lives inside the object); see topic 01 |
| `deque` | At either end: **all iterators**, **no** references or pointers. In the middle: **all** iterators, references, pointers | First or last element: only the erased elements (plus `end()` when erasing the last). In the middle: **all** | `shrink_to_fit`: all |
| `list`, `forward_list` | **None** | Only the erased elements | `splice`, `sort`, `merge`, `reverse`: none (spliced iterators now belong to the destination list) |
| `map`, `set`, `multimap`, `multiset` | **None** | Only the erased elements | `extract`: only the extracted element's iterators |
| `unordered_*` | If it causes a rehash: **all iterators**, **no** references or pointers. Otherwise none | Only the erased elements | `rehash`/`reserve`: all iterators. Details in topic 09 |
| `array` | n/a | n/a | Never invalidated while the array lives |
- Three groups to remember:
  - **Contiguous** (`vector`, `string`): elements move, so the rules depend on capacity and position.
  - **Node-based** (`list`, `forward_list`, ordered and unordered associative): elements never move; only the erased element dies.
  - **Mixed** (`deque`, unordered rehash): elements never move at the ends, but iterators carry bookkeeping that can be rebuilt.
- `swap` on any container except `string` and `array`: no element handle is invalidated; iterators keep pointing to the same elements, which now live in the **other** container. The `end()` iterator may be invalidated.
- Moving a container (`std::vector<int> b = std::move(a);`): in practice the buffer or nodes are stolen, so iterators into `a` now refer to elements of `b`.
  - An explicit guarantee (move construction, and move assignment when the allocator propagates; never for `array`) is proposed in LWG 2321, which is still an **open** issue. Today it rests on the general [container.reqmts] wording and on what every implementation does.
  - `std::string` is not covered: a short (SSO) string is copied on move, so its iterators do not follow.

#### 7. vector rules in detail
- Reallocation (new size > capacity): every iterator, pointer and reference is invalid; the old buffer is freed.
- `push_back` / `emplace_back` without reallocation:
  - All iterators, pointers and references **to elements** stay valid.
  - **Only `end()`** is invalidated: it used to be past-the-end, now it would point at the new element.
- `insert(pos, x)` without reallocation:
  - Elements before `pos`: valid.
  - Elements at and after `pos`: invalid. The memory is still there, but every element shifted one slot right, so a stale pointer now reads the element that used to be before it.
- `erase(pos)`: elements after `pos` shift left; everything at or after `pos` (including `end()`) is invalid. `capacity()` does not change.
- `erase` returns an iterator to the element that followed the erased one (or `end()`); `insert` returns an iterator to the inserted element. Always continue from the returned iterator.
- Growth policy, `reserve` and `emplace` are topic 05; this topic only states what they invalidate.

#### 8. Safe patterns for erasing while iterating
| Pattern | Use when | Complexity (vector) |
|---|---|---|
| `std::erase_if(v, pred)` (C++20) | Remove all elements matching a predicate | O(n) |
| `v.erase(std::remove_if(...), v.end())` | Same, before C++20 | O(n) |
| `it = c.erase(it); else ++it;` | Node containers, or you need side effects per erased element | vector: O(n) per erase, O(n²) total |
| Iterate by index backwards | Removing from a vector with simple index logic | O(n) per erase |
| Collect keys, erase after the loop | The loop body calls code that might also modify the container | depends |
- The canonical loop:
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <list>

int main() {
    std::list<int> l{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};
    for (auto it = l.begin(); it != l.end(); ) {
        if (*it % 2 == 0)
            it = l.erase(it);   // erase returns the next element
        else
            ++it;               // advance only when nothing was erased
    }
    for (int x : l) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';          // 1 3 5
}
```
- Two classic bugs: `l.erase(it); ++it;` (increments an invalid iterator) and `it = l.erase(it);` followed by the loop's own `++it` (skips the next element, and runs past `end()` if the erased element was the last).
- `std::remove_if` does not shrink the container: it moves the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end; the tail holds valid but unspecified values until `erase` removes them.

#### 9. Range-for hides two iterators
- `for (auto& x : v) body;` is defined as:
```cpp
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
    {
        auto&& range = v;
        auto first = range.begin();
        auto last = range.end();         // computed ONCE, before the first iteration
        for (; first != last; ++first) {
            auto& x = *first;
            x *= 2;                      // body
        }
    }
}
```
- Any body statement that invalidates `first` or `last` is UB: `push_back`, `insert`, `erase`, `clear` on the same container.
- Even when a `reserve` prevents reallocation, `last` is the stale old `end()`, so the code is still UB.
- Rule: never change the size of the container you are range-for looping over. Use an index loop or build a separate container.

#### 10. reverse_iterator and base()
- `std::reverse_iterator` stores a forward iterator `base()` that points **one past** the element it refers to: `*rit` is `*std::prev(rit.base())`.
- This is why `rbegin().base() == end()` and `rend().base() == begin()`, and why reverse ranges need no "before begin" position.
- Erasing through a reverse iterator: `v.erase(std::next(rit).base())`. Passing `rit.base()` directly erases the **next** element in forward order (off by one).
- To keep iterating in reverse after the erase: `rit = std::reverse_iterator(v.erase(std::next(rit).base()));`.

#### 11. Tools that catch invalid iterators
| Tool | Catches | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` (libstdc++ debug mode) | Dereferencing, incrementing or comparing singular iterators; iterators from the wrong container; invalid ranges | Stale old `end()` after `push_back` without reallocation (not flagged in GCC 11). Changes the ABI: build every translation unit with it |
| `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` | Cheap precondition checks: `operator[]` out of range, `front()` on empty | Does not track iterator validity at all |
| `-fsanitize=address` | Use after reallocation (heap-use-after-free), out-of-bounds | Insert or erase without reallocation (memory still valid) |
| ASan + `-D_GLIBCXX_SANITIZE_VECTOR` | Reads between `size()` and `capacity()` (container-overflow) | Shifted elements |
- Debug mode is slow (iterators keep a link to their container); run it in tests and CI, not in production builds.

#### 12. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "If there is no reallocation, all iterators stay valid." ✅ Insert and erase still invalidate everything at or after the position, and `push_back` invalidates `end()`.
- ❌ "The pointer still points into allocated memory, so it is valid." ✅ Validity is defined by the operation, not by the address. After a shifting insert it reads a different element.
- ❌ "Comparing an invalid iterator with `end()` is harmless." ✅ Any use other than assignment or destruction is UB.
- ❌ "`deque::pop_front()` invalidates all iterators because the structure changed." ✅ Erasing at either end invalidates only the erased element (and `end()` for `pop_back`).
- ❌ "deque `push_back` keeps iterators valid, like references." ✅ References and pointers survive; iterators do not.
- ❌ "Erasing from a `std::map` invalidates the iterators after it." ✅ Only the erased node's iterators die.
- ❌ "unordered_map rehash invalidates references." ✅ Only iterators; nodes do not move.
- ❌ "`std::advance(it, n)` is O(1)." ✅ Only for random access iterators.
- ❌ "`const iterator` means read-only access." ✅ That is `const_iterator`; a `const iterator` cannot move but can still write.
- ❌ "ASan will catch any stale iterator." ✅ It only sees freed or out-of-bounds memory; shifted elements look valid to it.

edge_cases.title: Insert without reallocation still breaks positions at and after the insert
push_back without reallocation invalidates end()
edge_cases.explanation:
- People say "no reallocation, nothing is invalidated". The precise rule: element iterators survive, the old `end()` does not.
- A loop written with an `end()` captured before the `push_back` is UB.
- libstdc++ debug mode (GCC 11) does not flag this case, so tests may pass. Re-read `end()` after every size change.

edge_cases.title: Comparing an invalid iterator is already UB
edge_cases.explanation:
- `v.erase(it); if (it != v.end()) ...` is UB at the comparison, before any dereference.
- In debug mode the comparison itself aborts with "attempt to compare a singular iterator". In release builds it usually "works", which hides the bug.

edge_cases.title: deque: references survive push_back, iterators do not
unordered rehash: iterators die, references live
edge_cases.explanation:
- An insert that pushes the load factor over `max_load_factor()` triggers a rehash.
- Rehash rebuilds the bucket array and relinks nodes; nodes do not move. So pointers and references stay valid, iterators do not, and iteration order changes.
- Rule of thumb: never insert into an unordered container while iterating it. Bucket mechanics are topic 09.

edge_cases.title: swap keeps iterators, but they move to the other container
edge_cases.explanation:
- After `a.swap(b)`, an iterator taken from `a` still refers to the same element, which now belongs to `b`. Comparing it with `a.end()` is meaningless.
- Exceptions:
  - `std::string`: swap may invalidate (short strings live inside the object, so they really are copied).
  - `std::array`: swap exchanges the values element by element; an iterator still points into the same array and now sees the other array's old value.
  - `end()` iterators may be invalidated by swap for any container.

edge_cases.title: Range-for plus push_back
edge_cases.explanation:
- `for (int x : v) v.push_back(x);` looks like "duplicate the vector".
- The hidden `last` iterator is the old `end()`. On reallocation, `first` points into freed memory: ASan reports heap-use-after-free.
- With enough capacity reserved, it often appears to work, but the cached `end()` is invalid, so it is still UB.
- Fix: `v.insert(v.end(), v.begin(), v.end())` is also wrong (source range aliases the destination and is invalidated). Copy first, or index: `auto n = v.size(); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) v.push_back(v[i]);` (topic 05 explains why `push_back(v[i])` itself is safe).

edge_cases.title: reverse_iterator base() is off by one
edge_cases.explanation:
- `rit.base()` points to the element **after** `*rit` in forward order.
- `v.erase(rit.base())` therefore erases the wrong element, and if `rit == v.rbegin()` it passes `end()` to `erase`, which is UB.
- Correct: `v.erase(std::next(rit).base())`.

edge_cases.title: Views dangle exactly like iterators
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::span<int>`, `std::string_view` and C++20 range views hold pointers or iterators internally.
- They follow the same invalidation rules as the container's iterators: a `span` over a vector dangles after a reallocation, a `string_view` over a string dangles after a growing append (topic 02).

interview_qa.question: What does it mean for an iterator to be "invalidated", and what are you still allowed to do with it?
interview_qa.answer: An invalidated iterator no longer refers to the element (or position) it used to, because the container changed in a way the rules say breaks it. You may only assign a new value to it or destroy it; dereferencing, incrementing and even comparing it is undefined behaviour.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The same rules apply separately to iterators, pointers and references; each container states which of the three survive each operation.
- Three causes: storage moved (vector reallocation), position shifted (vector insert or erase), bookkeeping rebuilt (deque map, unordered buckets).
- Invalid does not mean "points to freed memory". After an insert without reallocation the address is fine, but it now names a different element.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's invalid only if the memory was freed." The standard defines validity per operation; reading a shifted slot is still UB.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: even `it == c.end()` on an invalid iterator is UB, and libstdc++ debug mode aborts on that comparison.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Invalid means "no defined meaning", not "no memory"; only assignment and destruction are allowed.

interview_qa.question: `v.push_back(x)` does not reallocate. Which iterators, pointers and references are invalidated?
interview_qa.answer: Only the past-the-end iterator. Every iterator, pointer and reference to an existing element stays valid. If `push_back` does reallocate, everything is invalidated.
interview_qa.explanation:

interview_qa.question: With spare capacity, you insert at the front of a vector. Is a pointer to `v[2]` taken before the insert still valid?
interview_qa.answer: No. Without reallocation, `insert` invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference at or after the insertion point. The pointer still points into the vector's buffer, but slot 2 now holds what used to be `v[1]`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Elements before the insertion point stay valid; elements at or after it shift right by one.
- In practice the stale pointer reads the neighbouring value, so the bug produces wrong data, not a crash. ASan cannot detect it because the memory is still owned.
- Same for `erase`: everything at or after the erased position is invalid, including `end()`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Valid, the address didn't change." Address stability is not validity.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's invalid because the value changed." Right conclusion, wrong reason: it is invalid because the standard says so for that operation, whatever value it reads.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `insert` returns an iterator to the new element; continue from that, not from the old one.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Insert and erase invalidate from the position onwards even when no memory moves.

interview_qa.question: How do you catch iterator invalidation bugs, and what can each tool not see?

interview_qa.explanation:

- GCC 11 debug mode does not flag a stale `end()` after `push_back` without reallocation.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "ASan catches all iterator bugs." It catches memory errors, not logical invalidation.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: run unit tests in both debug mode and ASan builds in CI; they are complementary.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Debug mode checks the rules; ASan checks the memory; you need both.

interview_qa.question: A component keeps pointers to objects in a `std::vector` that keeps growing, and crashes appear after growth. How do you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: Stop handing out pointers into storage that relocates. - ✅ What a strong answer adds: name the trade-off: stable addresses cost locality; indices keep locality but need care on erase.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
(A) is well defined and prints 1.
(B) is undefined behaviour: last is the old end(), invalidated by push_back. In practice it prints 123.
```

**Explanation:**
- `push_back` without reallocation keeps every element iterator valid, so `first` is fine.
- It invalidates the past-the-end iterator: `last` no longer has a defined meaning, so comparing with it is UB.
- In practice the old `end()` equals the address of the new element, so the loop stops before 4. That "works" result is why the bug is hard to see.
- libstdc++ debug mode (GCC 11) does not flag this case either.
- **Key Concept:** `push_back` without reallocation invalidates exactly one thing: `end()`. Never cache it across a size change.

practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: it and the end() it is compared with come from two different
temporary vectors, and both temporaries are already destroyed.
In our run (GCC 11, -O0) it printed three garbage numbers, e.g. "-1847767897 5 -69165601".

practice_tasks.explanation:
- `ports()` returns by value, so every call makes a new vector. `cfg.ports().begin()` is an iterator into a temporary that dies at the end of the init statement: `it` is dangling before the first test.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
30 20 40 2
```

**Explanation:**
- `it + 2` moves by elements, not bytes: `*it` is `v[2]`.
- `it[1]` means `*(it + 1)`, relative to `it`, not to `begin()`: 40, not 30.
- `v.end() - it` is the number of elements from `it` to the end: 2.
- All of this needs random access iterators; on a `std::list` only `*it` would compile.
- **Key Concept:** Random access iterators support pointer arithmetic in element units; `it[n]` is relative to `it`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Does not compile. Only "++it;" fails:
error: passing 'const iterator' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers
```

**Explanation:**
- `const iterator` makes the iterator object constant: it cannot be moved, but it still yields `int&`, so `*it = 5` compiles.
- `std::vector<int>::const_iterator` is the opposite: `++it` compiles, `*it = 5` fails.
- Same as `int* const p` versus `const int* p`.
- **Key Concept:** `const iterator` fixes the position; `const_iterator` makes the element read-only. Use `cbegin()` for read-only iteration.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: after 50, it += 2 jumps to begin() + 6, one past end(), so
it != v.end() is never false. In our run it printed "10 30 50" followed by
thousands of garbage numbers, then crashed with a segmentation fault.
-fsanitize=address: "heap-buffer-overflow ... 4 bytes to the right of 20-byte region".
-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG: "attempt to advance a dereferenceable iterator 2 steps, which falls
outside its valid range".
```

**Explanation:**
- An iterator may only move inside `[begin(), end()]`. Forming `begin() + 6` on a 5-element vector is already UB, before any dereference (same rule as pointer arithmetic past one-past-the-end).
- With an even size the loop lands exactly on `end()` and "works", so the bug appears only for odd sizes.
- `std::next(it, 2)` and `std::advance(it, 2)` have the same problem: they do not check bounds.
- Writing `it < v.end()` usually stops the loop in practice, but `begin() + 6` is still formed, so it is still UB (and `<` does not compile for list iterators).
- **Key Concept:** Strided loops must check the remaining distance before stepping; `!=` only works when every step can land on `end()`.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); i += 2)      // index check, no overshoot
        std::cout << v[i] << ' ';
    // iterator form: if (v.end() - it <= 2) break; else it += 2;
    std::cout << '\n';                                 // 10 30 50
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
1 7
true true
```

**Explanation:**
- `vector::swap` exchanges the internal pointers; no element moves. `vit` still refers to the element 1, which now belongs to `vb`.
- `array::swap` cannot exchange buffers (the elements live inside the object), so it swaps the values one by one. `ait` still points into `aa`, which now holds 7, 8, 9.
- The same split applies to `std::string`: short strings live inside the object, so string swap may invalidate.
- **Key Concept:** For heap-backed containers, swap moves ownership and iterators follow the elements; for `array` the iterator stays and the values change.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
The map loop is correct and prints "map: 2".
The vector loop is undefined behaviour. In practice (libstdc++) it prints "vector: 3": one of the 2s survives.
```

**Explanation:**
- `m.erase(it++)`: the post-increment moves `it` to the next node first, then the old position is erased. Map erase invalidates only the erased node, so `it` stays valid. This was the standard idiom before C++11 gave `map::erase` a return value.
- For a vector, erase invalidates everything at or after the erased position, which includes the already incremented `it`. Every later use is UB.
- In practice the incremented iterator now points one slot too far (elements shifted left), so the element after each erased one is skipped: the second 2 is never tested.
- `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` aborts on the first use of the stale iterator.
- **Key Concept:** `erase(it++)` is safe only for node containers. `it = c.erase(it)` is correct for every container.

quick_reference.content:
#### Invalidation summary
| Operation | vector / string | deque | list / forward_list | map / set | unordered |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insert at end, no realloc | `end()` only | all iterators, no refs | none | none | none (no rehash) |
| Insert causing realloc / rehash | all | n/a | n/a | n/a | all iterators, no refs |
| Insert in middle | at/after pos (or all if realloc) | all iterators and refs | none | none | n/a |
| Erase at end | erased + `end()` | erased + `end()` | erased only | erased only | erased only |
| Erase at front | everything (all shift) | erased only | erased only | erased only | erased only |
| Erase in middle | at/after pos | all | erased only | erased only | erased only |
| `clear()` | all | all | all | all | all |
| `swap` | none (string: may) | none (except `end()`) | none | none | none |

#### Safe idioms
| Goal | Code |
|---|---|
| Erase by predicate | `std::erase_if(c, pred);` (C++20, every container except `array`) |
| Erase in a loop | `it = c.erase(it);` else `++it;` |
| Erase via reverse iterator | `c.erase(std::next(rit).base());` |
| Advance generic iterator | `std::next(it, n)`, constrain on `std::random_access_iterator` if O(1) matters |
| Read-only iteration | `cbegin()`, `cend()`, `const auto&` |
| Handle that survives growth | index, stable id, node container, `vector<unique_ptr<T>>` |
| Catch stale iterators in tests | `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` (rules), ASan (freed memory only) |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What can you do with an invalid iterator? | Assign to it or destroy it; nothing else (even `==` is UB) |
| vector push_back, no reallocation: what dies? | Only `end()` |
| vector insert, no reallocation: what dies? | Everything at or after the insertion point |
| deque push_back: refs? iterators? | Refs and pointers valid; all iterators invalid |
| deque pop_front: what dies? | Only the erased element |
| list / map erase: what dies? | Only the erased element |
| unordered rehash: what dies? | Iterators; refs and pointers survive |
| Why `it != end()` and not `it < end()`? | `<` exists only for random access; `!=` works for every category |
| `std::advance` on a list? | O(n); `it + n` does not compile |
| `const iterator` vs `const_iterator`? | Fixed position vs read-only element |
| `rit.base()`? | Points one past `*rit` in forward order |
| Does swap invalidate? | No (except string, array values, and `end()`); iterators follow the elements |
| Range-for and push_back? | UB: hidden `begin`/`end` are cached |
