topics.topic: deque, list, forward_list, array and Adaptors

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- Every sequence container keeps elements in insertion order; they differ in **memory layout**, and the layout decides everything else: cost of each operation, what invalidates, and cache behaviour.
- Four layouts:
  - **One contiguous heap buffer**: `vector` (topic 05), `string` (topic 01).
  - **Contiguous storage inside the object**: `std::array`, C++26 `std::inplace_vector`.
  - **Fixed-size blocks plus a map of block pointers**: `std::deque`.
  - **One heap node per element**: `std::list` (doubly linked), `std::forward_list` (singly linked).
- Adaptors (`stack`, `queue`, `priority_queue`) are not containers: they wrap one and expose a restricted interface.
- Default choice is `std::vector`. Reach for the others only for a concrete reason: growth at the front, stable element addresses, O(1) splicing, or a size fixed at compile time.

subsections.title: 2. std::deque: layout
subsections.content:
- A deque is an array of pointers (the **map**) to fixed-size **blocks**; elements live in the blocks.
- Block size is implementation-defined. libstdc++ (GCC, x86-64): 512 bytes per block when `sizeof(T) < 512`, otherwise one element per block. So 128 `int`s or 16 `std::string`s per block.
- Because all blocks (except the partly filled first and last) have the same size, `d[i]` is plain arithmetic: block = `(offset + i) / per_block`, slot = `(offset + i) % per_block`. That is O(1) random access **without** contiguity.
- `push_back`/`push_front`:
  - Constant time, exactly one element constructed, no existing element is moved or copied.
  - When the end block is full, a new block is allocated; when the map is full, the map (only the block pointers) is reallocated or recentered.
- `insert`/`erase` in the middle: linear in the distance to the **nearer** end, O(min(i, n - i)), because the deque shifts whichever side is shorter.
- No `capacity()` and no `reserve()`. `shrink_to_fit()` exists (non-binding).
- Costs to know (libstdc++, x86-64): `sizeof(std::deque<T>)` is 80 bytes, and even an empty deque allocates (the map plus one block). A `vector<deque<int>>` of many small deques wastes a lot of memory.
- No `data()`: you cannot pass a deque's elements to a C API expecting a contiguous array.

subsections.title: 3. std::deque: invalidation (why it is asymmetric)
subsections.content:
- Insert at either end: **all iterators invalid, all references and pointers valid**.
  - Elements never move, so references stay valid.
  - A deque iterator stores a pointer into the map (libstdc++: current element, block begin, block end, map slot). If the map is reallocated, that last pointer dangles; the standard therefore invalidates iterators on every end insertion.
- Erase at either end (`pop_front`, `pop_back`): only the erased element (and `end()` for the back).
- Insert or erase in the middle: everything.
- Full container comparison table: topic 06.
- Practical consequence: a deque grown only at the ends is a valid choice when other code holds `T*` or `T&` to its elements and also needs indexing.

subsections.title: 4. std::list
subsections.content:
- Doubly linked list: each element is a separate heap node with `prev` and `next` pointers.
  - libstdc++, x86-64: node for `list<int>` is 24 bytes (16 bytes of links + `int` + padding), plus the allocator's own per-allocation overhead.
  - `sizeof(std::list<int>)` is 24 bytes (sentinel node links + size). An empty list does not allocate.
- Operations:
  - `insert(pos, x)` inserts **before** `pos`, O(1), returns an iterator to the new element.
  - `erase(pos)` O(1), returns the next iterator.
  - `size()` is O(1) since C++11 (it was allowed to be O(n) before, to keep range `splice` O(1)).
  - Finding the position is O(n): "O(1) insertion" only helps if you already hold an iterator.
- `splice` moves nodes between lists without copying or allocating:
  - Whole list or a single element: O(1).
  - A range from **another** list: O(n) in the range length (the sizes must be updated). Within the same list: O(1).
  - Iterators and references to moved elements stay valid and now refer into the destination list.
- Member algorithms, because the generic ones need random access or would copy:
  - `sort()`: stable merge sort, O(n log n), relinks nodes; no iterator is invalidated.
  - `merge(other)`: both sorted; stable; `other` becomes empty.
  - `unique()`: removes **consecutive** duplicates.
  - `remove(v)`, `remove_if(p)`: unlink matching nodes; return the count since C++20.
  - `reverse()`: relinks.
- Iteration is pointer chasing: each step is a dependent load to an address the prefetcher cannot predict. A list traversal is typically several times slower than a vector traversal of the same size.

subsections.title: 5. std::forward_list
subsections.content:
- Singly linked, designed to have zero overhead over a hand-written C list: `sizeof(std::forward_list<int>)` is 8 bytes (one pointer, libstdc++), node is 16 bytes for `int`.
- No `size()` (keeping it would cost space), no `push_back`, no `--it`.
- Everything happens **after** a position, because a node can only change its successor:
  - `insert_after`, `emplace_after`, `erase_after`, `splice_after`.
  - `before_begin()` returns a position before the first element, so you can insert or erase at the front with the same API.
- To remove nodes while iterating, keep a `prev` iterator and call `erase_after(prev)`, or use `remove_if`.
- Use cases: intrusive-style free lists, hash bucket chains, very memory-tight node lists. Rare in application code.

subsections.title: 6. std::array
subsections.content:
- `template<class T, std::size_t N> struct array`: an **aggregate** wrapping `T[N]`. No heap, no pointer: the elements are inside the object, so `sizeof(std::array<int, 4>)` is 16.
- What it adds over a C array:
  - Does not decay to a pointer; can be copied, assigned, compared (`==`, `<`, `<=>` since C++20), and returned by value.
  - `size()`, iterators, `at()` with bounds checking, `fill()`, `swap()`.
  - Usable in `constexpr` code (most members `constexpr` since C++17, all since C++20).
- Initialization follows aggregate rules:
  - `std::array<int, 3> a;` default-initializes: in a function, the ints hold **indeterminate** values.
  - `std::array<int, 3> a{};` zero-initializes. `std::array<int, 3> a{1};` gives `1, 0, 0`.
- `std::to_array` (C++20) deduces N from a C array or a braced list: `auto a = std::to_array({1, 2, 3});`. CTAD also works: `std::array a{1, 2, 3};` (C++17).
- `swap` is O(N): elements are exchanged one by one; iterators keep pointing into the same array (topic 06).
- `std::array<T, 0>` is allowed: `begin() == end()`, and `front()`/`back()` are UB.
- Large `std::array` locals live on the stack; a 1 MB array in a function risks stack overflow.

subsections.title: 7. Container adaptors
subsections.content:
| Adaptor | Default container | Required operations | Interface |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::stack<T, C>` | `deque<T>` | `back`, `push_back`, `pop_back` | `push`, `pop`, `top` |
| `std::queue<T, C>` | `deque<T>` | `front`, `back`, `push_back`, `pop_front` | `push`, `pop`, `front`, `back` |
| `std::priority_queue<T, C, Cmp>` | `vector<T>`, `std::less<T>` | random access iterators, `front`, `push_back`, `pop_back` | `push`, `pop`, `top` |
- No iterators: you cannot loop over an adaptor. If you need to, use the underlying container directly.
- `pop()` returns `void`. Reason: returning the removed element by value could throw while copying it, after the element was already removed, losing it. Read `top()`/`front()`, then `pop()`.
- `stack<int, std::vector<int>>` works (vector has `push_back`/`pop_back`). `queue<int, std::vector<int>>` compiles until you call `pop()`, which needs `pop_front`.
- `priority_queue`:
  - A binary heap stored in the vector (`std::push_heap`/`std::pop_heap`): `push` and `pop` are O(log n), `top` O(1).
  - With `std::less` (default), `top()` is the **largest** element: a max-heap. The comparator means "lower priority than", so `std::greater<T>` gives a min-heap.
  - Not stable: equal-priority elements come out in unspecified order. Add a sequence number to the key for FIFO among equals.
  - `top()` returns `const T&`: you cannot move out of it without a `const_cast` trick; no decrease-key operation.
  - The underlying container is the protected member `c`, reachable from a derived class.
- C++23 adds iterator-pair and range constructors to `stack` and `queue`.

subsections.title: 8. Choosing a sequence container
subsections.content:
| Need | Choose | Why |
|---|---|---|
| General purpose, iteration, random access | `vector` | Contiguous, cache friendly, smallest overhead |
| Size fixed at compile time | `array` | No heap, constexpr friendly |
| Bounded size, no heap, size varies | `inplace_vector` (C++26) or a fixed-capacity vector type | Storage inside the object |
| Push/pop at both ends, indexing | `deque` | O(1) at ends, no element moves |
| FIFO queue of unknown length | `queue` over `deque`, or a ring buffer | Ring buffer if bounded and latency matters |
| Stable addresses with indexing | `deque` (ends only) or `vector<unique_ptr<T>>` | Elements never move |
| O(1) insert/erase/splice at known positions, iterators must survive | `list` | Node based |
| Minimal memory node list | `forward_list` | One pointer per node |
| Top-k, scheduling by priority | `priority_queue` | Binary heap |
- For small and medium N, a vector with an O(n) shift usually beats a list with an O(1) relink, because the shift is a sequential `memmove` and the list walk is a chain of cache misses.
- Measure before choosing a node container for speed; choose it for semantics (stable iterators, splice).

subsections.title: 9. Newer containers (C++23/26 notes)
subsections.content:
- `std::inplace_vector<T, N>` (C++26): vector interface, capacity N fixed, storage inside the object.
  - `push_back` on a full container throws `std::bad_alloc`; `try_push_back` returns a null pointer instead; `unchecked_push_back` makes it a precondition.
  - Not in GCC 14's library yet; similar types exist in many code bases as `static_vector` or `fixed_vector`.
- `std::hive` (C++26, P0447): a bucket-based container with stable element addresses, O(1) insert and erase, and skipping of erased slots during iteration. Useful for object pools; standard library support is still arriving (not in GCC 14), and the reference implementation is the `plf::colony`/`plf::hive` library.
- `std::flat_map`/`flat_set` (C++23) are adaptors over sorted sequences; they belong to the associative family (topic 08).

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "deque is a vector that can also grow at the front." ✅ It is a block map: not contiguous, no `data()`, no `reserve()`, bigger fixed cost.
- ❌ "deque blocks have varying sizes." ✅ In real implementations they are fixed per element type (libstdc++: 512 bytes), which is what makes indexing O(1).
- ❌ "deque push_back may invalidate references like vector." ✅ References never move on end insertion; only iterators are invalidated.
- ❌ "list insertion is O(1), so list beats vector for inserts." ✅ Only with an iterator in hand, and the traversal to find it dominates.
- ❌ "`list::size()` is O(n)." ✅ O(1) since C++11.
- ❌ "`std::sort` works on any container." ✅ It needs random access iterators; use `list::sort`.
- ❌ "`std::array<int, 3> a;` is zero-filled." ✅ Only `a{}` is; plain `a` in a function is indeterminate.
- ❌ "`priority_queue` with `std::greater` is a max-heap." ✅ It is a min-heap; the default `less` gives a max-heap.
- ❌ "`queue::pop()` returns the element." ✅ It returns `void`; read `front()` first.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- Every sequence container keeps elements in insertion order; they differ in **memory layout**, and the layout decides everything else: cost of each operation, what invalidates, and cache behaviour.
- Four layouts:
  - **One contiguous heap buffer**: `vector` (topic 05), `string` (topic 01).
  - **Contiguous storage inside the object**: `std::array`, C++26 `std::inplace_vector`.
  - **Fixed-size blocks plus a map of block pointers**: `std::deque`.
  - **One heap node per element**: `std::list` (doubly linked), `std::forward_list` (singly linked).
- Adaptors (`stack`, `queue`, `priority_queue`) are not containers: they wrap one and expose a restricted interface.
- Default choice is `std::vector`. Reach for the others only for a concrete reason: growth at the front, stable element addresses, O(1) splicing, or a size fixed at compile time.

#### 2. std::deque: layout
- A deque is an array of pointers (the **map**) to fixed-size **blocks**; elements live in the blocks.
- Block size is implementation-defined. libstdc++ (GCC, x86-64): 512 bytes per block when `sizeof(T) < 512`, otherwise one element per block. So 128 `int`s or 16 `std::string`s per block.
- Because all blocks (except the partly filled first and last) have the same size, `d[i]` is plain arithmetic: block = `(offset + i) / per_block`, slot = `(offset + i) % per_block`. That is O(1) random access **without** contiguity.
- `push_back`/`push_front`:
  - Constant time, exactly one element constructed, no existing element is moved or copied.
  - When the end block is full, a new block is allocated; when the map is full, the map (only the block pointers) is reallocated or recentered.
- `insert`/`erase` in the middle: linear in the distance to the **nearer** end, O(min(i, n - i)), because the deque shifts whichever side is shorter.
- No `capacity()` and no `reserve()`. `shrink_to_fit()` exists (non-binding).
- Costs to know (libstdc++, x86-64): `sizeof(std::deque<T>)` is 80 bytes, and even an empty deque allocates (the map plus one block). A `vector<deque<int>>` of many small deques wastes a lot of memory.
- No `data()`: you cannot pass a deque's elements to a C API expecting a contiguous array.

#### 3. std::deque: invalidation (why it is asymmetric)
- Insert at either end: **all iterators invalid, all references and pointers valid**.
  - Elements never move, so references stay valid.
  - A deque iterator stores a pointer into the map (libstdc++: current element, block begin, block end, map slot). If the map is reallocated, that last pointer dangles; the standard therefore invalidates iterators on every end insertion.
- Erase at either end (`pop_front`, `pop_back`): only the erased element (and `end()` for the back).
- Insert or erase in the middle: everything.
- Full container comparison table: topic 06.
- Practical consequence: a deque grown only at the ends is a valid choice when other code holds `T*` or `T&` to its elements and also needs indexing.

#### 4. std::list
- Doubly linked list: each element is a separate heap node with `prev` and `next` pointers.
  - libstdc++, x86-64: node for `list<int>` is 24 bytes (16 bytes of links + `int` + padding), plus the allocator's own per-allocation overhead.
  - `sizeof(std::list<int>)` is 24 bytes (sentinel node links + size). An empty list does not allocate.
- Operations:
  - `insert(pos, x)` inserts **before** `pos`, O(1), returns an iterator to the new element.
  - `erase(pos)` O(1), returns the next iterator.
  - `size()` is O(1) since C++11 (it was allowed to be O(n) before, to keep range `splice` O(1)).
  - Finding the position is O(n): "O(1) insertion" only helps if you already hold an iterator.
- `splice` moves nodes between lists without copying or allocating:
  - Whole list or a single element: O(1).
  - A range from **another** list: O(n) in the range length (the sizes must be updated). Within the same list: O(1).
  - Iterators and references to moved elements stay valid and now refer into the destination list.
- Member algorithms, because the generic ones need random access or would copy:
  - `sort()`: stable merge sort, O(n log n), relinks nodes; no iterator is invalidated.
  - `merge(other)`: both sorted; stable; `other` becomes empty.
  - `unique()`: removes **consecutive** duplicates.
  - `remove(v)`, `remove_if(p)`: unlink matching nodes; return the count since C++20.
  - `reverse()`: relinks.
- Iteration is pointer chasing: each step is a dependent load to an address the prefetcher cannot predict. A list traversal is typically several times slower than a vector traversal of the same size.

#### 5. std::forward_list
- Singly linked, designed to have zero overhead over a hand-written C list: `sizeof(std::forward_list<int>)` is 8 bytes (one pointer, libstdc++), node is 16 bytes for `int`.
- No `size()` (keeping it would cost space), no `push_back`, no `--it`.
- Everything happens **after** a position, because a node can only change its successor:
  - `insert_after`, `emplace_after`, `erase_after`, `splice_after`.
  - `before_begin()` returns a position before the first element, so you can insert or erase at the front with the same API.
- To remove nodes while iterating, keep a `prev` iterator and call `erase_after(prev)`, or use `remove_if`.
- Use cases: intrusive-style free lists, hash bucket chains, very memory-tight node lists. Rare in application code.

#### 6. std::array
- `template<class T, std::size_t N> struct array`: an **aggregate** wrapping `T[N]`. No heap, no pointer: the elements are inside the object, so `sizeof(std::array<int, 4>)` is 16.
- What it adds over a C array:
  - Does not decay to a pointer; can be copied, assigned, compared (`==`, `<`, `<=>` since C++20), and returned by value.
  - `size()`, iterators, `at()` with bounds checking, `fill()`, `swap()`.
  - Usable in `constexpr` code (most members `constexpr` since C++17, all since C++20).
- Initialization follows aggregate rules:
  - `std::array<int, 3> a;` default-initializes: in a function, the ints hold **indeterminate** values.
  - `std::array<int, 3> a{};` zero-initializes. `std::array<int, 3> a{1};` gives `1, 0, 0`.
- `std::to_array` (C++20) deduces N from a C array or a braced list: `auto a = std::to_array({1, 2, 3});`. CTAD also works: `std::array a{1, 2, 3};` (C++17).
- `swap` is O(N): elements are exchanged one by one; iterators keep pointing into the same array (topic 06).
- `std::array<T, 0>` is allowed: `begin() == end()`, and `front()`/`back()` are UB.
- Large `std::array` locals live on the stack; a 1 MB array in a function risks stack overflow.

#### 7. Container adaptors
| Adaptor | Default container | Required operations | Interface |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::stack<T, C>` | `deque<T>` | `back`, `push_back`, `pop_back` | `push`, `pop`, `top` |
| `std::queue<T, C>` | `deque<T>` | `front`, `back`, `push_back`, `pop_front` | `push`, `pop`, `front`, `back` |
| `std::priority_queue<T, C, Cmp>` | `vector<T>`, `std::less<T>` | random access iterators, `front`, `push_back`, `pop_back` | `push`, `pop`, `top` |
- No iterators: you cannot loop over an adaptor. If you need to, use the underlying container directly.
- `pop()` returns `void`. Reason: returning the removed element by value could throw while copying it, after the element was already removed, losing it. Read `top()`/`front()`, then `pop()`.
- `stack<int, std::vector<int>>` works (vector has `push_back`/`pop_back`). `queue<int, std::vector<int>>` compiles until you call `pop()`, which needs `pop_front`.
- `priority_queue`:
  - A binary heap stored in the vector (`std::push_heap`/`std::pop_heap`): `push` and `pop` are O(log n), `top` O(1).
  - With `std::less` (default), `top()` is the **largest** element: a max-heap. The comparator means "lower priority than", so `std::greater<T>` gives a min-heap.
  - Not stable: equal-priority elements come out in unspecified order. Add a sequence number to the key for FIFO among equals.
  - `top()` returns `const T&`: you cannot move out of it without a `const_cast` trick; no decrease-key operation.
  - The underlying container is the protected member `c`, reachable from a derived class.
- C++23 adds iterator-pair and range constructors to `stack` and `queue`.

#### 8. Choosing a sequence container
| Need | Choose | Why |
|---|---|---|
| General purpose, iteration, random access | `vector` | Contiguous, cache friendly, smallest overhead |
| Size fixed at compile time | `array` | No heap, constexpr friendly |
| Bounded size, no heap, size varies | `inplace_vector` (C++26) or a fixed-capacity vector type | Storage inside the object |
| Push/pop at both ends, indexing | `deque` | O(1) at ends, no element moves |
| FIFO queue of unknown length | `queue` over `deque`, or a ring buffer | Ring buffer if bounded and latency matters |
| Stable addresses with indexing | `deque` (ends only) or `vector<unique_ptr<T>>` | Elements never move |
| O(1) insert/erase/splice at known positions, iterators must survive | `list` | Node based |
| Minimal memory node list | `forward_list` | One pointer per node |
| Top-k, scheduling by priority | `priority_queue` | Binary heap |
- For small and medium N, a vector with an O(n) shift usually beats a list with an O(1) relink, because the shift is a sequential `memmove` and the list walk is a chain of cache misses.
- Measure before choosing a node container for speed; choose it for semantics (stable iterators, splice).

#### 9. Newer containers (C++23/26 notes)
- `std::inplace_vector<T, N>` (C++26): vector interface, capacity N fixed, storage inside the object.
  - `push_back` on a full container throws `std::bad_alloc`; `try_push_back` returns a null pointer instead; `unchecked_push_back` makes it a precondition.
  - Not in GCC 14's library yet; similar types exist in many code bases as `static_vector` or `fixed_vector`.
- `std::hive` (C++26, P0447): a bucket-based container with stable element addresses, O(1) insert and erase, and skipping of erased slots during iteration. Useful for object pools; standard library support is still arriving (not in GCC 14), and the reference implementation is the `plf::colony`/`plf::hive` library.
- `std::flat_map`/`flat_set` (C++23) are adaptors over sorted sequences; they belong to the associative family (topic 08).

#### 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "deque is a vector that can also grow at the front." ✅ It is a block map: not contiguous, no `data()`, no `reserve()`, bigger fixed cost.
- ❌ "deque blocks have varying sizes." ✅ In real implementations they are fixed per element type (libstdc++: 512 bytes), which is what makes indexing O(1).
- ❌ "deque push_back may invalidate references like vector." ✅ References never move on end insertion; only iterators are invalidated.
- ❌ "list insertion is O(1), so list beats vector for inserts." ✅ Only with an iterator in hand, and the traversal to find it dominates.
- ❌ "`list::size()` is O(n)." ✅ O(1) since C++11.
- ❌ "`std::sort` works on any container." ✅ It needs random access iterators; use `list::sort`.
- ❌ "`std::array<int, 3> a;` is zero-filled." ✅ Only `a{}` is; plain `a` in a function is indeterminate.
- ❌ "`priority_queue` with `std::greater` is a max-heap." ✅ It is a min-heap; the default `less` gives a max-heap.
- ❌ "`queue::pop()` returns the element." ✅ It returns `void`; read `front()` first.

edge_cases.title: deque is random access but not contiguous
The fixed cost of an empty deque
edge_cases.explanation:
- libstdc++: `sizeof(std::deque<int>)` is 80 bytes and a default-constructed deque performs 2 allocations (the map and one block, 512 bytes).
- So `std::vector<std::deque<int>> per_key(100000);` costs over 50 MB before anything is stored. A `vector` (24 bytes, no allocation while empty) is far cheaper for many small sequences.
- Also: an implementation is allowed to throw from the default constructor of a deque (it allocates); `std::vector`'s default constructor is `noexcept`.

edge_cases.title: list::insert inserts before the iterator
edge_cases.explanation:
- `l.insert(it, x)` places `x` **before** `*it` and returns an iterator to `x`. `it` itself is unchanged and still refers to the same element.
- People who expect "insert after" get an off-by-one; to insert after, use `l.insert(std::next(it), x)`.
- `forward_list` is the opposite: it only offers `insert_after`.

edge_cases.title: Generic algorithms on a list
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::sort(l.begin(), l.end())` does not compile (needs random access): use `l.sort()`.
- `std::remove_if` on a list compiles but moves values around instead of unlinking nodes, and the list size is unchanged until you `erase`. `l.remove_if(pred)` unlinks and is what you want.
- `std::binary_search` and `std::lower_bound` on a list compile and are correct, but each step walks the list: O(n) traversal for O(log n) comparisons.

edge_cases.title: Splice moves iterators to another container
edge_cases.explanation:
- After `b.splice(b.end(), a, it)`, `it` is valid but belongs to `b`. Calling `a.erase(it)` is UB (wrong container); debug mode reports it.
- Splicing a range from a different list is O(n) because both sizes must be updated; whole-list and single-element splices are O(1).
- Splicing between lists with unequal allocators is UB.

edge_cases.title: forward_list has no size() and works "after"
edge_cases.explanation:
- `fl.size()` does not compile; `std::distance(fl.begin(), fl.end())` is O(n).
- `erase_after(pos)` erases the element **after** `pos`. To erase the first element, use `erase_after(fl.before_begin())` or `pop_front()`.
- `before_begin()` must not be dereferenced; it exists only as an argument for the `_after` functions.

edge_cases.title: std::array and initialization
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::array<int, 4> a;` inside a function holds indeterminate values; reading them is UB. Write `std::array<int, 4> a{};`.
- `std::array<std::string, 4> s;` is fine: class types are default-constructed.
- `std::array<int, 3> a = {1, 2, 3, 4};` does not compile (too many initializers); `{1, 2}` compiles and zero-fills the rest.
- `a[5]` is UB without a check; `a.at(5)` throws `std::out_of_range`.

edge_cases.title: priority_queue order and comparator direction
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::priority_queue<int>` returns the largest first. Many people write `std::greater<int>` expecting "greater first" and get the smallest first.
- The comparator answers "is a lower priority than b?". The element for which no other element compares greater ends up on `top()`.
- For a custom comparator on events, "earliest time first" therefore needs `a.time > b.time`.
- `top()` and `pop()` on an empty `priority_queue` are UB, not exceptions.

edge_cases.title: queue over vector fails only when you pop
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::queue<int, std::vector<int>> q; q.push(1);` compiles: member functions of a class template are instantiated only when used.
- `q.pop();` then fails: "'class std::vector<int>' has no member named 'pop_front'".
- `std::stack<int, std::vector<int>>` is fully valid and avoids the deque's fixed cost.

interview_qa.question: How is `std::deque` implemented, and how can `d[i]` be O(1) if the storage is not contiguous?
interview_qa.answer: A deque is a map (an array of pointers) to fixed-size blocks that hold the elements. Because every block has the same capacity, `d[i]` computes the block as `(start + i) / per_block` and the slot as `(start + i) % per_block`: two loads and some arithmetic, independent of `n`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Block size is implementation-defined; libstdc++ uses 512-byte blocks (128 `int`s), or one element per block when `sizeof(T) >= 512`.
- O(1) random access needs a constant-time address computation, not contiguity.
- Each access costs one more indirection than a vector (map slot, then block), and iteration has a branch at every block boundary.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Blocks grow like vector capacity (30, 50, 50, ...), so index math walks the blocks." Real implementations use one fixed block size; variable blocks would make indexing O(number of blocks).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the deque iterator is a "fat" iterator (libstdc++: four pointers) that knows its block's bounds, which is also why end insertion invalidates it (topic 06).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: deque = map of fixed-size blocks; index math replaces contiguity.

interview_qa.question: When would you choose `std::deque` over `std::vector`, and what does it cost?
interview_qa.answer: Choose deque when you need O(1) insertion or removal at **both** ends, or when elements must not move as the sequence grows at its ends (stable references with indexing). It costs an extra indirection per access, no contiguity (`data()` does not exist), a larger fixed size, and allocation even when empty.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Growing a vector copies or moves all elements on reallocation; growing a deque allocates a new block and at most copies block pointers.
- libstdc++ numbers: `sizeof(std::deque<int>) == 80`, and an empty deque allocates the map plus one 512-byte block. Many tiny deques are expensive.
- Vector is faster for iteration and lookup; deque wins for FIFO patterns (`push_back` + `pop_front`), which on a vector would be O(n) per pop.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "deque is always better because it can do everything vector can." It loses contiguity, is slower to traverse, and has a bigger footprint.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for a bounded FIFO in a latency-sensitive path, a fixed-capacity ring buffer beats both (one contiguous array, no allocation after start-up).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: deque buys two cheap ends and stable element addresses; it pays with indirection and fixed overhead.

interview_qa.question: When is `std::list` actually the right choice?
interview_qa.answer: When you need iterators and references that survive every other insertion and erasure, O(1) insert or erase at positions you already hold iterators to, or O(1) splicing of elements between lists. The LRU cache (list plus hash map of iterators) is the textbook case.
interview_qa.explanation:
- "O(1) insert" is only O(1) with an iterator in hand; finding the position is O(n) pointer chasing.
- Each element is a separate allocation (libstdc++: 24-byte node for `int`, plus allocator overhead), and traversal is a chain of cache misses.
- For "insert in the middle" workloads with small or medium N, a vector's `memmove` usually beats walking a list to the position.
- Memory allocation per node can be tamed with a pool allocator (Memory & Ownership chapter, pmr topic).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Use list whenever there are many insertions." Insertions that need a search first are dominated by the search.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: choose list for its semantics (stable iterators, splice), not for raw speed.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: list is a semantics choice (stability, splice), rarely a performance choice.

interview_qa.question: Both traversals are O(n). Why is iterating a `std::list` much slower than a `std::vector`?
interview_qa.answer: A vector traversal reads consecutive memory, so every cache line brings several elements and the hardware prefetcher runs ahead. A list traversal must load each node's `next` pointer before it knows the next address, so every step can be a cache miss that cannot be overlapped.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Nodes allocated at different times end up scattered across the heap; even freshly built lists lose locality after some inserts and erases.
- Each node also carries two pointers of overhead, so less useful data fits in cache.
- The dependent-load chain also blocks out-of-order execution: the CPU cannot start load k+1 before load k finishes.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Same Big-O, so same speed." Big-O hides the constant, and memory access dominates that constant.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: deeper cache discussion (lines, prefetching, TLB) belongs to the Systems chapter; the interview point is "locality beats asymptotics for realistic N".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Pointer chasing makes list traversal latency-bound; vector traversal is bandwidth-bound.

interview_qa.question: How do `std::array`, a C array and `std::vector` compare?

interview_qa.question: What values does `std::array<int, 4> a;` hold inside a function?

interview_qa.question: What are container adaptors, and why does `pop()` return `void`?

- Adaptors have no iterators; if you need to iterate, use the container directly.

interview_qa.question: What is `std::inplace_vector` (C++26), and when would you use it?
interview_qa.answer: `std::inplace_vector<T, N>` is a vector with a compile-time capacity N whose elements are stored inside the object, so it never allocates. Its size varies from 0 to N. Use it for small bounded collections in hot paths or where heap allocation is forbidden.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Unlike `std::array<T, N>`, only `size()` elements are constructed; unlike `vector`, `reserve` cannot grow it past N.
- Full-container behaviour: `push_back` throws `std::bad_alloc`, `try_push_back` returns a null pointer, `unchecked_push_back` has a precondition (UB if full).
- Moving it moves each element (no pointer steal), so move is O(size), not O(1).
- Not yet in GCC 14's library; many code bases have an equivalent (`static_vector`, `fixed_vector`, `small_vector` with fallback to heap).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's the same as `std::array`." Array always holds N constructed elements.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a small-buffer vector (inline up to N, heap after) is a different trade-off: no hard limit, but a branch and possible allocation.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: inplace_vector = vector interface, array storage, hard capacity.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
2 true true
```

**Explanation:**
- Insertion at either end of a deque never invalidates pointers or references: the element 2 stays at the same address through all 1000 `push_front` calls (several new blocks and map reallocations happen).
- Its **index** changes: 1000 elements were added in front, so it is now `d[1001]`.
- The same code with a `std::vector` and `insert(v.begin(), ...)` would invalidate `p` on the first insert.
- **Key Concept:** deque end insertion keeps element addresses stable; only iterators (and indices, by meaning) change.

practice_tasks.answer:
Does not compile. The essence of the GCC 11 error (inside std::sort):
error: no match for 'operator-' (operand types are 'std::_List_iterator<int>' and 'std::_List_iterator<int>')
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::sort` needs random access iterators (it computes `last - first` and jumps to midpoints). `list` iterators are bidirectional.
- `l.sort()` is the member merge sort: stable, O(n log n), relinks nodes, keeps all iterators valid.
- With `std::ranges::sort(l)` (C++20) the error message names the unsatisfied constraint (`random_access_range`) instead of failing deep inside the algorithm.
- **Key Concept:** The iterator category decides which algorithms are available; list compensates with member algorithms.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
First line is guaranteed: "000 700".
The second line reads an indeterminate value: undefined behaviour. In practice it printed a different garbage number on each run (for example 28710).
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::array` is an aggregate. `a` is default-initialized, and for `int` elements that means no initialization at all.
- `b{}` value-initializes every element to 0. `c{7}` sets the first element and value-initializes the rest.
- GCC 11 warns ("'a' is used uninitialized", `-Wuninitialized`) only with optimization (`-O2`), not at `-O0`; MemorySanitizer (Clang) reports it at run time.
- **Key Concept:** `std::array` follows C array initialization rules; write `{}` to get zeros.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
5 4 2 1 | 1 2 4 5 
```

**Explanation:**
- The comparator means "lower priority than". With the default `std::less`, the largest value has the highest priority: max-heap.
- With `std::greater`, a larger value counts as lower priority, so the smallest comes out first: min-heap.
- `pop()` returns `void`; reading requires `top()` first.
- **Key Concept:** `std::greater` in a priority_queue gives a min-heap, the opposite of what the name suggests.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Does not compile, because of q.pop():
error: 'class std::vector<int>' has no member named 'pop_front'
```

**Explanation:**
- `queue::pop()` is implemented as `c.pop_front()`. `std::vector` has no `pop_front` (it would be O(n)).
- Without the `pop()` line the program compiles: a class template member function is only instantiated when it is called.
- Valid choices: `std::queue<int>` (deque) or `std::queue<int, std::list<int>>`. A `std::stack` over a vector is fine.
- **Key Concept:** Adaptors require specific operations from their container, and the error appears only when the member that uses them is instantiated.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.answer: processed charlie
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `top()` returns a reference to the first element of the underlying vector. `pop()` runs `std::pop_heap` (which moves the top to the back and moves the next largest to the front) and then `pop_back()`.
- `next` still refers to slot 0 of the vector, which now holds the new top, "charlie". The intended value, "delta", was destroyed by `pop_back`.
- With the default vector container this reads a live object (not a crash, nothing for ASan to find), so it is a silent logic bug. Holding a reference across `pop()` is never correct.
- **Key Concept:** Copy or move the value out of `top()` before `pop()`; references into an adaptor do not survive modification.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
0 5 2 1
```

**Explanation:**
- Whole-list `splice` relinks all three nodes of `a` into `b` in O(1); `a` becomes empty.
- `it` is still valid and still refers to 2, but it now iterates `b`: `b` is `1 2 3 10 20`, and 2 is at distance 1.
- Using `it` with `a` (for example `a.erase(it)`) would now be UB.
- **Key Concept:** splice moves nodes, not values; iterators follow their nodes into the destination list.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: insertion in the middle of a deque invalidates all references.
In practice (libstdc++) it prints "50 50".
```

**Explanation:**
- The standard: an insert anywhere except at the two ends invalidates **all** iterators and references to deque elements.
- libstdc++ shifts whichever side is shorter. Inserting at index 1 moves only the element 10 one slot towards the front, so 50 happens to stay at its address and `r` still reads 50.
- Insert near the back instead (`d.begin() + 5`) and the back elements move: then `r` reads 99 in practice, a different element. Code that "works" depends on an implementation detail and on the position.
- **Key Concept:** Middle insertion in a deque invalidates every reference by the standard, even when the implementation happens not to move a given element.

quick_reference.content:
#### Complexity
| Operation | vector | deque | list | forward_list | array |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `c[i]` | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | n/a | O(1) |
| push/pop back | O(1) amortized | O(1) | O(1) | n/a | n/a |
| push/pop front | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | n/a |
| insert/erase middle (at iterator) | O(n) | O(min(i, n - i)) | O(1) | O(1) (`_after`) | n/a |
| `size()` | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) (C++11) | not provided | O(1), constexpr |
| Contiguous | yes | no | no | no | yes |
| Iterator category | contiguous | random access | bidirectional | forward | contiguous |

#### Implementation facts (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64; not guaranteed)
| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| deque block size | 512 bytes (128 `int`, 16 `std::string`); 1 element if `sizeof(T) >= 512` |
| `sizeof(std::deque<int>)` | 80 bytes; empty deque allocates map + 1 block |
| `sizeof(std::list<int>)` | 24 bytes; node 24 bytes |
| `sizeof(std::forward_list<int>)` | 8 bytes; node 16 bytes |
| `sizeof(std::priority_queue<int>)` | 32 bytes (vector + empty comparator, padded) |

#### Adaptor rules
| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| `pop()` return type | `void` (exception safety); read `top()`/`front()` first |
| Default containers | `stack`, `queue`: deque; `priority_queue`: vector |
| Default `priority_queue` | max-heap (`std::less`); `std::greater` = min-heap |
| Stability | `priority_queue` is not stable; add a sequence number |
| Iteration | Not supported; adaptors hide the container |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is deque contiguous? | No: blocks plus a map; each block is contiguous |
| Why is `d[i]` O(1)? | Fixed block size: index math is division and modulo |
| deque push_back: refs? iterators? | Refs valid; iterators invalid |
| Empty deque cost? | libstdc++: 80 bytes plus two allocations |
| `list::insert(it, x)`? | Inserts before `it`; `it` still points to the same element |
| `list::size()`? | O(1) since C++11 |
| Sort a list? | `l.sort()`; `std::sort` needs random access |
| splice cost? | O(1), except a range from another list: O(range) |
| forward_list size? | No `size()`; use `std::distance` (O(n)) |
| `std::array<int, 3> a;` values? | Indeterminate; use `a{}` |
| Min-heap? | `std::priority_queue<T, std::vector<T>, std::greater<T>>` |
| Why does `pop()` return void? | Returning by value could throw after removal and lose the element |
| list vs vector for inserts? | vector usually wins for small/medium N: memmove beats pointer chasing |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::set<K>` and `std::map<K, V>` keep their elements **sorted by a comparator** (`std::less<K>` by default) and allow at most one element per key. `multiset`/`multimap` allow equivalent keys.
- The standard fixes the interface and the complexities, not the data structure:
  - find, insert, erase by key: O(log n).
  - In-order iteration: O(n) total.
  - Insert and erase never invalidate iterators or references to other elements.
- Every major implementation uses a **red-black tree**: a self-balancing binary search tree where each node stores a colour and three pointers (parent, left, right).
  - libstdc++, x86-64: node header 32 bytes, so a `map<int, int>` node is 40 bytes plus allocator overhead; `sizeof(std::map<...>)` is 48 bytes.
  - Balancing: insert needs at most 2 rotations, erase at most 3, plus O(log n) recolouring in the worst case.
- `map<K, V>::value_type` is `std::pair<const K, V>`: the key cannot change while the element is in the tree, because changing it would break the ordering.
- A lookup walks from the root, one comparison and one pointer dereference per level. It is "binary search over a tree", not over an array: every step is a potential cache miss.

subsections.title: 2. Lookup API: find, contains, count, at, operator[]
subsections.content:
| Call | Missing key | Requirements | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `m.find(k)` | `m.end()` | none | iterator |
| `m.contains(k)` (C++20) | `false` | none | bool |
| `m.count(k)` | 0 | none | 0 or 1 (multimap: n) |
| `m.at(k)` | throws `std::out_of_range` | none | `V&` / `const V&` |
| `m[k]` | **inserts** `{k, V{}}` | non-const map, `V` default-constructible | `V&` |
- `operator[]` is "find or insert": reading a missing key with `m[k]` adds an element. Accidental inserts change `size()`, iteration output, and memory use.
- `operator[]` does not exist on a `const map` (it may modify), so `const` code is forced to use `find`/`at`.
- For a read-and-use, `find` gives both the existence check and the value in one O(log n) walk; `contains` followed by `at` does two walks.

subsections.title: 3. Insertion API
subsections.content:
| Call | Key exists | Key missing | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `insert({k, v})` | no change, returns `{it, false}` | inserts | The pair is built **before** the call, even if unused |
| `emplace(args...)` | no change | constructs in place | May construct the node (consuming the arguments) before finding the duplicate |
| `try_emplace(k, args...)` (C++17) | no change, **arguments untouched** | constructs `V(args...)` | Best "insert if absent" |
| `insert_or_assign(k, v)` (C++17) | assigns `v` | inserts | Returns `{it, inserted}`; unlike `m[k] = v`, no default construction of `V` |
| `m[k] = v` | assigns | default-constructs, then assigns | Needs default-constructible `V` |
| `insert(hint, x)`, `emplace_hint` | no change | inserts | Amortized O(1) if the element goes right before `hint` |
- `insert` and `emplace` return `std::pair<iterator, bool>`; the `bool` is the only way to know whether the insert happened.
- `emplace` when the key exists:
  - The standard allows constructing the node first, so arguments passed as rvalues may already be moved from.
  - Observed: libstdc++ GCC 11 moves the string out even when the key exists; GCC 13 and GCC 14 look the key up first and leave it intact. Do not rely on either; use `try_emplace`.
- Hint insertion: inserting sorted data with `m.emplace_hint(m.end(), k, v)` is O(n) overall instead of O(n log n).

subsections.title: 4. Ordered queries: lower_bound, upper_bound, equal_range
subsections.content:
- Defined through the comparator `comp`, not through `>=`:
  - `lower_bound(k)`: first element `e` with `!comp(e, k)`, "not ordered before k".
  - `upper_bound(k)`: first element `e` with `comp(k, e)`, "ordered after k".
  - `equal_range(k)`: the pair `{lower_bound(k), upper_bound(k)}`; for a unique-key container it has 0 or 1 elements.
- With the default `less`: lower_bound = first key `>= k`, upper_bound = first key `> k`.
- With `std::greater` (descending order): lower_bound = first key `<= k`. People who think "lower_bound means >=" get this wrong.
- Range query `[a, b)`: iterate from `lower_bound(a)` to `lower_bound(b)`. Inclusive `[a, b]`: up to `upper_bound(b)`.
- "Greatest key `<= k`" with default order: `auto it = m.upper_bound(k); if (it != m.begin()) --it;`.
- Use the **member** functions: `std::lower_bound(m.begin(), m.end(), ...)` does O(log n) comparisons but O(n) iterator steps, because map iterators are bidirectional.

subsections.title: 5. Comparators and strict weak ordering
subsections.content:
- The comparator must be a **strict weak ordering**:
  - Irreflexive: `comp(a, a)` is false.
  - Asymmetric: `comp(a, b)` implies `!comp(b, a)`.
  - Transitive: `comp(a, b) && comp(b, c)` implies `comp(a, c)`.
  - Transitivity of equivalence: if `a ~ b` and `b ~ c`, then `a ~ c`, where `a ~ b` means `!comp(a, b) && !comp(b, a)`.
- Associative containers never call `operator==`. Two keys are "the same" when they are **equivalent** under `comp`.
- "Weak" means distinct objects may be equivalent (orders sorted by price only: two orders at the same price are equivalent). It does not mean "allowed to use `<=`".
- Violations are UB (a precondition of the container and of `std::sort`), with concrete symptoms:
  - `a <= b` breaks irreflexivity: a set inserts duplicates and then cannot find them; `std::sort` can read past the end of the array.
  - Floating-point keys with NaN: NaN is equivalent to every number, which breaks transitivity of equivalence; lookups and inserts misbehave.
  - Comparators that change behaviour over time (comparing mutable state) corrupt the tree's invariants.
- Compound keys: compare lexicographically with `std::tie(a.x, a.y) < std::tie(b.x, b.y)` or, in C++20, `auto operator<=>(const Key&) const = default;`.
- The comparator object must be callable as `const` (libstdc++ static-asserts: "comparison object must be invocable as const").
- Descending order: `std::map<K, V, std::greater<K>>`, or `std::greater<>` for heterogeneous lookup.

subsections.title: 6. Heterogeneous lookup with transparent comparators
subsections.content:
- Problem: `std::map<std::string, int> m; m.find(sv)` with a `std::string_view` does not compile, and `m.find("literal")` builds a temporary `std::string` (possibly allocating) for every lookup.
- Fix (C++14): use a transparent comparator, `std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>>`. `std::less<>` has a nested `is_transparent` type, which enables template overloads of `find`, `count`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, `equal_range`, and (C++20) `contains`.
- The key type and the lookup type must be comparable both ways (`std::string` vs `std::string_view` is).
- Version map:
  - C++14: heterogeneous `find`/`count`/bounds for ordered containers.
  - C++20: heterogeneous `contains`; unordered containers get heterogeneous lookup, needing both a transparent hash and a transparent equality (topic 09).
  - C++23 (P2077): heterogeneous `erase` and `extract`. Not yet in GCC 14's library.
  - C++26 (P2363): heterogeneous `operator[]`, `at`, `try_emplace`, `insert_or_assign`.
- Custom transparent comparator: add `using is_transparent = void;` and overloads for each mixed pair.

subsections.title: 7. Iterator and reference stability
subsections.content:
- Insert never invalidates anything. Erase invalidates only the erased elements. This holds for all four ordered containers (table in topic 06).
- Erase-in-loop: `it = m.erase(it);` or `std::erase_if(m, pred)` (C++20).
- Element references are stable for the element's lifetime in the container, which makes `map` a reasonable owner of objects that other code points to.
- `set` elements and map keys are `const`: you cannot modify them through an iterator. To change a key: `extract`, modify, re-insert (section 8).
- Range-for: write `const auto& [key, value]` or `const std::pair<const K, V>&`. Writing `const std::pair<K, V>&` (without `const K`) binds to a **temporary copy** of each element; GCC warns with `-Wrange-loop-construct`.

subsections.title: 8. Node handles: extract, insert, merge (C++17)
subsections.content:
- `m.extract(it)` or `m.extract(key)` unlinks a node and returns a **node handle** owning it. No allocation, no copy.
- With a node handle you can:
  - Change the key: `nh.key() = new_key;` (the only legal way to modify a key in place), then `m.insert(std::move(nh))`.
  - Move the node into another container with the same node type: `map` and `multimap` with the same `K`, `V`, allocator (comparator may differ).
- `insert(node_handle&&)` returns an `insert_return_type` with `position`, `inserted`, and `node` (the handle is given back if the key already existed).
- `dst.merge(src)` splices every node whose key is not already in `dst`; duplicates stay in `src`. No element is copied or moved, iterators to transferred elements stay valid and now refer into `dst`.
- Pointers and references to an extracted element stay valid; using them while the element is held by the node handle is UB, and they become usable again after re-insertion.

subsections.title: 9. multimap and multiset
subsections.content:
- Equivalent keys are allowed. A new element is inserted at the upper end of its equal range, so insertion order among equivalent keys is preserved (guaranteed since C++11).
- `equal_range(k)` gives all elements with key `k`; `count(k)` is O(log n + count).
- `erase(k)` removes **all** elements equivalent to `k` and returns how many. To remove one: `if (auto it = ms.find(k); it != ms.end()) ms.erase(it);`.
- `multimap` has no `operator[]` and no `at` (which value would they return?).

subsections.title: 10. Performance and alternatives
subsections.content:
| Structure | Lookup | Insert / erase | Ordered iteration | Memory and cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `std::map` | O(log n), pointer chasing | O(log n), one allocation per element | yes | 32-byte node header per element (libstdc++), scattered |
| `std::unordered_map` | O(1) average, O(n) worst | O(1) average, may rehash | no | buckets + nodes (topic 09) |
| Sorted `std::vector<pair>` | O(log n) binary search, contiguous | O(n) shift | yes | Compact, prefetch friendly |
| `std::flat_map` (C++23) | O(log n), contiguous keys | O(n) | yes | Separate key and value arrays; GCC 15+ library |
- Why a map can lose to a linear scan of a small vector: each tree level is a dependent load (cache miss), a branch the predictor cannot learn, and every node is a separate allocation. For tens of elements, scanning a contiguous array is often faster than O(log n) tree descent.
- Choose `map` for: ordered iteration, range queries (`lower_bound`), stable references, frequent inserts and erases interleaved with lookups.
- Choose a sorted vector or `flat_map` for: read-mostly data built once (configuration, symbol tables, static lookup tables).
- `flat_map` invalidates iterators on insert and erase (it is vector-backed) and needs movable keys and values.

subsections.title: 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`m[k]` is a lookup." ✅ It inserts a default value if `k` is missing.
- ❌ "Set uses `operator==` to detect duplicates." ✅ It uses equivalence: `!comp(a, b) && !comp(b, a)`.
- ❌ "`<=` is a fine comparator; it just allows equal keys." ✅ It violates irreflexivity: UB, duplicates and failed lookups.
- ❌ "`lower_bound(k)` returns the first key `>= k`." ✅ Only with the default `less`; in general it is the first key not ordered before `k`.
- ❌ "`std::lower_bound` on a map is O(log n)." ✅ O(n) iterator steps; use the member function.
- ❌ "`emplace` does nothing when the key exists." ✅ It may already have consumed (moved) its arguments; `try_emplace` does not.
- ❌ "A map is a binary search over an array." ✅ It is a tree walk; each step is a pointer dereference.
- ❌ "O(log n) map always beats O(n) vector scan." ✅ Not for small n: locality and branch prediction dominate.
- ❌ "Keys can be modified through a map iterator if the order stays the same." ✅ Keys are `const`; use `extract`.
- ❌ "Heterogeneous lookup works with the default comparator." ✅ It needs `std::less<>` (or another transparent comparator).

#### 1. Mental model
- `std::set<K>` and `std::map<K, V>` keep their elements **sorted by a comparator** (`std::less<K>` by default) and allow at most one element per key. `multiset`/`multimap` allow equivalent keys.
- The standard fixes the interface and the complexities, not the data structure:
  - find, insert, erase by key: O(log n).
  - In-order iteration: O(n) total.
  - Insert and erase never invalidate iterators or references to other elements.
- Every major implementation uses a **red-black tree**: a self-balancing binary search tree where each node stores a colour and three pointers (parent, left, right).
  - libstdc++, x86-64: node header 32 bytes, so a `map<int, int>` node is 40 bytes plus allocator overhead; `sizeof(std::map<...>)` is 48 bytes.
  - Balancing: insert needs at most 2 rotations, erase at most 3, plus O(log n) recolouring in the worst case.
- `map<K, V>::value_type` is `std::pair<const K, V>`: the key cannot change while the element is in the tree, because changing it would break the ordering.
- A lookup walks from the root, one comparison and one pointer dereference per level. It is "binary search over a tree", not over an array: every step is a potential cache miss.

#### 2. Lookup API: find, contains, count, at, operator[]
| Call | Missing key | Requirements | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `m.find(k)` | `m.end()` | none | iterator |
| `m.contains(k)` (C++20) | `false` | none | bool |
| `m.count(k)` | 0 | none | 0 or 1 (multimap: n) |
| `m.at(k)` | throws `std::out_of_range` | none | `V&` / `const V&` |
| `m[k]` | **inserts** `{k, V{}}` | non-const map, `V` default-constructible | `V&` |
- `operator[]` is "find or insert": reading a missing key with `m[k]` adds an element. Accidental inserts change `size()`, iteration output, and memory use.
- `operator[]` does not exist on a `const map` (it may modify), so `const` code is forced to use `find`/`at`.
- For a read-and-use, `find` gives both the existence check and the value in one O(log n) walk; `contains` followed by `at` does two walks.

#### 3. Insertion API
| Call | Key exists | Key missing | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `insert({k, v})` | no change, returns `{it, false}` | inserts | The pair is built **before** the call, even if unused |
| `emplace(args...)` | no change | constructs in place | May construct the node (consuming the arguments) before finding the duplicate |
| `try_emplace(k, args...)` (C++17) | no change, **arguments untouched** | constructs `V(args...)` | Best "insert if absent" |
| `insert_or_assign(k, v)` (C++17) | assigns `v` | inserts | Returns `{it, inserted}`; unlike `m[k] = v`, no default construction of `V` |
| `m[k] = v` | assigns | default-constructs, then assigns | Needs default-constructible `V` |
| `insert(hint, x)`, `emplace_hint` | no change | inserts | Amortized O(1) if the element goes right before `hint` |
- `insert` and `emplace` return `std::pair<iterator, bool>`; the `bool` is the only way to know whether the insert happened.
- `emplace` when the key exists:
  - The standard allows constructing the node first, so arguments passed as rvalues may already be moved from.
  - Observed: libstdc++ GCC 11 moves the string out even when the key exists; GCC 13 and GCC 14 look the key up first and leave it intact. Do not rely on either; use `try_emplace`.
- Hint insertion: inserting sorted data with `m.emplace_hint(m.end(), k, v)` is O(n) overall instead of O(n log n).

#### 4. Ordered queries: lower_bound, upper_bound, equal_range
- Defined through the comparator `comp`, not through `>=`:
  - `lower_bound(k)`: first element `e` with `!comp(e, k)`, "not ordered before k".
  - `upper_bound(k)`: first element `e` with `comp(k, e)`, "ordered after k".
  - `equal_range(k)`: the pair `{lower_bound(k), upper_bound(k)}`; for a unique-key container it has 0 or 1 elements.
- With the default `less`: lower_bound = first key `>= k`, upper_bound = first key `> k`.
- With `std::greater` (descending order): lower_bound = first key `<= k`. People who think "lower_bound means >=" get this wrong.
- Range query `[a, b)`: iterate from `lower_bound(a)` to `lower_bound(b)`. Inclusive `[a, b]`: up to `upper_bound(b)`.
- "Greatest key `<= k`" with default order: `auto it = m.upper_bound(k); if (it != m.begin()) --it;`.
- Use the **member** functions: `std::lower_bound(m.begin(), m.end(), ...)` does O(log n) comparisons but O(n) iterator steps, because map iterators are bidirectional.

edge_cases.title: Reading with operator[] inserts
operator[] needs a non-const map and a default-constructible value
edge_cases.explanation:
- In a `const std::map&` parameter, `m[k]` does not compile: "passing 'const std::map<...>' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers".
- If `V` has no default constructor, every use of `m[k]` fails to compile, even for assignment. Use `try_emplace`, `insert_or_assign`, or `at`.

edge_cases.title: A `<=` comparator
NaN keys silently break the set
emplace may consume its arguments even when nothing is inserted
edge_cases.explanation:
- `m.emplace(key, std::move(s))` with an existing key: libstdc++ GCC 11 constructs the node first, moving `s`, then discards it. GCC 13 and GCC 14 check the key first. The standard permits both.
- `m.insert({key, std::move(s)})` always moves `s`: the pair argument is constructed before `insert` runs.
- `m.try_emplace(key, std::move(s))` guarantees `s` is untouched if the key exists.
- This matters for retry logic: code that "inserts, and on failure uses the value elsewhere" loses the value.

edge_cases.title: The wrong pair type in range-for copies every element
edge_cases.explanation:
- `for (const std::pair<std::string, int>& p : m)` does not match `std::pair<const std::string, int>`; the compiler builds a temporary converted pair (copying the string) per iteration and binds the reference to it.
- Costs an allocation per long key, and `&p.first` is not the address of the key in the map.
- GCC warns: "loop variable 'p' ... binds to a temporary constructed from type 'std::pair<const ...>'" (`-Wrange-loop-construct`, part of `-Wall`).
- Write `const auto& [k, v]` or `const auto& p`.

edge_cases.title: lower_bound with a descending comparator
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::map<int, char, std::greater<int>> m{{10,'a'},{20,'b'},{30,'c'},{40,'d'}};` iterates 40, 30, 20, 10.
- `m.lower_bound(25)` is 20 (first key not ordered before 25, i.e. first key `<= 25` in this order), and `upper_bound(25)` is also 20.
- `lower_bound` follows the comparator, not numeric `>=`.

edge_cases.title: Algorithms that look logarithmic but are linear
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::lower_bound(m.begin(), m.end(), ...)` and `std::binary_search` on map iterators: O(log n) comparisons, but `std::advance` on bidirectional iterators makes it O(n) steps.
- `std::distance(m.begin(), m.find(k))` (the "rank" of a key) is O(n). Ordered containers have no O(log n) rank operation; an order-statistics tree or a sorted vector is needed.
- `std::find(m.begin(), m.end(), ...)` is a linear scan; use `m.find(k)`.

edge_cases.title: A non-const call operator does not compile
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Cmp { bool operator()(int a, int b) { return a < b; } };` (missing `const`) fails as soon as the set is used: libstdc++ static-asserts "comparison object must be invocable as const".
- Lookups are `const` member functions, so the comparator they store is `const` too. Mark `operator()` `const`, and keep comparators free of mutable state.

interview_qa.question: How is `std::map` typically implemented, and what complexity does the standard guarantee?
interview_qa.answer: As a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree with one heap node per element. The standard does not name the structure; it requires O(log n) find, insert and erase, sorted iteration, and that insert/erase do not invalidate iterators to other elements, which in practice forces a balanced node-based tree.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Red-black trees keep the height at most about 2·log2(n+1); insert needs at most 2 rotations and erase at most 3.
- libstdc++, x86-64: each node has a colour and parent/left/right pointers (32 bytes) before the value; `sizeof(std::map)` is 48 bytes.
- A lookup is a tree walk: each level is a comparison plus a pointer dereference to a node that may be anywhere in memory.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's a sorted array with binary search." That would make insert O(n) and invalidate iterators; that structure is `std::flat_map` (C++23).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: red-black versus AVL: AVL is more strictly balanced (faster lookups, more rotations on update); red-black has cheaper updates, which suits a general-purpose container.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: map = balanced tree of separately allocated nodes; O(log n) with a pointer dereference per level.

interview_qa.question: What is a strict weak ordering, and what goes wrong with `a <= b` as a comparator?
interview_qa.answer: A strict weak ordering is irreflexive (`comp(a, a)` is false), asymmetric, transitive, and has transitive equivalence. `<=` violates irreflexivity: no key is equivalent to itself, so a set inserts duplicates and `find` never matches. interview_qa.key_takeaway: Comparators must answer "strictly before"; `<=` is UB in every sorted container and algorithm.

interview_qa.question: What does "weak" mean in strict weak ordering?

interview_qa.question: Why can a linear scan over a small vector beat `std::map::find`, despite O(n) versus O(log n)?

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: measure with realistic sizes and access patterns; the crossover depends on key type, n and how often the data changes.

- Best for read-mostly data: build in bulk (or insert with the `sorted_unique` tag for pre-sorted input), then look up many times.
- Keys and values are separate arrays, so a key search touches only keys: better cache use than an array of pairs.
- Library support: libstdc++ ships `<flat_map>` from GCC 15; it is not available in GCC 14.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "flat_map is a drop-in replacement for map." Code that relies on stable references or frequent inserts changes behaviour or cost.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `flat_set`, `flat_multimap` and `flat_multiset` follow the same model.

**Key takeaway:** flat_map = sorted arrays with a map interface: fast reads, slow writes, no stability.

interview_qa.question: How do you write a correct comparator for a struct key with several fields?
interview_qa.answer: Compare lexicographically: first field, then the next field only if the earlier ones are equivalent. Before C++20, `return std::tie(a.x, a.y) < std::tie(b.x, b.y);`. In C++20, `auto operator<=>(const Key&) const = default;` generates it, and `std::less<Key>` uses it.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Hand-written `return a.x < b.x || a.y < b.y;` is a classic bug: `{1, 5}` < `{2, 1}` and `{2, 1}` < `{1, 5}` are both true, so it is not asymmetric.
- Include every field that distinguishes keys; otherwise distinct keys are treated as duplicates.
- Defaulted `<=>` compares members in declaration order, so declaration order is the sort order.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`a.x < b.x && a.y < b.y`." Then `{1, 1}` ~ `{1, 3}` and `{1, 3}` ~ `{2, 2}` (neither is less than the other), yet `{1, 1}` < `{2, 2}`: equivalence is not transitive.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: floating-point members bring back the NaN problem; normalize or reject NaN.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Use `std::tie` or defaulted `<=>`; hand-rolled multi-field comparisons are a frequent source of UB.

interview_qa.question: How do you build a large `std::map` from already sorted data efficiently?
interview_qa.answer: Insert with a hint at the end: `m.emplace_hint(m.end(), k, v)`. When the new element belongs right before the hint, insertion is amortized O(1), so the whole build is O(n) comparisons instead of O(n log n). The range constructor is guaranteed linear for input already sorted by the comparator.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Since C++11 the hint means "insert as close as possible to the position just before `hint`".
- A wrong hint is not an error, it just falls back to O(log n).
- Every element still costs one node allocation; for static data, a sorted vector avoids those entirely.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Hints are ignored by modern implementations." libstdc++ uses them; the gain is measurable for large sorted inputs.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `try_emplace` and `insert_or_assign` also have hint overloads.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Sorted input plus `emplace_hint(end())` turns an O(n log n) build into O(n).

With -fsanitize=address it stops with "heap-buffer-overflow" inside std::__unguarded_partition. Without ASan our run aborted with "free(): invalid size" (heap corruption); other runs may appear to work.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.explanation:
- For 25, `lower_bound` returns 30 and stepping back gives 20: correct.
- For 20 (a key that exists), `lower_bound` returns 20 itself; stepping back gives 10: wrong.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: p dangles. With -fsanitize=address it reports "stack-use-after-scope".
GCC also warns: loop variable 'e' ... binds to a temporary constructed from type 'std::pair<const std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>, int>' [-Wrange-loop-construct]
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The element type is `std::pair<const std::string, int>`. A `const std::pair<std::string, int>&` cannot bind to it directly, so each iteration builds a converted temporary pair (copying the string) and binds `e` to that.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**

```
Does not compile (GCC 11 and GCC 14 report this single error):
error: static assertion failed: comparison object must be invocable as const
```

**Explanation:**

- libstdc++ checks this with a `static_assert` as soon as the comparator is used.
- Fix: `bool operator()(int a, int b) const { return a < b; }`. Prefer stateless comparators; a comparator whose result changes over time corrupts the tree.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: ++it on an erased node.
GCC 11, -O0: segmentation fault.
-fsanitize=address,undefined: prints 1, no report at all.
-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG: "attempt to increment a singular iterator".
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Why ASan is silent although the node really was freed: `++it` on a map iterator calls `std::_Rb_tree_increment`, which lives in the prebuilt `libstdc++.so` (libstdc++ / GCC). That library is not compiled with `-fsanitize=address`, so the read of the freed node's links is never checked. ASan only instruments code that you compile.
- Debug mode does not depend on memory at all: it records that `erase` invalidated `it` and aborts on the next `++`. For node containers it is the reliable detector; ASan is the reliable one for vector reallocation (topic 06, which also has the general erase-while-iterating rule for every container).
- The mechanics: `erase(it)` destroys the node `it` points to, and the loop's `++it` then follows that freed node's parent/child pointers. Whether that crashes, skips elements or "works" depends on what the allocator did with the block.
- Fix: `it = sessions.erase(it);` with `++it` only in the else branch, or `std::erase_if(sessions, pred)` (C++20).
- **Key Concept:** A clean ASan run proves nothing for `std::map`/`std::set` iterator bugs, because the tree walk happens inside uninstrumented `libstdc++.so`; run such code under `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`. The rule itself is general: map erase invalidates only the erased element, but that includes the iterator you are holding.

quick_reference.content:
#### Operations and complexity
| Operation | Complexity | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `find`, `contains`, `count`, `at` | O(log n) | Never insert |
| `operator[]` | O(log n) | Inserts default `V` if missing |
| `insert`, `emplace`, `try_emplace` | O(log n) | Returns `{iterator, bool}` |
| `insert(hint, x)` / `emplace_hint` | amortized O(1) if right before hint, else O(log n) | Sorted bulk load |
| `erase(it)` | amortized O(1) | Returns next iterator |
| `erase(key)` | O(log n + count) | Returns number removed |
| `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, `equal_range` | O(log n) | Use members, not `std::` versions |
| Full iteration | O(n) | Sorted by comparator |
| `extract`, `insert(node)` | O(log n) (amortized O(1) by iterator) | No allocation |
| `merge` | O(n log(n + m)) | No copies; duplicates stay in source |

#### Insert or update?
| Want | Use |
|---|---|
| Insert if absent, never touch the argument otherwise | `try_emplace(k, args...)` |
| Insert or overwrite | `insert_or_assign(k, v)` |
| Insert if absent, check result | `auto [it, ok] = m.insert({k, v});` |
| Read, missing is an error | `at(k)` |
| Read, missing is normal | `find(k)` |
| Existence only | `contains(k)` (C++20) |
| Change a key | `extract`, `nh.key() = ...`, `insert(std::move(nh))` |

#### Comparator rules
| Rule | Breaks if |
|---|---|
| `comp(a, a)` is false | `<=`, `>=` |
| Equivalence transitive | NaN keys, tolerance-based comparisons (`abs(a - b) < eps`) |
| Stable over time | Comparator reads mutable or global state |
| Callable as const | `operator()` not marked `const` |
| Transparent for heterogeneous lookup | Missing `is_transparent` (`std::less<>` has it) |

#### Implementation facts (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64; not guaranteed)
| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Data structure | Red-black tree |
| `sizeof(std::map<K, V>)`, `sizeof(std::set<K>)` | 48 bytes |
| Node overhead | 32 bytes (colour + parent/left/right) + value |
| `map<int, int>` node | 40 bytes |
| `emplace` with existing key | GCC 11 consumes rvalue args; GCC 13/14 do not |
| `std::flat_map` | Library support from GCC 15 (not in GCC 14) |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How is std::map implemented? | Red-black tree in practice; standard mandates O(log n) and stable iterators |
| `m[k]` on a missing key? | Inserts `V{}` and returns a reference to it |
| How does set detect duplicates? | Equivalence: `!comp(a,b) && !comp(b,a)`, never `==` |
| `<=` as comparator? | UB: duplicates inserted, lookups fail, `std::sort` can overflow |
| `lower_bound` vs `upper_bound`? | First not before `k` vs first after `k` (per comparator) |
| Greatest key `<= k`? | `upper_bound(k)`, then step back if not `begin()` |
| `emplace` vs `try_emplace`? | try_emplace never consumes args when the key exists |
| Lookup `std::string` keys by `string_view`? | Use `std::less<>` (transparent comparator) |
| Change a key? | `extract` node handle, edit `key()`, re-insert |
| map erase invalidates? | Only the erased element |
| Why can a small vector beat a map? | Contiguous memory, no pointer chasing, no per-node allocation |
| map vs unordered_map? | Need order, ranges, or stable worst case: map; pure point lookups: unordered |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::unordered_map<K, V>` (and `unordered_set`, `unordered_multimap`, `unordered_multiset`, all C++11) is a **hash table with separate chaining**:
  - A **bucket array**: a contiguous array of pointers, one per bucket.
  - **Nodes**: every element lives in its own heap-allocated node (key, value, link pointer, sometimes a cached hash code).
  - `bucket = hash(key) mod bucket_count()` (how the index is reduced is implementation-defined).

subsections.title: 2. Complexity: average, worst and amortized
subsections.content:
| Operation | Average | Worst | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `find`, `count`, `contains` (C++20) | O(1) | O(n) | Worst case = every key in one bucket |
| `insert`, `emplace`, `operator[]` | O(1) amortized | O(n) | Plus an occasional O(n) rehash |
| `erase(key)` | O(1) | O(n) | `erase(it)` average O(1) |
| `rehash`, `reserve` | O(n) | O(n²) | Relinks every node; allocates a new bucket array |
| Full iteration | O(n) in libstdc++ | | Order is unspecified |

subsections.title: 3. Load factor and when rehash happens
subsections.content:
- `load_factor() = size() / bucket_count()`: average chain length.
- `max_load_factor()` defaults to **1.0**. You can set it: `m.max_load_factor(0.5f)` (shorter chains, more memory).
- Rule: the container keeps `size() <= bucket_count() * max_load_factor()`. The check happens **before** inserting: if adding the element would exceed the limit, the table rehashes first, then inserts.
- An insert whose key already exists does not grow the table (no element is added).
- Growth policy is implementation-defined. libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 (measured, mlf 1.0):

| Elements after insert | `bucket_count()` |
|---|---|
| 0 (default-constructed) | 1 |
| 1 | 13 |
| 14 | 29 |
| 30 | 59 |
| 60 | 127 |
| 128 | 257 |
| 1110 | 2357 |
- libstdc++ picks a **prime** about twice the old count; libc++ uses primes or powers of two depending on the request. Never rely on "doubling" or on a specific number.
- Erasing never shrinks the bucket array; neither does `clear()` (2357 buckets after clearing 2000 elements in the run above). `rehash(0)` asks for the minimum that fits the current size.

subsections.title: 4. reserve(n) vs rehash(n)
subsections.content:
| Call | Unit | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `m.reserve(n)` | elements | Same as `rehash(ceil(n / max_load_factor()))`: room for `n` elements without a further rehash |
| `m.rehash(n)` | buckets | `bucket_count() >= n` **and** `bucket_count() >= size() / max_load_factor()` |
- Neither gives an exact number: libstdc++ rounds up to the next prime in its table. `reserve(1000)` gave 1031 buckets; with `max_load_factor(2.0)`, `reserve(10000)` gave 5087 (not 5000).
- Both can be no-ops if the table is already big enough, and `rehash(n)` with a smaller `n` may shrink it.
- Practical rule: when the final size is known, call `reserve(n)` **once, before** inserting. That removes all rehash spikes from the insert loop and keeps iterators stable during it.
- `reserve` is not a memory pool: each element still allocates its own node (see Memory & Ownership, topic 11, for `std::pmr` to control node allocation).

subsections.title: 5. Invalidation rules (unordered containers only)
subsections.content:
- The full cross-container table lives in topic 06 (Iterators and Invalidation Rules). Here is the unordered part in depth.

| Operation | Iterators | References and pointers to elements |
|---|---|---|
| Insert, **no** rehash | Valid | Valid |
| Insert that **causes** a rehash | **All invalidated** | Valid |
| `reserve` / `rehash` (that changes buckets) | All invalidated | Valid |
| `erase` | Only to erased elements | Only to erased elements |
| `clear` | All | All |
| `extract` (C++17) | Only the extracted one | Stay valid, but using them while the node handle owns the element is UB; fine again after reinsertion |
| `swap` | Valid, now refer into the other container | Valid |

- Why iterators do not survive: an iterator may hold bucket information (implementation-specific), and the traversal order changes. Even where an old iterator still "works" on libstdc++, using it is UB by the standard.
- `end()` is also invalidated by a rehash.

  - Store **pointers or references** to values long-term if you must, never iterators.
  - Inserting while iterating is unsafe unless you reserved enough beforehand (and even then the new element may or may not be visited).

subsections.title: 6. The hash and equality contract
subsections.content:
- An unordered container needs two function objects: `Hash` (default `std::hash<K>`) and `KeyEqual` (default `std::equal_to<K>`, i.e. `operator==`).
- **Contract**: `a == b` implies `hash(a) == hash(b)`. The reverse is not required: different keys may collide.
- If violated, two equal keys land in different buckets: `find` misses, duplicates appear in a "unique" container.
- The bug can hide in small tests: since GCC 12, libstdc++ looks up small tables (up to 20 elements for non-"fast" hashes such as `std::string`) by a linear scan with the equality only, so a broken hash shows up only once the table grows.
- The hash of a key must not change while it is stored. Keys are `const` in the node for this reason; changing a key through `mutable` members or `const_cast` silently corrupts the table (lookups miss, the element is "lost").
- To change a key legally: C++17 `extract()` the node, modify `nh.key()`, `insert(std::move(nh))`. No reallocation of the node.
- Equality must be an equivalence relation. Floating-point keys break it:
  - `NaN != NaN`: every inserted NaN is a new element and `find(NaN)` never succeeds.
  - `0.0 == -0.0`: so `std::hash<double>` must return the same hash for both (libstdc++ returns 0 for both).

subsections.title: 7. std::hash: what exists and how to add your own
subsections.content:
- Provided for: arithmetic types, enums, pointers, `std::string`, `std::string_view`, `std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`, `std::optional`, `std::variant`, `std::bitset`, `std::thread::id`, `std::type_index`, `std::error_code` and a few more.

  - A functor passed as a template argument: `std::unordered_map<Point, V, PointHash>`.
  - A specialization `template<> struct std::hash<Point> { ... };` (allowed for program-defined types). Then `std::unordered_map<Point, V>` just works.
- `std::hash` for pointers hashes the **address**, not the pointee. `unordered_map<const char*, int>` compares and hashes addresses: lookups with an equal string at a different address miss.

subsections.title: 8. Hash quality and combining
subsections.content:
- A good hash for a hash table: cheap, deterministic, and spreads **similar** keys to different buckets (small key changes flip many bits: avalanche).
- The weak combiner seen in tutorials: `hash(x) ^ (hash(y) << 1)`.
  - With identity `std::hash<int>`: `hash(0,1) == hash(2,0) == 2`, and `(x,y)` and `(y,x)` stay close.
  - Measured (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64): 10000 grid points `(x,y)` in `[0,100)²`, 10273 buckets, longest chain **50** (a good hash gives a few).
- Better: a boost-style `hash_combine`, mixing each field into a running seed:
  - `seed ^= h + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 + (seed << 6) + (seed >> 2);`
  - Or pack two 32-bit fields into one 64-bit value and run a mixer (for example a splitmix64 finalizer).
