- **Hash flooding (DoS)**: if attackers control keys and the hash is predictable, they can force O(n) chains. Use a seeded/keyed hash for untrusted input.
- Equal keys must hash equally, so the hash must use exactly the fields `operator==` uses (no more, no fewer meaningful fields).

subsections.title: 9. API choices: lookup and insertion
subsections.content:
| You want | Use | Inserts? | Needs default-constructible `V`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read if present | `find(k)`, `contains(k)` (C++20), `count(k)` | No | No |
| Read, throw if absent | `at(k)` | No | No |
| Read or create default | `m[k]` | Yes | Yes |
| Insert if absent, never touch args otherwise | `try_emplace(k, args...)` (C++17) | If absent | No |
| Insert or overwrite | `insert_or_assign(k, v)` (C++17) | Yes | No |
| Insert if absent | `insert({k, v})`, `emplace(k, v)` | If absent | No |
- `operator[]` is non-const: it does not exist on a `const` map and inserts a value-initialized `V` for a missing key. `if (m[k] == 0)` silently grows the map.
- `emplace` must build the node (and the key) **before** it can look the key up. If the key exists, the node is destroyed: arguments may already have been moved from. Measured (libstdc++): `emplace(1, std::move(ptr))` on an existing key leaves `ptr` null; `try_emplace(1, std::move(ptr))` leaves it untouched.
- **Heterogeneous lookup** (C++20 for unordered): `find("literal")` on `unordered_map<std::string, V>` normally constructs a temporary `std::string`. If both `Hash` and `KeyEqual` declare `is_transparent`, `find`/`count`/`contains`/`equal_range` accept a `std::string_view` or `const char*` directly. (GCC 11 already supports it.)
- **Node handles** (C++17): `extract(k)` unlinks a node without freeing it; `insert(std::move(nh))` relinks it (possibly in another map with the same types); `merge(other)` moves all nodes whose keys are absent. No element copies, no allocations.
- Bucket interface (debugging tool): `bucket(k)`, `bucket_size(b)`, `begin(b)/end(b)` (local iterators). Useful for measuring chain lengths of a hash function.

subsections.title: 10. Performance: why std::unordered_map is often slow, and what replaces it
subsections.content:
- Costs the big-O hides:
  - One heap allocation per element (insert) and one free (erase).
  - Pointer chasing: bucket array, then node, then maybe the next node. Cache-hostile on large tables.
  - Hash computation on every lookup (strings: proportional to length).
  - Rehash spikes: a single insert that triggers a rehash touches every node: a tail-latency event on a hot path.
- Mitigations inside the standard container: `reserve` upfront, a cheap but good hash, `std::pmr` or a custom allocator for nodes, transparent lookup to avoid temporaries.
- **Flat (open-addressing) hash maps** (for example `boost::unordered_flat_map`, "Swiss table" designs): elements stored in one array, probing instead of chains, metadata bytes for SIMD matching. Typically 2x to several x faster for lookups, but they give up reference stability (elements move on rehash).
- Other options:
  - Sorted `std::vector` + binary search (or C++23 `std::flat_map`, topic 08) for read-mostly data.
  - A direct array indexed by a small dense ID: fastest of all.
  - A perfect hash generated at build time for a static key set.
- `std::map` vs `std::unordered_map`: choose `map` when you need ordering, range queries, `lower_bound`, deterministic iteration, or a guaranteed O(log n) worst case. Choose `unordered_map` for pure point lookups on large sets with a good hash.

subsections.title: 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Lookup is O(1)." ✅ Average O(1); worst O(n). Insertion is also amortized because of rehash.
- ❌ "Rehash invalidates everything." ✅ Iterators yes; references and pointers to elements stay valid (nodes do not move).
- ❌ "Insert invalidates iterators." ✅ Only if it triggers a rehash.
- ❌ "`reserve(n)` reserves n buckets." ✅ It reserves room for n **elements**; `rehash(n)` is the bucket request.
- ❌ "The table rehashes after load_factor exceeds max_load_factor." ✅ It rehashes before the insert that would exceed it; the limit is never exceeded.
- ❌ "Bucket counts are powers of two / are doubled." ✅ Implementation-defined; libstdc++ uses primes.
- ❌ "`erase` or `clear` frees the bucket array." ✅ The bucket count never shrinks on its own; use `rehash(0)` or swap with a fresh map.
- ❌ "Small int keys come out sorted." ✅ Order is unspecified and changes after rehash.
- ❌ "`hash(x) ^ hash(y)` is a fine way to hash a pair." ✅ Symmetric and collision-prone; use a real combiner.
- ❌ "`std::hash<std::pair>` exists." ✅ It does not; write one.
- ❌ "`unordered_map` is always faster than `map`." ✅ For small sizes, string keys with expensive hashes, or ordered access, `map` or a sorted vector can win.

- Mitigations inside the standard container: `reserve` upfront, a cheap but good hash, `std::pmr` or a custom allocator for nodes, transparent lookup to avoid temporaries.
- **Flat (open-addressing) hash maps** (for example `boost::unordered_flat_map`, "Swiss table" designs): elements stored in one array, probing instead of chains, metadata bytes for SIMD matching. Typically 2x to several x faster for lookups, but they give up reference stability (elements move on rehash).
- Other options:
  - Sorted `std::vector` + binary search (or C++23 `std::flat_map`, topic 08) for read-mostly data.
  - A direct array indexed by a small dense ID: fastest of all.
  - A perfect hash generated at build time for a static key set.
- `std::map` vs `std::unordered_map`: choose `map` when you need ordering, range queries, `lower_bound`, deterministic iteration, or a guaranteed O(log n) worst case. Choose `unordered_map` for pure point lookups on large sets with a good hash.

#### 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "Lookup is O(1)." ✅ Average O(1); worst O(n). Insertion is also amortized because of rehash.
- ❌ "Rehash invalidates everything." ✅ Iterators yes; references and pointers to elements stay valid (nodes do not move).
- ❌ "Insert invalidates iterators." ✅ Only if it triggers a rehash.
- ❌ "`reserve(n)` reserves n buckets." ✅ It reserves room for n **elements**; `rehash(n)` is the bucket request.
- ❌ "The table rehashes after load_factor exceeds max_load_factor." ✅ It rehashes before the insert that would exceed it; the limit is never exceeded.
- ❌ "Bucket counts are powers of two / are doubled." ✅ Implementation-defined; libstdc++ uses primes.
- ❌ "`erase` or `clear` frees the bucket array." ✅ The bucket count never shrinks on its own; use `rehash(0)` or swap with a fresh map.
- ❌ "Small int keys come out sorted." ✅ Order is unspecified and changes after rehash.
- ❌ "`hash(x) ^ hash(y)` is a fine way to hash a pair." ✅ Symmetric and collision-prone; use a real combiner.
- ❌ "`std::hash<std::pair>` exists." ✅ It does not; write one.
- ❌ "`unordered_map` is always faster than `map`." ✅ For small sizes, string keys with expensive hashes, or ordered access, `map` or a sorted vector can win.

edge_cases.title: operator[] inserts, and needs a default constructor
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if (m["missing"] == 0)` inserts `"missing"` with a value-initialized mapped value: the size grows on a read.
- `operator[]` is not available on a `const` map: `const auto& cm = m; cm["k"];` does not compile. Use `find` or `at`.
- If the mapped type has no default constructor, `m[k]` does not compile at all, even for keys that exist: the compiler must instantiate the "insert default" path. Use `try_emplace`, `insert_or_assign`, or `find`.

edge_cases.title: A rehash keeps references but kills iterators
edge_cases.explanation:
- `auto& r = m[1]; auto it = m.find(1); m.reserve(1000);`
  - `r` and `&r`: still valid; the node did not move.
  - `it` and `end()`: invalid; using `it` is UB even if libstdc++ happens to print the right value.
- Typical bug: caching `find()` results in a member variable and inserting later.
- Fix: cache a pointer to the value (`&it->second`), or `reserve` the final size before taking iterators.

edge_cases.title: Inserting while iterating
edge_cases.explanation:
- A range-for over a map that inserts into the same map can trigger a rehash in the middle of the loop: the loop's hidden iterator is invalidated (UB).
- Even without a rehash, whether newly inserted elements are visited is unspecified (they may go into a bucket already passed).
- Fix: collect new entries in a separate vector and insert after the loop.

edge_cases.title: Floating-point keys: NaN and negative zero
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::unordered_set<double> s; s.insert(NAN); s.insert(NAN);` gives size 2, and `s.count(NAN)` is 0: equality says NaN equals nothing, not even itself.
- `0.0` and `-0.0` compare equal, so they are one key; `std::hash<double>` must (and does) hash both to the same value.
- Prices as `double` keys also suffer from rounding (`0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`). Use integer ticks or fixed-point keys.

edge_cases.title: Pointer keys hash the address
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::unordered_map<const char*, int>` uses `std::hash<const char*>`, which hashes the pointer value, and `==` compares addresses.
- `m["abc"]` and then a lookup with a `char buf[] = "abc"` misses: same characters, different address.
- String literals with the same content may or may not share an address (unspecified), so even literal-to-literal lookups are not reliable.
- Fix: use `std::string` keys, or `std::string_view` keys **only** if the viewed strings outlive the map (see topic 02 on dangling views).

edge_cases.title: Keys that collide by construction
edge_cases.explanation:
- libstdc++ `std::hash<int>` is the identity. With bucket count `B`, keys `0, B, 2B, ...` all land in bucket 0.
- Real-world cases: IDs that are multiples of 1000, aligned addresses (pointer hashes: low bits are always zero), timestamps rounded to a tick.
- The prime bucket counts of libstdc++ make simple strides less likely to hit one bucket, but it remains possible; power-of-two tables (common in custom and flat maps) are far more sensitive.
- Fix: a mixing hash (multiply by a large odd constant and shift, or splitmix64).

edge_cases.title: emplace can consume arguments even when it does not insert
edge_cases.explanation:
- `m.emplace(k, std::move(p))` with an existing key: libstdc++ allocates a node, constructs the pair (moving from `p`), finds the duplicate, destroys the node. `p` is now null and the object it owned is gone.
- The standard allows this: `emplace` gives no guarantee that arguments are untouched on failure.
- `try_emplace(k, std::move(p))` (C++17) looks up first and moves only if it inserts. It also avoids the wasted allocation.
- Same issue with `insert({k, std::move(p)})`: the pair argument is built before the call.

edge_cases.title: The bucket array never shrinks by itself
edge_cases.explanation:
- Load a map with a million entries, `clear()` it: `bucket_count()` stays at about a million, and iteration in some implementations, plus `clear()` itself, stays proportional to the bucket count.
- Memory of the bucket array (8 bytes per bucket on x86-64) is held until destruction.
- Fix: `m.rehash(0)` after clear, or `std::unordered_map<K,V>().swap(m);`.

edge_cases.title: Same content, different iteration order
edge_cases.explanation:
- Two maps with the same elements can iterate in different orders (different insertion history, different bucket counts).
- `operator==` still says they are equal: it compares the containers as unordered collections.
- Never write tests or produce output (logs, serialized files, checksums) that depend on unordered iteration order. Sort the keys first if order matters.

interview_qa.question: How is std::unordered_map implemented internally?
interview_qa.answer: As a hash table with separate chaining: an array of buckets, where each bucket leads to a chain of individually heap-allocated nodes holding the key/value pair. The bucket index is computed from `hash(key)` reduced modulo the bucket count.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Lookup: hash the key, go to its bucket, compare keys in that chain with `key_equal` until one matches.
- One node allocation per element; the bucket array is a separate allocation that is replaced on rehash.
- The node design is forced by the standard: references to elements must stay valid across a rehash, so elements cannot live inside a probing array.
- libstdc++ detail: all nodes are on one singly linked list, each bucket points to the node before its first element, and the hash code is cached in the node for non-trivial hashes such as `std::string`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's a balanced tree like `std::map`, just unsorted." Trees give O(log n) and ordered iteration; this is a hash table.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: why this layout is slow in practice (allocation per insert, pointer chasing per lookup) and that open-addressing "flat" maps exist because of it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Buckets plus heap nodes: stable element addresses, at the price of allocations and cache misses.

interview_qa.question: Is lookup in unordered_map O(1)? What is the worst case and why?
interview_qa.answer: Average O(1), worst case O(n). The worst case happens when many keys land in the same bucket (bad hash, adversarial keys, or keys that collide by construction), so lookup degenerates into a linear scan of one chain.

interview_qa.question: What is the load factor, and exactly when does the table rehash?
interview_qa.answer: `load_factor() = size() / bucket_count()`, the average chain length. The container keeps it at or below `max_load_factor()` (default 1.0): an insert that **would** push the size above `bucket_count() * max_load_factor()` first grows the bucket array, then inserts the element.

- The new bucket count is implementation-defined: libstdc++ uses a prime about twice as large (13, 29, 59, 127, ...). The standard does not say "double".
- Inserting a key that already exists adds nothing and never rehashes.
- A lower `max_load_factor` means shorter chains and more memory.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "When the load factor exceeds the maximum, it rehashes." The check is done before the insert, so the limit is never exceeded.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the bucket array never shrinks on erase or clear.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between reserve(n) and rehash(n)?
interview_qa.answer: `reserve(n)` is in **elements**: it makes room for `n` elements without further rehashing, equivalent to `rehash(ceil(n / max_load_factor()))`. `rehash(n)` is in **buckets**: it requests at least `n` buckets (and enough for the current size).

- Neither preallocates nodes: every insert still allocates.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "call `reserve(final_size)` once before a bulk insert: no rehash spikes, iterators stay valid during the loop."

interview_qa.question: What is wrong with `hash(p.x) ^ (hash(p.y) << 1)` as a hash for a 2-D point? How would you combine hashes?
interview_qa.answer: With libstdc++'s identity `std::hash<int>`, it maps structured inputs into a tiny range with many collisions: `(0,1)` and `(2,0)` both hash to 2. On a 100x100 grid (10000 points, 10273 buckets) the longest chain was 50 instead of single digits. Use a proper combiner (boost-style `hash_combine`) or pack the fields and apply a mixing function.
interview_qa.explanation:
- XOR is commutative and loses information: plain `h(x) ^ h(y)` makes `(x,y)` and `(y,x)` collide and maps every `(x,x)` to 0. The `<< 1` only partly helps.
- With small coordinates, all values stay below 256, so 10000 keys fit in at most 256 buckets whatever the bucket count.
- Good options:
  - `seed ^= h + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 + (seed << 6) + (seed >> 2);` per field.
  - Pack `x` and `y` into one 64-bit integer and apply a splitmix64 / Murmur finalizer.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "XOR is fine because it's uniform for random bits." Inputs are rarely random; grids, IDs and prices are highly structured.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: measure with the bucket interface (`bucket_count`, `bucket_size`) instead of guessing.

interview_qa.question: libstdc++'s std::hash<int> is the identity function. When does that hurt?
interview_qa.answer: When keys share a stride related to the bucket count: the bucket is `key % bucket_count`, so keys that are all multiples of the bucket count (or of a common factor of it) pile into a few buckets. It also offers no protection against adversarial keys.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Identity is fast and perfect for random or sequential keys (sequential keys spread perfectly).
- Prime bucket counts (libstdc++) make the problem rarer; power-of-two tables (common in custom and flat maps) are badly hit by keys with zero low bits, e.g. aligned pointers or IDs that are multiples of 1024.
- Fix: a mixing hash (multiply-shift, splitmix64) as the `Hash` template argument.
- Untrusted input (network IDs): prefer a seeded hash so collisions cannot be precomputed.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "std::hash is cryptographic / randomized." It is neither, and its values are implementation-specific.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: hash quality is relative to the table's index reduction (modulo prime vs masking low bits).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Identity hashing is fast but fragile; structured or hostile keys need a mixer.

interview_qa.question: Can `m[k]` or `insert` invalidate the iterator you are looping with? How does `reserve` help?
interview_qa.answer: Yes, when they add a new element and that pushes `size()` above `max_load_factor() * bucket_count()`: the container rehashes and every iterator is invalidated (references and pointers survive). interview_qa.question: Can you store `std::hash` values in a file or send them to another process, for example to pick a shard?
interview_qa.answer: No. The standard only requires `std::hash` to return the same value for the same key **within one execution of the program**. Different standard libraries, versions, bitnesses (`size_t` width) and even runs may give different values, so persisted or shared hashes need a hash function you specify yourself.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `std::hash` is for in-memory tables; anything persisted or shared needs an explicitly specified hash.

interview_qa.question: Can you modify a key stored in an unordered_map?
interview_qa.answer: Not in place: the key is `const` in `value_type` because changing it would change its hash and bucket. C++17 lets you `extract` the node, modify `node.key()`, and `insert` it back without reallocating the node or copying the value.
interview_qa.explanation:

- `merge(other)` moves all nodes whose keys are absent from `*this`; colliding keys stay in `other`.
- Node handles can move elements between maps of the same key/value/allocator types (hash and equality may differ).
- Pointers and references taken before `extract` stay valid and refer to the element again after reinsertion; using them while the node handle owns the element is UB. References obtained from the handle (`nh.key()`) are invalidated by a successful insert.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`const_cast` the key and change it." UB, and in practice the element is now in the wrong bucket.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the same applies to `std::set` elements and `std::map` keys.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Change a key with extract, modify, insert: no allocation, no copy.

interview_qa.question: Is the iteration order of unordered_map defined? Are two maps with the same elements equal?
interview_qa.answer: Iteration order is unspecified and can change after any rehash. Two maps with the same key/value pairs compare equal with `==` regardless of insertion order or bucket count.
interview_qa.explanation:
- On libstdc++, inserting `0, 10, 20, 30, 40` iterates as `40 30 20 10 0`; after `rehash(1000)` it iterates `0 10 20 30 40`. Neither is guaranteed.
- Different standard libraries (and versions) give different orders: never let output, logs, tests or checksums depend on it.
- `operator==` is O(n) on average (O(n²) worst case) because it checks each element of one map in the other.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Small integer keys come out sorted." Sometimes, by accident.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: if you need deterministic output, copy keys into a vector and sort, or use `std::map`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: No order guarantee; equality is content-based.

interview_qa.question: map vs unordered_map: how do you choose, especially for latency-sensitive code?
interview_qa.answer: Use `std::map` when you need ordering, range queries (`lower_bound`), deterministic iteration or a guaranteed O(log n) worst case. Use `std::unordered_map` for point lookups on larger sets with a good hash. On hot paths, measure: both are node-based, and often a sorted vector or a flat hash map beats both.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `unordered_map` risks: rehash spikes (one insert relinks every node), hash cost for long strings, collision worst cases.
- `map` risks: O(log n) pointer chasing, one allocation per element too.
- For a fixed universe of small integer IDs, a plain array indexed by ID is fastest.
- For read-mostly data, a sorted `std::vector` (or C++23 `std::flat_map`, topic 08) wins on cache locality.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "unordered_map is O(1) so it's always faster." Small maps (tens of entries) are often faster as a sorted vector or even a linear scan.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `reserve` upfront and a pool allocator remove most of the unordered_map tail-latency spikes.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Choose by required operations first (order? ranges?), then by measured latency, not by big-O alone.

interview_qa.question: Why is std::unordered_map slower than open-addressing ("flat") hash maps, and what do flat maps give up?
interview_qa.answer: `std::unordered_map` allocates a node per element and follows at least two pointers per lookup (bucket, then node), costing cache misses. Flat maps store elements directly in one array and probe neighbouring slots, often with SIMD-matched metadata, so a lookup touches one or two cache lines. They give up reference and pointer stability: elements move on rehash (and sometimes on erase).
interview_qa.explanation:
- The standard requires references to survive rehash, which forces the node design for `std::unordered_*`.
- Flat maps also usually require a good hash: with power-of-two capacities, poor low bits cause clustering.
- Examples: `boost::unordered_flat_map`, Swiss-table style maps in common open-source libraries.
- Typical measured gain: 2x to several x faster lookups and fewer allocations; benchmark on your data.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Flat maps are faster because they have a better hash function." The big win is memory layout.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: if you need stable addresses with a flat map, store indices into a separate vector or `unique_ptr` values.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: std's design buys reference stability with allocations and pointer chasing; flat maps make the opposite trade.

interview_qa.question: How do you erase elements while iterating over an unordered_map?
interview_qa.answer: Use the iterator returned by `erase`: `for (auto it = m.begin(); it != m.end(); ) { if (cond) it = m.erase(it); else ++it; }`, or C++20 `std::erase_if(m, pred)`. Erase invalidates only the erased element, so the returned iterator is safe to continue from.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The bug: `for (auto it = m.begin(); it != m.end(); ++it) if (cond) m.erase(it);` increments an iterator to a freed node: UB (ASan: heap-use-after-free).
- Erasing does not reorder or rehash, so other elements are still visited exactly once.
- `std::erase_if` returns the number of erased elements.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Erase invalidates all iterators, so collect keys and erase later." That works but is unnecessary for unordered containers.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: insertion inside the loop is different: it can rehash and invalidate all iterators.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `it = m.erase(it)` or `std::erase_if`; never `++` an erased iterator.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between unordered_map and unordered_multimap, and how do you find all values for a key?
interview_qa.answer: `unordered_multimap` allows several elements with equivalent keys and has no `operator[]` or `at`. Use `equal_range(k)` to get the range of all elements with that key; equal keys are guaranteed to be adjacent in iteration order.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Multimap allows duplicates; iterate a key's group with `equal_range`.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Lines A and B are well-defined and print "one".
Line C is undefined behaviour (the rehash invalidated `it`), even though
libstdc++ happens to print "one" as well and ASan reports nothing.
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: the first emplace rehashes (13 -> 29 buckets on libstdc++),
which invalidates it. The reference first stays valid.
GCC 11, -O0 and with -fsanitize=address,undefined: prints "14 1" (only one shadow
id was added instead of 13) and ASan reports nothing.
-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG: aborts with "attempt to increment a singular iterator".
practice_tasks.explanation:
- With `max_load_factor()` 1.0 and 13 elements in 13 buckets (libstdc++ bucket counts), adding a 14th element exceeds the limit, so `emplace` rehashes. A rehash invalidates **all** iterators, including the loop's `it`.
- References and pointers survive: nodes are relinked, not moved. That is why `first` still prints 1 (Q3 shows the same split with `reserve`).
- Why ASan is silent: no memory was freed except the old bucket array, and the iterator holds a pointer to a live node. Why only one shadow: libstdc++ keeps all nodes in one singly linked list; the rehash rebuilt that list, the node `it` pointed to (key 13, visited first) ended up last, and `++it` reached `end()` immediately. The result is quietly wrong data, not a crash.
- Debug mode compares the bucket count before and after each insert and marks every iterator singular when it changes, so it catches what ASan cannot.
- `ids.reserve(2 * ids.size())` before the loop makes it well defined (no rehash, an insert without rehash invalidates nothing) and prints `26 1`; whether the loop also visits the new keys is unspecified, so the `< 1000` guard is still needed.
- **Key Concept:** In an unordered container, inserting can rehash and kill every iterator while every reference stays valid; ASan sees nothing, debug mode does. Reserve first, or collect and insert after the loop.

- The range-for holds `begin()`/`end()` iterators. Any insert that triggers a rehash invalidates them; on large maps this crashes or skips elements.
- Even without a rehash, a newly inserted element may land before or after the current position, so it may or may not be processed.
- Fix: collect the new keys in a separate vector, insert after the loop (and `reserve` first if the size is known).
- **Key Concept:** Do not insert into an unordered container while iterating over it.

invalidate the loop's hidden iterator. Whether new elements are visited is also
unspecified, so the size is not reliable (libstdc++ printed 3 here: no rehash, and
the new key 3 was inserted at a position the loop had already passed).

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
true false false
(the second and third values are libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64 results; only "true" is guaranteed)
```

**Explanation:**
- `operator==` compares unordered containers as sets of key/value pairs: insertion order and bucket count are irrelevant.
- The iteration order of the two maps differs (different history, different bucket counts), so their first elements are different keys.
- `b` was rehashed to at least 4096 buckets; `a` grew naturally to a much smaller prime.
- **Key Concept:** Unordered equality is content-based; iteration order is not part of a container's value.

practice_tasks.answer:
0 1
(GCC 11, 13 and 14 / libstdc++; it can print 1 1 if "ABCD" happens to land in the same bucket)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The equality says `"ABCD" == "abcd"`, but `std::hash<std::string>` hashes the raw bytes, so the two get different hashes and usually different buckets.
- That violates the contract (`a == b` implies `hash(a) == hash(b)`); the equality is never even called for the right element.
- The 30 extra symbols matter: since GCC 12, libstdc++ searches a table with at most 20 elements (for non-"fast" hashes such as `std::string`) by a linear scan using only the equality. With just `"abcd"` inserted, GCC 13/14 print `1 1` and GCC 11 prints `0 1`: the bug hides in small tests and appears in production-sized tables.
- Violating the hash/equality requirement is a precondition violation of the container, so no result is guaranteed.
- Fix: hash the same normalized form the equality compares (lowercase each character while hashing).
- **Key Concept:** Hash and equality must agree: hash exactly what equality compares, in the same way.

practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error: no matching function for call to
'std::unordered_map<std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>, int>::find(std::string_view&)'
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Without heterogeneous lookup, `find` takes `const key_type&`. `std::string_view` to `std::string` is an **explicit** conversion, so no overload matches.
- The C++20 template `find(const K&)` overload is enabled only when both the hash and the key equality are transparent (`is_transparent`). The default `std::hash<std::string>` and `std::equal_to<std::string>` are not.
- `limits.find(std::string(field))` compiles but allocates a temporary for long keys.
- **Key Concept:** Heterogeneous lookup needs a transparent hash **and** `std::equal_to<>`.

quick_reference.content:
#### Core facts
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Structure | Bucket array + one heap node per element (chaining) |
| Default `max_load_factor` | 1.0 |
| Rehash trigger | Before an insert that would make `size() > bucket_count() * mlf` |
| Bucket growth | Implementation-defined (libstdc++: next prime, about 2x) |
| Shrinks on erase/clear? | No; `rehash(0)` or swap with an empty map |
| Iteration order | Unspecified; changes on rehash |
| Key requirements | `Hash` + `KeyEqual`; `a == b` implies `hash(a) == hash(b)` |
| `std::hash<pair/tuple>` | Not provided |

#### Invalidation (unordered only; full table in topic 06)
| Operation | Iterators | References / pointers |
|---|---|---|
| Insert without rehash | Valid | Valid |
| Insert with rehash, `reserve`, `rehash` | Invalid | Valid |
| `erase(x)` | Only `x` | Only `x` |
| `clear()` | All | All |

#### Lookup and insert cheat sheet
| Code | Inserts on miss | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `m[k]` | Yes (default `V`) | Non-const; needs default ctor |
| `m.at(k)` | No | Throws `std::out_of_range` |
| `m.find(k)`, `m.contains(k)` | No | `contains` is C++20 |
| `m.try_emplace(k, a...)` | Yes | Args untouched if key exists (C++17) |
| `m.insert_or_assign(k, v)` | Yes | Overwrites (C++17) |
| `m.emplace(k, v)` | Yes | May build and discard a node |
| `m.extract(k)` / `m.merge(o)` | | Move nodes, no allocation (C++17) |

#### Implementation facts (libstdc++ / GCC, x86-64; not standard)
| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| `sizeof(std::unordered_map<int,int>)` | 56 bytes |
| Empty map `bucket_count()` | 1 |
| Growth sequence | 13, 29, 59, 127, 257, 541, 1109, 2357, ... |
| `std::hash<int>` | Identity |
| `std::hash<double>(0.0)` and `(-0.0)` | Both 0 |
| Hash code cached in node | For non-fast hashes (e.g. `std::string`), not for integers |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| How is `unordered_map` built? | Buckets of chained nodes; one allocation per element |
| Lookup complexity? | Average O(1), worst O(n) |
| When does it rehash? | Before the insert that would exceed `max_load_factor` |
| `reserve` vs `rehash`? | Elements vs buckets |
| What does rehash invalidate? | Iterators only; references and pointers survive |
| What does erase invalidate? | Only the erased element |
| Custom key needs? | Hash + equality, consistent with each other |
| Why is `h1 ^ (h2 << 1)` bad? | Nearly symmetric, small range, many collisions |
| Avoid a temporary string in `find`? | Transparent hash + `equal_to<>` (C++20) |
| Change a key? | `extract`, modify `key()`, `insert` |
| Faster alternative? | Flat open-addressing map, sorted vector, or direct array |
| `map` instead? | Need ordering, ranges, or a hard O(log n) bound |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A template is a **recipe**, not code. The compiler generates a concrete function or class (a **specialization**) when the template is used with specific arguments: this is **instantiation**.
- Each distinct argument set produces a separate entity: `max<int>` and `max<double>` are two different functions in the binary.
- Consequences:
  - The definition must be visible where it is instantiated, so templates normally live in **headers**. A template defined only in a `.cpp` file gives "undefined reference" link errors for other translation units.
  - Errors appear at instantiation, often deep inside library code (concepts, topic 11, move them to the call site).
  - Code size grows with every distinct instantiation (template bloat).
- Control instantiation explicitly:
  - `template class Matrix<double>;` (explicit instantiation definition) in one `.cpp`.
  - `extern template class Matrix<double>;` (C++11) in the header: other TUs do not instantiate it, which saves compile time.
- Kinds of template parameters:
  - Type: `template <class T>` (`typename` and `class` are identical here).
  - Non-type (NTTP): `template <int N>`, `template <auto V>` (C++17), class types (C++20).
  - Template template: `template <template <class> class C>`.
- Kinds of templates: function, class, variable (`template <class T> constexpr bool is_big_v = sizeof(T) > 8;`, C++14), alias (`template <class T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;`), and concepts (C++20).

subsections.title: 2. Function template argument deduction
subsections.content:
- The compiler deduces `T` by matching each **parameter type** against the corresponding **argument type**. The rules depend on the form of the parameter.
- Forwarding references (`T&&`) and `auto` deduction are covered in Core Language (Ch1); here are the other three forms.

| Parameter | Argument | Deduced `T` | Parameter type |
|---|---|---|---|
| `T` (by value) | `int` | `int` | `int` |
| `T` | `const int` | `int` (top-level const dropped) | `int` |
| `T` | `const int*` | `const int*` (low-level const kept) | `const int*` |
| `T` | `int[3]` | `int*` (array decays) | `int*` |
| `T` | function `void(int)` | `void(*)(int)` | pointer to function |
| `T&` | `int` | `int` | `int&` |
| `T&` | `const int` | `const int` | `const int&` |
| `T&` | `int[3]` | `int[3]` (no decay) | `int(&)[3]` |
| `T&` | `42` (rvalue) | deduction succeeds (`int`), but `int&` cannot bind: error | |
| `const T&` | `const int` | `int` | `const int&` |
| `const T&` | `42` | `int` | `const int&` |
- By value means "a new copy": the copy's own constness is not inherited, so top-level `const` and references are stripped.
- `T&` keeps everything the argument has, which is why `template <class T, std::size_t N> std::size_t size(T (&)[N])` can recover array sizes.
- **Every** deducible parameter is deduced independently, and the results must agree: `template <class T> T add(T, T); add(10, 20.5);` deduces `T = int` and `T = double`: deduction fails, "no matching function". No conversion is tried during deduction.
- Fixes: `add<double>(10, 20.5)` (explicit argument: now only conversions are needed), `add(10.0, 20.5)`, two parameters `template <class A, class B> auto add(A, B)`, or block deduction on one parameter with `std::type_identity_t<T>` (C++20).
- **Non-deduced contexts**: `T` cannot be deduced from `typename Wrapper<T>::type`, from a default argument, or from `std::function<void(T)>` when passing a lambda (the lambda is not a `std::function`).
- **Explicit arguments** fill parameters left to right; the rest are deduced: `std::make_unique<Order>(1, 2)` specifies `T`, deduces `Args...`.
- Return types are never deduced from the call site: `template <class R> R parse(std::string_view)` must be called as `parse<int>("42")`.

subsections.title: 3. Overloading vs specialization of function templates
subsections.content:
- Two ways to customize a function template for some types:
  - **Overloading**: declare another function template or a plain function with the same name.
  - **Explicit (full) specialization**: `template <> void f<int>(int);` gives a different body for one exact argument set.
- Overload resolution only looks at **primary templates and non-template functions**. Specializations are not candidates; they are used only after their primary template has won.
- Ranking (simplified):
  1. Best conversion sequences win.
  2. On a tie, a non-template function beats a template.
  3. On a tie between templates, **partial ordering**: the more specialized template wins (`f(T*)` beats `f(T)` for `int*`, because every `T*` call could go to `f(T)` but not the reverse).
  4. Still tied: ambiguous.
- **Function templates cannot be partially specialized**. `template <class T> void f<T*>(T*)` is an error ("non-class, non-variable partial specialization ... is not allowed"). Use an overload instead.
- The classic trap (often called the Dimov/Abrahams example): a full specialization `f<int*>` of `f(T)` is ignored if an overload `f(T*)` exists and wins partial ordering. The specialization's body never runs.
- Guideline: prefer overloading (or `if constexpr`, or a class template with partial specialization) over explicit specialization of function templates.

subsections.title: 4. Class template specialization: full and partial
subsections.content:
- Full specialization: `template <> struct Traits<bool> { ... };` a completely separate class for one argument set; it shares nothing with the primary (no members are inherited from it).
- Partial specialization: a pattern that matches a family of arguments:
  - `template <class T> struct Traits<T*>` (any pointer)
  - `template <class T> struct Traits<std::vector<T>>`
  - `template <class T> struct Same<T, T>` (both arguments equal)
- Selection: the compiler finds all partial specializations that match; if one is more specialized than all others it is used; if two match equally, the use is ambiguous; if none match, the primary is used.
- A specialization must be declared before the first use that would instantiate it; otherwise the program is ill-formed, no diagnostic required (in practice the primary is often used silently).
- This is how `<type_traits>` is built (`std::is_pointer<T*>`, `std::remove_const<const T>`); writing traits is covered in topic 11.
- Member specialization: a single member function of a class template can be fully specialized (`template <> void Box<int>::print() { }`) without rewriting the class.
- Variable templates can be partially specialized too (`template <class T> constexpr bool is_ptr_v<T*> = true;`).

subsections.title: 5. Two-phase lookup and dependent names
subsections.content:
- Templates are checked twice:
  - **Phase 1** (definition): non-dependent names are looked up and non-dependent code is checked. `undeclared_function();` with no dependent argument is an error even if the template is never used (GCC, Clang).
  - **Phase 2** (instantiation): names that depend on template parameters are resolved, with ADL at the point of instantiation.
- A **dependent name** is one whose meaning depends on `T`: `T::value_type`, `obj.size()` where `obj` is a `T`, `Base<T>::member`.
- Disambiguators, because in phase 1 the compiler cannot know what a dependent name is:
  - `typename T::value_type x;` says "this is a type" (without it, it is parsed as a value; error).
  - `obj.template get<0>()` says "`get` is a template, `<` is not less-than".
  - C++20 relaxed `typename` in many places where only a type can appear (alias declarations, return types, parameter types of member declarations).
- **Dependent base classes**: members of `Base<T>` are not found by unqualified lookup in a derived class template. `helper()` alone fails ("there are no arguments to 'helper' that depend on a template parameter"). Write `this->helper()` or `Base<T>::helper()` or add `using Base<T>::helper;`.
- Reason: `Base<T>` could be specialized later to not have `helper`, so the compiler refuses to assume.

subsections.title: 6. Non-type template parameters (NTTP)
subsections.content:
- Values known at compile time: integers, enums, pointers/references to objects with static storage, `std::nullptr_t`; C++20 adds floating point and **structural class types** (all members public and themselves structural).
- `template <auto V>` (C++17) deduces the NTTP's type: `Constant<42>`, `Constant<'x'>`.
- Classic uses: `std::array<T, N>`, fixed-size buffers, compile-time configuration, `std::get<I>`.
- String literals cannot be NTTP arguments directly (`Tag<"x">` with `const char*` is an error), but C++20 allows a class type that copies the characters: `template <FixedString S> struct Field;` used as `Field<"price">`.
- Each distinct value is a distinct type: `Buffer<64>` and `Buffer<128>` share nothing at runtime, which is both the speed (constants folded) and the bloat.

subsections.title: 7. Class template argument deduction (CTAD, C++17)
subsections.content:
- `std::pair p{1, 2.5};` deduces `std::pair<int, double>`; `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` deduces `std::vector<int>`; `std::lock_guard lk(m);` deduces the mutex type.
- The compiler builds deduction candidates from the constructors (implicit guides) and from **user-written deduction guides**:
  ```cpp
  template <class T> struct Wrapper { Wrapper(T) {} };
  Wrapper(const char*) -> Wrapper<std::string>;   // guide: literals become strings
  ```
- Surprises:
  - `std::pair p{1, "x"};` is `pair<int, const char*>`, not `pair<int, std::string>`.
  - `std::vector v{other_vec};` is a **copy** (`vector<int>`), not a vector of vectors: the copy deduction candidate is preferred for a single argument of the same template.
  - `std::vector v{it1, it2};` with braces deduces `vector<iterator>` (initializer_list of two iterators); `std::vector v(it1, it2)` with parentheses uses the iterator-pair guide and deduces the element type.
  - CTAD is all-or-nothing: `std::array<int> a{1, 2};` is an error; write `std::array a{1, 2}` or specify both arguments.
- C++20: CTAD for aggregates and alias templates.

subsections.title: 8. Variadic templates and fold expressions
subsections.content:
- `template <class... Ts> void log(const Ts&... args);` declares a **template parameter pack** and a **function parameter pack**.
- `sizeof...(Ts)` gives the count at compile time.
- **Pack expansion** `pattern...` repeats the pattern for each element: `f(std::forward<Ts>(args)...)`, `std::tuple<std::vector<Ts>...>`, `g(h(args)...)`.
- Before C++17, processing a pack needed recursion: a base case plus `head, tail...` overload.
- **Fold expressions** (C++17) reduce a pack with a binary operator:

| Form | Name | Expansion for `(a, b, c)` |
|---|---|---|
| `(args op ...)` | Unary right | `a op (b op c)` |
| `(... op args)` | Unary left | `(a op b) op c` |
| `(args op ... op init)` | Binary right | `a op (b op (c op init))` |
| `(init op ... op args)` | Binary left | `((init op a) op b) op c` |
- Direction matters for non-associative operators: `(args - ...)` on `(10, 3, 2)` is `10 - (3 - 2) = 9`; `(... - args)` is `(10 - 3) - 2 = 5`.
- **Empty pack** in a unary fold: only three operators have a value:
  - `&&` gives `true`, `||` gives `false`, `,` gives `void()`.
  - Any other operator (`+`, `*`, ...) is a compile error ("fold of empty expansion over operator+"). Use a binary fold with an init: `(0 + ... + args)`.
- Comma fold for "do this for each": `(std::cout << ... << args);` (binary left fold over `<<`), or `((std::cout << args << ' '), ...);`.
- The comma fold evaluates left to right (the built-in comma operator sequences its operands).

subsections.title: 9. CRTP and deducing this
subsections.content:
- **CRTP** (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern): `struct Derived : Base<Derived>`. The base knows the derived type at compile time and calls into it with `static_cast<Derived&>(*this).step()`.
- Uses: static polymorphism (no virtual call, no vptr, inlinable), mixins that add operators or counters to a class, compile-time "interface" enforcement.
- Limits:
  - `Base<A>` and `Base<B>` are unrelated types: no `std::vector<Base*>` of mixed derived objects, no runtime choice of type. Use `virtual` (or `std::variant`, topic 04) for that.
  - Writing `struct B : Base<A>` by mistake compiles and casts `*this` to the wrong type: UB. Guard with a private constructor plus `friend Derived;` in the base.
  - It removes the virtual dispatch and *enables* inlining; the optimizer still decides whether to inline.
- **Deducing this** (C++23, explicit object parameter): `void process(this auto& self) { self.step(); }`.
  - `self` is deduced as the actual object type (the derived class) at the call site: no template base, no cast.
  - An error (derived class has no `step`) is reported when `process` is instantiated for that class, at the call.
  - Also removes const/non-const/`&&` overload duplication: one `this auto&& self` member covers all.
  - Needs GCC 14 or Clang 18 (or newer); GCC 11 and 13 do not support it.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Templates are type-checked when defined." ✅ Only non-dependent parts; dependent code is checked at instantiation.
- ❌ "`add(10, 20.5)` converts 10 to double." ✅ Deduction does no conversions; it fails.
- ❌ "Pass by value deduces `const int` from a `const int`." ✅ Top-level const is dropped; `T` is `int`.
- ❌ "A full specialization is an overload." ✅ It is not a candidate in overload resolution; only its primary template is.
- ❌ "Function templates can be partially specialized like classes." ✅ They cannot; overload instead.
- ❌ "`typename` and `class` differ in a template parameter list." ✅ Identical there; `typename` is additionally the disambiguator for dependent types.
- ❌ "Members of a templated base are visible like normal inheritance." ✅ Not for unqualified names; use `this->`.
- ❌ "`std::vector v{a, b}` always makes a vector of the element type." ✅ CTAD with braces prefers the initializer list: two iterators make a `vector<iterator>`.
- ❌ "An empty fold is fine for any operator." ✅ Only `&&`, `||` and `,`.
- ❌ "CRTP guarantees inlining." ✅ It removes the virtual call; inlining is still the optimizer's decision.
- ❌ "Templates must go in headers because of a language rule about `.cpp` files." ✅ The rule is visibility at instantiation; explicit instantiation in a `.cpp` works for a closed set of types.

| `T` | `int[3]` | `int*` (array decays) | `int*` |
| `T` | function `void(int)` | `void(*)(int)` | pointer to function |
| `T&` | `int` | `int` | `int&` |
| `T&` | `const int` | `const int` | `const int&` |
| `T&` | `int[3]` | `int[3]` (no decay) | `int(&)[3]` |
| `T&` | `42` (rvalue) | deduction succeeds (`int`), but `int&` cannot bind: error | |
| `const T&` | `const int` | `int` | `const int&` |
| `const T&` | `42` | `int` | `const int&` |
- By value means "a new copy": the copy's own constness is not inherited, so top-level `const` and references are stripped.
- `T&` keeps everything the argument has, which is why `template <class T, std::size_t N> std::size_t size(T (&)[N])` can recover array sizes.
- **Every** deducible parameter is deduced independently, and the results must agree: `template <class T> T add(T, T); add(10, 20.5);` deduces `T = int` and `T = double`: deduction fails, "no matching function". No conversion is tried during deduction.
- Fixes: `add<double>(10, 20.5)` (explicit argument: now only conversions are needed), `add(10.0, 20.5)`, two parameters `template <class A, class B> auto add(A, B)`, or block deduction on one parameter with `std::type_identity_t<T>` (C++20).
- **Non-deduced contexts**: `T` cannot be deduced from `typename Wrapper<T>::type`, from a default argument, or from `std::function<void(T)>` when passing a lambda (the lambda is not a `std::function`).
- **Explicit arguments** fill parameters left to right; the rest are deduced: `std::make_unique<Order>(1, 2)` specifies `T`, deduces `Args...`.
- Return types are never deduced from the call site: `template <class R> R parse(std::string_view)` must be called as `parse<int>("42")`.

#### 3. Overloading vs specialization of function templates
- Two ways to customize a function template for some types:
  - **Overloading**: declare another function template or a plain function with the same name.
  - **Explicit (full) specialization**: `template <> void f<int>(int);` gives a different body for one exact argument set.
- Overload resolution only looks at **primary templates and non-template functions**. Specializations are not candidates; they are used only after their primary template has won.
- Ranking (simplified):
  1. Best conversion sequences win.
  2. On a tie, a non-template function beats a template.
  3. On a tie between templates, **partial ordering**: the more specialized template wins (`f(T*)` beats `f(T)` for `int*`, because every `T*` call could go to `f(T)` but not the reverse).
  4. Still tied: ambiguous.
- **Function templates cannot be partially specialized**. `template <class T> void f<T*>(T*)` is an error ("non-class, non-variable partial specialization ... is not allowed"). Use an overload instead.
- The classic trap (often called the Dimov/Abrahams example): a full specialization `f<int*>` of `f(T)` is ignored if an overload `f(T*)` exists and wins partial ordering. The specialization's body never runs.
- Guideline: prefer overloading (or `if constexpr`, or a class template with partial specialization) over explicit specialization of function templates.

#### 4. Class template specialization: full and partial
- Full specialization: `template <> struct Traits<bool> { ... };` a completely separate class for one argument set; it shares nothing with the primary (no members are inherited from it).
- Partial specialization: a pattern that matches a family of arguments:
  - `template <class T> struct Traits<T*>` (any pointer)
  - `template <class T> struct Traits<std::vector<T>>`
  - `template <class T> struct Same<T, T>` (both arguments equal)
- Selection: the compiler finds all partial specializations that match; if one is more specialized than all others it is used; if two match equally, the use is ambiguous; if none match, the primary is used.
- A specialization must be declared before the first use that would instantiate it; otherwise the program is ill-formed, no diagnostic required (in practice the primary is often used silently).
- This is how `<type_traits>` is built (`std::is_pointer<T*>`, `std::remove_const<const T>`); writing traits is covered in topic 11.
- Member specialization: a single member function of a class template can be fully specialized (`template <> void Box<int>::print() { }`) without rewriting the class.
- Variable templates can be partially specialized too (`template <class T> constexpr bool is_ptr_v<T*> = true;`).

#### 5. Two-phase lookup and dependent names
- Templates are checked twice:
  - **Phase 1** (definition): non-dependent names are looked up and non-dependent code is checked. `undeclared_function();` with no dependent argument is an error even if the template is never used (GCC, Clang).
  - **Phase 2** (instantiation): names that depend on template parameters are resolved, with ADL at the point of instantiation.
- A **dependent name** is one whose meaning depends on `T`: `T::value_type`, `obj.size()` where `obj` is a `T`, `Base<T>::member`.
- Disambiguators, because in phase 1 the compiler cannot know what a dependent name is:
  - `typename T::value_type x;` says "this is a type" (without it, it is parsed as a value; error).
  - `obj.template get<0>()` says "`get` is a template, `<` is not less-than".
  - C++20 relaxed `typename` in many places where only a type can appear (alias declarations, return types, parameter types of member declarations).
- **Dependent base classes**: members of `Base<T>` are not found by unqualified lookup in a derived class template. `helper()` alone fails ("there are no arguments to 'helper' that depend on a template parameter"). Write `this->helper()` or `Base<T>::helper()` or add `using Base<T>::helper;`.
- Reason: `Base<T>` could be specialized later to not have `helper`, so the compiler refuses to assume.

#### 6. Non-type template parameters (NTTP)
- Values known at compile time: integers, enums, pointers/references to objects with static storage, `std::nullptr_t`; C++20 adds floating point and **structural class types** (all members public and themselves structural).
- `template <auto V>` (C++17) deduces the NTTP's type: `Constant<42>`, `Constant<'x'>`.
- Classic uses: `std::array<T, N>`, fixed-size buffers, compile-time configuration, `std::get<I>`.
- String literals cannot be NTTP arguments directly (`Tag<"x">` with `const char*` is an error), but C++20 allows a class type that copies the characters: `template <FixedString S> struct Field;` used as `Field<"price">`.
- Each distinct value is a distinct type: `Buffer<64>` and `Buffer<128>` share nothing at runtime, which is both the speed (constants folded) and the bloat.

#### 7. Class template argument deduction (CTAD, C++17)
- `std::pair p{1, 2.5};` deduces `std::pair<int, double>`; `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` deduces `std::vector<int>`; `std::lock_guard lk(m);` deduces the mutex type.
- The compiler builds deduction candidates from the constructors (implicit guides) and from **user-written deduction guides**:
  ```cpp
  template <class T> struct Wrapper { Wrapper(T) {} };
  Wrapper(const char*) -> Wrapper<std::string>;   // guide: literals become strings
  ```
- Surprises:
  - `std::pair p{1, "x"};` is `pair<int, const char*>`, not `pair<int, std::string>`.
  - `std::vector v{other_vec};` is a **copy** (`vector<int>`), not a vector of vectors: the copy deduction candidate is preferred for a single argument of the same template.
  - `std::vector v{it1, it2};` with braces deduces `vector<iterator>` (initializer_list of two iterators); `std::vector v(it1, it2)` with parentheses uses the iterator-pair guide and deduces the element type.
  - CTAD is all-or-nothing: `std::array<int> a{1, 2};` is an error; write `std::array a{1, 2}` or specify both arguments.
- C++20: CTAD for aggregates and alias templates.

#### 8. Variadic templates and fold expressions
- `template <class... Ts> void log(const Ts&... args);` declares a **template parameter pack** and a **function parameter pack**.
- `sizeof...(Ts)` gives the count at compile time.
- **Pack expansion** `pattern...` repeats the pattern for each element: `f(std::forward<Ts>(args)...)`, `std::tuple<std::vector<Ts>...>`, `g(h(args)...)`.
- Before C++17, processing a pack needed recursion: a base case plus `head, tail...` overload.
- **Fold expressions** (C++17) reduce a pack with a binary operator:

| Form | Name | Expansion for `(a, b, c)` |
|---|---|---|
| `(args op ...)` | Unary right | `a op (b op c)` |
| `(... op args)` | Unary left | `(a op b) op c` |
| `(args op ... op init)` | Binary right | `a op (b op (c op init))` |
| `(init op ... op args)` | Binary left | `((init op a) op b) op c` |
- Direction matters for non-associative operators: `(args - ...)` on `(10, 3, 2)` is `10 - (3 - 2) = 9`; `(... - args)` is `(10 - 3) - 2 = 5`.
- **Empty pack** in a unary fold: only three operators have a value:
  - `&&` gives `true`, `||` gives `false`, `,` gives `void()`.
  - Any other operator (`+`, `*`, ...) is a compile error ("fold of empty expansion over operator+"). Use a binary fold with an init: `(0 + ... + args)`.
- Comma fold for "do this for each": `(std::cout << ... << args);` (binary left fold over `<<`), or `((std::cout << args << ' '), ...);`.
- The comma fold evaluates left to right (the built-in comma operator sequences its operands).

#### 9. CRTP and deducing this
- **CRTP** (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern): `struct Derived : Base<Derived>`. The base knows the derived type at compile time and calls into it with `static_cast<Derived&>(*this).step()`.
- Uses: static polymorphism (no virtual call, no vptr, inlinable), mixins that add operators or counters to a class, compile-time "interface" enforcement.
- Limits:
  - `Base<A>` and `Base<B>` are unrelated types: no `std::vector<Base*>` of mixed derived objects, no runtime choice of type. Use `virtual` (or `std::variant`, topic 04) for that.
  - Writing `struct B : Base<A>` by mistake compiles and casts `*this` to the wrong type: UB. Guard with a private constructor plus `friend Derived;` in the base.
  - It removes the virtual dispatch and *enables* inlining; the optimizer still decides whether to inline.
- **Deducing this** (C++23, explicit object parameter): `void process(this auto& self) { self.step(); }`.
  - `self` is deduced as the actual object type (the derived class) at the call site: no template base, no cast.
  - An error (derived class has no `step`) is reported when `process` is instantiated for that class, at the call.
  - Also removes const/non-const/`&&` overload duplication: one `this auto&& self` member covers all.
  - Needs GCC 14 or Clang 18 (or newer); GCC 11 and 13 do not support it.

#### 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "Templates are type-checked when defined." ✅ Only non-dependent parts; dependent code is checked at instantiation.
- ❌ "`add(10, 20.5)` converts 10 to double." ✅ Deduction does no conversions; it fails.
- ❌ "Pass by value deduces `const int` from a `const int`." ✅ Top-level const is dropped; `T` is `int`.
- ❌ "A full specialization is an overload." ✅ It is not a candidate in overload resolution; only its primary template is.
- ❌ "Function templates can be partially specialized like classes." ✅ They cannot; overload instead.
- ❌ "`typename` and `class` differ in a template parameter list." ✅ Identical there; `typename` is additionally the disambiguator for dependent types.
- ❌ "Members of a templated base are visible like normal inheritance." ✅ Not for unqualified names; use `this->`.
- ❌ "`std::vector v{a, b}` always makes a vector of the element type." ✅ CTAD with braces prefers the initializer list: two iterators make a `vector<iterator>`.
- ❌ "An empty fold is fine for any operator." ✅ Only `&&`, `||` and `,`.
- ❌ "CRTP guarantees inlining." ✅ It removes the virtual call; inlining is still the optimizer's decision.
- ❌ "Templates must go in headers because of a language rule about `.cpp` files." ✅ The rule is visibility at instantiation; explicit instantiation in a `.cpp` works for a closed set of types.

edge_cases.title: Conflicting deduction
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T> T add(T a, T b);` with `add(10, 20.5)`: `T` deduced as `int` from the first argument and `double` from the second.
- GCC: `no matching function for call to 'add(int, double)'`, note: `deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')`.
- `add<double>(10, 20.5)` compiles: with `T` given, deduction is skipped and 10 converts to `10.0`.
- Similar trap: `std::max(1, 2L)` (int vs long) and `std::min(x, 0)` with `size_t x`.

edge_cases.title: The specialization that is never called
Partial specialization of a function template
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T> void print<T*>(T* p);` is rejected: `non-class, non-variable partial specialization 'print<T*>' is not allowed`.
- Workarounds:
  - Overload: `template <class T> void print(T* p);`
  - `if constexpr (std::is_pointer_v<T>)` inside one template.
  - Forward to a class template that can be partially specialized: `PrintImpl<T>::run(x)`.

edge_cases.title: Missing typename, template or this->
edge_cases.explanation:
- `T::value_type x;` is parsed as a value expression: error "need 'typename' before 'T::value_type' because 'T' is a dependent scope".
- `t.get<0>()` where `t` depends on `T`: may parse `<` as less-than; write `t.template get<0>()`.
- In `template <class T> struct D : Base<T> { void g() { helper(); } };`, `helper` is not found in the dependent base: "there are no arguments to 'helper' that depend on a template parameter, so a declaration of 'helper' must be available". Fix: `this->helper()`.
- Some compilers in permissive modes historically accepted these; GCC and Clang reject them.

edge_cases.title: Empty packs and unary folds
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class... T> auto sum(T... v) { return (v + ...); }` compiles, but `sum()` fails: "fold of empty expansion over operator+".
- `(v && ...)` with no arguments is `true`; `(v || ...)` is `false`; `(v , ...)` is `void()`.
- Fix: `(0 + ... + v)` (binary fold with an identity) or `if constexpr (sizeof...(v) == 0)`.
- With a binary fold, the init also fixes the result type: `(0.0 + ... + v)` sums in `double`.

edge_cases.title: CTAD that deduces the "wrong" type
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::vector<int> src{1, 2, 3};`
  - `std::vector a{src};` is `vector<int>` (copy), size 3.
  - `std::vector b{src, src};` is `vector<vector<int>>`, size 2.
  - `std::vector c{src.begin(), src.end()};` is `vector<vector<int>::iterator>`, size 2.
  - `std::vector d(src.begin(), src.end());` is `vector<int>`, size 3.
- `std::pair p{"key", 1};` stores a `const char*`; comparing `p.first == other` compares pointers if `other` is also `const char*`.
- Use an explicit type when the element type matters for correctness.

edge_cases.title: Template defined in a .cpp file
edge_cases.explanation:
- Header declares `template <class T> T clamp01(T);`, `clamp.cpp` defines it, `main.cpp` calls `clamp01(0.5)`.
- Compiles, then fails at link time: `undefined reference to 'double clamp01<double>(double)'`. `clamp.cpp` never instantiated the `double` version because nothing there used it.
- Fixes: define the template in the header, or add `template double clamp01<double>(double);` (explicit instantiation) in `clamp.cpp` for each supported type.

edge_cases.title: Arrays: decay by value, size by reference
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T> void by_val(T)` with `int arr[10]` gives `T = int*`: `sizeof(T)` is 8 (x86-64), the size is lost.
- `template <class T> void by_ref(T&)` gives `T = int[10]`: `sizeof(T)` is 40.
- `template <class T, std::size_t N> constexpr std::size_t count(T (&)[N]) { return N; }` is how `std::size` works for arrays.
- String literals are arrays too: `by_ref("abc")` deduces `T = const char[4]`, so `by_ref("abc")` and `by_ref("abcd")` are two different instantiations.

interview_qa.question: What does "instantiating a template" mean, and why do template definitions usually live in headers?
interview_qa.answer: Instantiation is the compiler generating a concrete function or class from the template for specific arguments, at the point where it is used. To do that it needs the full definition in the same translation unit, so definitions go in headers; otherwise other translation units fail at link time with "undefined reference".
interview_qa.explanation:
- Each distinct argument set is a separate entity: `Stack<int>` and `Stack<double>` share no code unless the optimizer folds identical functions.
- Explicit instantiation lets you keep the definition in a `.cpp`: `template class Stack<int>;` there, plus `extern template class Stack<int>;` in the header to stop other TUs from instantiating it (C++11). This works when the set of types is closed.
- Duplicate implicit instantiations across TUs are merged by the linker (they are inline-like entities), so the ODR is not violated.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Templates are compiled once into generic machine code." C++ templates are expanded per argument set; it is not type erasure like Java generics.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: compile-time cost and binary bloat grow with instantiations; `extern template`, explicit instantiation and moving type-independent code into a non-template base reduce both.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A template is a recipe compiled per use; the recipe must be visible where it is used.

To do that it needs the full definition in the same translation unit, so definitions go in headers; otherwise other translation units fail at link time with "undefined reference".

**Explanation:**
- Each distinct argument set is a separate entity: `Stack<int>` and `Stack<double>` share no code unless the optimizer folds identical functions.

- Duplicate implicit instantiations across TUs are merged by the linker (they are inline-like entities), so the ODR is not violated.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Templates are compiled once into generic machine code." C++ templates are expanded per argument set; it is not type erasure like Java generics.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: compile-time cost and binary bloat grow with instantiations; `extern template`, explicit instantiation and moving type-independent code into a non-template base reduce both.

**Key takeaway:** A template is a recipe compiled per use; the recipe must be visible where it is used.

interview_qa.question: Given `template<class T> void f(T)`, `template<class T> void g(T&)` and `const int c = 1;`, what is T in `f(c)` and in `g(c)`? What about an array argument?
interview_qa.answer: `f(c)`: `T = int` (by-value parameters drop top-level const). `g(c)`: `T = const int` (a reference must preserve the const). For `int arr[3]`: `f(arr)` gives `T = int*` (decay) and `g(arr)` gives `T = int[3]` (no decay).
interview_qa.explanation:
- By value creates a new object; whether the caller's object was const is irrelevant to the copy.
- Low-level const is kept: `const int* p; f(p)` deduces `T = const int*`.
- `const T&` with `const int` gives `T = int` (the const is already in the pattern); it also accepts rvalues like `42`, while `T&` does not.
- `T&` preserving array types is how `template <class T, std::size_t N> std::size_t size(T (&)[N])` recovers `N`.
- Forwarding references `T&&` follow different rules (Ch1, Core Language).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`f(c)` deduces `const int`, so `x` can't be modified inside." Inside `f` the parameter is a mutable `int` copy.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: string literals are `const char[N]` arrays, so `g("abc")` and `g("abcd")` are two different instantiations.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: By value strips top-level const and decays arrays; by reference keeps both.

interview_qa.question: Why does `add(10, 20.5)` fail for `template<class T> T add(T, T)`, and how do you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: `T` is deduced independently from each argument: `int` from `10` and `double` from `20.5`. The two deductions conflict and deduction performs no conversions, so there is no viable function ("deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T'"). Fix with `add<double>(10, 20.5)`, matching argument types, or two template parameters.
interview_qa.explanation:
- With an explicit `T`, deduction is skipped and normal implicit conversions apply: `10` converts to `10.0`.
- Two-parameter version: `template <class A, class B> auto add(A a, B b) { return a + b; }` returns `double` here.
- C++20 `std::type_identity_t<T>` on one parameter makes it non-deduced, so only the other argument decides `T`.
- Same root cause as `std::max(1, 2L)` failing.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It compiles and returns 30 because 20.5 is truncated." Nothing is converted during deduction; it fails to compile.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: quoting the GCC note "deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Deduction must agree across all arguments and never converts; specify `T` to allow conversions.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
`T` is deduced independently from each argument: `int` from `10` and `double` from `20.5`. The two deductions conflict and deduction performs no conversions, so there is no viable function ("deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T'"). Fix with `add<double>(10, 20.5)`, matching argument types, or two template parameters.

**Explanation:**
- With an explicit `T`, deduction is skipped and normal implicit conversions apply: `10` converts to `10.0`.
- Two-parameter version: `template <class A, class B> auto add(A a, B b) { return a + b; }` returns `double` here.
- C++20 `std::type_identity_t<T>` on one parameter makes it non-deduced, so only the other argument decides `T`.
- Same root cause as `std::max(1, 2L)` failing.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It compiles and returns 30 because 20.5 is truncated." Nothing is converted during deduction; it fails to compile.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: quoting the GCC note "deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')".

**Key takeaway:** Deduction must agree across all arguments and never converts; specify `T` to allow conversions.

interview_qa.question: Should you specialize a function template or overload it? Why?
interview_qa.answer: Overload. Explicit specializations do not take part in overload resolution: the compiler first picks the best primary template (or non-template function), and only then checks whether that primary has a specialization for the deduced arguments. A specialization of a primary that loses is silently ignored.
interview_qa.explanation:
- With `template<class T> void f(T)`, a specialization `f<int*>`, and an overload `template<class T> void f(T*)`, the call `f(&x)` picks the overload `f(T*)` (more specialized) and the specialization never runs.
- Moving the specialization after `f(T*)` changes which primary it belongs to (now `f(T*)` with `T = int`) and it is called: the behaviour depends on declaration order.
- Overloads are visible, rank by normal rules, and cannot be "attached" to the wrong primary.
- Exception: specializing `std::` customization points such as `std::hash<MyType>` (a class template) is correct and expected (see topic 09).

interview_qa.question: What is two-phase lookup, and why do you sometimes need `typename` and `template` inside templates?
interview_qa.answer: Templates are checked in two phases: at definition, non-dependent names are looked up and checked; at instantiation, names that depend on template parameters are resolved. interview_qa.question: What is CTAD, what are deduction guides, and what are its pitfalls?

interview_qa.question: How do variadic templates work, and how was a pack processed before C++17?
interview_qa.answer: `template <class... Ts> void f(Ts... args)` declares type and value packs; `pattern...` expands a pattern once per element (`g(args)...`, `std::forward<Ts>(args)...`), and `sizeof...(Ts)` gives the count. Before C++17 you processed a pack by recursion: an overload taking `(Head, Tail...)` that handles `Head` and calls itself with `Tail...`, plus a base case.
interview_qa.explanation:
```cpp
#include <iostream>

void print() { std::cout << '\n'; }                      // base case

template <class Head, class... Tail>
void print(const Head& h, const Tail&... t) {
    std::cout << h << (sizeof...(t) ? ", " : "");
    print(t...);                                         // recurse on the tail
}

int main() { print(1, "two", 3.5); }                     // 1, two, 3.5
```
- Recursion creates one instantiation per pack length: more compile time and deeper call chains (usually inlined away).
- C++17 fold expressions or `if constexpr (sizeof...(t) > 0)` remove the need for a separate base case.

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`args...` loops over the arguments at runtime." Expansion happens at compile time; there is no loop.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: C++26 pack indexing `Ts...[0]` removes much of the remaining recursion.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Packs are expanded at compile time; recursion was the pre-C++17 way to walk them.

interview_qa.question: Explain the four forms of fold expressions. What do `(a - ...)` and `(... - a)` give for (10, 3, 2), and what happens with an empty pack?
interview_qa.answer: Unary right `(a op ...)`, unary left `(... op a)`, binary right `(a op ... op init)`, binary left `(init op ... op a)`. - Binary folds supply an identity for the empty case and fix the result type: `(0.0 + ... + a)`.
- `(std::cout << ... << args)` is a binary left fold; `((std::cout << args << ' '), ...)` is a unary comma fold that prints with separators.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: GCC's error text "fold of empty expansion over operator+".

interview_qa.question: What is CRTP, what does it buy you over virtual functions, and what can't it do?
interview_qa.answer: CRTP is `class D : public Base<D>`: the base is parameterized by the derived class, so it can call derived members with `static_cast<D&>(*this)` resolved at compile time. It removes the virtual call and the vptr and lets the compiler inline. It cannot give runtime polymorphism: `Base<A>` and `Base<B>` are unrelated, so no heterogeneous container or runtime type choice.
interview_qa.explanation:

- Inlining is enabled, not guaranteed; the optimizer still decides.
- Each derived type instantiates its own copy of the base code (binary size).
- Trap: `struct B : Base<A>` compiles and invokes UB; guard with a private base constructor and `friend D;`.
- Virtual call cost itself is small when predicted; the larger win is inlining and keeping the object free of a vptr.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "CRTP is faster than virtual in every case." With one hot type, devirtualization (`final`, LTO) can make virtual just as fast; with many types chosen at runtime CRTP does not apply.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: when runtime choice is needed among a closed set of types, `std::variant` + `std::visit` is the middle ground (topic 04).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CRTP = compile-time polymorphism: no vptr, inlinable, but no runtime type choice.

- Recursive lambdas become possible: `auto fib = [](this auto self, int n) -> int { return n < 2 ? n : self(n - 1) + self(n - 2); };`.
- Restrictions: such a function cannot be `virtual`, `static`, or have cv/ref qualifiers; `this` is not available inside (use `self`).
- Compiler support: GCC 14, Clang 18 and newer. GCC 11 and 13 reject it.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "You still need to cast `self` to the derived type." No cast: `self` already has the derived type.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: unlike CRTP, there is no way to name the wrong derived class.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `this auto& self` gives the base the real object type at each call: CRTP without the template plumbing.
interview_qa.full_content:

interview_qa.question: Why does a template sometimes beat a non-template function that looks like a perfect fit?
interview_qa.answer: The non-template is preferred only when the conversion sequences are equally good. A template deduces the exact argument type, so if the non-template needs any conversion (for example `int` to `double`, or adding `const` through a reference), the template's exact match wins first.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Better conversions beat the non-template preference; templates win by being exact.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
The non-template is preferred only when the conversion sequences are equally good. A template deduces the exact argument type, so if the non-template needs any conversion (for example `int` to `double`, or adding `const` through a reference), the template's exact match wins first.

**Explanation:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>

void note(double) { std::cout << "note(double)\n"; }
template <class T> void note(T) { std::cout << "note(T)\n"; }

int main() {
    note(1.0);  // tie on exact match: non-template wins
    note(1);    // note<int> is exact; note(double) needs int->double: template wins
}
```
- Output: `note(double)` then `note(T)`.
- The same mechanism makes a forwarding-reference constructor hijack copy construction from a non-const lvalue (Ch1).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Non-template functions are always preferred over templates." Only as a tie-breaker.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: to force the non-template path, constrain the template (concepts, topic 11) or delete the unwanted instantiation.

**Key takeaway:** Better conversions beat the non-template preference; templates win by being exact.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: no matching function for call to 'add(int, double)'
note: deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')
Fix: add<double>(10, 20.5), which prints 30.5
```

**Explanation:**
- `T` is deduced from each argument separately: `int` from `10`, `double` from `20.5`. The results must agree, and deduction never applies conversions.
- With an explicit template argument there is nothing to deduce, so `10` is converted to `10.0` as for any normal function call.
- Alternatives: `add(10.0, 20.5)`, or two template parameters with `auto` return type.
- **Key Concept:** All deductions of the same `T` must match exactly; conversions only happen after `T` is fixed.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
explicit specialization
```

**Explanation:**
- The specialization is declared after `f(T*)`, so `template <> void f<>(int*)` matches the more specialized primary: it is `f(T*)` with `T = int`.
- Overload resolution between the two primaries picks `f(T*)` (partial ordering); its specialization for `T = int` exists, so that body runs.
- Swap the order (specialization right after `f(T)`) and it becomes `f(T)` with `T = int*`: the same call then prints `f(T*)` and the specialization is never used.
- **Key Concept:** Explicit specializations attach to whichever primary they match at their point of declaration and do not take part in overload resolution. Prefer overloads.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
8 64 8
(typical x86-64: 8-byte pointers and doubles)
```

- `count` deduces both the element type and `N` from the array reference; this is how `std::size(arr)` is implemented.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
16 4
```

**Explanation:**
- `(v / ...)` is a unary right fold: `64 / (8 / 2) = 64 / 4 = 16`.
- `(... / v)` is a unary left fold: `(64 / 8) / 2 = 4`.
- The position of the dots shows the grouping: dots on the right, grouping from the right.
- **Key Concept:** Fold direction changes the result for non-associative operators.

practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error: fold of empty expansion over operator*
(any_negative() alone is fine: an empty || fold is false)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- An empty unary fold is valid only for `&&` (true), `||` (false) and `,` (void()).

practice_tasks.answer:
Compile error: there are no arguments to 'reset' that depend on a template parameter,
so a declaration of 'reset' must be available
practice_tasks.explanation:

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
4 2 4
```

**Explanation:**
- `a{src}`: CTAD prefers the copy deduction candidate for a single argument of the same template, so `a` is a `vector<int>` copy.
- `b{src.begin(), src.end()}`: braces make the `initializer_list` constructor win, so `b` is a `vector<vector<int>::iterator>` holding two iterators.
- `c(src.begin(), src.end())`: parentheses select the iterator-pair constructor and its deduction guide: `vector<int>` with 4 elements.
- **Key Concept:** CTAD plus braces can deduce a container of iterators; use parentheses or spell out the element type.
