practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: ambiguous template instantiation for 'struct Pair<int*, int*>'
(the two static_asserts on their own are fine)
```

**Explanation:**
- `Pair<int*, int*>` matches both partial specializations, and neither is more specialized than the other (each accepts arguments the other rejects).
- The compiler does not fall back to the primary when specializations tie: it is an error.
- Fix: add a specialization for the overlap, `template <class T, class U> struct Pair<T*, U*>`, which is more specialized than both.
- **Key Concept:** Among matching class partial specializations, a unique most specialized one must exist.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
2 1 1
```

**Explanation:**
- Every instantiation is a separate class with its own static members. `Counter<int>`, `Counter<double>` and `Counter<const int>` share nothing.
- `const int` and `int` are different template arguments, so they are different classes too.
- To share a counter across all instantiations, move it into a non-template base class.
- **Key Concept:** A class template's statics exist once per instantiation, not once per template.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.answer:
Compiles, but undefined behaviour: Shape<Square>::area casts a Circle to Square&.
At -O0 on GCC it printed 1 (Circle's r = 1.0 read as Square::side), not 3.14159.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `Circle` derives from `Shape<Square>`, so `c.area()` runs `static_cast<const Square&>(*this)` on an object that is not a `Square`: UB.
- It calls `Square::area_impl` on Circle's memory: `side` overlays `r`, so it computes `1 * 1`.
- Guard against this at compile time: give `Shape` a private constructor and `friend Derived;`. Then `Circle c;` fails ("use of deleted function 'Circle::Circle()'"), because only `Square` may construct `Shape<Square>`.
- C++23 deducing this (`double area(this const auto& self)`) cannot be pointed at the wrong type at all.
- **Key Concept:** CRTP trusts you to pass the right derived type; enforce it with a private constructor plus `friend Derived`.

quick_reference.content:
#### Deduction summary
| Parameter | Drops top-level const | Array/function decays | Binds rvalues |
|---|---|---|---|
| `T` | Yes | Yes | Yes (copy) |
| `T&` | No (`T` may become `const X`) | No | No |
| `const T&` | n/a (`const` added) | No | Yes |
| `T&&` (forwarding) | See Ch1 | No | Yes |

#### Specialization rules
| Construct | Allowed? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Function: full specialization | Yes | Not an overload; avoid, prefer overloads |
| Function: partial specialization | No | Overload or forward to a class |
| Class: full specialization | Yes | Unrelated to the primary's members |
| Class: partial specialization | Yes | Most specialized match wins; ties are ambiguous |
| Variable template: partial | Yes | C++14 |
| Single member of a class template | Full only | `template <> void Box<int>::f()` |

#### Disambiguators
| Situation | Write |
|---|---|
| Dependent type | `typename T::value_type` |
| Dependent member template | `x.template get<0>()` / `T::template rebind<U>` |
| Member of dependent base | `this->m` / `Base<T>::m` / `using Base<T>::m;` |

#### Folds
| Code | Empty pack |
|---|---|
| `(a + ...)` | Error |
| `(0 + ... + a)` | `0` |
| `(a && ...)` | `true` |
| `(a \|\| ...)` | `false` |
| `(f(a), ...)` | `void()` |

#### Version map
| Feature | Standard |
|---|---|
| Variadic templates, `extern template`, alias templates | C++11 |
| Variable templates | C++14 |
| Folds, CTAD, `template <auto>`, `if constexpr` | C++17 |
| Class-type NTTP, aggregate/alias CTAD, concepts, `type_identity` | C++20 |
| Deducing this (explicit object parameter) | C++23 |
| Pack indexing `Ts...[0]` | C++26 |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| `add(10, 20.5)` with `T add(T, T)`? | Deduction conflict, no match; `add<double>` works |
| `f(T)` with `const int`? | `T = int` |
| `f(T&)` with `const int`? | `T = const int` |
| Specialize or overload a function template? | Overload |
| Partial specialization of a function? | Not allowed |
| Which wins, `f(T)` or `f(T*)` for `int*`? | `f(T*)`, more specialized |
| Why `typename`? | Dependent name is assumed to be a value |
| Why `this->` in a template derived class? | Dependent base members are not found otherwise |
| Why are templates in headers? | Definition needed at instantiation |
| `(a - ...)` on 10,3,2? | 9; `(... - a)` gives 5 |
| CRTP vs virtual? | Compile-time type, no vptr; no heterogeneous containers |
| Deducing this? | C++23 `this auto& self`: CRTP without the template base |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- An unconstrained template `template <class T> void f(T)` accepts **every** type and fails late, deep inside its body, with long errors. Constraining means: decide at the **call site** whether a template applies to a type, and pick between alternatives by type properties.
- Three generations of tools, all still seen in interviews and codebases:

| Era | Tool | How it selects |
|---|---|---|
| C++98/11 | SFINAE, `std::enable_if`, tag dispatch | Make the signature invalid so the overload disappears; or overload on tag types |
| C++17 | `if constexpr`, `std::void_t`, `_v` traits | One template, branches discarded at compile time |
| C++20 | Concepts, `requires` | Named constraints checked before overload resolution, with ordering (subsumption) |
- Everything is compile-time: none of these tools costs anything at runtime; they decide which code is generated.
- Type traits (`<type_traits>`) are the vocabulary for all three: compile-time questions about types (`is_integral`) and type transformations (`remove_cvref`).

subsections.title: 2. Type traits: how they work
subsections.content:
- A trait is a class template whose result is a static member:
  - **Predicate** traits derive from `std::integral_constant<bool, B>` (`std::true_type`/`std::false_type`), exposing `::value`.
  - **Transformation** traits expose `::type`.
- Helpers: `std::is_integral_v<T>` (C++17) = `std::is_integral<T>::value`; `std::remove_cvref_t<T>` (C++20) = `typename std::remove_cvref<T>::type` (C++14 added the `_t` aliases).
- Implemented with partial specialization (topic 10):
  ```cpp
  template <class T> struct is_ptr : std::false_type {};
  template <class T> struct is_ptr<T*> : std::true_type {};
  ```
  Note: this version says `is_ptr<int* const>` is false; the real `std::is_pointer` handles cv-qualified pointers too.
- Most used traits:

| Trait | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `is_same_v<A, B>` | Exact type equality (`int` vs `const int` differ) |
| `is_integral_v`, `is_floating_point_v`, `is_arithmetic_v` | Number categories (`bool` and `char` are integral) |
| `is_pointer_v`, `is_reference_v`, `is_const_v` | Shape of the type |
| `is_trivially_copyable_v` | Safe to `memcpy` (Ch2) |
| `is_nothrow_move_constructible_v` | Decides vector's move-vs-copy on growth (Ch2) |
| `remove_cvref_t`, `decay_t` | Strip `const`/`&` (decay also turns arrays/functions into pointers) |
| `conditional_t<B, X, Y>` | Compile-time type selection |
| `common_type_t<A, B>` | Type both convert to (`int`, `double` give `double`) |
| `underlying_type_t<E>` | Integer type of an enum |
| `is_invocable_v<F, Args...>`, `invoke_result_t` | Can `F` be called with `Args`? With what result? |
- Many traits need compiler intrinsics (`is_trivially_copyable`, `is_enum`, `is_union`): they cannot be written in portable C++.
- Pitfall: `is_const_v<const int&>` is false (a reference itself is never const); strip the reference first: `is_const_v<std::remove_reference_t<T>>`.

subsections.title: 3. SFINAE: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
subsections.content:
- During overload resolution, for each function template the compiler deduces `T` and **substitutes** it into the **signature** (parameter types, return type, template parameter defaults, a C++20 `explicit(bool)` condition).
- If substitution produces an invalid type or expression in that **immediate context**, the template is silently removed from the candidate set. That is SFINAE.
- After that, the remaining **viable** candidates (substitution succeeded, constraints satisfied, arguments convertible) are ranked; the best one wins.
- What is **not** SFINAE (a hard error):
  - Errors inside the function **body** (the body is instantiated only after the function is chosen).
  - Errors inside a class template instantiated as a side effect (e.g. a trait whose definition itself fails).
  - The `noexcept` specifier: it is substituted only when it is needed, after deduction, so `noexcept(T::value)` with `T = int` is a hard error, not SFINAE ([temp.deduct.general]).
  - Return type deduction with `auto`: the signature is just `auto`, so substitution cannot fail and the template stays viable. If it is selected (or its return type is needed), the body is instantiated and errors there are hard. Measured: `template <class T> auto len(T t) { return t.size(); }` plus `long len(...)`, called with `len(5)`: the template is an exact match, beats the `...` fallback, and its body fails: "request for member 'size' in 't', which is of non-class type 'int'".
- Typical SFINAE spots:
  - Trailing return type: `auto f(T t) -> decltype(t.size(), void())`.
  - Template parameter default: `typename = std::enable_if_t<Cond>`.
  - Non-type template parameter: `std::enable_if_t<Cond, int> = 0`.
  - Return type: `std::enable_if_t<Cond, R> f(T)`.

subsections.title: 4. std::enable_if: the forms and their traps
subsections.content:
- `std::enable_if<true, T>::type` is `T`; `std::enable_if<false, T>` has no `type`: using it is a substitution failure.
- Forms:

| Form | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Return type | `template <class T> std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>, T> twice(T x)` | Clutters the return type; no use for constructors |
| Type template parameter default | `template <class T, class = std::enable_if_t<C>>` | **Trap**: two overloads differing only in the default are a redefinition |
| NTTP | `template <class T, std::enable_if_t<C, int> = 0>` | Preferred form: different conditions give different signatures |
| Function parameter | `void f(T x, std::enable_if_t<C>* = nullptr)` | Changes the arity; not for operators |
- The redefinition trap: default template arguments are not part of the function template's signature, so `template <class T, class = enable_if_t<is_integral_v<T>>> void f(T)` and the same with `is_floating_point_v` declare the **same** template twice: "redefinition of 'template<class T, class> void f(T)'".
- The **ambiguity trap** (a common wrong textbook answer):
  - `template <class T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0> void foo(T);` plus an unconstrained `template <class T> void foo(T);`.
  - `foo(10)`: both are viable with identical parameter types; SFINAE conditions do not take part in partial ordering, so neither is more specialized: "call of overloaded 'foo(int)' is ambiguous". (`foo(3.14)` works: only the generic one is viable.)
  - Fixes: make the generic overload exclusive (`!is_integral_v<T>`), use a priority tag, use `if constexpr`, or use concepts (where a constrained template **does** beat an unconstrained one).

subsections.title: 5. Detection idiom: void_t and declval
subsections.content:
- Question: "does `T` have a `.size()` member?" without a compile error when it does not.
- `std::void_t<Ts...>` (C++17) is `void` for any valid types; if any type is invalid, substitution fails.
- `std::declval<T>()` produces a `T&&` in unevaluated contexts (`decltype`, `sizeof`, `noexcept`) without constructing a `T`; calling it in evaluated code is an error.
- The idiom:
  ```cpp
  template <class T, class = void>
  struct has_size : std::false_type {};

  template <class T>
  struct has_size<T, std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<const T&>().size())>>
      : std::true_type {};
  ```
- How it works: `has_size<T>` means `has_size<T, void>`. The partial specialization matches only if its second argument can be formed and equals `void`; for types without `size()` substitution fails and the primary (false) is used.
- C++20 replaces it with a one-liner: `template <class T> concept HasSize = requires(const T& t) { t.size(); };`.

subsections.title: 6. Tag dispatch and priority tags
subsections.content:
- Tag dispatch: pass a tag object whose **type** encodes a property, and overload on the tag type. No SFINAE needed, and normal overload resolution (with inheritance) does the ranking.
- Classic example: `std::advance` on iterator categories:
  - `random_access_iterator_tag` derives from `bidirectional_iterator_tag`, which derives from `forward_iterator_tag` ...
  - `advance_impl(it, n, std::random_access_iterator_tag)` does `it += n`; the bidirectional version loops in both directions; the input version loops forward.
  - A tag type with no exact overload converts to its base: the most derived matching overload wins.
- Priority tags fix the SFINAE ambiguity: `template <int N> struct priority : priority<N - 1> {}; template <> struct priority<0> {};`
  - Call `impl(x, priority<1>{})`; the preferred overload takes `priority<1>`, the fallback takes `priority<0>` (a derived-to-base conversion, so it ranks lower).
  - If the preferred overload is removed by SFINAE, the fallback is still viable.
- Tag dispatch is also the cleanest pre-C++17 way to branch on `std::true_type`/`std::false_type`.

subsections.title: 7. if constexpr (C++17) and the discarded statement
subsections.content:
- `if constexpr (cond)` requires a constant expression; the branch not taken becomes a **discarded statement**.
- Inside a template, when the condition depends on a template parameter, the discarded branch is **not instantiated**: it may contain code that would not compile for this `T` (`v.size()` for an `int`).
- Limits (the parts source explanations usually skip):
  - Outside a template, or when the condition is not value-dependent, the discarded branch is still fully checked. `void g(int v) { if constexpr (true) { } else { v.size(); } }` is an error: "request for member 'size' in 'v', which is of non-class type 'int'".
  - The discarded branch must still parse, and non-dependent constructs in it are still checked.
  - `return` statements in a discarded branch do not participate in `auto` return type deduction.
- `static_assert(false, "...")` in a discarded branch:
  - Before C++23 (P2593R1, applied as a defect report), the program was ill-formed because the assertion does not depend on `T`. GCC 11 rejects it: "static assertion failed".
  - GCC 13 and newer accept it (in every `-std` mode, as a DR): it fires only if the branch is instantiated.
  - Portable old workaround: `static_assert(always_false<T>, "...")` with `template <class> constexpr bool always_false = false;`.
- `if constexpr` vs SFINAE: one template with branches (simpler, one place) vs separate overloads (extensible by others: users can add an overload, but cannot add a branch to your function).

subsections.title: 8. Concepts and requires (C++20)
subsections.content:
- A **concept** is a named compile-time predicate on template arguments:
  ```cpp
  template <class T>
  concept Hashable = requires(const T& a) {
      { std::hash<T>{}(a) } -> std::convertible_to<std::size_t>;
  };
  ```
- Four ways to apply a constraint (equivalent for simple cases):
  - `template <Hashable T> void f(T);` (type-constraint)
  - `template <class T> requires Hashable<T> void f(T);` (requires-clause)
  - `template <class T> void f(T) requires Hashable<T>;` (trailing requires-clause; works on non-template members of class templates)
  - `void f(Hashable auto x);` (abbreviated function template, C++20)
- A **requires-expression** `requires (params) { requirements; }` is a `bool` constant expression. Kinds of requirements:

| Kind | Syntax | Checks |
|---|---|---|
| Simple | `a + b;` | Expression is valid (not its value) |
| Type | `typename T::value_type;` | Type exists |
| Compound | `{ a.size() } -> std::convertible_to<std::size_t>;` | Valid, optionally `noexcept`, result satisfies a concept |
| Nested | `requires sizeof(T) <= 8;` | A constant expression is **true** |
- Trap: `requires { sizeof(T) > 4; }` is a simple requirement: it checks that the expression compiles, which it always does, so the concept is always true. Use `requires (sizeof(T) > 4);` as a nested requirement, or just `sizeof(T) > 4` in the concept definition.
- `requires requires (T x) { x + x; }`: a requires-clause whose condition is an ad hoc requires-expression. Legal, but name it as a concept instead.
- Errors move to the call site. GCC: "no matching function ... constraints not satisfied ... the required expression 'a.size()' is invalid".
- Standard concepts (`<concepts>`, `<iterator>`, `<ranges>`): `same_as`, `convertible_to`, `derived_from`, `integral`, `floating_point`, `invocable`, `predicate`, `equality_comparable`, `totally_ordered`, `copyable`, `movable`, `regular`, `input_iterator` ... `random_access_iterator`, `ranges::range`.

subsections.title: 9. Constraint ordering: subsumption
subsections.content:
- When two constrained templates are both viable and otherwise equal, the one whose constraints **subsume** the other's (is "more constrained") wins. An unconstrained template loses to a constrained one.
- Constraints are normalized into conjunctions (`&&`) and disjunctions (`||`) of **atomic constraints**. `A && B` subsumes `A`.
- Atomic constraints are compared by **identity of the expression as written in the source**, not by meaning:
  - `template <class T> requires std::is_integral_v<T>` and `template <class T> requires (std::is_integral_v<T> && sizeof(T) == 4)`: the two `is_integral_v<T>` are different atomic constraints (different source locations), so no subsumption: `f(1)` is ambiguous (verified with GCC 11).
  - Define named concepts (`concept Int = ...; concept Int4 = Int<T> && sizeof(T) == 4;`) and the same calls resolve: `Int4` subsumes `Int` because concepts are expanded to the same atomic constraint.
- Standard concepts are designed for this: `std::random_access_iterator` subsumes `std::bidirectional_iterator`, so concept overloads can replace tag dispatch.
- SFINAE/`enable_if` conditions are never compared: that is why the enable_if ambiguity trap exists and concepts fix it.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Any compile error during overload resolution is SFINAE." ✅ Only failures in the immediate context of substitution into the signature.
- ❌ "An `enable_if`-constrained overload is more specialized than an unconstrained one." ✅ Partial ordering ignores SFINAE conditions; the call is ambiguous. Concepts do order.
- ❌ "Two `enable_if` overloads with `typename = ...` defaults are fine." ✅ Redefinition; use `enable_if_t<C, int> = 0`.
- ❌ "`if constexpr` never compiles the other branch." ✅ Only inside a template with a value-dependent condition.
- ❌ "`static_assert(false)` in an `if constexpr` else is always an error." ✅ Accepted since P2593 (GCC 13+); older compilers need a dependent `false`.
- ❌ "`requires { sizeof(T) > 4; }` checks the size." ✅ It checks the expression is valid; use a nested `requires`.
- ❌ "Concepts change the generated code." ✅ They only choose which template is used; no runtime cost.
- ❌ "`is_const_v<const int&>` is true." ✅ False; references are not cv-qualified.
- ❌ "Concepts with the same meaning subsume each other." ✅ Subsumption compares atomic constraints by source identity, so reuse named concepts.

- Three generations of tools, all still seen in interviews and codebases:

| Era | Tool | How it selects |
|---|---|---|
| C++98/11 | SFINAE, `std::enable_if`, tag dispatch | Make the signature invalid so the overload disappears; or overload on tag types |
| C++17 | `if constexpr`, `std::void_t`, `_v` traits | One template, branches discarded at compile time |
| C++20 | Concepts, `requires` | Named constraints checked before overload resolution, with ordering (subsumption) |

- Type traits (`<type_traits>`) are the vocabulary for all three: compile-time questions about types (`is_integral`) and type transformations (`remove_cvref`).


edge_cases.title: enable_if overload vs a generic overload is ambiguous
The decltype-SFINAE overload is not "better" either
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T> void process(T);` and `template <class T> auto process(T t) -> decltype(t.size(), void());`
- `process(std::string("x"))`: both viable, same parameter types: "call of overloaded 'process(std::string)' is ambiguous". `process(10)` works (only the first survives).
- Fix: priority tags (`process_impl(t, priority<1>{})` vs `priority<0>`) or a `requires` clause.

edge_cases.title: Two overloads that differ only in a default template argument
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T, class = std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>>> void f(T);` plus the same with `is_floating_point_v`.
- GCC: "redefinition of 'template<class T, class> void f(T)'": default arguments are not part of the signature, so both declare `template <class, class> void f(T)`.
- Fix: `template <class T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0>`: now the condition is part of the template parameter's **type**, so the two templates differ.

edge_cases.title: Errors outside the immediate context are hard errors
edge_cases.explanation:
- SFINAE only protects the signature. Examples that still fail to compile:
  - `auto` return type deduction: the body is instantiated to find the type. `template <class T> auto len(T t) { return t.size(); }` with a `long len(...)` fallback: `len(5)` is a hard error.
  - A trait or helper class whose own definition errors for `T` (e.g. it uses `typename T::type` in its body, not in a partial specialization pattern).
  - Default member initializers, lambdas in the body, `static_assert` in the body.
- Fix: put the check in the signature (`-> decltype(t.size())`) or in a constraint.

edge_cases.title: if constexpr in a non-template function
static_assert(false) in a discarded branch
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) { ... } else { static_assert(false, "unsupported type"); }`
- GCC 11: "static assertion failed: unsupported type" even when only `int` is used (pre-P2593 rule: a non-dependent false assertion makes the template ill-formed).
- GCC 13+ (any `-std`, P2593R1 as a defect report): compiles; fires only if the else branch is instantiated.
- Portable form: `static_assert(always_false<T>, "...")` (`template <class> constexpr bool always_false = false;`).

edge_cases.title: Ad hoc constraints do not subsume
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T> requires std::is_integral_v<T> int f(T);` and `template <class T> requires (std::is_integral_v<T> && sizeof(T) == 4) int f(T);`
- Intuitively the second is "more constrained", but `f(1)` is ambiguous: atomic constraints from different source expressions are never identical.
- With named concepts, `concept Int4 = Int<T> && sizeof(T) == 4;`, the same calls resolve to the `Int4` overload.

edge_cases.title: A requires-expression checks validity, not truth
edge_cases.explanation:
- `template <class T> concept Big = requires { sizeof(T) > 4; };` is true for `char`: the expression `sizeof(char) > 4` is valid (and false), and only validity is checked.
- Correct: `concept Big = sizeof(T) > 4;` or `requires { requires sizeof(T) > 4; }`.
- Similarly `requires (T a) { a == a; }` checks that `==` exists, not that it returns true or even `bool`; use a compound requirement `{ a == a } -> std::convertible_to<bool>;`.

edge_cases.title: Traits and references
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::is_const_v<const int&>` is false; `std::is_integral_v<int&>` is false; `std::is_same_v<T, int>` is false for `T = const int`.
- In a forwarding function `template <class T> void f(T&& x)`, `T` is `int&` for lvalues, so `is_integral_v<T>` silently fails. Use `std::remove_cvref_t<T>` (C++20) or `std::decay_t<T>` before testing.

interview_qa.question: What is SFINAE, and what exactly counts as a "substitution failure"?
interview_qa.answer: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: when the compiler substitutes deduced template arguments into a function template's signature and gets an invalid type or expression, that template is quietly dropped from the overload set instead of causing an error. Only failures in the immediate context of the signature count; errors in the body are hard errors.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Immediate context: parameter types, return type (including trailing `decltype`), template parameter defaults, the C++20 `explicit(bool)` condition. Not the `noexcept` specifier: it is substituted only when needed, so an invalid `noexcept(T::value)` is a hard error.
- Hard errors (not SFINAE):
  - The function body (instantiated only after the function is selected).
  - `auto` return type deduction, because finding the type needs the body.
  - Errors inside another template that gets instantiated while forming the signature.
- After substitution, the surviving viable candidates are ranked by normal overload resolution.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "If any overload fails to compile, the compiler tries the next one." Only signature substitution failures are forgiven.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the `auto len(T t) { return t.size(); }` example where `len(5)` is a hard error even with a `len(...)` fallback.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: SFINAE removes candidates whose signature cannot be formed; it never rescues errors inside bodies.

interview_qa.question: What is a "viable function", and how is the best one picked among templates?
interview_qa.answer: A viable function is a candidate whose template arguments were deduced and substituted successfully, whose constraints (C++20) are satisfied, and whose parameters can accept the arguments through implicit conversions. interview_qa.explanation:
- Steps: name lookup builds candidates; deduction + substitution (SFINAE drops some); constraint checking; viability (conversions); ranking.
- If two remain equally good: "call of overloaded ... is ambiguous".
- `enable_if` conditions never enter ranking, only viability.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Viable means it is the one that gets called." Several can be viable; only the best one is called.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the tie-breakers in order, including that constraints only break ties between otherwise equivalent templates.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Viability is pass/fail; ranking picks the winner; SFINAE only affects viability.

interview_qa.question: What is a type trait, and how is one implemented?
interview_qa.answer: A class template that answers a compile-time question about a type (`::value`, usually by deriving from `std::true_type`/`std::false_type`) or transforms a type (`::type`). interview_qa.key_takeaway: Traits are compile-time functions on types, built from partial specialization.

interview_qa.question: Explain the void_t detection idiom. What does std::declval do?

- The default argument `void` is what makes `has_x<T>` match the specialization's second argument.
- `declval` works for types that are not default-constructible or are abstract.
- Calling `declval` in evaluated code is a compile error (it is declared, never defined to be used).

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the specialization's argument must be exactly `void` (the default); `void_t` guarantees that.

interview_qa.question: What is tag dispatch, and what are priority tags?
interview_qa.answer: Tag dispatch passes an empty object whose type encodes a property (for example `std::random_access_iterator_tag`) and lets ordinary overload resolution pick an implementation by that type. interview_qa.explanation:
- `std::advance` / `std::distance` are classic: O(1) for random access, a loop otherwise. Tag inheritance (`random_access` derives from `bidirectional` ...) makes the most derived matching overload win.
- Priority tags turn an ambiguous SFINAE pair into an ordered one: the derived-to-base conversion to `priority<0>` ranks below the exact `priority<1>`.
- Pure compile-time: tags are empty and optimized away.
- In C++20, concept subsumption on `std::random_access_iterator` etc. replaces both.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Tag dispatch is a runtime switch on a type enum." The choice is made at compile time.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: tag dispatch keeps each implementation a separate, unconstrained function, which gives clear errors and easy extension.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Encode the property in a type, overload on it; inheritance between tags gives ordering.

interview_qa.question: Compare `if constexpr`, a normal `if`, and `enable_if` inside a template.
interview_qa.answer: A normal `if` requires both branches to compile for every `T`, even if the condition is a constant. `if constexpr` (C++17) discards the untaken branch, and inside a template with a dependent condition the discarded branch is not instantiated. `enable_if` works at the overload level: whole functions are added or removed from overload resolution.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `if constexpr` = compile-time branch in one template; `enable_if`/concepts = compile-time choice between functions.

interview_qa.question: What are concepts, and what do they improve over SFINAE?
interview_qa.answer: A concept (C++20) is a named compile-time predicate on template arguments, used to constrain templates: `template <std::integral T> T gcd(T, T)`. interview_qa.explanation:
- Constraints are checked after deduction, before the function is considered viable.
- No runtime cost: like SFINAE, they only decide which template is used.
- They also work on non-template members of class templates (`void push(T) requires std::copyable<T>;`), which SFINAE cannot do without making the member a template.

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Concepts are like interfaces with virtual functions." There is no runtime dispatch or vtable; types satisfy them structurally, without inheriting.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the subsumption rule and its source-identity limitation.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Concepts = named, ordered, readable constraints; same zero runtime cost as SFINAE.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between a requires-clause, a requires-expression, and `requires requires`?

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`requires` always introduces a block of requirements." The keyword has two different roles depending on position.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: named concepts are not just style: ad hoc expressions never subsume each other.

interview_qa.question: What kinds of requirements can a requires-expression contain? What is the classic mistake?
interview_qa.answer: Simple (`a.size();`: valid expression), type (`typename T::value_type;`: type exists), compound (`{ a.size() } noexcept -> std::convertible_to<std::size_t>;`: valid, optionally noexcept, result satisfies a concept) and nested (`requires sizeof(T) <= 8;`: value is true). The classic mistake is `requires { sizeof(T) > 4; }`: a simple requirement only checks validity, so it is true for every complete type.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `template <class T> concept Big = requires { sizeof(T) > 4; };` gives `Big<char> == true`.
- Correct: `concept Big = sizeof(T) > 4;` or `requires { requires sizeof(T) > 4; };`.
- Compound requirement return checks use a concept, not a type: `-> std::same_as<int>`, not `-> int`.
- `{ a == b }` alone checks only that `==` exists; add `-> std::convertible_to<bool>` to check the result.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Every line in a requires block must evaluate to true." Lines must only be valid, except nested requirements.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: verifying concepts with `static_assert(MyConcept<GoodType> && !MyConcept<BadType>);` in tests.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Requires-expressions test validity; only a nested `requires` tests truth.

interview_qa.question: What is constraint subsumption, and why can two "obviously ordered" constraints still be ambiguous?
interview_qa.answer: Subsumption decides which of two viable constrained templates is more constrained: constraints are normalized into conjunctions/disjunctions of atomic constraints, and P subsumes Q if P implies Q structurally. Atomic constraints are only identical if they come from the same expression in the source (typically the same concept), so `requires is_integral_v<T>` and `requires (is_integral_v<T> && sizeof(T) == 4)` written separately do not subsume: the call is ambiguous.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `concept Int = std::is_integral_v<T>; concept Int4 = Int<T> && sizeof(T) == 4;`: `Int4` subsumes `Int`, so `f(1)` picks the `Int4` overload and `f(short{1})` the `Int` overload.
- The compiler does not reason about meaning (it will not prove that `sizeof(T) == 4` implies anything); it only matches atoms.
- Standard library concepts are built to subsume (`std::totally_ordered` refines `std::equality_comparable`, `random_access_iterator` refines `bidirectional_iterator`).
- An unconstrained template is always less constrained than a constrained one.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The compiler picks the logically stricter constraint." Only structurally, through named concepts.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: build concept hierarchies (`Base`, `Refined = Base<T> && extra`) whenever you overload on them.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Subsumption is structural, by concept identity; ad hoc trait expressions never order.

interview_qa.question: What are abbreviated function templates, and how does `auto` in a parameter interact with concepts?
interview_qa.answer: In C++20, a function with an `auto` parameter is a function template: `void log(const auto& x)` equals `template <class T> void log(const T& x)`. Prefixing a concept constrains it: `void send(std::integral auto id)` equals `template <std::integral T> void send(T id)`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Each `auto` parameter introduces its own template parameter: `void f(auto a, auto b)` has two, so `f(1, 2.0)` deduces `int` and `double` (no conflict, unlike `T, T`).
- Because it is a template, the definition must be visible at the call site (usually in a header).
- Constrained `auto` also works for variables: `std::integral auto n = compute();` fails to compile if `compute` returns `double`.
- Same idea as generic lambdas (C++14), now for ordinary functions.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`auto` parameters are dynamically typed like in scripting languages." Each call with a new type instantiates a new function.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: you cannot name the type directly; use `decltype(x)` or switch to the full template syntax when you need `T`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `auto` parameter = implicit template parameter; `Concept auto` = constrained template parameter.

interview_qa.question: How do you check "can F be called with these arguments" in C++17 and in C++20?
interview_qa.answer: C++17: `std::is_invocable_v<F, Args...>` (and `std::is_invocable_r_v<R, F, Args...>`, `std::invoke_result_t<F, Args...>` for the result type). C++20: the concept `std::invocable<F, Args...>` (or `std::predicate`, `std::regular_invocable`), usable directly as a constraint.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `is_invocable_v` (C++17) or `std::invocable` (C++20), both based on `std::invoke` semantics.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between std::decay_t and std::remove_cvref_t, and when do you need them?
interview_qa.answer: Both remove references and top-level cv-qualifiers. `decay_t` additionally converts arrays to pointers and functions to function pointers (what pass-by-value does). `remove_cvref_t` (C++20) only strips; use it when you want the "plain" type of a forwarded argument without changing arrays.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `decay_t<const int&>` and `remove_cvref_t<const int&>` are both `int`.
- `decay_t<int[3]>` is `int*`; `remove_cvref_t<int[3]>` stays `int[3]`.
- Needed in forwarding templates: with `template <class T> void f(T&& x)`, `T` is `int&` for an lvalue, so `std::is_integral_v<T>` is false and `std::is_same_v<T, int>` is false.
- `std::decay_t` is what `std::thread` and `std::bind` use to store copies of arguments (`std::make_pair` uses `std::unwrap_ref_decay_t`: decay plus unwrapping `std::reference_wrapper`).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`decay` and `remove_reference` are the same." `remove_reference` keeps `const` and arrays.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: test traits on `std::remove_cvref_t<T>` in any constraint on a forwarding reference.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `decay_t` = "type after pass by value"; `remove_cvref_t` = "strip const and reference only".

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: call of overloaded 'print(double)' is ambiguous
(print(7) alone would compile and print "generic 7")
```

**Explanation:**
- `print(7)`: the `enable_if` overload is removed by SFINAE (`int` is not floating point), only the generic one is viable.
- `print(2.5)`: both overloads are viable, both take a `double`. Partial ordering compares parameter types only, and the `enable_if` condition is not part of that comparison, so neither is more specialized.
- Fix: add `std::enable_if_t<!std::is_floating_point_v<T>, int> = 0` to the generic overload, or use `template <std::floating_point T>` (a constrained template beats an unconstrained one).
- **Key Concept:** SFINAE only removes candidates; it never makes one candidate better than another.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <concepts>
#include <iostream>

template <std::floating_point T>
void print(T v) { std::cout << "floating " << v << '\n'; }

template <class T>
void print(T v) { std::cout << "generic " << v << '\n'; }

int main() {
    print(7);     // generic 7
    print(2.5);   // floating 2.5
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: redefinition of 'template<class T, class> void scale(T)'
```

**Explanation:**
- Default template arguments are not part of a function template's signature. Both declarations are `template <class T, class> void scale(T)`: the same template defined twice.
- The error is at the second definition, before any call is considered.
- Fix: put the condition into the template parameter's type: `std::enable_if_t<Cond, int> = 0`. Now the two templates have different non-type parameter types and are distinct.
- **Key Concept:** Use the `enable_if_t<C, int> = 0` form when overloading on conditions.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <type_traits>

template <class T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0>
void scale(T v) { std::cout << "int " << v * 2 << '\n'; }

template <class T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_floating_point_v<T>, int> = 0>
void scale(T v) { std::cout << "float " << v * 2 << '\n'; }

int main() {
    scale(3);     // int 6
    scale(1.5);   // float 3
}
```

practice_tasks.answer:
GCC 11: compile error: static assertion failed: encode: unsupported type
GCC 13 and newer: compiles and prints 42
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Old rule: `static_assert(false)` does not depend on `T`, so it is evaluated at template definition time, and a template that can never be valid in some branch was ill-formed.
- P2593R1 (C++23, applied as a defect report to earlier modes) changed it: a `static_assert` in a discarded branch of a template is checked only when the branch is instantiated. GCC 13 implements it, even with `-std=c++17`.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: call of overloaded 'kind(int)' is ambiguous
(kind(5u) alone is fine: only the first overload is satisfied)
```

**Explanation:**
- For `int` both constraints are satisfied. The second looks "more constrained", but subsumption compares **atomic constraints by source identity**: the two `std::is_integral_v<T>` expressions are written in different places, so they are different atoms and neither constraint subsumes the other.

```cpp
template <std::signed_integral T>

int main() {
    std::cout << kind(5u) << '\n';   // integral
    std::cout << kind(5) << '\n';    // signed integral
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: request for member 'size' in 'v', which is of non-class type 'const int'
```

**Explanation:**
- The template's signature is `auto length(const T&)`, which substitutes fine for `int`; SFINAE has nothing to remove.
- The template is an exact match for `int`, so it beats the `...` fallback (an ellipsis conversion ranks last) and is selected.
- Its body is then instantiated (also to deduce `auto`), and `v.size()` fails there: a hard error, not a substitution failure.
- Fix: move the expression into the signature (`-> decltype(v.size())`) or constrain the template with `requires`.
- **Key Concept:** A deduced `auto` return type puts nothing checkable in the signature, so SFINAE cannot remove the template; body errors are never SFINAE.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

template <class T>
auto length(const T& v) -> decltype(v.size()) { return v.size(); }   // SFINAE-friendly

long length(...) { return -1; }

int main() {
    std::cout << length(std::string("abc")) << ' ' << length(5) << '\n';   // 3 -1
}
```

quick_reference.content:
#### Which tool?
| Need | C++11/14 | C++17 | C++20 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Remove an overload for some types | `enable_if` (NTTP form) | same | `requires` / concept |
| Pick behaviour inside one function | Tag dispatch | `if constexpr` | `if constexpr` + `requires` expression |
| "Does T have member X?" | `decltype` + SFINAE | `void_t` detection | `requires (T t) { t.x(); }` |
| Prefer one overload over another | Priority tags | Priority tags | Subsumption |
| Readable errors | No | No | Yes (constraint failure at call site) |

#### enable_if forms
| Form | Overload two conditions? |
|---|---|
| `template <class T, class = enable_if_t<C>>` | No: redefinition |
| `template <class T, enable_if_t<C, int> = 0>` | Yes |
| `enable_if_t<C, R> f(T)` (return type) | Yes |
| `f(T, enable_if_t<C>* = nullptr)` | Yes |

#### SFINAE vs hard error
| Failure location | Result |
|---|---|
| Parameter types, return type, template parameter defaults | SFINAE: overload removed |
| Function body | Hard error |
| `auto` return type deduction (needs the body) | Hard error |
| Inside a class template instantiated by the signature | Hard error |

#### requires-expression cheat sheet
| Requirement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `expr;` | `expr` compiles |
| `typename T::X;` | `T::X` names a type |
| `{ expr } -> C<...>;` | compiles and result satisfies concept `C` |
| `{ expr } noexcept;` | compiles and is `noexcept` |
| `requires cond;` | `cond` is true |

#### Version map
| Feature | Standard |
|---|---|
| `enable_if`, `integral_constant`, `declval`, most traits | C++11 |
| `_t` aliases (`enable_if_t`) | C++14 |
| `_v` variables, `void_t`, `if constexpr`, `conjunction` | C++17 |
| Concepts, `requires`, abbreviated templates, `remove_cvref_t`, `type_identity` | C++20 |
| `static_assert(false)` in discarded branch (P2593, DR) | C++23 (GCC 13+) |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is SFINAE? | Invalid substitution in the signature removes the overload instead of erroring |
| Does a body error count? | No, hard error |
| enable_if overload vs generic `T` for `int`? | Ambiguous |
| Concept-constrained vs unconstrained? | Constrained wins |
| Why `enable_if_t<C, int> = 0`? | Conditions become part of the signature: no redefinition |
| `if constexpr` in a non-template? | Both branches are checked |
| `static_assert(false)` in a discarded branch? | OK since P2593 (GCC 13+); use a dependent false before |
| `requires { sizeof(T) > 4; }`? | Always true if it compiles; use `requires (sizeof(T) > 4)` |
| What decides subsumption? | Atomic constraints identical by source: use named concepts |
| `declval`? | Fake object in unevaluated context |
| Tag dispatch? | Overload on a tag type; inheritance ranks the tags |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- The compiler contains an **interpreter** for a subset of C++ (constant evaluation). Some expressions **must** be evaluated by it (array bounds, template arguments, `static_assert`, `case` labels, `constexpr` variable initializers); everything else is ordinary code that runs on the CPU.
- The keywords control eligibility and requirements, not "speed":

| Keyword | Applies to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `constexpr` (variable) | Variables | Must be initialized by a constant expression; implicitly `const`; usable in constant expressions |
| `constexpr` (function) | Functions, lambdas, constructors | **May** be evaluated at compile time when called in a constant-expression context; otherwise a normal run-time call |
| `consteval` (C++20) | Functions | **Must** be evaluated at compile time: every call is an immediate invocation |
| `constinit` (C++20) | Static / thread-local variables | Must be constant-initialized; the variable stays **mutable** |

- A `constexpr` function is a promise "this can be computed at compile time for suitable arguments", not a request "compute it at compile time if possible". Whether a given call is compile-time is decided by the **context** of the call.
- Optimizers also fold constants at `-O2`, but that is unrelated to the language rules: it is not guaranteed, it does not change `std::is_constant_evaluated()`, and it cannot make a value usable as a template argument.

subsections.title: 2. constexpr variables
subsections.content:
- `constexpr T x = init;` requires:
  - `T` is a **literal type** (scalars, references, arrays of literal types, classes with a `constexpr` constructor and a trivial or `constexpr` destructor).
  - `init` is a constant expression. Otherwise: "the value of 'n' is not usable in a constant expression" or "call to non-'constexpr' function".
- Implicitly `const`: assigning later fails ("assignment of read-only variable").
- At namespace scope a `constexpr` variable has internal linkage (like `const`): each translation unit gets its own copy. Use `inline constexpr` (C++17) in headers for one shared object.
- Pointers: `constexpr` applies to the pointer, not to the pointee.
  - `constexpr const char* s = "hi";` constant pointer to constant chars.
  - `constexpr int* p = &global;` valid (address of a static-storage object is a constant), and `*p = 6;` is allowed: the `int` is not const.
  - `constexpr int* p = &local;` fails: the address of an automatic variable is not a constant expression.
- `const int n = 10;` (integral, constant initializer) is also usable in constant expressions; `const double d = 1.5;` is not. `constexpr` removes that special case: use it for every compile-time constant.

subsections.title: 3. constexpr functions: when do they run at compile time?
subsections.content:
- A call to a `constexpr` function is evaluated at compile time **only** when it appears in a context that is manifestly constant-evaluated:

| Context | Compile time guaranteed? |
|---|---|
| `constexpr int a = f();` | Yes |
| `static_assert(f() == 3);` | Yes |
| `std::array<int, f()>`, `int arr[f()]`, template argument `X<f()>` | Yes |
| `case f():`, enumerator `= f()`, `alignas(f())`, `if constexpr (f())` | Yes |
| `const int c = f();` (integral or enum type) | Tried first, like static init: if `f()` is a constant, `c` is usable in constant expressions; otherwise a run-time call |
| `static int s = f();` / global `int g = f();` | Constant initialization is tried first; succeeds if `f()` is a constant |
| `int b = f();` (local, non-const) | **No**: ordinary run-time call (may be folded by the optimizer) |
| `f(runtime_value)` | No; cannot be |

- Parameters are **never** constant expressions inside the function body, even when the call is compile-time: `constexpr int f(int n) { std::array<int, n> a; ... }` fails with "'n' is not a constant expression". Pass compile-time values as template parameters instead.
- `constexpr` functions are implicitly `inline`: define them in headers.
- A `constexpr` function that can never produce a constant (it always calls a non-`constexpr` function): before C++23 the program is ill-formed, no diagnostic required (GCC 11 diagnoses some cases, e.g. a `std::cin` read: "call to non-'constexpr' function"). C++23 (P2448, also applied by GCC 13 in `-std=c++20`) drops the rule: it is only an error when such a call is actually constant-evaluated.

subsections.title: 4. How constexpr grew, standard by standard
subsections.content:
| Standard | What became allowed in constexpr functions / evaluation |
|---|---|
| C++11 | A single `return` statement (recursion and `?:` for logic); constexpr constructors with empty bodies; member functions implicitly `const` |
| C++14 | Local variables, loops, `if`/`switch`, multiple statements, mutation of local objects; member functions no longer implicitly `const` |
| C++17 | `constexpr` lambdas (implicit when possible), `if constexpr`, `inline` variables (static constexpr members implicitly inline), more of the library (`std::array`, `std::string_view`, `std::char_traits`) |
| C++20 | `consteval`, `constinit`, `std::is_constant_evaluated()`; virtual functions, `dynamic_cast`, `typeid`; `try`/`catch` blocks (a `throw` still cannot be evaluated); changing the active union member; uninitialized locals (`int x;` if never read before assignment); `new`/`delete` with **transient** allocation; constexpr `std::vector`, `std::string`, most `<algorithm>` |
| C++23 | `if consteval`; `static` and `thread_local` locals, `goto` and labels in constexpr functions (only if not evaluated at compile time); `static constexpr` locals; relaxed "must be able to produce a constant" rule (P2448); constexpr `std::unique_ptr`, `std::bitset`, `<cmath>` parts (`std::abs`, `fmin`, ...) |
| C++26 | Placement new in constant evaluation, constexpr exceptions (P3068), more containers and algorithms |

- Library support lags: libstdc++ made `std::vector` and `std::string` constexpr in GCC 12; GCC 11 accepts the C++20 language features but not those library parts.

subsections.title: 5. What constant evaluation forbids
subsections.content:
- Any **undefined behaviour** in the evaluated path: signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, reading an uninitialized variable, reading an object outside its lifetime, invalid pointer arithmetic, division by zero. The compiler must diagnose it, so a compile-time test is a free UB detector for the inputs you test.
- Calls to non-`constexpr` functions (I/O, `malloc`, most C APIs), `reinterpret_cast`, inline assembly, evaluating a `throw` (until C++26), modifying an object that was not created during this evaluation (e.g. a global).
- Non-transient allocation: memory allocated with `new` (or by `std::vector`, `std::string`) during constant evaluation must be freed before the evaluation ends. `constexpr std::vector<int> v{1, 2};` fails: "is not a constant expression because it refers to a result of 'operator new'". Copy results into a `std::array` instead.
- Implementation limits (GCC defaults): recursion depth 512 (`-fconstexpr-depth`), 262144 loop iterations per loop (`-fconstexpr-loop-limit`), 33554432 operations in total (`-fconstexpr-ops-limit`). Exceeding them is a compile error, not a fallback to run time.

subsections.title: 6. consteval: immediate functions
subsections.content:
- Every call to a `consteval` function must produce a constant at compile time; calling it with a run-time value is an error ("the value of 'n' is not usable in a constant expression").
- Use cases:
  - Guarantee compile-time evaluation without forcing the caller to write `constexpr auto x = ...` (e.g. hashes of string literals used as IDs).
  - Validate arguments at compile time: a `consteval` constructor can reject a malformed format string or symbol code; `std::format` (C++20) checks format strings this way.
  - Remove the function from the binary entirely: no run-time symbol exists.
- Restrictions: you cannot take its address outside an immediate context ("taking address of an immediate function"), and a `constexpr` function cannot call it with its own (run-time) parameters unless the call is in an `if consteval` branch.
- C++23 P2564 ("consteval needs to propagate up", GCC 14) lets some constexpr functions that call consteval functions become immediate automatically; the basic rule above is what interviews expect.

subsections.title: 7. std::is_constant_evaluated() and if consteval
subsections.content:
- `std::is_constant_evaluated()` (C++20, `<type_traits>`) returns `true` when the current evaluation is manifestly constant-evaluated. It lets one function choose a compile-time-friendly algorithm and a run-time-fast one (e.g. a loop vs a SIMD intrinsic or `memcpy`).
- Trap 1: `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` is **always true**: the `if constexpr` condition is itself a constant-evaluated context. GCC warns: "'std::is_constant_evaluated' always evaluates to true in 'if constexpr'".
- Trap 2: `if (std::is_constant_evaluated()) return consteval_fn(x);` does not compile: the call to the consteval function is still checked as an immediate invocation with a non-constant `x`.
- `if consteval { ... } else { ... }` (C++23) fixes both: the first branch is an immediate function context, so it may call consteval functions with the parameters; no `<type_traits>` include needed. `if !consteval` also exists.
- Its result depends on the **context**, not on the optimization level: in `int b = where();` it is `false` at `-O0` and at `-O2`.

subsections.title: 8. constinit and static constexpr data members
subsections.content:
- `constinit` (C++20): a static or thread-local variable must be constant-initialized (no dynamic initialization, no static-initialization-order problem), but stays modifiable. `constinit int x = f();` is an error unless `f()` is a constant expression. Not allowed on automatic locals; allowed on `static` locals and `thread_local`. Full treatment (initialization order, function-local statics, TLS): Memory & Ownership, topic 01.
- `constinit` is not a thread-safety tool: it fixes *when* the initial value is set; concurrent `++x` is still a data race (use `constinit std::atomic<int>`).
- `static constexpr` data members:
  - C++11/14: `struct S { static constexpr int N = 5; };` is only a declaration. Using it by value (`int a = S::N;`) is fine, but **odr-using** it (binding to `const int&`, taking its address, passing to `std::max` or `push_back(const T&)`) needs an out-of-class definition `constexpr int S::N;` in one .cpp, or the link fails with "undefined reference to 'S::N'".
  - C++17: `static constexpr` members are implicitly `inline`: the in-class declaration is the definition; no out-of-class definition needed (it is redundant and deprecated).

subsections.title: 9. Compile-time tables and the cost trade-off
subsections.content:
- A `constexpr` function filling a `std::array` (lookup tables, CRC tables, bit-count tables, perfect hashes for known keys) runs at compile time and lands in read-only data: no start-up cost, no static-initialization order issue, and the table can be `static_assert`-tested.
- Patterns:
  - `constexpr auto table = make_table();` at namespace scope or `static constexpr` in a function (C++23 for function-local in constexpr functions).
  - Hash of string literals with a `consteval` function to get compile-time IDs usable in `case` labels.
  - `std::array` results instead of `std::vector` (no allocation can escape constant evaluation).
- Costs:
  - Compile time: the constant evaluator is an interpreter, typically far slower than running the same code natively (it interprets every step); large tables slow builds and can hit the ops limit.
  - Binary size: every table is stored in the executable; a 1 MB table is 1 MB of `.rodata`.
  - Debuggability: no breakpoints inside constant evaluation; write the function so it can also be called and tested at run time.
- Low-latency angle: moving work from run time to compile time removes it from the hot path entirely (configuration constants, dispatch tables, bit masks), and `static_assert` protects layout assumptions (`sizeof`, field offsets) at build time.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "A `constexpr` function is evaluated at compile time." ✅ Only in contexts that require a constant expression; elsewhere it is a normal function call.
- ❌ "The compiler tries compile time and silently falls back to run time." ✅ There is no "try" in the rules; the context decides. Constant folding by the optimizer is a separate, unguaranteed thing.
- ❌ "`constexpr` and `const` are the same." ✅ `const` = not modifiable (initializer may run at run time); `constexpr` = known at compile time (and const).
- ❌ "`consteval` is just a stricter `constexpr`." ✅ It is a different kind of function: no run-time version exists, its address cannot escape, and every call must be constant.
- ❌ "`constinit` means constant." ✅ It means "initialized at compile time"; the variable is mutable.
- ❌ "Inside a constexpr function called at compile time, my parameter is a constant expression." ✅ Parameters never are; use template parameters.
- ❌ "`if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` selects the compile-time path." ✅ It is always true; use plain `if` or C++23 `if consteval`.
- ❌ "C++20 lets me have a `constexpr std::vector` global." ✅ Only transient allocations: the vector must be destroyed before constant evaluation ends.
- ❌ "UB in a constexpr function is caught at compile time." ✅ Only for the evaluations that actually happen at compile time; the same call at run time is ordinary UB.
- ❌ "More constexpr is always better." ✅ It shifts cost to compile time and binary size; use it where the value is truly static.

#### 7. std::is_constant_evaluated() and if consteval
- `std::is_constant_evaluated()` (C++20, `<type_traits>`) returns `true` when the current evaluation is manifestly constant-evaluated. It lets one function choose a compile-time-friendly algorithm and a run-time-fast one (e.g. a loop vs a SIMD intrinsic or `memcpy`).
- Trap 1: `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` is **always true**: the `if constexpr` condition is itself a constant-evaluated context. GCC warns: "'std::is_constant_evaluated' always evaluates to true in 'if constexpr'".
- Trap 2: `if (std::is_constant_evaluated()) return consteval_fn(x);` does not compile: the call to the consteval function is still checked as an immediate invocation with a non-constant `x`.
- `if consteval { ... } else { ... }` (C++23) fixes both: the first branch is an immediate function context, so it may call consteval functions with the parameters; no `<type_traits>` include needed. `if !consteval` also exists.
- Its result depends on the **context**, not on the optimization level: in `int b = where();` it is `false` at `-O0` and at `-O2`.

#### 8. constinit and static constexpr data members
- `constinit` (C++20): a static or thread-local variable must be constant-initialized (no dynamic initialization, no static-initialization-order problem), but stays modifiable. `constinit int x = f();` is an error unless `f()` is a constant expression. Not allowed on automatic locals; allowed on `static` locals and `thread_local`. Full treatment (initialization order, function-local statics, TLS): Memory & Ownership, topic 01.
- `constinit` is not a thread-safety tool: it fixes *when* the initial value is set; concurrent `++x` is still a data race (use `constinit std::atomic<int>`).
- `static constexpr` data members:
  - C++11/14: `struct S { static constexpr int N = 5; };` is only a declaration. Using it by value (`int a = S::N;`) is fine, but **odr-using** it (binding to `const int&`, taking its address, passing to `std::max` or `push_back(const T&)`) needs an out-of-class definition `constexpr int S::N;` in one .cpp, or the link fails with "undefined reference to 'S::N'".
  - C++17: `static constexpr` members are implicitly `inline`: the in-class declaration is the definition; no out-of-class definition needed (it is redundant and deprecated).

#### 9. Compile-time tables and the cost trade-off
- A `constexpr` function filling a `std::array` (lookup tables, CRC tables, bit-count tables, perfect hashes for known keys) runs at compile time and lands in read-only data: no start-up cost, no static-initialization order issue, and the table can be `static_assert`-tested.
- Patterns:
  - `constexpr auto table = make_table();` at namespace scope or `static constexpr` in a function (C++23 for function-local in constexpr functions).
  - Hash of string literals with a `consteval` function to get compile-time IDs usable in `case` labels.
  - `std::array` results instead of `std::vector` (no allocation can escape constant evaluation).
- Costs:
  - Compile time: the constant evaluator is an interpreter, typically far slower than running the same code natively (it interprets every step); large tables slow builds and can hit the ops limit.
  - Binary size: every table is stored in the executable; a 1 MB table is 1 MB of `.rodata`.
  - Debuggability: no breakpoints inside constant evaluation; write the function so it can also be called and tested at run time.
- Low-latency angle: moving work from run time to compile time removes it from the hot path entirely (configuration constants, dispatch tables, bit masks), and `static_assert` protects layout assumptions (`sizeof`, field offsets) at build time.

#### 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "A `constexpr` function is evaluated at compile time." ✅ Only in contexts that require a constant expression; elsewhere it is a normal function call.
- ❌ "The compiler tries compile time and silently falls back to run time." ✅ There is no "try" in the rules; the context decides. Constant folding by the optimizer is a separate, unguaranteed thing.
- ❌ "`constexpr` and `const` are the same." ✅ `const` = not modifiable (initializer may run at run time); `constexpr` = known at compile time (and const).
- ❌ "`consteval` is just a stricter `constexpr`." ✅ It is a different kind of function: no run-time version exists, its address cannot escape, and every call must be constant.
- ❌ "`constinit` means constant." ✅ It means "initialized at compile time"; the variable is mutable.
- ❌ "Inside a constexpr function called at compile time, my parameter is a constant expression." ✅ Parameters never are; use template parameters.
- ❌ "`if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` selects the compile-time path." ✅ It is always true; use plain `if` or C++23 `if consteval`.
- ❌ "C++20 lets me have a `constexpr std::vector` global." ✅ Only transient allocations: the vector must be destroyed before constant evaluation ends.
- ❌ "UB in a constexpr function is caught at compile time." ✅ Only for the evaluations that actually happen at compile time; the same call at run time is ordinary UB.
- ❌ "More constexpr is always better." ✅ It shifts cost to compile time and binary size; use it where the value is truly static.

edge_cases.title: The same call is compile-time in one line and run-time in the next
edge_cases.explanation:
- With `constexpr int where() { return std::is_constant_evaluated() ? 1 : 0; }`:

| Declaration | `where()` evaluated at |
|---|---|
| `constexpr int a = where();` | Compile time (1) |
| `int b = where();` (local) | Run time (0), even at `-O2` |
| `const int c = where();` | Compile time (1): const integral with a constant initializer is usable in constant expressions |
| `const double e = where();` | Run time (0): a `const double` is not usable in constant expressions |
| `static int d = where();` / global `int g = where();` | Compile time (1): constant initialization |
| `std::array<int, where() + 1>` | Compile time (size 2) |

- The `const int` vs `const double` difference surprises most people: it is the C++98 rule that integral `const` variables with constant initializers are constants.

edge_cases.title: Function parameters are never constant expressions
edge_cases.explanation:
- `constexpr std::size_t f(std::size_t n) { std::array<int, n> a{}; return a.size(); }` does not compile ("'n' is not a constant expression"), even if every call is `f(3)` in a constant context.
- The function body must be valid for run-time calls too, where `n` is unknown.
- Fix: make it a template parameter: `template <std::size_t N> constexpr std::size_t f() { std::array<int, N> a{}; ... }`, or return a value computed with `n` without using it as a type parameter.
- `static_assert(n > 0)` inside the function fails for the same reason; check with `if (n == 0) throw ...;` (a throw evaluated at compile time is a compile error, a free check) or use `consteval`.

edge_cases.title: is_constant_evaluated inside if constexpr
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` is always `true` because the `if constexpr` condition is itself manifestly constant-evaluated. The run-time branch is discarded.
- GCC warns with `-Wall` (not by default): "'std::is_constant_evaluated' always evaluates to true in 'if constexpr' [-Wtautological-compare]".
- Same trap in `static_assert(std::is_constant_evaluated())` (always passes) and in template arguments.
- Use plain `if (std::is_constant_evaluated())` or C++23 `if consteval`.

edge_cases.title: Calling a consteval function from a constexpr function
edge_cases.explanation:
- `constexpr int f(int x) { if (std::is_constant_evaluated()) return twice(x); return x; }` with `consteval int twice(int)` fails: "'x' is not a constant expression" (GCC 13). The call `twice(x)` is checked as an immediate invocation regardless of the surrounding `if`.
- `if consteval { return twice(x); } else { return x; }` (C++23) compiles: inside the consteval branch, the parameters may be passed to immediate functions.
- GCC 14 implements P2564: the error message changes ("call to consteval function 'twice(x)' is not a constant expression"), but the plain-`if` version still fails when `f` is also called at run time.

edge_cases.title: UB, throw and limits are compile errors, not silent fallbacks
edge_cases.explanation:
- In a constant evaluation: `INT_MAX + 1` → "overflow in constant expression"; `arr[3]` on `int arr[3]` → "array subscript value '3' is outside the bounds"; `*nullptr` → "dereferencing a null pointer"; reading an uninitialized local → "the value of 'x' is not usable in a constant expression".
- A `throw` on the evaluated path → "expression '<throw-expression>' is not a constant expression" (until C++26). Useful as a compile-time assertion inside a constexpr function.
- 1,000,000 iterations of one loop → "'constexpr' loop iteration count exceeds limit of 262144"; deep recursion → "evaluation depth exceeds maximum of 512"; huge total work → "operation count exceeds limit of 33554432" (GCC defaults, adjustable with `-fconstexpr-loop-limit`, `-fconstexpr-depth`, `-fconstexpr-ops-limit`).
- None of these silently turn into run-time computation for a `constexpr` variable: the program does not compile.

edge_cases.title: constexpr pointers and references
edge_cases.explanation:
- `constexpr` makes the **pointer** constant: `constexpr int* p = &g;` then `*p = 6;` compiles (if `g` is a non-const global) but `p = &h;` does not.
- `constexpr int* p = &local;` fails: "'& local' is not a constant expression". The address of an automatic variable differs per call; only static-storage addresses are constants. `static int local;` would work.
- `constexpr const char* name = "order";` is fine (string literals have static storage).
- A `constexpr` reference must bind to a static-storage object: `constexpr const int& r = 42;` at namespace scope works (the temporary gets static storage), the same inside a function does not.

edge_cases.title: static constexpr members and the C++14 link error
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Limits { static constexpr int Max = 100; };` then `std::max(x, Limits::Max)` or `v.push_back(Limits::Max)` binds `const int&` to `Max`: an **odr-use**.
- C++14: "undefined reference to 'Limits::Max'" at link time (sometimes only at `-O0`, because the optimizer may inline the value and remove the reference).
- C++17: `static constexpr` data members are implicitly `inline`; it links. Prefer C++17, or write `int(Limits::Max)` / `+Limits::Max` to pass a prvalue copy in old code.

edge_cases.title: A constexpr function that can never be constant
edge_cases.explanation:
- `constexpr int read_qty() { int x = 0; std::cin >> x; return x; }` can never be constant-evaluated.
- C++11 to C++20: ill-formed, no diagnostic required. GCC 11 diagnoses this one at the definition ("call to non-'constexpr' function"), but not every variant (a `std::scanf` version passed silently).
- C++23 (P2448): allowed; it is only an error if a call is actually constant-evaluated. GCC 13 accepts it even with `-std=c++20` (treated as a defect fix).
- Practical rule: do not mark functions `constexpr` unless you test at least one compile-time call (`static_assert`), otherwise the keyword promises nothing.

edge_cases.title: constexpr containers must not leak out of constant evaluation
edge_cases.explanation:
- C++20 allows `std::vector`/`std::string` inside a constexpr function (GCC 12+): build, sort, accumulate, return a scalar or an `std::array`.
- `constexpr std::vector<int> v{1, 2};` fails (GCC 13): the allocation would have to survive into run time. Same for returning a `std::string` into a `constexpr std::string` variable.
- Pattern: compute size first, then copy into `std::array<T, N>` (two-pass), or return a fixed-capacity structure.

interview_qa.question: A function declares `constexpr auto table = make_table();` as a local. Is the table built at compile time, and why is `static constexpr` usually what you want?
interview_qa.answer: The **values** are computed at compile time, but a non-static local is still an automatic object: every call creates a fresh copy on the stack and fills it in. `static constexpr` makes it one object with static storage, emitted once in read-only data, so a call only reads from it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `constexpr` fixes the values; `static` decides there is one object. For tables, write `static constexpr`.

interview_qa.question: `constexpr int sq(int x) { return x * x; }` then `int b = sq(10);`. Is `sq(10)` computed at compile time?
interview_qa.answer: Not by the language rules. `int b` is a non-const local, so its initializer is an ordinary run-time call. The optimizer may fold it to `100` at `-O2`, but that is an optimization, not a guarantee, and `std::is_constant_evaluated()` would still report `false` there.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Compile time is guaranteed only in contexts that require a constant: `constexpr int a = sq(10);`, `static_assert`, array bounds, template arguments, `case` labels. For `const` integral initializers and statics the constant evaluation is attempted first and used when it succeeds.
- At `-O0` GCC emits a real call to `sq` for `int b = sq(10);`.
- To force it: `constexpr int b = sq(10);`, or make `sq` `consteval`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Yes, the arguments are constants, so the compiler evaluates it at compile time."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in the `const int c = sq(10);` case the answer flips to yes, because a const integral variable with a constant initializer is usable in constant expressions; for `const double` it does not.

interview_qa.question: Why does `constexpr int f(int n) { std::array<int, n> a{}; return 0; }` not compile, even if you only call `f(3)` in constant expressions?
interview_qa.answer: Function parameters are never constant expressions. A constexpr function body must be valid for run-time calls too, where `n` is unknown, so `n` cannot be a template argument. GCC: "'n' is not a constant expression".

interview_qa.question: What happens if a constexpr function hits undefined behaviour during constant evaluation?
interview_qa.answer: The program does not compile: the compiler must diagnose UB in a constant evaluation (signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, reading uninitialized or dead objects). - Unspecified behaviour and implementation limits are not covered the same way (e.g. comparing unrelated pointers is rejected as "not a constant expression").

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: some teams write unit tests as `static_assert`s for constexpr utilities (parsers, bit manipulation) precisely to get this checking.

interview_qa.question: How has `constexpr` evolved from C++11 to C++23?
interview_qa.answer: C++11: a single return statement. C++14: loops, locals, multiple statements, mutation. C++17: constexpr lambdas, `if constexpr`, inline static constexpr members. C++20: `consteval`, `constinit`, `is_constant_evaluated`, virtual functions, `try`/`catch`, transient `new`/`delete`, constexpr `std::vector`/`std::string`/algorithms. C++23: `if consteval`, `static` locals in constexpr functions (not evaluated), relaxed "must be constant-able" rule.
interview_qa.explanation:
- C++11 style: `constexpr int fact(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); }`.
- C++14 removed the implicit `const` on constexpr member functions.
- C++20's transient allocation means memory obtained during constant evaluation must be released before it ends.
- C++26 adds constexpr exceptions (throw/catch evaluated at compile time) and placement new.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "C++20 made everything constexpr." I/O, `reinterpret_cast`, inline asm and non-transient allocations are still excluded.

interview_qa.question: Can you have a `constexpr std::vector` in C++20?

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between `const int c = f();` and `const double d = f();` when `f` is constexpr?

interview_qa.question: Why might `struct S { static constexpr int N = 5; };` cause a link error?
interview_qa.answer: Before C++17, the in-class `static constexpr` member is only a declaration. If the program odr-uses it (binds it to a reference, e.g. `std::max(x, S::N)` or `v.push_back(S::N)`, or takes its address), a definition is needed in one .cpp file; without it the linker reports "undefined reference to 'S::N'". Since C++17 such members are implicitly `inline`, so the declaration is the definition.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Using the value (`int a = S::N;`) is not an odr-use and always worked.
- The C++14 error may appear only at `-O0`: with optimization the value is often inlined and the reference disappears.
- C++14 fix: `constexpr int S::N;` in exactly one .cpp, or pass a copy (`+S::N`).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "constexpr values have no storage, so they cannot cause link errors."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: namespace-scope `constexpr` variables have internal linkage; in headers use `inline constexpr` (C++17) to get one shared object instead of one per translation unit.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: In C++17 static constexpr members are inline; in C++14 an odr-use needs an out-of-class definition.

interview_qa.question: Is it an error to mark a function `constexpr` if it can never be evaluated at compile time?
interview_qa.answer: Up to C++20: yes, but "ill-formed, no diagnostic required": compilers may or may not complain. C++23 (P2448) removed the rule: it is an error only if such a call is actually constant-evaluated.

- The change helps generic code: a constexpr function template may be instantiated with types whose operations are not constexpr.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: keep at least one `static_assert` that calls each constexpr function, otherwise the keyword promises nothing.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A constexpr that can never be constant was IFNDR until C++23; test with static_assert.

interview_qa.question: What does a class need to be usable in constant expressions? Can virtual functions be constexpr?
interview_qa.answer: It must be a literal type: a `constexpr` constructor (or be an aggregate), a trivial destructor (or a `constexpr` destructor in C++20), and literal-type members. interview_qa.question: What are the costs and limits of compile-time computation?
interview_qa.answer: Compile time (the constant evaluator is an interpreter, much slower than native code), binary size (every table is stored in `.rodata`), and hard limits: GCC defaults are 512 recursion depth, 262144 iterations per loop, 33554432 total operations. Exceeding a limit is a compile error.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Messages: "'constexpr' loop iteration count exceeds limit of 262144 (use '-fconstexpr-loop-limit=' to increase the limit)", "'constexpr' evaluation depth exceeds maximum of 512", "operation count exceeds limit of 33554432".
- Clang has its own limits (`-fconstexpr-steps`, `-fconstexpr-depth`).
- Debugging is harder: no debugger inside constant evaluation; keep functions callable at run time to unit test them normally.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Compile-time work is free."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in low-latency code, precomputing small tables and constants is worth it; generating megabytes of tables usually is not (I-cache, D-cache and build time).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Compile-time work trades build time and binary size for zero run-time cost.

interview_qa.question: How do you build a lookup table at compile time, and why prefer it to filling one at start-up?
interview_qa.answer: Write a `constexpr` function that returns a filled `std::array`, and initialize a `constexpr` variable with it at namespace scope (or `static constexpr` inside a function): `constexpr auto table = make_table();`. interview_qa.question: Does `constinit` make a global safe to use from several threads?
interview_qa.answer: No. `constinit` only guarantees that the initial value is set at compile time (so no thread can see it uninitialized and there is no initialization-order problem). Later concurrent writes, or a write concurrent with reads, are still a data race. Use `constinit std::atomic<int>` or a mutex for that.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `constinit std::atomic<int> counter{0};` works because `std::atomic`'s constructor is `constexpr`.
- Function-local `static T x = make();` is thread-safe *initialization* (C++11 "magic statics"), a different mechanism with a run-time guard; `constinit` needs no guard at all.
- `thread_local constinit int t = 0;` avoids the per-access TLS initialization check that dynamic `thread_local` initialization needs.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It is initialized before main, so it is thread-safe."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: initialization and access are separate concerns; details are in Memory & Ownership, topic 01 and the Concurrency chapter.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: constinit fixes when a variable is initialized, not how it is shared.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
-1 100 100 -1 -1
```

**Explanation:**
- `a`: a `constexpr` variable requires a constant: compile time.
- `b`: a plain local `int`: ordinary run-time call, even though the argument is a literal. At `-O2` the optimizer may fold `10 * 10`, but folding does not change what `is_constant_evaluated()` returns.

- `e`: a `const int` with a constant initializer is usable in constant expressions, so its initializer is constant-evaluated. (`const double` would print 100.)
- **Key Concept:** The context of the call decides compile vs run time, never the arguments alone.
